title: GOP’s ‘rubberstamp’ of Trump puts US Senate in play, Dem campaign chair says
text: WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Democrats believe they could pick up as many as six seats following this November’s midterm elections, despite Republicans having better fundraising numbers and break-even polling in several states. Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand said during a sit-down interview Tuesday that the president's low approval ratings and the ongoing war in Iran remind her of the 2006 election cycle, when the party flipped both chambers of Congress.“We may be outspent in all the races, but we will not be outworked,” she said. “Our candidates are better and they are stronger and they are on-message to what voters actually care about.”The National Republican Senatorial Committee holds a slim fundraising advantage over the DSCC, with $176 million to $163 million in contributions this cycle as of Aug. 31, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission.But the Republican National Committee has a nine-digit cash advantage over the Democratic National Committee. And Trump's MAGA Inc. super PAC has more than $400 million ready to spend.Gillibrand, of New York, said she was confident Democrats will be able to keep Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire, while possibly flipping seats in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas. “All six are viable. All six we can win. And so we're excited about all of them,” she said. “And on top of those six, there's other races that we continue to watch.”The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates seats held by Republicans in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas as tossup races, with North Carolina leaning toward Democrats. The forecaster lists seats Democrats are defending in Michigan and New Hampshire as tossups, with Georgia Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff a slight favorite to win reelection.Control at stakeDemocrats need a net gain of four seats to flip the Senate from Republican to Democratic control. A 50-50 split would leave the GOP with the majority since the vice president casts the tie-breaking vote in that chamber of Congress. Gillibrand said during the interview with States Newsroom and a dozen other reporters in the Regional Reporters Association that Americans are frustrated with what Republicans have done during their two years with unified control of Washington. She expects many Americans who voted for a Republican during the 2024 presidential election will decide to vote for a Democratic candidate this fall. “I think it's going to be a groundswell,” Gillibrand said. “I think it's a lot like 2006.”Two decades ago, following the second midterm election of a Republican president involved in an unpopular Middle East war, Democrats went from holding 45 Senate seats to 51. In the House of Representatives, Democrats went from 202 seats to 233. The six states Democrats are focused on flipping, Gillibrand said, are largely in play because of actions by President Donald Trump as well as his Republican allies in Congress. "Republicans' roster of corruption and candidates who have been a rubber stamp to Trump is very much affecting their campaigns,” she said. “And our focus on just the issues that are affecting voters where they are — cost of groceries, cost of housing, cost of healthcare, along with fraud and corruption — it’s resonating, pretty much everywhere.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sand supports letting Iowa prison workers bargain as public safety employees
description: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand said he would support classifying prison employees as public safety workers to give them access to more bargaining rights under Iowa law. Sand met Tuesday with correctional officers and others working in the state’s prison system for a roundtable discussion at the Des Moines headquarters for AFSCME Council 61, a […[...]
text:
Iowa Auditor Rob Sand, left, running for Iowa governor, held a roundtable discussion with Todd Copley, AFSCME Council 61 President and employees in state correctional facilities at the AFSCME Council 61 headquarters in Des Moines Sep. 22, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand said he would support classifying prison employees as public safety workers to give them access to more bargaining rights under Iowa law.
Sand met Tuesday with correctional officers and others working in the state’s prison system for a roundtable discussion at the Des Moines headquarters for AFSCME Council 61, a public sector union. Roundtable participants told Sand, who currently serves as Iowa auditor, about problems they saw in Iowa’s prison system.
Neil Lemaster, who works at the Iowa State Penitentiary in Fort Madison, said Iowa prisons are overcrowded and understaffed, putting prison employees in more potentially dangerous situations. Lemaster said while private-sector jobs offered better pay, he made the choice to work in the state prison system because of access to Iowa Public Employees’ Retirement System (IPERS). But, he said, low wages, increased overtime and unsafe working conditions have made him feel “trapped” in his job.
“I never looked at it like that until recently, where I felt trapped in my job because I can’t leave because I’m close to retirement,” he said. “I’m 52 years old, and and I got to wait three years to retire — I have over 30 (years) in, but it’s getting so bad. I was telling my wife, who’s a retired correctional officer, I was like, ‘I feel like I’m like sacrificing my safety.’ I’m like, ‘I don’t know if I’m going to be murdered at work for retirement.'”
Lemaster and other speakers said they believed the staffing shortage could be solved by providing higher wages for prison employees. However, they said the 2017 law making major changes to Chapter 20 of Iowa Code significantly limited their ability to bargain for benefits, safety and hours. The law, which limits public employee unions to bargaining only for base wages, does contain exemptions for public safety employees, like law enforcement and firefighters — but does not include workers in Iowa’s correctional facilities.
Sand said he planned to look further into the problems facing prison employees, but said he believed looking at changing Chapter 20 to classify Department of Corrections staff as public safety officials makes sense.
“I think if you ask the average Iowan, ‘Hey, somebody who’s working in prison, are they public safety workers?’ They’d say. … yeah, like, ‘What? Of course they are. What are you talking about?’ And so I don’t think that request is anything outside of common sense. And then when you talk about the fact that you got people doing it here — and they could be making $15 or more per hour working at a nursing home, well, how are you going to staff prisons? It makes a great point. If you’re building more and you can’t staff the ones we have, how’s that going to work out? So clearly, what we’re doing right now is not working, and nobody knows that better than the people who’ve been injured on the job, or the families of those that have been injured on the job, or even killed on the job.”
The Legislative Services Agency, a nonpartisan entity, estimated in June there were 230 vacant positions in Iowa’s prison system, with more than half of vacancies being for correctional officer positions. Iowa prisons are also over capacity by 28.47%, according to daily statistics from the Iowa Department of Corrections.
Prison populations are expected to rise further after Gov. Kim Reynolds signed House File 2542 into law earlier this year, a version of Republicans’ “three strikes” proposal that requires individuals to face a seven-year mandatory prison sentence after they have been convicted of their third felony offense. LSA projected this change will result in 4,363 more individuals in Iowa prisons by fiscal year 2030, which would require building three new medium-security prisons to house the increased prison population.
Sand shared a story about getting his concealed carry permit when he was prosecuting an armed robbery case in Hancock County, seeking a sentence above the mandatory minimum against an individual who was not in custody. Sand said, “You’re not going to find anybody, probably running for office anywhere, who has put their own safety on the line to extend somebody’s prison term.” 
However, he also said it was cause for concern that the higher population could cause further strain on Iowa’s prison system, according to DOC staff comments at the roundtable.
“I don’t think that that law was thought through a deep sense, because clearly you have a lot of people who are involved with that around the table here today, who know a lot about the situation, who have some beef with a decision that they made,” Sand said. “That said, changes are going to have to originate in the Legislature. If there are legislators who think there are better ways to protect public safety than what they went with last year, I’d be all ears for listening.”
Sand is running against Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn in the Nov. 3 election. Lahn announced endorsements from 40 sheriffs Tuesday, who said in a news release they supported Lahn and conservatives who back public safety. Dan Capodilupo, a spokesperson for Lahn’s campaign, said the endorsements come “because he is the only candidate in this race who stands up for law enforcement.”
Marion County Sheriff Jason Sandholt said in a statement he was backing Lahn as a candidate who shares his belief in “accountability.”
“What does accountability mean to me? Accountability is holding criminals accountable for their actions and not having a catch and release program where they’re in and out of prison,” Sandholt said. “I want a governor who has those same conservative beliefs that I have, and that’s why I’m supporting Zach.”
Sand was backed by group of law enforcement officials, prosecutors, and other public safety workers earlier in September.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Free school meal ballot measure debated at North Dakota policy summit
description: A proponent of the free school meal ballot measure touted the benefits to North Dakota families Tuesday while an opponent cautioned against adding the program to the state constitution. The two sides presented their arguments during the Greater North Dakota Chamber Policy Summit in Bismarck. Voters will decide the fate of Measure 2 in November, […]
text:
From the left, Robin Nelson, chair of Together for School Meals, and Sen. Paul Thomas, R-Velva, speak during the Greater North Dakota Chamber Policy Summit in Bismarck on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photos by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)A proponent of the free school meal ballot measure touted the benefits to North Dakota families Tuesday while an opponent cautioned against adding the program to the state constitution.
The two sides presented their arguments during the Greater North Dakota Chamber Policy Summit in Bismarck.
Voters will decide the fate of Measure 2 in November, a constitutional measure that would provide free breakfast and lunch to North Dakota K-12 students at no cost to the student. Funding would be provided through earnings from the state Legacy Fund if lawmakers do not identify an alternative funding source.
Sponsor, opponent debate need for North Dakota ballot measure to change constitution

Robin Nelson, chair of Together for School Meals, told event attendees Measure 2 would be like giving every North Dakota family with a K-12 student a tax break.
“About $1,000 per child, per family, and this would affect, if passed, 105,000 households in North Dakota,” Nelson said.
She said about 35% of North Dakotans rent apartments or houses and did not benefit from the property tax credit passed by lawmakers in 2025, which provides up to $1,600 for homeowners.
Nelson took issue with an income threshold that qualifies K-12 students for free or reduced price school meals in North Dakota by pointing out the property tax credit did not require a similar income requirement.
“What is so wrong with providing meals to the kids, regardless of income?” she said. “Let’s be consistent.”
The projected cost to provide meals to students is between $124.3 million to $134.3 million every two years, according to an analysis conducted by the Department of Public Instruction. 
Lawmakers have previously rejected bills to provide free school meals to all students, most recently in January during a special session of the Legislature.
Lawmakers adopt cost estimate for North Dakota school meal ballot measure

Nelson said the initiated measure committee chose to pursue a constitutional measure petition because it was available to them as citizens of North Dakota. 
Sen. Paul Thomas, R-Velva, opposes Measure 2 and said the free school meals program should not be included in the state’s constitution with mandatory spending. He added the measure isn’t really about providing breakfast and lunch to students at no cost.
“Measure 2 asks if we should permanently rewrite our state constitution to mandate a specific government program with a specific funding stream,” Thomas said. “That is a very different question.”
He highlighted that constitutional measures would take another vote of the people to change, while state law can be adjusted by lawmakers during a legislative session if programs are not working or the state’s financial position changes.
If Measure 2 passes, Thomas said it would establish a dangerous precedent for in-state and out-of-state interest groups, if they don’t like how state lawmakers vote.
“Today it’s school meals. Tomorrow, it could be a mandated funding level program for childcare, healthcare, paid family leave, tax incentives, minimum wage, anything a coalition believes deserves a permanent, unamendable priority over every other state need,” he said.
The remedy for lawmakers not adhering to concerns of citizens isn’t a constitutional measure, it’s elections, Thomas said.
“That is how self-government is supposed to work,” he said. “What that argument does not justify is treating the constitution as an escape hatch every time a Legislature declines to pass a particular bill.”
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: The tyranny of uncertainty
description: The most damaging feature of this system may not be the arrests that make the news. It is the uncertainty imposed on families who have followed the rules, filed their papers, paid their fees and waited—sometimes for well over a year—for the government to act.
text:
Expansive view of downtown Juneau and waterfront, Alaska. Morning, waterfalls and fog nestled in the mountains. Mount Roberts tram operating at right.The ICE dragnets that dominated headlines earlier this year and led to the deaths of two United States citizens and several immigrant victims in communities around the country may now attract less attention. But the machinery of detention and deportation continues to hum along—perhaps more quietly, but no less relentlessly. 
According to Homeland Security records, in July alone 50,208 immigrants were arrested and 65,000 were in detention. According to the Deportation Data Project, less than 30 percent of the arrestees and detainees had criminal convictions.   
The low-hanging fruit for these arrests are local jails and prisons that may be holding an immigrant. Homeland Security’s enlistment of state and local law enforcement agencies to do immigration stops have also contributed to the surge in arrests and detentions. In recent weeks, there are also reports of arrests at airport boarding gates for domestic flights. More pernicious are the arrests made at immigration offices when immigrants are directed to appear for status hearings on their individual cases.   
Yet the most damaging feature of this system may not be the arrests that make the news. It is the uncertainty imposed on families who have followed the rules, filed their papers, paid their fees and waited—sometimes for well over a year—for the government to act.
These enforcement activities are achieving one of their intended effects: to scare individuals and families enough that they self-deport. In Juneau that has meant that every member of our small Haitian community felt compelled to abandon their new home when they, along with some 350,000 other Haitians in the country, lost their temporary protected status on July 27th.   Juneau lost some fine healthcare workers and school aides.  
Here is the psychological war being waged on countless families across our nation: Families wait for long periods to be scheduled for interviews on their status, not knowing when these will happen—while anxiety builds over what for many will be a life-or-death outcome. With ICE’s apprehension of people who show for interviews, each applicant must ask: Do I skip the interview, resulting in an automatic case denial for abandonment, or do I attend and take the chance that I could be arrested, detained and permanently separated from my family?
I mentor several Ukrainian and Central American families in Juneau and have assisted them in filing papers for temporary protected status, authorizations for work and the like. Without exception, they are contributing to our community through their service jobs and small businesses. 
As I write this, I have before me seven Homeland Security Notices of Action, known as I-797s,  on applications for temporary protected status or for employment authorization filed between January 10 and March 17, 2025.  These specific Notices of Action acknowledge the applications and all are dated in August 2026, more than 17 months after these immigrants applied. The forms indicate that the applicants are conditionally approved to remain and work in the country. The catch: the temporary protected status will expire on October 19. In short, these families have been held in suspended animation.  
One immigrant I mentor  applied for and received an initial authorization to work, helping to support his family. Many months before that authorization was due to expire, he filed for renewal and paid the requisite fee. When his work authorization expired, he was forced to quit his job. Finally last month he received confirmation that his application for renewal was being reviewed. When we called the department’s Contact Center to learn when the review would be complete, we were informed that the government might get to it by November. The family survives only because his adult daughter and niece are employed.
Another immigrant and his wife have established a successful business in Juneau. They paid nearly $1,000 for a renewal of their employment authorization documents on the first day they were eligible to do so — immigrants are allowed to apply no more than 180 days in advance. Once their current authorization expired, they could no longer lawfully work. USCIS can’t say when their renewal will be processed.
Without a valid work permit or an active status determination, all of these immigrants are stripped of their ability to earn an income. They lose employer-sponsored health insurance, stable housing options and are unable to receive or renew a driver’s license. The result is not merely delay. It is enforced poverty.
Another immigrant and his wife have worked multiple jobs to buy a home for their teenage children and themselves. Mikhail has successfully built his own construction-related business and has an unwavering belief that the United States government will reward his industry and dedication by granting a more permanent status to him and his family. His 18-year-old son struggles with his future, finding it difficult to set roots here because of the incessant fear that the rug will be pulled out from under them and that they will soon be forced to look to another country to start a new life yet again.
This war of nerves is taking a visible toll on countless thousands of people in limbo: parents suffering depression, panic attacks and sleep deprivation; children haunted by the possibility that they will be separated from their parents.
Most of us sleep at night because we live with the ordinary security of knowing where we will live, how we will work, whom we can count on and what we can offer our children. Those are not extravagant privileges. They are the basic conditions of a stable life.
The cruelty of the present immigration system lies not only in detention and deportation. It lies in forcing our neighbors to live without those basic assurances—day after day, month after month, while the government that demands their compliance leaves their futures unresolved.

title: Nurse claims clinic put patients at risk and retaliated against her
description: An advanced registered nurse practitioner is suing a central Iowa medical clinic for allegedly firing her after she complained of patients being put at risk. Tracy Drinkard is suing DoctorsNow Walk-In Care of Polk County in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa. Drinkard is an Iowa-licensed advanced registered nurse practitioner, and DoctorsN[...]
text:
(Photo via Getty Images)An advanced registered nurse practitioner is suing a central Iowa medical clinic for allegedly firing her after she complained of patients being put at risk.
Tracy Drinkard is suing DoctorsNow Walk-In Care of Polk County in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa. Drinkard is an Iowa-licensed advanced registered nurse practitioner, and DoctorsNow, which is owned by Dr. David Stanek Jr. and Dr. Eric Stanek, operates medical clinics in West Des Moines, Johnston and Altoona, offering urgent and primary care, as well as weight-loss and dermatology services.
According to the lawsuit, DoctorsNow hired Drinkard on Jan. 15, 2023, to provide primary care services to patients in return for an hourly wage of $62.50. The lawsuit asserts Drinkard routinely worked more than 40 hours per week without being paid overtime wages.
Drinkard contacted a DoctorsNow human resources administrator in October 2025 and formally complained about the company’s failure to pay overtime, according to the lawsuit.
Months before, in the spring of 2025, Drinkard alleges, she had informed David Stanek that she believed the clinic was carrying unsafe patient volumes and providing inadequate clinical staffing. The lawsuit asserts Drinkard suggested patient care might be compromised because she was required to see patients at seven-minute intervals and because there was only one clinical support staff member to assist two medical providers.
According to the lawsuit, Drinkard resigned in October 2025, effective Jan.15, 2026, citing the “ongoing high patient volumes and lack of adequate support” that she said “made it increasingly difficult to provide safe and effective care.”
On Oct. 20, 2025, she allegedly reported DoctorsNow to the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals, and Licensing for remaining open and continuing to see patients at a clinic where the building’s water supply was shut off for one to two hours. Days later, the lawsuit claims, Drinkard also reported to DIAL that David Stanek had suggested she dispense pharmaceutical samples to cash-paying, weight-loss patients while they awaited delivery of their mail-order medications.
That complaint alleged DoctorsNow was charging patients for a medical weight-loss plan and then providing them with free samples while also failing to record the distribution of those samples in the appropriate logbook.
On Nov. 21, 2025, Drinkard’s attorney asked DoctorsNow for contact information for the company’s attorney. According to the lawsuit, DoctorsNow prematurely terminated Drinkard’s employment the next day.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages for violations of the overtime provisions of the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, for workplace retaliation, and for wrongful discharge in violation of public policy.
In response to the allegations, DoctorsNow has denied any wrongdoing and asserted that every element of the claims made under the Fair Labor Standards Act is barred by the statute of limitations.
A trial date in the case has yet to be scheduled.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Task force recommends New Mexico education department consider eliminating K-2 screen time
description: A task force studying the impact of screens in classrooms on Tuesday recommended New Mexico education officials consider issuing guidelines that would eliminate screen time for students from kindergarten through second grade. The task force also recommended to lawmakers to define 'screen time' in upcoming legislative session.
text:
New Mexico’s interim Legislative Education Study Committee heard recommendations on Sept. 22, 2026 from a task force that studied screen time use in elementary classrooms.A task force studying the impact of screens in classrooms on Tuesday recommended New Mexico education officials consider issuing guidelines that would eliminate screen time for students from kindergarten through second grade. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Screen Use Legislative Task Force formed after House Memorial 2, a bill signed last legislative session, tasked the Legislative Education Study Committee with conducting a study on screen time use in elementary classrooms. The task force included LESC analysts, New Mexico Public Education Department officials, district administrators, teachers and students.
The task force’s study cites research conducted by the University of Michigan that shows the average age at which kids engage with screen media on a regular basis is four months old.
Excessive screen time for young children is a public health concern, as research shows it causes negative impacts on social and emotional growth, as well as language development. Additionally, excessive screen time is linked to a rise in obesity, sleep disorders and mental health conditions including depression and anxiety.
The New Mexico Public Education Department requires computer-based testing in elementary schools for reading, math, and science. In kindergarten through second grade, the state requires use of Amira, an AI-program, to assess and track student reading development.
Numerous lawmakers have expressed concern about the program and according to NMPED, as of earlier this month, 18 local education agencies had opted out of one or more components of Amira’s assessment process.
On Tuesday, LESC Principal Analyst Marit Andrews presented recommendations to state lawmakers, which include having NMPED issue K-12 guidelines for daily screen use. In addition to eliminating screen time for kindergarten through second grade students, the task force suggested PED consider minimizing screen time deemed nonessential to active learning and limiting access to entertainment and social media apps.
But LESC Chair Sen. William Soules (D-Las Cruces) expressed concern over what the legislative committee’s role should be toward implementing the guidelines come the next legislative session.
“We can request the PED to do something — it doesn’t compel them to do anything unless it is directly in statute,” Soules said. 
The task force advised lawmakers to leave the screen time guidelines to NMPED code rather than state statute so they remain “adaptable to change,” LESC Principal Analyst Marit Andrews explained.
But the task force did recommend lawmakers push legislation that defines screen time, as New Mexico law does not currently set parameters for acceptable screen time use for the purpose of K-12 instruction. The definition, Andrews said, should distinguish between “active” and “passive” use of technology.
Benjamin Barlow, a member of the task force and principal of North Star Elementary School in Albuquerque, explained to lawmakers that not all screen time is created equal. In one scenario, he said, students could be using a computer in an active way to collect data for a science project. In a separate scenario he posed, a student could use a computer to watch an instructional video without discussion or reflection, which he calls passive use. 
“So for me, as an administrator, the question isn’t simply how many minutes was a student on a screen. The question is what is the student doing on that screen and why was technology the right tool,” Barlow told lawmakers.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: 160 miles of transmission lines planned for eastern SD, costing upward of $2 billion
description: South Dakota regulators are considering permit applications for projects that would add about 160 miles of electrical transmission lines along the eastern edge of the state.  Transmission lines carry high-voltage power over long distances. The larger proposal is part of the PowerOn Midwest Project, from companies including Xcel Energy and Otter Tail Power. I[...]
text:
Electric transmission lines stand near Clark, South Dakota, in 2024. Pending proposals would add about 160 miles of transmission lines along the eastern edge of the state. (Photo by Robert Zullo/States Newsroom)South Dakota regulators are considering permit applications for projects that would add about 160 miles of electrical transmission lines along the eastern edge of the state. 
Transmission lines carry high-voltage power over long distances.
The larger proposal is part of the PowerOn Midwest Project, from companies including Xcel Energy and Otter Tail Power. It calls for about 90 miles of 765-kilovolt transmission line in South Dakota through Grant, Deuel and Brookings counties. It would run south from the Big Stone South Substation in Grant County, in the northeastern corner of the state, and turn into Minnesota at a point east of Brookings. 
It also includes expansions at the Big Stone and Brookings County substations and about 5 miles of 345-kilovolt transmission line. Further segments would be constructed across southern Minnesota.
The companies estimate construction of the South Dakota segment would cost between $1.3 and $1.7 billion, with completion in 2034.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The route includes a 250-foot-wide right-of-way for the 765-kilovolt line and a 150-foot-wide right-of-way for the 345-kilovolt line, according to the project application. The 765-kilovolt line has landowner access agreements, known as easements, for 81 of the required 274 parcels in South Dakota, or 30%. The 345-kilovolt line has 7 of 19, or 37%. 
The second proposal, filed by Otter Tail Power Company, is the Big Stone South to Hankinson to Bison Project. That proposal would run 71 miles of 345-kilovolt transmission line in South Dakota from the Big Stone South Substation north through Grant and Roberts counties into North Dakota. The project would continue to a substation west of Fargo.
The line would have a 150-foot right of way, and the South Dakota segment is estimated to cost $191 million to $229 million with completion in 2034. The project application says the company “will work collaboratively with landowners to obtain necessary rights through voluntary agreements.” The application does not say how many agreements have been obtained. 
The companies say the projects are intended to improve reliability and increase transmission capacity for more power plants and customers consuming large amounts of electricity, including “data centers and other industrial demands.” South Dakota has some small data centers but none of the larger hyperscale data centers proliferating across the country, including in North Dakota and Minnesota.

The South Dakota Public Utilities Commission has scheduled the following meetings to receive public input about proposed transmission-line projects.

title: Trump DOJ uses case of Utah letter carrier to highlight allegations of voting fraud
text: Federal officials charged a Utah letter carrier Tuesday with throwing 300 primary ballots in a church parking lot dumpster, an incident that a top U.S. Justice Department official said made the case for stricter regulations of voting.The prosecution of Damon Matai Seei, of Payson, Utah, showed “voting fraud is real,” acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said at a press conference at DOJ headquarters in Washington.The Justice Department gave the arrest an unusually high profile, spotlighting the administration’s efforts to combat voter fraud after the U.S. Supreme Court this month blocked a new U.S. Postal Service rule limiting mail voting from going into effect for this year’s elections.The regulation was meant to “address the chronically abused mail-in ballot system,” McCotter said. He criticized the trial judge who initially blocked the rule, which would have required special tracking and design features, among other things such as creating a national database of eligible voters.“Election integrity should not be a political or partisan issue,” McCotter said. “Who could be against properly tracking mail-in ballots? Unfortunately, but entirely predictably, that regulation was blocked by a judge in Massachusetts. … The Trump administration, however, will continue taking aggressive actions to protect our elections.”Postal Service ruleU.S. District Judge Indiria Talwani’s order blocking the rule is only in effect for the Nov. 3 elections, a provision meant to preserve the status quo because the rule was finalized mere months before the midterms. The merits of the case are still being argued. The U.S. Supreme Court upheld Talwani’s decision.The prosecution of Seei, and the attention the administration sought to give it, undercut a key argument the administration made in the case: The rule included only “modest” technical specifications for a category of mail and should not be interpreted as an election regulation.The U.S. Constitution grants states the authority to administer elections, with policy oversight from Congress. In siding with the Democratic states and voting rights groups who filed suit, Talwani and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit said the rule was clearly an attempt to affect election policy and was not restricted to a modest mail regulation.Trump and mail-in votingPresident Donald Trump has railed against mail-in voting and claimed, without evidence, that it is a major source of election fraud and contributed to his 2020 loss to President Joe Biden.Since Trump retook office in January 2025, the department has charged 70 immigrants with illegally voting, compared with only 13 in the four years of Biden’s term, McCotter said Tuesday.“And we intend to bring many more,” he added.Homeland Security Investigations, a Homeland Security Department agency, has made 160 recent arrests, from 1,600 open voter fraud cases, HSI acting Deputy Executive Associate Director Matthew Millhollin said.A reporter in the room noted that 70 prosecutions amounted to a bare fraction of the 150 million votes cast in the 2024 election.McCotter responded that the Utah case involved 300 ballots, and that law enforcement had only scratched the surface of possible incidents. “Thousands more” cases were being investigated, he said.“The folks on the other side, the opponents of the president, insist this has never happened, that there is no voting fraud,” he said. “And so when we have dozens of cases … I think that discourages and defeats their characterization.”No partisan motive allegedSeei, who is no longer a postal worker, intentionally threw out about 300 mail ballots on June 3 that were being mailed to voters in advance of the June 23 primary in Utah, according to charging documents.In an interview with law enforcement, he indicated he did not have a political motive but said he threw away the mail, which also included advertisements, “because he wanted to ‘lighten his workload’ so he could presumably go home earlier,” prosecutors said.Melissa Holyoak, the top federal prosecutor for Utah, traveled to Washington, D.C., for Tuesday’s press conference. She noted that 95% of the state’s voters cast their ballots by mail.Many people in Seei’s delivery area in Eagle Mountain, Utah, complained to the Utah County Clerk that they hadn’t received ballots, Holyoak said. Using county databases, the clerk found that voter participation was “remarkably low” in the area where complaints originated.“As American citizens, we have certain freedoms and rights,” Holyoak said. “And one of those fundamental rights is the right to vote. But when defendant allegedly tossed the mail-in ballots into a parking lot dumpster, those citizens' right to vote were also thrown away.”The federal public defender representing Seei did not immediately return a call seeking comment.

title: Average Idaho gas prices jump 10 cents overnight, as Boise, IF and other towns hit $5 per gallon
description: The state’s average price for regular gasoline jumped 10 cents overnight to $4.96 per gallon, while drivers in Boise and Idaho Falls are seeing average prices that are 17 and 16 cents higher than Monday, respectively. Idaho’s average for regular gas is 10 cents more than a day ago, 14 cents more than a week […]
text:
The state’s average price for regular gasoline jumped 10 cents overnight to $4.96 per gallon, while drivers in Boise and Idaho Falls are seeing average prices that are 17 and 16 cents higher than Monday, respectively. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The state’s average price for regular gasoline jumped 10 cents overnight to $4.96 per gallon, while drivers in Boise and Idaho Falls are seeing average prices that are 17 and 16 cents higher than Monday, respectively.
Idaho’s average for regular gas is 10 cents more than a day ago, 14 cents more than a week ago, 47 cents more than a month ago, and $1.44 more than a year ago, according to AAA Idaho. Several of Idaho’s largest cities now join rural counties above the $5 mark, including Boise ($5.04), Idaho Falls ($5.00), Pocatello ($5.02), and Twin Falls ($5.02), according to AAA.
AAA has compiled the statistics for the average price for a gallon of regular gasoline in Idaho, compared to the national average, over time. (Graphic courtesy of AAA Idaho)
The average price for diesel in Idaho spiked to $6.59 on Tuesday, the highest average price ever recorded by AAA.
“The causes are the same, but the symptoms are more severe – global conflict putting pressure on crude oil affects the price of everything you can make by refining the crude,” said AAA Idaho public affairs director Matthew Conde in the press release.  “These price jumps are simply shocking.”
The West Texas Intermediate benchmark for crude is currently trading near $91 per barrel, a drop of nearly $10 from late last week, the press release said.  
“Market instability could continue in the short term, and consumers will have to cope as best we can,” Conde said. “Please follow the fuel grade requirements in your owner’s manual. If you’ve been purchasing a higher grade of gasoline with the belief that you’re giving your car a ‘treat,’ you could be spending unnecessary money for a marginal benefit.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Report shows steady improvement in Long Island Sound water quality
description: From 2023 to 2025, water quality in Long Island Sound improved following wastewater treatment and infrastructure upgrades in CT and NY.
text:
Billions of dollars spent on wastewater treatment and other infrastructure upgrades in Connecticut and New York have resulted in apparent improvements in Long Island Sound’s water quality, according to a report from the ecological nonprofit Save the Sound.
Published every two years, the group’s report divides Long Island Sound into five segments: the eastern, central and western basins that cover the widest portions of the Sound between New York and Connecticut, and the western and eastern narrows around lower Fairfield County, Westchester County and New York City.
The three basin segments all received “A” grades in the latest report, which relied on data from water samples taken in 2025.
The eastern narrows received a “B” grade for the second consecutive report and the western narrows — the smallest by total area, covering the waters directly around New York City — rose from an “F” grade to a “D,” for the first time since Save the Sound began publishing its report in 2008.
“It’s a remarkable success story in that the investments paid dividends, the water quality is improving,” said Peter Linderoth, Save the Sound’s director of healthy waters and lands. 
Still, he and other officials said Tuesday that Long Island Sound continues to face challenges from climate change, coastal development and occasional overflows from combined stormwater and sewer systems that can send millions of gallons of untreated wastewater flowing into rivers and, eventually, the Sound.
“It could take time,” to address lingering points of concern, Linderoth added. 
The report also published letter grades for dozens of smaller inlets, bays and other bodies of water around the Sound. Of the 28 sites within Connecticut that were measured, 19 recieved “A” or “B” grades. 
Researchers looked at several key indicators from water samples in their grading rubric, including measurements of dissolved oxygen, organic carbon, populations of phytoplankton and water clarity. Samples taken from harbors were also tested for oxygen saturation and levels of seaweed — which, in moderate amounts, is typical of healthy ecosystems, while too much seaweed can be a sign of of nitrogen pollution.
Water sampling in the open-water areas of the Sound was conducted by the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, the Interstate Environmental Commission and the New York City Department of Environmental Protection. Samples from smaller coastal areas were taken by over a dozen partner organizations working with Save the Sound as part of the group’s Unified Water Study.
At a press conference to unveil the report’s findings Tuesday at Weed Beach in Darien, officials credited “billions” of dollars in state and federal investments — particularly on fixing antiqued wastewater treatment systems — with helping to improve the heavily-polluted Sound’s reputation.
Approximately $1.2 billion has been spent in Connecticut alone over the last 20 years to address the problem of combined sewer overflows, according to DEEP.
“Save The Sound’s report reflects the improvements to the quality of Long Island Sound waters as a result of the investments the state of Connecticut has made through its Clean Water Fund, and the General Permit for Nitrogen Discharges to reduce nutrient pollution from the state’s wastewater treatment facilities,” DEEP spokesman Bill Flood said in a statement Tuesday.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also provides funding to support conservation projects in both Connecticut and New York through its Long Island Sound Program. Overall funding for that program reached $40 million in the most recent fiscal year, up from just $1 million a decade ago.
U.S. Rep. Jim Himes, D-4th District, said support for conservation projects in and around Long Island Sound has historically been bipartisan. He said that continues to be the case under current EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, who is a former Republican congressman from Long Island.
“The [Trump] administration has taken a particularly aggressive stance in certain areas, like wind,” Himes said. “But I haven’t seen that same animus out of this administration with respect to conservation projects. For the moment, we’re in — I think — pretty good shape.”
In 2025, Zeldin’s EPA closed the agency’s dedicated Long Island Sound office in Stamford as part of a wave of government cost-cutting. Staff members were reassigned to the agency’s regional offices in New York City. An EPA spokesperson  said at the time there were no impacts to the work of the agency’s Long Island Sound Program. 
Also last year, officials with the Long Island Sound Partnership reported that areas of hypoxia — where low levels of dissolved oxygen kill off fish — had reached their lowest levels since data collection began in the 1980s. However, the Save the Sound report noted that rising water temperatures in the Sound due to climate change could reverse that trend, as warmer water holds less oxygen.
Bill Lucey of Save the Sound said Tuesday that while there had been some “ups and downs” in dealing with the current Trump administration, work improving water quality has continued unabated.
“In the future, it’s going to be wide open for fish consumption, shellfish consumption, no more closure days for swimming,” Lucey said.  “We’re so much farther along than we were 15 years ago.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Consumer Advocate calls for proof that Alliant gas plant is cost effective
description: The Office of Consumer Advocate is asking the Iowa Utilities Commission to require additional information and a hearing for an Iowa gas peaker plant planned for Cerro Gordo County.  Interstate Power and Light Company, an Iowa branch of Alliant Energy, applied for a certificate of public convenience, use and necessity with IUC for its Riverhawk […]
text:
The Office of Consumer Advocate is asking the Iowa Utilities Commission to require additional information before approving a certificate for a gas peaker plant.  (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)The Office of Consumer Advocate is asking the Iowa Utilities Commission to require additional information and a hearing for an Iowa gas peaker plant planned for Cerro Gordo County. 
Interstate Power and Light Company, an Iowa branch of Alliant Energy, applied for a certificate of public convenience, use and necessity with IUC for its Riverhawk Energy Center project, a 1,200-megawatt natural gas turbine plant. The consumer advocate and clean energy groups have urged the utilities commission to require evidence that the project is cost effective before it approves the certificate. 

About the Office of Consumer Advocate
The Office of Consumer Advocate, a division of the Iowa attorney general’s office, represents “Iowa consumers and the public interest in all forums with the goal of maintaining safe, reliable, reasonably-priced, and nondiscriminatory utility services for all consumers in all market settings while informing and educating the public on utility related issues,” according to the agency’s website.

In a Sept. 11 filing to the IUC, the Office of Consumer Advocate said estimated capital costs of building the plant and its ongoing expenses are “significant and raise additional concerns concerning affordability for IPL’s current customers, if the costs are passed onto customers.” 
The consumer advocate’s filing argues the company is potentially taking advantage of the system to approve and build the facility before proving it is cost effective and necessary. The company, however, argues that costs from the project cannot be passed on to customers without IUC review at a rate proceeding. 
“IPL should not be allowed to exploit the (certificate of public convenience) and advance ratemaking statute in a manner that would allow for the development of the largest natural gas facility on record with essentially no upfront review of the need for, cost of, or ongoing fuel cost impacts relative to other generation resource choices,” the Office of Consumer Advocate wrote in its objection. 
In a filed response to the Office of Consumer Advocate objection, Interstate Power and Light said the issue of “whether a project is prudent, necessary, and cost-effective” is not “relevant” in approving a certificate of public convenience, use and necessity, which the company seeks from the IUC.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Company argues this is not the format for proving necessity

IPL argued in the filing, and in a previous response to concerns raised by the Office of Consumer Advocate, that IUC has previously approved certificates of public convenience without evaluating if the project is “prudent, necessary, and cost-effective.” 
“Consistent with the numerous rulings of the Commission, IPL is not required to present additional evidence relating to cost-effectiveness and need in this docket – such information must be resolved in a ratemaking proceeding, not this docket,” the filing reads. “A ruling to the contrary would be inconsistent with the prior precedents of the Commission and would implicate Iowa Code.” 
The latest filings follow calls from Iowa Business for Clean Energy for greater public scrutiny of Interstate Power and Light’s generation plans and their connection to the company’s contracts with data centers. 
Bob Rafferty, Iowa Business for Clean Energy’s executive director, said in a news release Tuesday that utilities should be required to demonstrate “that projects are truly needed, are the most cost-effective option available, and that the customers driving the need are paying their fair share” before customers are “exposed to billions of dollars in risk.” 
“Consumers deserve full transparency about the need, cost-effectiveness, fuel cost impacts, and customer impacts of the proposed power-generation facilities before customers are committed to decades of costs and risks,” Rafferty said. “If these projects are truly needed and represent the best choice for customers, the utility should have no problem demonstrating that through a rigorous public review process.” 
The OCA filing estimates that Alliant’s Riverhawk facility, combined with the Morgan Valley Energy Center, another flexible energy natural gas plant project from company, will cost between $2.1 billion and $3.2 billion, “without considering the ongoing costs of operating the facilities.” 
Coal increased its share of Iowa electricity generation in 2025, report shows

IPL’s Sept. 17 filed response to the Office of Consumer Advocate does not address the multibillion-dollar cost estimate from OCA. 
A spokesperson for Growing Iowa’s Economy, a group promoting “responsible” data center development and of which Alliant is a member, said “siting approval of a project does not automatically mean its costs are included in customer rates.” 
“Any request for cost recovery must be reviewed in a future rate proceeding, where the Commission determines whether the investment was prudent and what costs can be included in customer rates,” the spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement. “One of our members, Alliant Energy, has committed to keeping electric base rates stable through the end of the decade.” 
Interstate Power and Light’s response to the OCA objection notes precedent set by the Iowa Utilities Commission’s decision to grant a certificate of public convenience to MidAmerican Energy for a proposed 50-megawatt solar project. In IUC’s final order for the certificate, commissioners said whether the project was prudent, necessary or cost-effective, “are questions that fall outside the scope of this proceeding.” 
Office of Consumer Advocate argued that IUC has not approved a certificate of public convenience and necessity “for a gas-fired generating facility of the size and scale presented in this case without underlying resource planning support.” 
The OCA comments also argue that the Riverhawk project is “more than a mere peaking facility” which are constructed with the intent of running when electric demands are “peaking,” like during a heat wave for example. OCA, and comments from Iowa Business for Clean Energy point to IPL filings that indicated the facility could run more frequently depending on market conditions.
In their response, IPL said the “the legal standard for a certificate is the same regardless of how frequently the facility is expected to operate” and that the issue would be more appropriately considered in a ratemaking proceeding. 
The Clean Energy Districts of Iowa and Iowa Business Energy Coalition also submitted comments on the docket sharing some of the concerns of the Office of Consumer Advocate. 
The comments ask commissioners to require a resource evaluation study and evidence of cost-effectiveness and need before IPL’s certificate for the Riverhawk facility can be approved. 
“This issue warrants the filing of testimony and a hearing,” the OCA comment reads. “If IPL does not provide evidence demonstrating that its proposed generation is cost effective, including in relation to fuel costs, the Commission must deny the certificate.”
IPL’s response said the only issues asserted by the groups are “legal in nature” over whether prudency, necessity and cost-effectiveness must be proven in a certificate of public convenience application. The utility company argued the IUC has already made that determination in previous dockets. 
“The legal issues over the applicability of cost-effectiveness and need have been fully addressed and can be resolved without the need for an evidentiary hearing,” the company said and requested IUC waive the hearing.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Bridgeport’s police union wants chief sidelined during probe
description: Mayor Joe Ganim has agreed to a probe, but the Bridgeport police union called on him to remove Chief Roderick Porter until it is done.
text:
Despite his recent public statements in support of Police Chief Roderick Porter, Bridgeport Mayor Joe Ganim had also agreed to hire a legal firm to conduct an independent investigation into internal allegations of misconduct against the city’s top cop.
But members of the city’s police union gathered Tuesday to reiterate their calls for the probe and to call on Ganim to place him on administrative leave while the review is undertaken. Members of the department have accused Porter of retaliation, discrimination, abuse of authority and other misconduct.
At a press conference Tuesday, members of AFSCME Local 1159 and AFSCME Council 4 said Bridgeport police officers have filed roughly 20 complaints with the state Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities and about six federal lawsuits. The complaints against Porter include allegations of retaliation, discrimination, interference with investigations, violations of due process and collective bargaining agreements, whistleblower retaliation and improper interference with promotions and assignments.
“When there’s a massive amount of complaints, it’s not just an isolated incident,” said Michael Salemme III, president of AFSCME Local 1159.
Porter denied the accusations and said the complaints are largely coming from officers who are unhappy with changes he has made since he became chief in 2022. He said he has worked to make promotions and assignments more equitable and increase accountability within the department.
Porter also denied threatening officers, one of the allegations raised against him.
“I’ve never threatened anybody,” he said.
In a statement, City Attorney Tyisha Toms noted the city’s previous decision to hire the firm Jackson Lewis to investigate the officers’ complaints, but declined to answer questions about when the probe would start or how long it would take.
“As an employer, the City has an obligation to take workplace complaints seriously and to make reasonable efforts to understand and address concerns that may affect its employees, the effective operation of the Department, and ultimately the public it serves,” Toms said. “Given the number and continuing nature of the concerns being raised, the City has determined that it is appropriate and necessary to resume an independent review of the workplace environment within the Bridgeport Police Department. Because this process involves personnel matters and pending litigation, the City will not comment publicly on the review while it is ongoing.”
The Bridgeport Police Union held a vote of no confidence against Porter last year, resulting in roughly 180 of the union’s 315 members casting ballot. Of that number, only 27 officers voted in support of the chief. 

Michael Salemme III, president of the Bridgeport Police Union (Local 1159), poses for a photo in Bridgeport. Credit: Reginald David / CT Mirror

Salemme and other union leaders said the number and nature of the complaints against Porter should warrant an investigation outside of the Police Department. They also questioned why officers facing allegations are typically placed on administrative leave during investigations while Porter remains in his position.
The Bridgeport Guardians, an organization representing minority law enforcement officers, also expressed support for the union’s call for an investigation. The group referenced the department’s history of federal oversight stemming from past discrimination lawsuits and said it did not want to see that history repeat itself.
On Tuesday, the union also called on the Federal Bureau of Investigation, U.S. Department of Justice and Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to intervene. Leaders said they believe the existing grievance process is too slow to adequately address the allegations, with some complaints taking years to reach a resolution.
Porter, meanwhile, pointed to what he described as improvements to the department under his leadership, including more than 100 new officers, promotions, new technology and vehicles, assignments to federal task forces and historically low crime. He also said community engagement with the department is at an all-time high.
Porter said he believes some officers had become accustomed to receiving special assignments, promotions and other opportunities without the level of oversight he has implemented. He said complaints increased after he began enforcing what he described as a more consistent approach to discipline and accountability.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Former VP Kamala Harris stumps with Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, highlighting Black maternal health
description: Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed appeared with former Vice President Kamala Harris Tuesday, with the latter flying in for a roundtable event in Detroit focused on Black maternal health. Harris’ willingness to hit the trail with El-Sayed was yet another show of national Democratic Party unity as he faces a general election battle with […]
text:
Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed appears with former Vice President Kamala Harris on Sept. 22, 2026, for a roundtable event in Detroit focused on Black maternal health. (C-SPAN screenshot)
Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed appeared with former Vice President Kamala Harris Tuesday, with the latter flying in for a roundtable event in Detroit focused on Black maternal health.
Harris’ willingness to hit the trail with El-Sayed was yet another show of national Democratic Party unity as he faces a general election battle with Republican nominee Mike Rogers in November. 
Speaking to Black mothers in Detroit about maternal healthcare outcomes and the struggles of healthcare workers writ large, Harris outlined the stakes of the 2026 election — and what it means for healthcare, a key plank of El-Sayed’s campaign.
The former vice president and 2024 presidential candidate said that one in 12 women in the U.S. are living in what she called maternal healthcare deserts. Harris also noted that President Donald Trump had cut funding for Medicaid and that his administration’s attacks on diversity, equity and inclusion programs was, in its own way, a direct attack on maternal healthcare.
“These are the facts when we talk about what is at stake in this moment as it relates to these midterms and who occupies seats in one of the most important bodies in our nation, if not the world,” Harris said. “The United States Senate should be a stopgap on the abuses of this administration and I would suggest to you that this fellow sitting to my right would be one of them when elected.”
In turn, El-Sayed said the race between him and Rogers was an opportunity “to decide that we are going to invest in more health, we are going to invest in more care.”
Shanay Watson‑Whittaker, the director of Michigan campaigns at Reproductive Freedom for All, was also in attendance, and said Rogers was against Michigan’s 2022 ballot proposal that enshrined reproductive rights into the Michigan Constitution.
“What we have with Mike Rogers is we have someone who is a blank check for Trump,” Watson-Whittaker said.


The campaign visit was significant because Harris appears poised to reenter public life in some fashion, which could mean another run at the White House after losing to Trump in 2024. Some Democrats have been wary of tying their respective ships to Harris after that defeat, which Rogers alluded to in a social media post just prior to Tuesday’s event.
“Just like he begged Chuck Schumer for money, Conman Abdul El-Sayed has begged Kamala Harris to come to Michigan today. Can we expect your endorsement of her 2028 campaign, Abdul?,” the Facebook post asked.
Regardless, El-Sayed has embraced Harris’ support — the former vice president was one of the first few national establishment Democrats to endorse him after his primary win over U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham).
Harris going all in on El-Sayed was also a sign that there was no bad blood between them after El-Sayed was a member of the “uncommitted” movement, which involved Arab and Muslim voters, particularly in southeast Michigan, withdrawing their support for Biden over his embrace of Israel’s war on Hamas in Gaza following the Oct. 17, 2023 terrorist attack that killed more than 1,200 Israelis, most of them civilians.
El-Sayed and other former members of the have since said that the pushback was squarely against Biden and his reelection bid in 2024, and not aimed at Harris or any other member of the Biden administration. When Harris became the Democratic nominee that year, and only after Biden dropped out of the race, El-Sayed was one of the first Michigan Democrats to endorse her.
Some Michigan members of the pro-Palestinian movement continued to hammer Harris over the Israel-Hamas war during the tail end of the 2024 cycle, but El-Sayed was not one of them.
Still, Republicans and some centrist-Democrats in the 2026 cycle tried to paint El-Sayed’s opposition to Biden as opposition to Harris, all in an attempt to drive a wedge between supporters of Harris and galvanize momentum around Stevens’ primary campaign.
That effort was put to rest when Harris eventually endorsed El-Sayed.
Following the roundtable discussion, Harris was asked why she was supporting the Michigan nominee, and more importantly, why she was appearing with him on the campaign trail. The event was not open to local press, but the vice president told pool reporters that she was in El-Sayed’s corner because of his stances on affordable healthcare, childcare and housing.
Although the event was not open to all Michigan press, Harris took a swipe at Trump’s recent banning of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, calling it “abhorrent.”
“That man is afraid of the voice of the people and that the people understand and know what he’s doing,” Harris said. 
Michigan progressive rabbis use Harris visit to press El-Sayed on ‘nonnegotiable’ Jewish concerns
Meanwhile, a group of Michigan rabbis who say they are both longtime Democrats and supporters of Harris’ 2024 campaign, have been pressing El-Sayed to publicly address concerns they have for Jewish safety and identity, Jewish statehood in Israel and self-determination in the Holy Land. 
Those concerns are predicated on El-Sayed’s firm stance that Israel is committing a genocide in Gaza and that the leadership of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is to blame, but also his primary campaign stops with influencer Hasan Piker and their respective rhetoric against the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
El-Sayed says Hasan Piker does not speak for his campaign amid comments about Jewish candidate

The rabbis raised concerns about El-Sayed and asked him to come to the table to address those concerns in early September. The group, known as Nonnegotiable Michigan, has said since that El-Sayed has yet to do so.
On Tuesday, in anticipation of Harris’ visit, the group issued an open letter to the former vice president and asked her to push El-Sayed to address their grievances.
“Throughout your admirable public service career, you have never asked us to choose between our commitment to social justice and our Jewish safety or identity,” the letter said. “You made Jewish life proud and visible inside the Vice President’s residence for the first time in American history, inviting many of us to celebrate Hanukkah at the Naval Observatory. As Vice President, you told us plainly that antisemitism ‘must be condemned unequivocally’ — no caveats, no context, no hesitation. … Dr. El-Sayed has had every opportunity to meet our request to support our basic needs. So far, he has declined even to respond.”
The rabbis also noted that Harris’ visit comes the day after the Yom Kippur holiday, “a season we spend personally confronting questions of accountability, repentance, and the possibility of change and growth.”
“That is the same spirit with which we have approached Dr. El-Sayed’s candidacy. We have appealed to him directly, and been met with silence,” the letter said. “We believe he needs to be urged by Democratic Party leaders who understand that Jews have been one of the strongest, most committed voting blocs in the Democratic coalition, and by someone who understands that a Democratic Party that is not safe for Jews will not be able to protect our democracy.”

title: Democrats, experts call for revocation of school voucher program under adoption by states
text: WASHINGTON — Education experts and advocates on Tuesday urged Congress to repeal an incoming national school voucher program over concerns that it will divert critical funds away from public schools to private institutions.  U.S. Sen. Mazie Hirono convened a Democratic-led panel to sound the alarm on the sweeping program, which marks a key pillar of President Donald Trump’s and congressional Republicans’ efforts surrounding school choice. The Hawaii Democrat blasted the federal initiative, set to launch in early 2027, as a “tax break for wealthy families whose children are already enrolled in private schools, disguised as support for education.” At least 30 states have already opted in to the program, which allocates up to $1,700 in federal tax credits for people donating to organizations that provide K-12 scholarships for education-related services at private or public schools. The program is baked into the GOP’s “big, beautiful” bill that Trump signed into law in 2025. The U.S. Treasury Department is slated to release proposed regulations by the end of this month. Repeal attemptsHirono and Arizona Democratic U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly, joined by more than two dozen of their colleagues, introduced legislation in April to repeal the program. Wisconsin Democratic U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore introduced a companion bill in June with Reps. Suzanne Bonamici of Oregon, Maxwell Frost of Florida, Adelita Grijalva of Arizona, Mark Pocan of Wisconsin and dozens more original cosponsors. But any measure to roll back the program faces a dismal path in the GOP-controlled House and Senate.The umbrella term “school choice” centers on alternative programs to a student’s assigned public school. Opponents say these efforts drain critical funds and resources from school districts, while advocates argue the initiatives are necessary for parents who are dissatisfied with their local public schools.Augustus Mays, vice president of partnerships and engagement at the nonprofit policy and advocacy group EdTrust, said “our conclusion is clear: This is not free money or a targeted investment in students with the greatest needs.” “It is an uncapped federal tax subsidy that steers public resources toward private education with few safeguards,” he added. Mays pointed out that “a voucher does not guarantee access or quality,” noting that private schools are not bound by the same civil rights protections and obligations extended under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, or IDEA. Diverting funds?The Education and Treasury departments have said that the credit “does not divert money from local or state taxes, which make up the large majority of school funding,” according to a fact sheet. The agencies have also pointed to examples of education expenses the scholarships can be used for, such as “tuition for students to attend private schools of choice, tutoring at public schools, and support services for students with disabilities.” But Jessica Levin, litigation director at the advocacy group Education Law Center, said it’s a “major misconception” that “this is free money without cost to public schools” or that “currently underfunded public schools will benefit from the voucher program.” “Tax credit voucher programs are funded with public dollars because the money sent to scholarship granting organizations is money that would otherwise have been paid in state or federal taxes and gone into the state or federal treasury,” Levin said.Trump administration defends tax creditMeanwhile, Savannah Newhouse, a spokesperson for the Education Department, defended the tax credit, saying opponents of the program are “resorting to fearmongering by falsely labeling it a voucher because the phrase ‘we don’t want families to have more options to succeed in education’ isn’t a winning message,” in a statement shared with States Newsroom.  “The truth is that this provision does not take a single dollar away from public schools because it is funded by the generosity of private donors that supplement — not supplant — existing education dollars,” she added. “A word of advice: resisting change to the failed status quo in education makes you part of the problem, not the solution.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Postal Service’s plan to speed up delivery in South Dakota is a ‘good first step,’ US senator says
description: The U.S. Postal Service announced plans Tuesday to improve delivery speed in South Dakota, following years of complaints about service in the state. Beginning Jan. 1, a Sioux Falls processing and distribution center will become a regional center thanks to new machinery. The plant will handle more of the mail leaving and arriving in South […]
text:
U.S. Postal Service trucks parked in a line. (Photo by Stefania Pelfini la Waziya/Getty Images)The U.S. Postal Service announced plans Tuesday to improve delivery speed in South Dakota, following years of complaints about service in the state.
Beginning Jan. 1, a Sioux Falls processing and distribution center will become a regional center thanks to new machinery. The plant will handle more of the mail leaving and arriving in South Dakota without the need for processing out of state.
The change is expected to reduce travel time for some letters by one to two days.
“We are pleased that we can make these modernization improvements for our South Dakota customers, and we believe they will see noticeable changes,” the Postal Service said in a news release.
US senator from South Dakota subjects Postal Service to multiple pressure points

The release attributed slower delivery in South Dakota during the past few years to “unintended service issues” resulting from system-wide reforms.
U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, said in a speech last month that his office has received thousands of complaints about mail service. He said his staff conducted a test by sending mail from his Rapid City office to Pierre, which is a distance of about 170 miles by car. Rounds said the letter’s 10-day journey took it to Postal Service plants in Denver, then to Des Moines, Iowa, and to Fargo, North Dakota, before it was delivered in Pierre.
“This letter traveled over 1,800 miles across four different states just to end up back in South Dakota,” Rounds said.
The senator has exerted pressure on the Postal Service for improvement. He was part of an effort that convinced the service last year to keep some processing capabilities at its Huron plant, he introduced legislation last month to eliminate bonuses for Postal Service executives, and he placed a hold in June on Senate confirmations of Postal Service Board of Governors nominees that he pledged to keep in place until “service returns to levels at least equal to the days of the Pony Express.”
Rounds’ office issued a written statement Tuesday from Rounds about the Sioux Falls announcement.
“This is a good first step in improving our mail service, and I hope it will begin to reduce delivery times in our state,” the statement said.
The statement also said Rounds is looking forward to additional recommendations from the Postal Service Office of the Inspector General “in the coming days,” following an investigation Rounds requested.
Rounds previously said he had several conditions for lifting his hold on the Board of Governor nominees, including a commitment from the Postal Service to fully implement all findings from the inspector general investigation.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Fired police officer sues city over claims surrounding his private security work
description: A former Charles City police officer is now suing the city, alleging he was unfairly fired amid allegations he had falsified payroll records at his second job. Casey Mallory is suing the City of Charles City, Police Chief Hugh Anderson and City Manager Tyler Trout in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Iowa. […]
text:
(Photo via Getty Images)A former Charles City police officer is now suing the city, alleging he was unfairly fired amid allegations he had falsified payroll records at his second job.
Casey Mallory is suing the City of Charles City, Police Chief Hugh Anderson and City Manager Tyler Trout in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Iowa. Mallory was employed by the city as a police officer from 2011 through Jan. 16, 2026, most recently as a lieutenant.
The lawsuit alleges that in 2017, Mallory, while still working as a Charles City police officer, took a second job working security at a local poultry processing plant run by Pure Prairie Farms. In 2025, the lawsuit asserts, a rumor began circulating within the police department that Mallory was “double dipping” by being paid by both the plant and the city for some of the same hours worked.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In September 2025, the lawsuit alleges, Chief Anderson directed one of Mallory’s fellow officers, who also worked at the plant, to surreptitiously collect Mallory’s timesheets from the plant and deliver them to city officials. According to the lawsuit, Anderson then hired a third-party investigator, retired police officer Joseph Leibold of Pear Tree Investigations & Consulting, to investigate the matter.
Days later, Anderson notified Mallory he was being placed on paid administrative leave due to suspected misconduct, according to the lawsuit.
The written notice informed Mallory that “on numerous days in 2025, while on duty for the Charles City Police Department, Lt. Mallory allegedly submitted compensation (claims) to Pure Prairie Poultry for overlapping work hours.” According to the lawsuit, Anderson shared with Floyd County Sheriff Jeff Crooks information about the allegations against Mallory — although, the lawsuit claims, “there was no need for Anderson to disclose information about the complaint made against Mallory to Sheriff Crooks.”
According to the lawsuit, Leibold delivered his final investigative findings to Anderson on Nov. 21, 2025. The findings “confirmed that the plant did not pay Mallory for any hours during which Mallory was not performing work for the plant,” and also confirmed that the police department did not pay Mallory for any hours in which he was “not performing work for the department,” the lawsuit claims.
“In other words, Leibold’s investigation confirmed that the ‘double dipping’ rumor about Mallory was false,” the lawsuit asserts, adding that despite those findings, Anderson and Trout decided to terminate Mallory’s employment.
According to the lawsuit, Anderson and Trout then offered Mallory a severance agreement and told him if he signed it and agreed to resign, he could avoid having a termination on his record. Mallory declined the offer, the lawsuit asserts, and he was then fired for allegedly submitting claims for 46.5 hours of compensation from Pure Prairie Farms that “did not accurately reflect the time or manner in which the work was performed.”
According to the lawsuit, Mallory continues to be employed at the plant and has never been disciplined by the company for any reason.
As part of his lawsuit against the city, Mallory alleges he was denied the opportunity to respond to charges of misconduct and was given no explanation as to the city’s evidence against him. The lawsuit also alleges the city violated state law by disclosing to to the Floyd County sheriff confidential information about the complaint against Mallory.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages related to lost wages, compensation for emotional distress, court costs and attorney fees.
The city has yet to file a response to the lawsuit. The city’s attorney, Brad Sloter, did not return calls seeking comment Tuesday.
