	The FBI spoke to the other Navatek executives at Corner Bakery, who confirmed the meeting took place. One, David Kring, the company’s top scientist, told ProPublica he had no memory of what was discussed.
The other, Duke Hartman, told an FBI agent it was just “a get to know you meeting” with the chair of the super PAC and they did not discuss the “particulars of a donation.” Agents, records show, came to believe Hartman was lying about his role in Kao’s pay-to-play operation and would name him as a formal subject of a future investigation. Hartman was not charged. He did not respond to a detailed request for comment.
A few weeks after the $150,000 check to the Collins super PAC cleared, in February 2020, Kao and his team met with Collins’ office and secured a new round of funding.
“We were very warmly received,” Kao reported to his colleagues in an email obtained by the FBI. “Excellent meeting. Total of $32M will be supported.” Records show the Senate allocated at least $10 million that year based on Navatek’s proposals.
Navatek’s ambitions peaked in mid-2020. As the company waited to see if Collins would survive her reelection campaign, executives prepared to ask their champion on the appropriations committee for even more funding the following spring, internal documents show.
Other documents from that time show the company was courting senators from seven additional states and gunning for more than $200 million in new appropriations. Navatek expected to have offices in more than a dozen states by the end of the following year, including a new 15,000-square-foot facility in the Portland, Maine, harbor.
Kao, meanwhile, closed on a $4.5 million beachside home in an exclusive Honolulu neighborhood; the backyard pool had a waterfall feature. He renamed the company Martin Defense Group after himself, joking that it would simplify his future takeover of Lockheed Martin.
“It was working well, and it would have continued to work well,” said Schiff, the former executive. “Martin got greedy. Just got damn greedy.”
Downfall, cover-up
In early 2020, the Campaign Legal Center, a nonprofit good government group, noticed something strange in the public filings for the Collins super PAC. The PAC had received a $150,000 donation from a newly created LLC with a typo in its name: the Society of Young Women Scientist and Engineers, with no S at the end of “Scientist.”
This was the $150,000 Kao donated after the Corner Bakery meeting. The money had come from Navatek’s account, not Kao’s, violating a ban on government contractors making donations.
The center suspected the society was not a real group but a pass-through to hide the identity of a major political donor. It filed a complaint with the Federal Election Commission. It took only a few days for a Hawaii journalist to discover Kao’s wife’s name on the society’s paperwork, linking the shell company to Navatek.
Inside Navatek, Kao shifted into damage control mode. He spoke to Reed and the super PAC’s lawyer, Cleta Mitchell, and began to hatch a cover-up. In an email released in civil litigation, Mitchell suggested the society make charitable donations — preferably in Maine — which would make it seem like a legitimate nonprofit. “I want to be sure that the LLC proceeds with the ideas we discussed — giving scholarships and recognition to women in engineering, etc.,” wrote Mitchell. “That would help both of us, I think.”
Mitchell added, “We should develop a plan and timetable, so there are some scholarships given over the next several months, and particularly, perhaps in Maine, where the bad press was.”
Mitchell, who later played a major role in Trump’s attempts to overturn the results of the 2020 election, did not respond to requests for comment.
Kao and his team settled on donating scholarships to women in STEM. They offered between $5,000 and $25,000 apiece to state universities where they were angling to win government contracts — that way, the cover-up would benefit them politically, too.
But Navatek’s and Kao’s problems were just beginning. Undeterred by scrutiny from the FEC, Kao defrauded the COVID-era Paycheck Protection Program newly passed by Congress. He inflated Navatek’s payroll to amass loans of $13 million, according to a federal indictment. The Navatek founder, Loui, had long since soured on his chosen successor. This was the final straw. He reported Kao to federal authorities.
“This is not how Navatek behaved or conducted business before I sold the company to Martin Kao,” Loui wrote to ProPublica. He said Navatek was successful before Kao’s ownership and had many sources of government funding. After Kao’s arrest, he added, the company fully cooperated with law enforcement.
Loui has since regained control of the company and renamed it PacMar. He is dedicated to restoring its reputation and ability to execute government contracts, he continued. Loui said he fired employees hired during Kao’s tenure who were “not capable of performing quality, professional engineering and science tasks.”
“The company received no Collins-supported funding after Martin Kao’s arrest, nor should it,” Loui added. “What Martin Kao and his cabal did was wrong.”
On Sept. 30, 2020, law enforcement raided Navatek’s Honolulu offices and arrested Kao for fraud. Federal agents in windbreakers seized his laptop and ordered the company’s IT staff to copy the company’s internal servers.
Navatek’s public flameout attracted the attention of Michelle Ball and Kevin Gounaud, two experienced agents in the FBI’s elite anti-corruption unit. Gounaud was a 20-year FBI veteran who had worked on elaborate undercover operations. Ball had made a name for herself taking on politically sensitive cases. In 2018, she led the investigation into Maria Butina, the Russian agent convicted of infiltrating the National Rifle Association in an attempt to influence the Trump campaign.
The agents began digging through thousands of records for details of Navatek’s lobbying operation, donation strategy and ties to politicians.
They zeroed in on Kao’s relationship with Collins. In a 60-slide presentation agents prepared for prosecutors, they highlighted contributions that Kao and his wife made to the senator in 2018, right before Collins placed the $8 million in research funding into the federal budget. Kao had also given Navatek money to various relatives to donate to Collins in 2019, sending her around $33,000 through these illegal straw donors, the indictment said. Kao’s wife and father did not reply to requests for comment.
Collins christens a Navatek-designed boat at a University of Maine engineering lab in October 2019. (Photo via U.S. Sen. Susan Collins Facebook)
The government charged Kao in two separate cases: one for defrauding the loan program and another for his campaign finance crimes. His love of talking like a wheeler-dealer — including over email — was a gift to investigators. In one email, he all but admitted the scholarships to young women were a diversion. “Whatever… just a pack of bitches getting free $,” he wrote.
In the face of overwhelming evidence, Kao pleaded guilty in both cases in the fall of 2022. Navatek by then was under court-ordered new management. Awaiting sentencing, Kao worked as a line cook at a Cheesecake Factory.
He began meeting with the same FBI agents and prosecutors who brought him down. For the agents, he was a rare witness: a contractor with deep ties to elected officials saying he would speak candidly about how Washington works.
Kao faced nearly a decade in prison. “My world and life imploded,” he would later recall in a letter to the Hawaii U.S. District Court. “I was fooled and foolish enough to believe that the power elected officials wielded, and [were] actively willing to sell to anyone wealthy enough to pay, was….‘smart business.’”
Over the next two years, Kao sat with agents for at least three dayslong interviews. He told them that politicians, Collins in particular, had been willing participants in his scheme. “It takes two to tangle,” he told them.
Taxpayers funded Navatek’s entire political operation, Kao said. “Most companies of our size do not have the resources to endlessly hire expensive lobbyists and make political donations,” he told the FBI. Navatek solved this by using money from government contracts to hire lobbyists and make campaign contributions, according to interviews, court testimony and internal company records. Diverting money from contracts for lobbying and political donations can be illegal.
For their final meeting, in September 2024, Kao handed the FBI the 50-page document detailing Navatek’s dealings with more than a dozen members of Congress and their staff. It was not only a confession but a road map, with the email addresses and phone numbers of people Kao thought agents ought to subpoena.
Last year, Kao was sentenced to 87 months in prison. The judge in his case offered no leniency based on his cooperation with the FBI. Loui is battling Kao in court to recover the millions he contends Kao stole from the company.
Both Scott Reed and Amy Abbott remain in Collins’ inner circle. Abbott is the finance director for her 2026 reelection effort, and Reed again chairs the main Collins super PAC. Abbott, who is married to Collins’ campaign manager, referred questions to the senator’s communications staff. Clark told ProPublica that Abbott and other campaign staff were interviewed by the FBI and that the campaign was never a target of the investigation.
Earlier this year, Kao agreed to meet a ProPublica reporter at the Federal Prison Camp in Yankton, South Dakota, where he is incarcerated. But on two occasions when guards summoned Kao over the intercom, he refused to enter the visitation room. Over email, he said he was no longer willing to meet, citing the ongoing litigation. He declined through his lawyer to respond to detailed questions.
By late 2024, Ball and Gounaud, the FBI agents, had come to believe there was enough evidence to warrant a broader investigation into bribery of members of Congress, according to a memo seen by ProPublica.
Before they could embark on their new mission, however, they became casualties of Trump’s retribution campaign.
Ball and Gounaud worked for the FBI’s elite anti-corruption unit known as CR-15, which specialized in investigating misconduct by elected officials. When Trump retook power, his new FBI director, Kash Patel, purged the unit agent by agent.
Ball was targeted for her work on the special counsel investigation of Trump’s failed bid to overturn the 2020 election. She was fired in October 2025 in a one-page letter stating she had “weaponized” the Justice Department. She is challenging her firing in a lawsuit. Gounaud was pushed out in early 2026. Both agents declined to comment through their attorney.
Trump also targeted the Justice Department attorneys who worked with CR-15. The team, known as the Public Integrity Section, collapsed spectacularly in February 2025 after staff were ordered to drop a case against New York City Mayor Eric Adams, a Trump ally. The unit’s leadership quit en masse. Trump appointees ordered the remaining prosecutors to halt new corruption cases, just months after Kao made his detailed confession.
Before Ball was fired, however, she managed to take a key step forward.
Based on all the evidence, she persuaded her supervisors to approve a new investigation. It centered on South Carolina, one of the states Navatek eyed for a rapid expansion. The FBI had questions about a steak dinner Kao shared with Sen. Lindsey Graham.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Most Florida universities fell in national rankings, per U.S. News & World Report
description: Of the eight Florida universities recognized nationally, five dropped in the U.S. News & World Report’s annual national rankings. Two universities climbed and one stayed steady.  Florida’s two top-25 public universities, University of Florida and Florida State University, each dropped — UF by one spot, from No. 7 last year to No. 8; and FSU […]
text:
Century Tower and University Auditorium on the University of Florida  campus in Gainesville. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Of the eight Florida universities recognized nationally, five dropped in the U.S. News & World Report’s annual national rankings. Two universities climbed and one stayed steady. 
Florida’s two top-25 public universities, University of Florida and Florida State University, each dropped — UF by one spot, from No. 7 last year to No. 8; and FSU by three spots, from No. 21 last year to No. 24.
Staying in the top 50 were Florida International University, which maintained its place at No. 46, and University of South Florida, which dropped three spots from No. 43 to No. 46. FIU is the best university in Florida, according to state Board of Governors metrics. 
Two universities increased their ranks. Florida A&M University leaped 13 places, from No. 92 to No. 79. Florida Atlantic University moved into the double-digits, improving by one spot to No. 99. 
The University of Central Florida dropped a spot, from 57th to 58th, and the University of North Florida dropped from No. 122 to No. 128.
The rankings consider metrics such as graduation rates, retention rates, student debt, a peer assessment, and Pell Grant recipients’ graduation rates.
The top public school was the University of California, Berkeley, followed by the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Michigan; the University of Virginia; and the University of North Carolina. 
Among various rankings throughout the year, U.S. News & World Report’s are perhaps the most widely cited. In walking around some of the campuses, university display their ranking on light-post banners, for example.
Lee Hall on the Florida A&M University campus. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)
FAMU lost a spot among all historically Black colleges and universities, falling from No. 5 to No. 6. It was passed by North Carolina A&T State University. 
That means FAMU lost its seven-year streak as the No. 1 public HBCU in the nation. 
New College of Florida dropped six places in the national liberal arts colleges category, from No. 10 to No. 16, among 39 schools in that category.
In a new category, UF and FSU rank in the Top 10 for “Best Value Schools for In-State Students,” with the Gainesville university ranked No. 3 and the Tallahassee university No. 7.
FIU maintained its No. 1 rank in the nation as the top performer for social mobility.
Some university leaders not happy with Legislature’s enrollment oversight

Rankings are frequently mentioned by university leaders, including by UF Board of Trustees Chair Mori Hosseini, in arguing against increasing the ratio of in-state students who attend state institutions.
During a Board of Governors meeting earlier this month, Hosseini said UF is pursuing a Top Five rank, and to do so will decrease enrollment to maintain the state’s required ratio of in-state students to out-of-state students and maintain higher GPA, SAT, and ACT score expectations.
Florida Gulf Coast University was ranked No. 170 last year, but was not ranked this year.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Amendment 6 could make another Missouri congressional gerrymander much harder
description: The Missouri Supreme Court had barely settled the immediate question of which congressional map is legally in effect before some Republicans began looking ahead to drawing another one. Minutes after the court ruled unanimously against use of a gerrymandered map drawn by Republicans last year, GOP state Sen. Nick Schroer posted “8-0 2027” on social […]
text:
Protesters gather in the Missouri Capitol rotunda Sept. 10, 2025, in opposition to a gerrymandered congressional district map (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).The Missouri Supreme Court had barely settled the immediate question of which congressional map is legally in effect before some Republicans began looking ahead to drawing another one.
Minutes after the court ruled unanimously against use of a gerrymandered map drawn by Republicans last year, GOP state Sen. Nick Schroer posted “8-0 2027” on social media and later said his caucus would discuss “implementing an eight-zero map” in the next couple of years. Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said in a radio interview that he could “most certainly” see lawmakers revisiting congressional redistricting in the 2027 legislative session.
But two measures on the Nov. 3 ballot could make another mid-decade redraw extraordinarily difficult — and potentially complicate Missouri’s redistricting fights for years to come.
If voters reject Proposition A, the congressional boundaries enacted in 2022 would remain in place. And if they also approve Amendment 6, lawmakers could face an 80% threshold in both the House and Senate, as well as another statewide vote, before changing the map again prior to the 2030 census.
Travis Crum, a Washington University law professor who specializes in election law and redistricting, said he believes Amendment 6 would require lawmakers to clear the 80% threshold if they attempted another redraw for the 2028 or 2030 elections.
“A new map would be viewed as similar in effect to the map that was rejected,” Crum said, “and so therefore the 80% requirement would apply.”
Asked specifically about Republicans passing an 8-0 map, or a different 7-1 map that targeted St. Louis instead of Kansas City, Crum said he believed those scenarios would fall under Amendment 6.
The unusual intersection of the two ballot measures stems from the Missouri Supreme Court’s Sept. 3 rulings putting both before voters. The court found that opponents of the 2025 congressional map gathered enough signatures to force a referendum and separately ordered Amendment 6 onto the ballot.
The immediate fight over which map will be used in November remains unresolved. On Monday, the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Missouri must use the 2025 map, but put its decision on hold until Sept. 28 to give opponents time to seek relief from the U.S. Supreme Court.
Election officials are continuing for now under the 2022 map.
Appeals court backs Missouri’s gerrymandered map, but decision is put on hold

One provision of Amendment 6 says the legislature could not pass, propose or refer a law or constitutional amendment “similar in effect” to a law voters rejected through referendum unless at least 80% of both the House and Senate agree to send the proposal back to voters.
That is a high bar even for Missouri’s Republican supermajority. Republicans won 111 of 163 House seats in 2024 and hold 24 of 34 Senate seats going into the election. 
Clearing 80% in both chambers would require Democratic votes.
Hoskins, who opposes Amendment 6, argues its impact would reach far beyond redistricting.
“If Amendment 6 passed,” he said in an email to The Independent, “it will basically cut our legislature off at the knees as far as being able to pass laws to reduce crime and cut taxes.”
Allen Rostron, a constitutional law professor at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, said an effort by lawmakers simply to reenact the gerrymandered map before the census, if it were rejected by voters, would be the kind of scenario most likely to trigger Amendment 6’s 80% threshold.
“That would seem like the General Assembly would be ignoring the spirit of what the voters decided,” Rostron said, “and it might be more tempting to interpret Amendment 6 as being meant to prevent that.”
Exactly what counts as “similar in effect,” however, is not defined in the amendment. A lawsuit would likely follow any new redistricting effort, leaving a state judge — and ultimately the Missouri Supreme Court — to interpret the new constitutional language.
The picture gets murkier after the 2030 census.
A literal reading of the amendment, Rostron said, could support the argument that even a future post-census map similar to the rejected 2025 plan would require 80% legislative approval and a statewide vote.
But Rostron said he doubts courts would apply Amendment 6 that broadly after the 2030 census.
“I’d lean a little toward doubting that Amendment 6 would be treated as changing what would be required for redistricting in the future, such as after the 2030 census,” he said.
Among the problems with a broader interpretation, Rostron said, is that Amendment 6 includes no expiration date for its protections. If a referendum rejection permanently restricts future legislation that is “similar in effect,” he said, courts could face difficult questions about how long that restriction lasts and how much resemblance is enough to trigger it.
Crum also sees the 2030 census as a potentially important dividing line.
Once new census numbers arrive, he said, population changes and the federal constitutional requirement that congressional districts contain roughly equal populations create a strong argument that Missouri must start over with a new map. In that circumstance, Crum said, Amendment 6’s 80% requirement would be unlikely to apply to the map drawn for the 2032 election.
But he stressed that the question is unsettled and would likely be litigated.
The campaign supporting Amendment 6, called Respect MO Voters, says the restriction is intended to prevent lawmakers from simply overriding a referendum result, not permanently freeze Missouri’s congressional districts.
“Amendment 6 makes it more difficult for politicians to overturn voter-approved or rejected measures,” the campaign said in an emailed statement. “By its very nature, the new census every decade will produce a unique map and enabling legislation. What politicians will have a harder time doing is passing legislation that’s similar to what was rejected by Missourians through a vote of the people on a referendum.”
But Amendment 6 could also raise the stakes of future redistricting referendums after the 2030 census, Crum said.
If lawmakers enact new districts in 2031 and opponents gather enough signatures to force a referendum, the new map could be suspended while voters decide its fate. And if voters ultimately reject it, Amendment 6 would bar lawmakers from passing a similar replacement without 80% support in each chamber and another statewide vote.
In the meantime, even suspending the new map would leave in place districts based on the 2020 census, likely violating the federal requirement that congressional districts contain roughly equal populations.
That could leave Missouri without a legally usable congressional map in time for the 2032 election. Under that scenario, Crum said, “you’re almost certainly going to have a court-drawn map used for 2032.”
Amendment 6’s 80% threshold could make replacing those court-drawn districts more difficult, potentially extending their use beyond 2032.
Lawmakers could try to avoid a referendum by passing the map with an emergency clause, which requires a two-thirds vote in each chamber. That’s what they had to do in 2022, when pandemic-related delays in census data helped push congressional redistricting past candidate filing and left little time before the August primary.
A law genuinely necessary for the “immediate preservation of the public peace, health or safety” is exempt from referendum, though Missouri courts ultimately decide whether that standard is met.
Amendment 6, Crum said, could fundamentally change the calculus surrounding future attempts to redraw congressional districts between censuses.
“The de facto result of all this,” he said, “is that mid-decade redistricting could become much harder in Missouri.”

name: Nevada Current
title: In first election since being appointed, higher ed regent draws challenge from math professor
description: Patrick Villa, a mathematics professor at the College of Southern Nevada, will face higher education Regent Jennifer McGrath, the incumbent who was appointed to the seat in 2025, during the upcoming general election.  No candidate running for Nevada System of Higher Education District 2 won more than 50% of the vote in the June primary […]
text:
Jennifer McGrath, Patrick Villa. (Candidate photos)Patrick Villa, a mathematics professor at the College of Southern Nevada, will face higher education Regent Jennifer McGrath, the incumbent who was appointed to the seat in 2025, during the upcoming general election. 
No candidate running for Nevada System of Higher Education District 2 won more than 50% of the vote in the June primary election resulting in the top two facing off again in November. 
McGrath came close, garnering roughly 49% of the vote while Villa, one of three candidates who challenged her, received about 25% of the vote.
The Southern Nevada district covers areas of the central Las Vegas Valley as far south as Spring Valley and as far north as Centennial Hills. 
Villa has been a math professor at CSN for 22 years, was chair of the Department of Mathematics for six years, and previously served as the CSN Faculty Senate Chair in 2024.
It’s his perspective working in higher education, he said, that he thinks the board could use. 
“I feel I know what’s best for students, for faculty, and for staff,” he said, adding he knows firsthand  “what makes a quality education and what changes we can make.”
“Being here on the ground and being a Nevadan for this many years is what I feel I can offer versus my opponent or some other board members,” he said. 
McGrath didn’t respond to requests to be interviewed. She also didn’t respond to requests for comment ahead of the primary election.
NSHE regents had previously served six year terms but 2023 legislation decreased it to four years. The legislation also mandates whoever wins the election will serve a two-year term before the seat reverts to a four-year cycle.
Villa had previously considered running to become a regent but didn’t want to challenge former regent Lois Tarkanian, who was elected to the seat in 2020.
After Tarkanian died in 2024, McGrath, an attorney, was appointed to fill the seat in 2025 by Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. 
As an attorney McGrath represented more than 300 women who claimed they were sexually abused by University of California, Los Angeles gynecologist Dr. James Heaps. UCLA settled and agreed to pay the victims $375 million in 2022.
Serving as a senate faculty chair, Villa has had the opportunity to present to the board on various occasions. At times, he said he grew frustrated watching the board misunderstand aspects of higher education or even sometimes the votes they were taking. 
Though the board already has a current professor, Jeffery Downs, serving as a regent, Villa thinks his perspective as a faculty member is often dismissed by others on the board.
There have been times, Villa added, when the board has not only dismissed the views and concerns of other faculty members, but disregarded the opinions of students who testify during public comment. 
“I just think we owe it to them to hear them out,” he said. “We’ve all seen it where somebody gets cut off, or someone’s told to hurry up, or they cut public comment, or they just say, ‘okay, we’re done talking about this.”
The election comes months after the regents approved a measure to increase tuition over the next three years by 12% for universities and upper-division courses at community colleges.
McGrath voted for the increase. 
Villa thought the proposal was premature. 
“At some point we may have no choice, but at this point, I felt like that was really rushed, and they didn’t properly consider alternatives,” he said of the proposal to hike tuition. 
Part of the problem is that higher education isn’t funded to the degree it should be by the state, he said
“The NSHE budget may have increased every biennium, but (as a) percent of the state budget has drastically gone down every year, so it doesn’t rise with other projects,” Villa said. 
In the meantime, NSHE could do more to deal with revenue gaps by tackling budget redundancies and audit wasteful spending, he said. 
“I want to show (the state) we are not wasting and that we’re efficient with the money,” he said, adding maybe that would lead lawmakers to “consider funding us more because you see we’re doing better with the money that you’re giving us.”

 Catching Our Eye

• Attorney deserts. Ideastream’s Amanda Pirani reports, “In rural Ohio, it’s getting harder to find lawyers for people who can’t afford one.”
In between juggling a growing caseload, Ashland Municipal Court Judge John Good spends a lot of his time trying to find lawyers. He said it’s time he doesn’t have to spare.
“I need to be working on other cases that I have, but I gotta find a lawyer to represent this lady,” he said referring to a case on his docket.
A declining number of local attorneys in the county means Good is down to two people who will serve as court appointed counsel.
• Everybody who shares the blame. In a Cleveland.com opinion column, Brent Larkin writes, “Disgustingly willing partners in Trump’s lethal overreach have been many.”
In an age of Donald Trump’s tyranny, we are surrounded by sellouts.
Millions of Americans now believe that. In his tremendous new book, “Profiles in Cowardice,” veteran journalist Jacob Weisberg goes a way towards proving it.
The book focuses on some of the many so-called leaders Weisberg describes as “the weak and the too willing,” those “who have betrayed their most important civic responsibilities” by capitulating to President Trump’s authoritarian ways.
As Weisberg notes, many in politics, business, the law and education fit that description. His book, labeled “valuable and dauntless” by The New York Times, focuses on a select few. Among this group are Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, former Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos, Sen. Mitch McConnell, journalist Megyn Kelly and former President George W. Bush.
• The rich. The Cincinnati Enquirer’s Haadiza Ogwude reports, “Ramaswamy could become second-richest U.S. governor ever, Forbes says.”
Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy could become the third-richest elected official if elected later this year, according to Forbes.
If Ramaswamy wins Ohio’s 2026 gubernatorial election in November, the 41-year-old businessman-turned-politician would become the nation’s second-richest governor and third-wealthiest elected official, wrote the global media company known for its business and finance reporting.
Per the Sept. 20 report, Ramaswamy, whose net worth Forbes estimates at $2.3 billion, would rank behind only President Donald Trump, worth an estimated $7 billion, and Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker, whose fortune is estimated at $4.2 billion.
• AI and the future of humanity. The Columbus Dispatch’s Samantha Hendrickson reports, “Is AI a threat? What Ohio experts say about worrying AI revelations.”
AI developers and executives are warning of potential threats to humanity from the rapidly evolving technology. Some experts are unsurprised by these warnings, noting researchers have discussed these risks for years.
Proposed solutions include more transparency, stricter regulations and implementing new safety guidelines before such worries come to fruition.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Gun owners challenge NJ restrictions on nonfirearm weapons
description: New Jersey restricts when people can use weapons like knives, slingshots, and pepper spray in public for self-defense. Gun owners are challenging that law in federal court.
text:
New Jersey restricts when people can use weapons like knives, slingshots, and pepper spray in public for self-defense. Gun owners are challenging that law in federal court. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Gun rights advocates have a new target in their crusade to strike down New Jersey’s longstanding prohibitions on weapons, suing Monday to overturn state restrictions on the use of items like knives, stun guns, slingshots, brass knuckles, bear spray, and bats for self-defense.
The Association of New Jersey Rifle & Pistol Clubs, Arizona-based Knife Rights, and four New Jersey gun owners are asking a federal judge to declare the restrictions illegal and unenforceable under the Second Amendment, saying they prevent people from using less-lethal tools than guns for self-defense.
“The Second Amendment protects all common arms not just guns,” attorney Daniel Schmutter wrote in the complaint filed Monday in federal court.
But anything can be a prohibited weapon under New Jersey law, he added.
“A baseball bat, a hammer, a screwdriver, any knife, a box cutter, pepper spray, bear spray, a stick, anything,” Schmutter wrote. “And if you happen to have a baseball bat in your car but you are not on your way to a baseball game, you can be arrested, prosecuted, and imprisoned under New Jersey law.”
The new lawsuit comes four years after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that people have a constitutional right to carry firearms outside their homes, toppling restrictions like New Jersey’s that required gun owners to prove a need to carry arms in public.
Under that decision, known as Bruen, the justices decreed that any gun restrictions had to be rooted in historical traditions that existed when the Second Amendment was ratified in the late 1700s.
At that time, arms were defined as “anything that a man wears for his defence, or takes into his hands, or useth in wrath to cast at or strike another,” Schmutter wrote, citing a 1771 legal dictionary.
“Arms come in many forms, not just guns,” Schmutter wrote. “While the Bruen decision has forced New Jersey to allow the carry of guns for self-defense, New Jersey law still explicitly bans and punishes the carry of common, everyday objects other than firearms specifically for the purpose of self-defense. That flies in the face of Bruen and must change. This case aims to do just that.”
The suit names as defendants Attorney General Jen Davenport and Jeanne Hengemuhle, acting superintendent of the New Jersey State Police.
A spokesman for Davenport’s office, which also oversees the state police, vowed to defend the state against the lawsuit “and do all we can to end violence in our state.”
“New Jersey’s commonsense restrictions on weapons keep our residents safe,” spokesman Mike Symons said.
The named plaintiffs include Wendy Copenhaver of Hammonton and her brother Wayne Viden of Glassboro, who own a gun range in Glassboro; Walter Everard Jr. of Hopatcong, a hunter, retired pipefitter, and Navy veteran; and Salvatore Marsilla of Emerson, who owns an automotive retail store.
The lawsuit is just the latest of more than a dozen gun-rights advocates have filed in recent years to challenge restrictions they say violate the Second Amendment. They also have challenged a law banning guns in places deemed sensitive, a law allowing the state to sue gun manufacturers for creating a “public nuisance,” and state restrictions on large-capacity magazines and certain semiautomatic firearms, among others.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Disability watchdog group says lacking state oversight contributed to deaths of 3 Utahns
description: A watchdog organization accuses Utah of allowing private agencies to serve Utahns with complex needs without enough oversight.
text:
The Capitol in Salt Lake City is pictured on Monday, May 6, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Months after three Utahns with disabilities died in the care of a Utah company, its license has been revoked and a caretaker charged with murder. 
And now a watchdog organization is calling attention to its view of the state’s role in what happened that day in February, when authorities say the group was left alone in a vehicle for hours.
“This tragedy occurred because DHHS (the Utah Department of Health and Human Services) allows high risk providers to serve individuals with complex support needs and large budgets to support those needs without appropriate oversight and accountability,” the Disability Law Center said in a report released Monday. 
Program for Utahns with disabilities loses its license following deaths of 3 clients left in van

The report reiterates criticisms the agency has been raising for more than a decade, said Nate Crippes, the center’s public affairs supervising attorney, in a prepared statement.
“Too often, Utah has prioritized facilities and profits over the wellbeing of Utahns with disabilities, and we, once again, urge State Officials to review our recommendations and make the necessary reforms to protect those in long-term care settings,” Crippes said. 
In its report, titled “Profits Over People,” the center says the department should have known that Safe and Sound Services was a “dangerous provider.” The state agency had been told of problems like physical assaults and failure to provide medical care for injuries prior to the deaths of the three men last winter, the center said. 
The Department of Health and Human Services conducted inspections of the company in the years leading up to the tragedy and found employees worked with clients unsupervised even though they hadn’t done required background checks, among other issues, the report notes. 
But it says those evaluations were either conducted remotely or when no clients were present — giving inspectors little opportunity to talk with clients and see for themselves how the company administered services. Safe and Sound could not be reached at a publicly listed number Monday.
Nate Crippes with the Disability Law Center speaks during a news conference held by the Protect Medicaid Utah Coalition at Sacred Circle Healthcare’s offices in Salt Lake City on July 30, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
After the men’s deaths, the department checked on the company’s residential sites and noted a variety of issues, including a foul smell and no heat or running water in one location, staff admitting to locking residents in a basement at night in another, and employees reporting a resident returned from a day program with a broken tooth, black eyes and scratches on his neck, the report states. 
“These complaints all demonstrate the provider was not using the money appropriated by DHHS to provide even basic utilities or a clean environment,” the report states. “Staffing ratios were dangerously low and insufficient to provide the care the state had contracted for.”
The Department of Health and Human Services did not make its executive director, Tracy Gruber, or any other administrator available for an interview Monday. 
In a prepared, unsigned statement, the department said “the stories outlined in the Disability Law Center’s report weigh heavily on us. When safety is compromised and lives are lost, we feel it deeply. We absolutely agree that taxpayer dollars should be used as intended.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The department said it identified many of the same concerns through an internal review process and in response, it has hired a contractor “to assess and mitigate the risk of abuse, neglect, and exploitation for people with disabilities.” The statement did not identify the contractor. 
Among the other changes the department has made: hiring a new quality assurance administrator, along with four new employees working in oversight and technical assistance. 
Looking forward, it said it’s also exploring ways to keep problematic providers from getting contracts in the first place and to raise the qualifications needed for agencies to serve those with disabilities. 
In Utah’s 3rd District Court, transport driver Isaiah Vaughn Pulu, 26, has not yet entered pleas to three counts of murder in the February deaths of Colton Warren Moser, 25; Mosa’ati Moa, 22; and Tim Jones, 39. An attorney for Pulu has previously said the deaths were a “tragic accident.”
Transport driver charged with murder after 3 Utahns with disabilities died in state custody

Prosecutors allege he drove the men who required round-the-clock supervision — two of them nonverbal — to his home in West Valley City. The men remained in the vehicle while investigators say Pulu went inside to eat and watch television, reporting he left the garage door open, but when he returned about four hours later the door was closed and the men were unconscious. 
He had been reprimanded a month earlier for “client abandonment” after leaving three people unsupervised for a half-hour, prosecutors alleged, without identifying those clients. 
The Disability Law Center report also identified issues in facilities serving other populations, including the Provo Canyon School, a youth residential treatment center that was shut down by the state earlier this year. It laid out a host of recommendations for the state, including requiring service providers to show they can safely care for clients before receiving a license. It also urged the state to bring on more employees helping to oversee such companies and raise their pay.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington’s medication collection program faces hurdles despite success
description: Washington’s program to collect medication so it doesn’t end up in the wrong hands has brought in over 1 million pounds of drugs since 2020, according to a state audit. But it’s still beset with some challenges, like a lack of sites to return unused pills in rural areas, a limited sense of the program’s […]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)Washington’s program to collect medication so it doesn’t end up in the wrong hands has brought in over 1 million pounds of drugs since 2020, according to a state audit.
But it’s still beset with some challenges, like a lack of sites to return unused pills in rural areas, a limited sense of the program’s effectiveness and the recent withdrawal of one of the two companies collecting the drugs in the state, according to the report from Washington’s Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee released this month.
Under this program, drug manufacturers pay companies to collect unused medication, including prescription and over-the-counter drugs, for incineration free of charge to patients. Those two companies have been MED-Project and Inmar, but the latter pulled out at the end of June. 
The state Department of Health collects fees from MED-Project, and previously Inmar, to oversee the program. Inmar’s absence means fewer sites for members of the public to bring in medication and less funding for state oversight. 
The company decided to bow out of Washington “after evaluating the long-term sustainability of the program and determining that the current model was not viable going forward,” said Brian Nightengale, the president of the company’s healthcare division.
Inmar also stopped doing this work in other states, according to auditors. 
Seven counties had similar programs before the statewide version launched six years ago. The goals are to avoid medication misuse, and stop the unused or expired drugs from polluting waterways.
The report comes as the state inches closer to sunsetting the program in 2029, a date the Legislature could extend.
Washington now has more than 400 drug collection sites with secure dropboxes to return unused medication. The number has gone down significantly in recent years with the closures of numerous Bartell Drugs and Rite Aid locations. 
Not everywhere in Washington has these kiosks. Over 100 cities and towns don’t meet requirements to have one per 50,000 residents, according to data from February. These are mostly small towns with just a few thousand residents or less. For example, in places with under 1,000 people, 91% don’t meet the kiosk requirement. In Seattle, on the other hand, there are more than 40 kiosks.
The average driving time from the city center to the nearest kiosk in places that have them is five minutes, according to the audit. But it’s 25 minutes in many of these small communities.
Only Washington’s two smallest counties, Columbia and Garfield counties, don’t have any drop-off sites. All counties have a mail option to allow residents to send medication directly to a disposal site with prepaid envelopes. Almost all of the drugs have been returned via kiosk. This is common across states with similar programs, said Carly Bartz-Overman, who runs the office in the Department of Health that oversees this initiative.
State lawmakers suggested increasing mail medication returns to get more drugs collected.
“With so many of our communities facing pharmacy deserts,” said Rep. Gerry Pollet, D-Seattle, “it seems like the likelihood of improving performance from kiosks is pretty low compared to the potential for improving performance through mailers.”
Bartz-Overman said she was also surprised the mail isn’t used more often to return pills but doesn’t believe people will start using that option more.
State law requires some smaller communities to have a dropbox even if there isn’t an eligible site for one. Federal law only allows them in places like pharmacies, hospitals and police stations, but eligible sites don’t have to participate under state law.
“Overall, the current program requirements may not be achievable,” Sydney Romero, a research analyst with the committee, said in a hearing on the audit last week. She noted similar programs elsewhere have less restrictive mandates.
Washington’s requirement makes it hard for state officials to provide oversight, as they don’t have a way to recognize progress toward complying with an unreachable benchmark, according to the audit.
It’s also been difficult for the Department of Health to measure the program’s efficiency and cost effectiveness, and the lack of data makes it harder to know what to prioritize.
No data is collected on which types of drugs are collected.
To assess the program’s success, the Legislature required three separate evaluations, but all are incomplete, according to auditors.
The audit recommends the Legislature continue the program past 2029 with changes to address these challenges.
“We look forward to working with the Legislature and operator on determining what measures and goals the department should put in place to ensure the program continues to serve Washington residents,” Bartz-Overman said.
Earlier this year, auditors recommended lawmakers amend how the program is funded, because otherwise, health officials warn, the program may not have the money to support its two full-time staffers. Almost every year, expenditures have surpassed revenue. The Department of Health has needed to use other money and an infusion from the Legislature to close that gap, according to the audit.
But last fiscal year, the program’s revenue was $533,000 from the operators. The Department of Health spent $405,000. Estimated revenue this year is expected to be under $300,000 with Inmar’s departure.
Bartz-Overman said she hopes the state will revamp the fee structure to “keep our program whole.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Believe what you are seeing and feeling: The climate is changing
description: Back in 1990, I attended a talk by Jim Hansen, a lead climate modeler and director of the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies. He concluded that the models were working well and could now reasonably predict global warming trends. An audience member asked when the public would believe the results of climate modeling. My […]
text:
A hot hazy day in Minneapolis, July 15, 2026. Wildfire smoke has moved south from fires in northeastern Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Back in 1990, I attended a talk by Jim Hansen, a lead climate modeler and director of the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies. He concluded that the models were working well and could now reasonably predict global warming trends. An audience member asked when the public would believe the results of climate modeling. My recollection is that his response was “never,” before adding, “They won’t believe it until they personally experience it.” 
Thirty-six years later, nearly all climate scientists believe that climate warming has occurred as the result of human activities, but do you see it and feel it, plainly? Do you believe it?
Even before the multiple climate crises of 2026, majorities of Minnesotans surveyed in 2025 agreed “that global warming is caused mostly by human activities,” and they were “somewhat or very worried about global warming.” Majorities of Minnesotans also responded that global warming affects sea levels, flooding, droughts, wildfires and extreme heat.
In the past few years, the soot has hit the fan. Minnesota has been smothered by smoke produced by wildfires in Canada and the western U.S. for several years. Smoke from the 2026 Canadian wildfires caused the air quality index in Grand Portage to reach the highest level ever recorded in Minnesota (800, on June 2). For young children and Minnesotans with respiratory diseases — including 5% with COPD and 8% with asthma — this is a crisis. Many who are less vulnerable still suffered for our affected friends and families. Have you seen the smoke? Have you heard the coughing and wheezing? Did you take someone to an emergency room? Did you buy an air filtration device? 
Do you think wildfires in recent years have become more severe because of climate warming? Older readers: Do you remember smoke events as severe as our recent events 20 or 50 years ago? Probably not. More than half of the total acres burned by wildfires in the US over the past 41 years occurred in the most recent 15 years. The trend is less clear in Canada, but the area of wildfires in the memorable 2023 season was more than twice as high as any prior year since 1983.  
In Europe, the wildfire situation this year was far worse. As of mid-July, an estimated 300,000 people had been evacuated from wildfire areas. An estimated 440 deaths were attributed to the fire, either directly or indirectly.  
Do you remember the vivid photos of the 2025 Los Angeles area fire? It forced the evacuation of 200,000 people and destroyed 17,000 homes and businesses. Minnesota’s wildfires earlier this year forced “only” 8,000 evacuations because the 2026 wildfires were in sparsely populated areas. But what about future years? Perhaps in outer ring suburbs on the edge of combustible wildlands? Many Minnesotans grew up learning about the 1893 Hinkley fire, which virtually destroyed the city and killed more than 400. 
Extreme heat in Europe has also caused a surge of deaths in recent years, mostly in cities. Heat waves in 2025 caused 24,400 estimated heat deaths, with climate change being responsible for 16,500 of these. 
Should this be a cautionary tale for Minnesota? Maybe. Throughout Minnesota, the number of days per year with a heat index (a measure of how heat feels) over 90 increased between the periods 1986-1995 and 2016-2025. For example, in Hennepin County, it went from 18 days to 30 days. Several counties in southern Minnesota now have 35 days with heat indexes over 90. Have you felt the summers get hotter in recent years? Do you avoid going out for a walk on these hot days? Do you start to feel overheated doing a half hour of light gardening? Are your kids’ soccer games being canceled? Remember when the Twin Cities marathon was canceled in 2023? 
The high death rate during Europe’s 2025 heat wave occurred in part because most Europeans do not have air conditioning, which would have prevented many of these deaths. In contrast, about 95% of Minnesotans have air conditioning. This gives us a false sense of security — our power supply could be interrupted at the time it is most needed. Would some of our most vulnerable Minnesotans, especially the very young and very old, die in a heat wave, as they did in Europe? Should we be upgrading our electrical grid to improve its reliability?
Is this the year that the soot hit the fan? Thirty-six years after Hansen’s talk, have our eyes and ears and our experiences finally shown us that climate warming is very real and very dangerous, even in Minnesota?

name: Mississippi Today
title: Survey ordered by Gov. Reeves shows many Mississippi agencies are embracing AI use
description: Cover art of Mississippi Agency AI Inventory survey report.
text:
As Mississippi’s state government agencies embrace artificial intelligence, or AI, in their work, officials say human oversight remains essential.
Mississippi defines AI in part as “a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments.“
In January 2025, Gov. Tate Reeves issued an executive order directing the Mississippi Department of Information Technology Services to survey and evaluate state agencies’ use of AI and develop AI use policy recommendations. For the survey, called the Mississippi State Agency AI Inventory, each state agency had to submit either a standardized report listing current and potential AI use or a letter stating no plans to use any. 
Out of 98 entities that responded, a little over half were using or planning to use AI. 
The Mississippi Department of Transportation, for instance, is working on AI projects for querying crash data, automating quality control across documentation and more.
The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality uses Grammarly, ChatGPT, Microsoft CoPilot and other programs for things such as research, drafting emails and calculations. The agency also uses several cybersecurity services, including Rubrik, Proofpoint and Silversky.
A cumulative total of 243 active or planned AI projects were reported across 44 agencies. The majority of AI projects, or 82%, were rated low-risk, and 69.5% relied solely on human decision making.

MDOT and MDEQ are among the five agencies that, when combined, account for a significant amount of AI usage across all state agencies, or 35%. The other three are the Department of Employment Security, the Department of Information Technology Services and the Mississippi Arts Commission.

Mississippi Today made a public records request for the completed inventory surveys from the these five agencies, and asked further questions about their AI use. 
ITS did not fulfill the public records request, citing an exception in the executive order. The Department of Employment Security and the Arts Commission provided their completed surveys, but did not respond to detailed questions. 
“Our annual AI inventory is designed to capture a point-in-time snapshot during the second quarter of each calendar year,” explained ITS chief strategy officer Stephanie Hedgepeth. “We then analyze the data during the third quarter, with the report targeted for publication on the ITS website early in the fourth quarter.”
Stephanie Hedgepeth, chief strategy officer for the Mississippi Department of Information Technology Services at MDITS headquarters, Thursday, March 19, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Hedgepeth said that while AI isn’t new, what is new is how accessible it’s become because of generative AI tools. Generative AI is an advanced form of AI that can create new content.
She, as well as leaders and spokespeople for the departments of Environmental Quality and Transportation, emphasized that AI is a tool to assist humans, not replace them. 
Paul Katool, MDOT’s deputy director of public affairs, explained that AI use is rapidly growing across the agency. 
“It enhances efficiency, enabling our existing staff to complete more work – often faster – without increasing headcount or overall labor costs,” he said.
“The reality is that we have fewer staff than we have ever had historically,” said Chris Wells, the Department of Environmental Quality’s executive director. At the same time, their workload has arguably increased. 
A 2025 national report found that MDEQ’s staff decreased by 17% between 2010 and 2024, and funding decreased by 71% in the same time frame. Records show that the agency’s total appropriations, including state funding and fees collected for services, dropped by over a quarter between fiscal year 2011 and fiscal year 2025.
Though most AI projects took a careful approach, the report found that governance hasn’t kept pace with adoption. The findings include recommendations for improvement, such as stronger protections for confidential data and communication, stronger accessibility and mitigating bias and misinformation for public-facing AI tools.
“Each agency is responsible for governing its use of AI in accordance with applicable laws, regulations, policies and requirements,” wrote Hedgepeth in an email.
ITS adopted the Acceptable Use Policy for Artificial Intelligence, which is meant to be a resource for state agencies to create their own AI policies.
The Mississippi Artificial Intelligence Regulation Task Force was established in 2025 to analyze all things related to regulating AI in Mississippi until 2027, and to report its findings and recommendations to the state Legislature annually. One of the recommendations the task force adopted was that state agencies disclose to citizens when they are engaging with an AI system.
The Department of Transportation issued its AI use policy in February. The Department of Environmental Quality and the Arts Commission are still developing theirs. 
Even without an AI policy, agencies still have rules. For the tools identified in their AI inventory report, employees at the Department of Environmental Quality are responsible for reviewing AI-generated information before using it. AI is not used to make decisions, either. The Arts Commission recently started requiring grant applications to disclose AI use.
Mississippi currently has a handful of AI laws, but the attorney general’s office determined that Mississippi has no overarching AI framework, according to the state’s Artificial Intelligence Regulation task force’s report.
Last year, President Donald Trump issued an executive order seeking to limit states’ ability to regulate AI. 
Republican Sen. Bart Williams of Starkville, co-chair of the Artificial Intelligence Regulation task force and chair of the Mississippi Senate Technology Committee, doesn’t believe the president’s executive order will impact AI regulation in Mississippi.
“I think we’re gonna look at what’s best for our citizens and what we need to do for them,” he said.
Williams said AI will definitely be a topic of conversation in the 2027 legislative session. Many legislators are concerned about AI as it relates to children’s safety online and the workforce. However, he doesn’t know if it will be regulated.
The task force’s panelists recommended taking a “wait and see” approach. The report states the AG’s office recommended monitoring how the order impacts existing computer-related state laws that do not mention AI specifically.
Kollin Napier is chief AI officer of the Mississippi Artificial Intelligence Network, the nation’s first statewide AI initiative. MAIN is in partnership with ITS to spearhead usage and adoption. It does not have a regulatory role.
Napier spoke about the importance of governance.     
“That comes as acceptable use. It comes as a statewide framework, structured pilots and so much more. So that way, you don’t have agencies just sort of experimenting in the dark, so to speak,” he said.
The AI Innovation Hub, established by ITS, Amazon Web Services and MAIN, has student teams work on solving AI use cases for state agencies. The teams presented their work at a showcase in May. 
Napier said the return-on-investment for the innovation hub and MAIN’s workforce development efforts are “tremendous.”
Mississippi governmental agencies are part of a growing trend. AI use is prevalent in governmental agencies across the country.
A 2024 survey found that 51% of state, local and federal government employees who responded used AI daily or several times a week. In a Google Public Sector survey of 250 federal IT professionals, 90% said their agencies were already using or planning to use AI.  
Federal agencies are using AI for a variety of projects, from facial recognition systems to helping the public search through historical records.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri’s ‘unprecedented’ budget vote leaves schools around Kansas City in the lurch
description: School districts around Kansas City know it’s possible, maybe even likely, that Missouri’s governor and lawmakers will choose to not fully fund public schools next year. The state’s foundation formula, the calculation of how much money schools should receive, is enshrined in law. That doesn’t mean lawmakers always choose to provide the full formula amount, [[...]
text:
A student at Ingels Elementary School in the Hickman Mills School District. Superintendent Dennis Carpenter said he’s disappointed by the Missouri State Board of Education’s decision not to request full funding for schools (Vaughn Wheat/The Beacon).School districts around Kansas City know it’s possible, maybe even likely, that Missouri’s governor and lawmakers will choose to not fully fund public schools next year.
The state’s foundation formula, the calculation of how much money schools should receive, is enshrined in law. That doesn’t mean lawmakers always choose to provide the full formula amount, especially when money is tight. The most recent statewide school budget fell $190 million short.
Still, some local and statewide education leaders were caught off guard when the Missouri State Board of Education at its Sept. 15 meeting approved a budget request that didn’t even ask for the full amount required to fund the formula.
They said the decision is unprecedented, to their knowledge, and undersells how much money schools need according to the framework that the legislature itself created. 
Instead, the state school board’s request asks the governor and the legislature to keep foundation formula funding flat compared to the current year’s already underfunded budget. That means that in the coming fiscal year, state school funding would fall more than $270 million under what is laid out in state law. 
Hickman Mills Superintendent Dennis Carpenter said he’s disappointed by the board’s decision, suggesting the move gives lawmakers an easy pass to continue depriving Missouri schools of deeply needed resources.
It “makes it more likely that we’ll get less than we received last year, because we remove the ability to have a strong conversation about the foundation formula not simply being something that’s on a spreadsheet,” he said. “It represents what the state determined was necessary to effectively educate children.”
The latest decision is just one way school funding is “under assault” at the local, state and federal levels, Carpenter said.
Jackson County schools are preparing for property tax refunds to cut millions of dollars out of their budgets, and schools have seen federal funding delayed, cut or threatened.
“We keep asking the system to do more with less,” Carpenter said. “At some point, the system can’t function at a level that we all can be proud of.”
 The board’s discussion

The decision came after the state board voted 4-4 on a budget recommendation that did include full foundation formula funding. The tie meant the proposal did not pass.
Democrats Jordan Bradberry and Vincent Schoemehl Jr., Republican Kerry Casey and Jon Otto, an independent, voted in favor of full funding. Republicans Kenneth “Brooks” Miller Jr., Michael Matousek and Robbie Myers, along with independent Gretchen Shull, voted no.
The board also has a new nonvoting member, Mike McDonald, who is a math teacher in the Park Hill School District.
Board members are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Missouri Senate. Their political affiliations are reported because no more than four may belong to the same party.
Matousek, a member from Kansas City, called for the board to disregard the funding formula, arguing that the department shouldn’t request a funding increase at all while it lacks a strategic plan and a permanent commissioner.
“I think we’re asking for a lot of money without a real justification for spending it,” he said.
“This board, this department, has a credibility problem, and I think sending over a nine-plus billion dollar budget to people who make these decisions doesn’t help.”
He said that while state law requires the department to calculate the full foundation formula amount, it doesn’t require that the budget request match.
“I think we’re asking for money that doesn’t exist,” he said, alluding to a tightening state budget.
In June, Missouri Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick warned that the state’s general revenue surplus is being depleted.
Casey said it isn’t the board’s role to determine whether funding is available. That’s the responsibility of the state’s legislative and executive branches.
“It’s our job to present the need,” she said. The governor and legislature “are the ones to determine how that works in the scheme of all of the bigger priorities within the budget. That is not our job.”
After the tie vote, the board reached a compromise to leave in budget requests tied to new initiatives ordered by Gov. Mike Kehoe, the legislature or the courts. Those include a plan to grade public schools and districts on an A-to-F scale, new antisemitism reporting requirements and increased oversight of athletics.
It approved a nearly $4.3 billion request for the foundation formula, the same as formula spending in fiscal year 2027. That’s $270 million less than full funding for the formula.
McDonald clarified that the only change from the budget the board voted down was a cut to school budgets.
“I guess my concern is that the easiest place to cut is from the funding of the districts,” he said.
 Local impact

Carpenter, whose south Kansas City district is digging itself out of a financial hole and fighting to earn full accreditation, said it’s striking that the board voted to underfund schools shortly after approving a framework to grade them on an A-to-F scale.
“I think it’s pretty interesting that we literally up the ante on accountability,” he said, “and we reduce the ante on the resources necessary to be successful.”
The foundation formula isn’t just his personal opinion about how much schools should receive, Carpenter said. “The state made that determination, and now we’ve gotten so comfortable with underfunding it that we’re now comfortable for not even asking for full funding.”
In the Lee’s Summit School District, about 28% of funding comes from the state, said Chad Hertzog, assistant superintendent of business services. 
When state funding lags, the district has to rely even more on local funding, he said, including potentially raising residents’ property taxes. Once the district hits the tax rate ceiling set by voters, it has to reduce expenses such as by cutting supplies, services and staff.
The district could also ask taxpayers to raise the tax ceiling.
“It’s not (an option) that we like to consider because again, we’re asking our local voters to ultimately fund shortfalls at the state level at even a higher rate than they already are,” he said.
Hertzog said the district’s most pressing problem is Jackson County property taxes, but state funding reductions add to budget concerns. KCUR reports that the district is anticipating a revenue reduction of $7 million to $10 million this year after it reduced the tax rate in 2023 in response to growing property assessments.
The county has since determined that those assessments were handled incorrectly and is planning to refund money to taxpayers, cutting into schools’ revenue.
Hertzog said the difference between full formula funding from the state and what the district is actually receiving is nearly $7 million. The district’s overall operating budget is more than $280 million.
Carter Taylor, a Kansas City Public Schools elementary teacher and legislative chair of the Kansas City Federation of Teachers union, said the state board’s decision felt in line with “the current era in Missouri politics.”
“This is just another move that says public education doesn’t deserve support or funding,” she said. “It is another not-so-subtle attempt to say that we shouldn’t really exist.”
School districts’ percentage of state funding varies widely depending on factors such as the value of property that can be taxed locally. KCPS is one district that receives relatively little from the state, but Taylor said that every dollar counts.
“We take the least, and we try so hard to put in the most, but there’s only so much that a good teacher can do,” she said.
Matt Michelson, director of education policy for the Missouri State Teachers Association, said that even flat funding represents a practical decrease for schools as costs rise.
“I think all of us see in our daily lives everything is getting more expensive,” he said. Schools are “not immune to those increases in costs that everyone’s experienced over the last year,” including raises for teachers who also experience the effects of inflation.
Sarah Laub, a parent of two in the Blue Springs School District, said she’s concerned that state funding decisions could lead to her kids losing teachers and extracurricular activities. She’s also worried rural school districts — like the one she left in search of more educational opportunities for her kids in a better-funded district — could be hit the hardest.
Laub was referred to The Beacon by the Will of the People PAC, which aims to flip Missouri legislative seats. She also worked to oppose Amendment 5 with Parents for Missouri Public Schools based on its predicted impact on school funding.
She said the board’s decision should be seen in the context of a political climate where Kehoe and the legislature haven’t supported full school funding.
“It sounds like the board made their decision to not request that funding, not based on the belief that the schools don’t need it, but instead based on the belief that they no longer have faith that the lawmakers would listen to them or provide it,” she said.
But she thinks the board’s decision could contribute to lower school funding.
“I am concerned that this has created a vicious cycle where now the legislature will use it as a reason to cut even more funds,” she said.
 The message to lawmakers and the public

Lindsey Baker, research director with the Missouri Budget Project, a center-left think tank, said there are plenty of historical examples of fully funding the state’s formula and the lack of full funding. But whatever the ultimate outcome, the education department always requested full funding from lawmakers.
“This is not something I have ever seen, certainly, and I’ve talked to many other people who have been around a lot longer than I have, who have never seen this before either,” Baker said.
“I think this is an indication that this is going to be a very painful budget year.”
Baker attributed state budget issues to years of tax cuts that she said have caused a “serious revenue problem.”
The board’s decision could have a mixed reception in the legislature, said Caitlin Whaley, senior director of advocacy for the Missouri School Boards’ Association (MSBA). Those against higher school funding might use it to their advantage, while others won’t be pleased.
“It certainly gives legislators something to hang their hat on if they can say, ‘Well, why should we fully fund it if the very board that we confirmed to oversee public education doesn’t think this funding is necessary?’” she said.
But “there are absolutely supporters of public education in the legislature,” she said, “that will now have a decidedly more negative view of the state board.”
Whaley said lawmakers shouldn’t be surprised by increased costs because the legislature had projections of the financial impact when they voted on the changes that have caused some of the increases to the foundation formula. Those changes include incentives for five-day school weeks and relying less on attendance when computing enrollment for funding purposes.
Attendance-based calculations of enrollment tend to penalize schools that have higher poverty rates.
A task force is working on a proposal to modernize Missouri’s school funding formula, which could further increase the cost of the formula.
Whaley said that as the budget process continues, MSBA will highlight stories of school districts that are facing budget challenges and emphasize that the state should fulfill its commitments.
“If we’re going to pass legislation that says we’re going to pay districts money, that we need to, as a state, be responsible for those decisions that are made,” she said.
In an emailed news release, Missouri Association of School Administrators Executive Director Mark Penny also criticized the board decision.
“This is a failure of the board’s most basic responsibility: advocating for Missouri’s public schools and the students they serve,” the statement read in part. “The board’s job is to tell the governor and the General Assembly what our schools need. Instead, this board has made the unprecedented choice to recommend that public schools remain underfunded, an action that reflects a board increasingly hostile to public education.”
Michelson said he’s not sure how legislators will respond, but he sees the recommendation as a poor start to the budget process.
“It sends a horrible message to our educators, our kids and our communities that the state board doesn’t believe that it’s necessary to even ask the legislature to fully fund our schools,” Michelson said.
This article first appeared on Beacon: Kansas City and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.

name: WyoFile
title: Barrasso loves attention from the media, but not protecting press freedoms
description:
Wyoming’s U.S. senator backs President Trump’s ban  on news outlets that say negative things about administration, columnist Kerry Drake writes.
The post Barrasso loves attention from the media, but not protecting press freedoms appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming’s senior U.S. Sen. John Barrasso had a golden opportunity to defend the constitutionally protected freedom of the press Sunday. Instead, he predictably launched into a feeble defense of President Donald Trump’s White House ban on three news organizations that have criticized him.

Opinion

In an interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Barrasso compared Trump’s vindictive action against CNN, MS NOW and Politico to the president being banned from Twitter (now X) and Facebook during his first term. 
“I didn’t see people come to his defense,” the senator said. “So, it goes both ways.”
I can’t believe Barrasso doesn’t recognize the difference between private corporations, which have the right to enforce their own rules for participating on their social media platforms, and the First Amendment’s mandate to allow the media to report the news without interference from the federal government.
Of course, he knows better. But Barrasso apparently views his job as the Senate’s majority whip, the chamber’s No. 2 leadership position, to defend whatever nonsense the president spouts no matter how much it lays waste to the guarantees enshrined in the Bill of Rights.
Throughout his 19 years in the Senate, Barrasso has been a frequent guest on cable TV news shows, including CNN and MS NOW (formerly MSNBC), whenever he wanted to express his views to a national audience. That usually included sticking it to the Democratic administrations of former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, and bashing Trump’s critics.
It’s no secret to his constituents that one of Barrasso’s top priorities seems to be getting in front of TV cameras and next to powerful politicians. While climbing the GOP Senate leadership ladder, he always hovered over the shoulder of then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell at news conferences.
“We all respect and value the freedom of the press, it’s in the Constitution,” Barrasso told NBC’s Kristen Welker, but it was just lip service from a politician who has adroitly used the media to get free air time.
If Barrasso truly values a free press, why won’t he even criticize Trump’s personal war against members of the media, whom he disturbingly calls “the enemy of the people?”
If Barrasso truly values a free press, why won’t he call out the president for threatening last Friday to revoke the White House press credentials of other news organizations as he sees fit, creating a climate of fear and intimidation?
“The press has an obligation to report fairly,” Barrasso told Welker. “The president doesn’t see it happening that way.”
No, Trump just brands everything that doesn’t show him in a favorable light as “fake news.” He has a particularly cruel way of trying to humiliate women reporters who are just doing their jobs when they ask Trump valid questions.
Like Welker, who saw Trump storm off her “Meet the Press” set in June when she asked a follow-up question after the president made an unsubstantiated claim about U.S. elections being rigged.
Trump called her “either crooked or stupid.”
When Bloomberg’s Catherine Lucey asked about the release of files related to Jeffrey Epstein, the president of the United States said, “Quiet, piggy.” Katie Rogers of The New York Times wrote an article about Trump’s age and health — perfectly reasonable topics about an 80-year-old commander-in-chief — and Trump lashed out, calling her a “third-rate reporter who is ugly, both inside and out.”
This is the guy Barrasso trusts to assess the fairness of journalists? And decide which news organizations have the right to ask him questions?
Trump has played this game of yanking White House media credentials before, and lost. After a contentious exchange at a news conference in 2018, the president revoked CNN correspondent Jim Acosta’s press pass to the White House grounds. CNN sued, and a Trump-appointed judge overturned the restriction.
“What’s going on here is a flagrant violation of the First Amendment,” Connor Fitzpatrick of the free speech advocacy group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expressions told The Washington Times. “The precedent on this point is clear.” 
Barrasso was so at a loss for ammunition to back his argument on NBC, he resorted to pulling a 2020 campaign trope out of the mud: Hunter Biden’s laptop.
“When you take a look at this president, and you take a look at the Hunter Biden laptop,” he said, appearing confused, “if you want to really get into things where the press ignored the reality for a long period of time, said it was a Russian hoax.” Huh?
Then Barrasso abruptly summed up what seemed to be his main point: of course Republicans will win and stay in power.
“The bottom line on all of this is, this is not going to have an impact on an election 44 days from now,” he said. “People are going to go to the voting booth, they’re going to make a decision based on their life, their future, what they believe is best for them and their families.”
Barrasso said the choice is between “common sense Republicans and crazy Democrats.” He claimed Democrats are in “dire straits, as they’re even less popular than Republicans.”
Well, that’s a strange way to put it, since Barrasso admits that Republicans are unpopular. And it turns out to be fake news: A New York Times/Sienna poll last week showed that likely voters favored Democratic congressional candidates over Republicans by nearly 9 percentage points. It’s a metric, the New York Times reported, that is “closely watched by both parties as a leading indicator of political momentum.”
It appears Barrasso’s assessment of where this midterm election is going — which will largely determine Trump’s ability to get anything done in the next two years — is equal parts fake news and wishful thinking. That makes it, like his statements on Trump’s press ban, another example of Barrasso favoring the company line over the truth.
