name: Mississippi Today
title: Grand jury issues no indictments in death of Nolan Wells, DA says
description: Friends and family of Nolan Xavier Wells gather for his funeral at Center Pointe Church in Ocean Springs on Monday, July 20, 2026.
text:
This story is developing and will be updated. 
A grand jury found no evidence of criminal wrongdoing in the death of Nolan Xavier Wells, a Black teenager whose body was found near a barrier island off the Mississippi Gulf Coast two days after he went missing on the Fourth of July.
The condition of his body was consistent with drowning, according to a redacted copy of the Jackson County grand jury report that District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath released Monday night on Facebook.
In this screenshot of a video released on Monday, Sept. 21, 2026, Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath says that a grand jury issued no indictments in the death of Nolan Wells. Credit: Jackson County District Attorney's Office
“In addition to bringing prosecutions against the guilty, the grand jury must also exonerate those who have been falsely accused,” McIlrath said in a video that accompanied the report. 
The grand jury issued 132 subpoenas during its investigation and heard from 43 witnesses as it reviewed whether criminal wrongdoing had occurred when Wells did not return from an excursion to Horn Island with friends on the Fourth of July, according to the report. 
As part of that review, the grand jury considered physical and digital evidence and heard testimony from witnesses and investigators. The grand jury reviewed cell phone data and forensic reports, with photographs, videos and GPS data. 
The decision by the grand jury not to indict someone is not the same as an acquittal of a potential crime. There is no statute of limitations for murder charges in Mississippi. If new evidence ever surfaces in connection with Wells’ death, a grand jury can meet in the future to consider whether that evidence shows someone may have committed a crime. 
McIlrath said she took her oath as district attorney a little over a year after burying her own child.
“When I was sworn in, I promised to fight for and protect you and your children as I would my own. I meant it then, and I mean it now,” she said. “The death of Nolan Wells has devastated our community. Outsiders and influencers have attempted to exploit Nolan’s death and create chaos here. But we are better together.”
Emails released to social media by the district attorney’s office also show she shared the report with attorneys representing Wells’ family and his estate. 
Correction, 9/21/2026: This story has been updated to correct the spelling of McIlrath.

name: Mississippi Today
title: DA Colom urges judge to end murder case against Tameshia Shelton, arguing evidence could point to suicide: ‘State does not have evidence’
description: Tameshia Shelton beams at a crowd of family members after her release from the Clay County Detention Center on June 29, 2026. She walked out in a shirt from her niece, featuring a photo of her taken before she was sentenced to life in prison 11 years before.
text:
Columbus-area District Attorney Scott Colom urged a judge Monday to dismiss the murder indictment against Tameshia Shelton, months after the state Supreme Court let stand a Court of Appeals ruling that threw out her conviction for the death of her sister’s boyfriend. 
Shelton served 11 years behind bars in the 2009 shooting death of 21-year-old Danelle Young. She was freed from prison in June after the Mississippi Supreme Court ruling. The Mississippi Court of Appeals had stated that prosecutors failed to prove “beyond a reasonable doubt” that Shelton murdered Young. The mother of four, now 48, is supposed to face a new murder trial in Clay County on Oct. 5.
If Circuit Judge James T. Kitchens Jr. grants the district attorney’s request, it could put an end to a case that has followed Shelton the last 17 years.
The office of District Attorney Forrest Allgood, Colom’s predecessor, oversaw the 2015 prosecution. Now Colom is arguing the state doesn’t have evidence to prove “beyond a reasonable doubt” that Young didn’t kill himself. 
Upon hearing the news about Colom’s request to the judge Monday, Shelton screamed and said, “Oh, my gosh, oh, my gosh, oh, my gosh! I’m so overwhelmed.” She said she feels like doing cartwheels.
The Clay County Circuit Clerk’s Office told Mississippi Today on Monday that the judge had not determined whether to dismiss Shelton’s indictment, but would reach a decision by the time of the retrial. 
A crumbling case
On June 1, Mississippi Today published its four-year investigation that found much of the evidence in Young’s death suggested he killed himself. A key piece was Young’s apparent suicide note, but the jury in Shelton’s 2015 trial never saw it before convicting her of murder.
Days after the story ran, the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled in Shelton’s favor, and she was freed on bond, awaiting trial.
Not long after arriving at Young’s fatal shooting on Oct. 16, 2009, Clay County sheriff’s deputies concluded his death was a homicide. Shelton, who has maintained her innocence, became the prime suspect because she was the last known person to see Young alive. 
A pathologist with the Mississippi Medical Examiner’s Office ruled Young’s death a homicide, based on the trajectory of the bullet, but reversed that decision in a 2021 hearing, concluding that the death should have been “undetermined,” most likely suicide.
District Attorney Scott Colom of Mississippi’s 16th Judicial District stands in his office in Columbus on May 12, 2026, beside a photo of Levon Brooks, middle, and Kennedy Brewer, who were two of the six people convicted under Colom’s predecessor, Forrest Allgood, for murder and later exonerated. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
In his motion, Colom wrote that he asked the Mississippi Medical Examiner’s Office to review the pathologist’s autopsy and that the office told him it could not provide any additional services. 
“In light of this development,” Colom wrote, “the State does not have evidence upon which a reasonable jury could rely to find beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Young’s death was a homicide rather than a suicide.”
Shelton also called 911 to report Young’s death to officers and get him medical aid, which could make her innocent in the eyes of a “reasonable jury,” Colom wrote.
Colom: ‘The evidence sounded thin’
For years as district attorney, Colom had supported a second look at Shelton’s murder conviction. 
Her case first came to his attention in 2018, after Shelton’s family came to him in an effort to get her out of prison. He had inherited a prosecutor’s office that oversaw six tossed-out murder convictions, all under Allgood. If the judge grants Colom’s new request, Shelton would become the seventh.
Allgood previously told Mississippi Today that he and his staff never tried anyone they thought was innocent, but that he did not recall the Shelton case, which other prosecutors in his office tried.
After Colom looked into her case, he started to have questions. “The evidence sounded thin,” he told Mississippi Today. “There was not much motive.”
Colom reached out to the Mississippi Innocence Project, whose attorneys ultimately secured the reversal of Shelton’s murder conviction and her freedom from prison. He also wrote a sworn statement supporting a hearing to determine whether she deserved a new trial.
When the state Supreme Court unanimously ordered such a hearing in 2020, Judge Kitchens removed Colom from the case because of that statement and had the attorney general’s office replace him.
“Eight years ago, Scott Colom met with Tameshia’s family to hear their concerns that she had been convicted of a crime that never happened,” Shelton’s current attorney, Sandra Levick, said in a statement Monday. “He had nothing to gain in taking that meeting. He had nothing to gain in signing an affidavit urging the Court of Appeals to allow a hearing so that the facts could be known.”
An apparent suicide note goes unseen
When Young was found shot outside Shelton’s trailer, he had been in town to visit his girlfriend and her younger sister, Ketina Tutton. The couple had been planning on living together, and Young wanted to get married. But Tutton changed her mind after getting a new job, her family said.
At about 8 p.m. on the evening of Young’s death, the couple’s dreams of a new life together had deteriorated into a verbal spat that lasted 15 to 20 minutes. “I had just told him that we were not – that I was not going to move in January like we had planned,” Tutton later told deputies. “This was something we had planned … until I got the job.”
The argument ended with the couple parting ways. She said she walked inside her mother’s house, and Young headed to Shelton’s trailer. 
It was dark when Shelton said Young knocked on her bedroom window. She was already in bed with her two daughters.
When she came to the front door, she said Young told her there was a raccoon in the tree and that he needed Shelton’s revolver and only one bullet to kill it.
She said she replied that he might need more than one bullet, so she loaded the .22 pistol and handed it to Young.
She said she heard a shot, and when Young didn’t return, she went outside to check on him and found him under a tree.
A scan of the apparent suicide note that Danelle Young signed and addressed to his girlfriend’s sister, Tameshia Shelton, before his death. Credit: Mississippi Supreme Court records
Weeks after Young’s death, Shelton said she found an apparent suicide note in which he wrote, “I have no life without (Ketina). These are my last words.”
She shared the note with her defense lawyer, Rod Ray, who failed to introduce the note as evidence at trial.
Mississippi Today shared the note with five jurors in Shelton’s original murder trial. Three said they believed the note created reasonable doubt about her guilt. 
In Mississippi, a person can’t be convicted of murder unless every juror agrees on a guilty verdict. 
In his Monday request, Colom wrote the note is another piece of evidence that “undermines” any prosecution against Shelton for murder.
“Today, he moved to dismiss the indictment because the facts are known and they show that a grave injustice has taken place,” Levick said in a statement Monday. “We join in urging the Court to grant the motion to put an end to this nightmare for Tameshia Shelton and her family.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas corrections department abandons restrictions on physical books, newspapers
description: The Arkansas Department of Corrections will shift its focus away from creating a policy restricting access to physical books in an effort to prevent illegal drugs from entering prisons, officials told the state corrections board Monday.  Officials instead plans to tighten the language of a 2022 policy and give the department more authority to ban […]
text:
Board of Corrections Chairman Jamie Barker (center) and board member Nathan Lee (left) listen to department staff during a Sept. 21, 2026 board meeting. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)The Arkansas Department of Corrections will shift its focus away from creating a policy restricting access to physical books in an effort to prevent illegal drugs from entering prisons, officials told the state corrections board Monday. 
Officials instead plans to tighten the language of a 2022 policy and give the department more authority to ban “misbehaving” third-parties selling publications laced with drugs to incarcerated people, said Tawnie Hughes, the department’s chief legal officer. 
The ability to purchase physical newspapers, books and other publications will not be taken away, based on the draft policy obtained by the Advocate.
Arkansas inmates restricted from receiving physical books, other media directly under new policy

“Please do not print a headline that says we’re banning books, because we’re not,” said corrections board chairman Jamie Barker during Monday’s meeting.
The department first proposed banning incarcerated people from receiving physical books last year in order to tamp down on drugs making their way into prisons. Physical books in state prison libraries were not affected under that proposal, but books that incarcerated people purchased from businesses like Amazon or Barnes & Noble were. 
The proposal faced pushback from civil liberties and prison reform groups, and the families of incarcerated people. 
Officials paused implementation of the proposal earlier this year so it could go through the formal rulemaking process.
Critics of such restrictions have said they severely limit access for people in prison to reading materials because offerings in prison libraries and on prison-issued tablets can be limited or outdated. But prison officials said they were needed to combat a surge of illegal drugs.
Rowell said the Baxter County sheriff tried implementing a policy similar to the one proposed by the corrections department, but it was blocked in federal court.
“You really have to be demonstrative that you’ve taken all of the steps before moving to something that’s that extreme,” Rowell said.
Corrections Secretary Linsday Wallace said the changes to the initial proposal that were discussed with the board Monday were made for several reasons, including that digital reading options for incarcerated people did not meet the standards necessary to enable a ban on physical books. 
“If we could get some library options that were bolstered and they had more opportunities to get what they wanted, I don’t have a problem with that,” Wallace said. “But also, not everybody gets tablets.” 
Prison-issued tablets often do not bridge the gap when access to physical books is curtailed, according to the Prison Policy Initiative, a nonpartisan, nonprofit advocacy group.
Wallace said department officials would see if the new proposal discussed Monday made a difference before attempting more restrictive policies. 
The conversation about the book policy came during a broader discussion about overdose deaths within state prisons. Incarcerated people have been overdosing on drugs that don’t respond to naloxone, an opioid-overdose antidote, department staff told board members, and the ever-evolving nature of the illicit drugs that make their way into the prisons means there’s no single test for identifying them.
“This is not an Arkansas-unique problem,” Wallace said. “It’s happening everywhere. Everybody is dealing with these drugs coming in and their deaths.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: 5th District candidates disagree on Iran war, public food assistance
description: Democrats and Republicans running for Congress in Louisiana’s 5th District have sharp differences over how to handle the Iran war as well as whether restoring food assistance benefits should be a priority for lawmakers.
text:
The Public Affairs Research Council of Louisiana hosted an online forum for selected 5th Congressional District candidates Monday, Sept. 21, 2026. Pictured are, top row from left: PAR Research Director Melinda Deslatte, state Rep. Pat Moore and Board of Regents Chair Misti Cordell. Middle row: State Rep. Mike Echols, attorney Dan McKay and state Rep Gabe Firment. Bottom row: State Sen. Stewart Cathey and PAR President Steven Procopio. (Photo by Julie O'Donoghue/Louisiana Illuminator) Democrats and Republicans running for Congress in Louisiana’s 5th District have sharp differences over how to handle the Iran war as well as whether restoring food assistance benefits should be a priority for lawmakers. 
Six candidates took part in an online forum Monday hosted by the Public Affairs Research Council of Louisiana, a nonpartisan group that promotes civic engagement and government transparency. The group limited its event to candidates who are elected officials or had raised $100,000 for the race.  
The two Democrats in the race, attorney Dan McKay of Bunkie and state Rep. Pat Moore of Monroe, said they would work to end the war with Iran if elected. 

“The first and most obvious thing to do about inflation and affordability is to end the war in Iran that Donald Trump started,” McKay said. “That was totally ill-advised. There’s no basis for it.”
All four Republicans — state Sen. Stewart Cathey of Monroe, Board of Regents chair Misti Cordell of Monroe, state Rep. Michael Echols of Monroe and state Rep. Gabe Firment of Pollock — said they supported Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. 

“Have there been some short-term pain points? Absolutely. And should we end this as soon as possible? Absolutely,” Echols said when asked if he backs the war. “But I do appreciate the president holding the bully accountable.”

The forum participants are among the nine candidates seeking to replace U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, in the 5th District. The congresswoman is the GOP’s nominee for Louisiana’s open U.S. Senate seat in the Nov. 3 election. 

The mostly rural 5th district covers all or parts of two dozen parishes, extending from Northeast Louisiana to the outskirts of Baton Rouge and the Florida Parishes. 
Democratic and Republican candidates also differed during the forum on what to prioritize in the federal farm bill, a massive multiyear package that drives public assistance to farmers, oversees agriculture policy and funds the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as food stamps. 
Congress is currently struggling to pass the farm bill, in part, because Senate Democrats won’t vote for one that keeps SNAP cuts enacted in 2025 in place. 
Over the past year, 166,000 Louisiana residents have lost SNAP benefits, which help low-income households purchase food each month. Others stayed in the program but saw them drastically reduced, in some cases from $300 to just $24 per month, after Congress approved Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

McKay and Moore, as Democrats, said restoring SNAP funding would be a priority if elected. Many Democrat-leaning policy organizations have argued that a more robust SNAP program would provide a boost to farmers because it increases demand for American agricultural products. 

“People that have been removed from the SNAP benefit, that of course impacts the farmers,” Moore said. 

Republicans Cordell and Echols implied SNAP should not be such a point of focus in the farm bill.

“SNAP is a very large part of the farm bill, and of course, no one, Republican or Democrat, wants anyone in America to go hungry. But there’s a lot of that farm bill that SNAP eats up,” Cordell said. 

Echols said he believed SNAP should be removed from the farm bill altogether because the fight over funding food aid holds up other crucial farming assistance. 

On the controversial topic of data centers and artificial intelligence regulation, McKay was the only candidate to call for a moratorium on the facilities. 

Cathey and Cordell said it is in Americans’ best interest to be friendly toward data center and AI development in order to protect  national security interests. Cathey said he favors minimal federal regulation of the industry for that reason. 

“They’re going to construct these somewhere. I’d much rather us have an inviting environment here in America rather than them go to China, where there will be absolutely no regulation, no oversight and no controls to protect your date,” he said. 

Firment and Echols said the AI and data center boom could provide opportunities for the state’s timber industry. Woody biomass, which can be produced easily by Louisiana companies, could be used to help power the new data centers, they said. 

Firment said it’s also crucial that Louisiana residents don’t end up paying for the energy and water resources needed to power data centers. 

“It’s absolutely critical that the cost of energy infrastructure and transmission is not passed along to the ratepayer,” Firment said. 

“Energy really is the biggest issue when we’re talking about data centers,” he said.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Appeals court backs Missouri’s gerrymandered map, but decision is put on hold
description: A federal appeals court ruled Monday that Missouri must use the congressional map passed by Republicans in 2025 for the Nov. 3 election, but the decision was put on hold for a week — leaving election officials to proceed for now under the map they were already using. The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals […]
text:
The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals in St. Louis ruled Monday that Missouri should use the 2025 congressional map drawn to favor Republicans in the 2026 election. the court is housed at the Thomas F. Eagleton U.S. Courthouse (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).A federal appeals court ruled Monday that Missouri must use the congressional map passed by Republicans in 2025 for the Nov. 3 election, but the decision was put on hold for a week — leaving election officials to proceed for now under the map they were already using.
The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals issued its order just before 5 p.m. Monday, ruling the election in November must use the same district lines that were used in the Aug. 4 primary election. But the judges stayed the order until Sept. 28 to give opponents time to seek relief from the U.S. Supreme Court.
That means Monday’s ruling does not immediately change how the election will proceed. The first ballots went out Friday for overseas voters, and absentee voting begins Tuesday for people who are unable to make it to the polls on Election Day because of travel or mobility issues.
The ruling reverses a decision of the Missouri Supreme Court that a referendum petition to force a vote on the 2025 map also negated the legal effect of the legislation enacting the plan. The U.S. Supreme Court has intervened twice already in the dispute, most recently on Sept. 10, when it blocked a federal judge’s order requiring use of the 2025 map while the case moved through the 8th Circuit. 
The court’s order changes nothing in how the election will proceed, said Boone County Clerk Brianna Lennon. She tested voting tabulators Monday using the 2022 map and will mail 1,000 ballots on Tuesday to people who requested them.
People who have not voted could be given a new ballot if the district lines do change, Lennon said. She’s not certain what message, if any, she will send to those voters.
“That is what I am going to spend tonight trying to figure out,” Lennon said.
Missouri election officials begin mailing ballots as they await ruling on congressional map

People Not Politicians, the political action committee that circulated the referendum petition, plans to appeal, attorney Chuck Hatfield said in a text to The Independent.
The judges “make it clear that we have until the 28th to get a stay and that there is no requirement to switch back to (the 2025 map) until then,” Hatfield wrote. “So we have a couple of days.”
In a statement, Richard von Glahn, director of People Not Politicians, said he is confident the U.S. Supreme Court will again find that the map used in the 2022 and 2024 elections will be used in November.
“Ballots have been printed, and Missourians have already voted,” von Glahn said. “Thousands more will vote before this order seeks to take effect. Officials should stop wasting taxpayers’ money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections.
The appeals court concluded that equal protection rights would be violated if the map lines change between the primary to the general election. That, the court ruled, means “some Missouri voters will have more say than others on who represents them in Congress.”
The order directed U.S. Chief District Judge Stephen Clark of the Eastern District of Missouri to issue a permanent injunction barring Missouri from using any map except the one passed by lawmakers in 2025.
He issued the order shortly after the 8th Circuit decision, including the one-week stay to allow for an appeal.
The 8th Circuit ruled in the appeal of a temporary restraining order, issued by Clark on Sept. 8, barring Secretary of State Denny Hoskins from using any map except the 2025 map for this year’s election. Clark ruled in a lawsuit brought by U.S. Rep. Bob Onder, an incumbent Republican running for re-election in the 3rd District; state Sen. Rick Brattin, the Republican nominee in the 5th District, and two voters who will change districts from the primary.
Onder and Brattin sued Hoskins after the state Supreme Court decision, arguing that the change in maps violated their rights and federal election law as interpreted by the courts. People Not Politicians intervened when Hoskins agreed with Onder and Brattin as they sought an order to restore the 2025 map.
The 2025 map puts Onder’s entire home county in the 3rd District and redraws the 5th District to shift its partisan composition toward Republicans. The 5th District is currently represented by Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.
If it takes effect next week, the 8th Circuit order would mark the fourth shift since Sept. 3 in which congressional map election officials have been directed to use. The appeals court blamed the confusion on the Missouri Supreme Court.
The 2025 map was in place for candidate filing and the primary, the opinion noted. 
“During that time, Missourians filed to run for Congress, met candidates, watched campaign advertisements, received campaign mail, and voted under the 2025 map,” the court wrote. “Any confusion stems from the last-minute decision by a state court to switch the congressional map.”
The 8th Circuit also rejected arguments that it was improperly interfering with a state-law question or improperly taking over a role that belongs to state courts.
“Allowing state courts to issue, without any federal-court review, lastminute decisions affecting the conduct of federal elections would increase the volume of last-minute requests to state courts, decrease the public’s confidence in the election results, and potentially allow a handful of state judges to render decisions that decide the outcome of a presidential election or party control of Congress,” the opinion stated.
Brattin issued a statement praising the ruling.
“I am hopeful the U.S. Supreme Court will agree,” Brattin said. “Voters cast their primary ballots under this map, and they should be able to vote in the same districts for the general election.”
If the district lines must change next week, Lennon said, it will not be a simple process.
“There is a fundamental difference between just removing and adding a candidate and creating entirely new ballot styles,” Lennon said.
Boone County has five Missouri House districts and the congressional lines do not conform to the legislative district lines. Local ballot questions mean that voters in some polling locations will get a ballot with questions that others do not. Each distinct ballot is what election officials call a ballot style.
And she would have to start over, Lennon said.
“We have to regenerate the entire election because the districts are completely different, so the make-up of the voters is different for each of those ballot styles,” she said. “I have to reprogram, reproof and create a new order for our vendor for printing, retest the absentee voting machines and get all of that done while absentee voting is happening.”

name: WyoFile
title: No Mollie’s Pack, Yellowstone wolves killed, state reports after hunt area’s quick close
description:
Hunters fill a four-wolf limit in just four days, closing down two hunt areas for the season and sparing a wandering wolf pack. 
The post No Mollie’s Pack, Yellowstone wolves killed, state reports after hunt area’s quick close appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
EVANSTON—Yellowstone National Park’s last original wolf pack, Mollie’s Pack, emerged unscathed from a hunting season that opened last week and has already closed, Wyoming wildlife officials announced Monday. 
Dan Smith, a Wyoming Game and Fish Department interim deputy director, provided the update, allaying concern that had run rampant online and in circles of wolf-watching devotees. Worries centered on the Mollie’s Pack, named after the late U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Mollie Beattie, who died of cancer during the historic 1995-96 reintroduction. 

U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Mollie Beattie helps hoist the first wolf for reintroduction into Yellowstone’s Crystal Bench pen in 1995. Five years later, the reintroduced wolves were renamed Mollie’s Pack in memory of Beattie, who died in 1996. (Jim Peaco/National Park Service)

Today, Mollie’s Pack is the last remaining wolf pack still intact since reintroduction three decades ago. The famous pack had been making headlines for leaving the safety of its longtime territory in Yellowstone’s Pelican Valley and mostly spending late 2025 and the first half of this year in Wyoming’s wolf hunt area one, located northwest of Cody.
“Wolf hunt areas one and two did close on Saturday, after reaching the mortality limit of four wolves,” Smith told the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission. “None of the wolves taken were from wolf packs previously assigned to Yellowstone National Park.”
Recent movements had put Mollie’s Pack in a good position to survive Wyoming’s hunt. Ahead of hunting season, the National Park Service had reported to WyoFile that the pack, which consisted of five adults and five pups in July, was “mostly” back in Yellowstone, where hunting isn’t allowed. 
Wildlife advocates had been pressuring Wyoming wildlife managers to close down the hunt area where Mollie’s Pack had been spending time. Monday’s news came as a relief.
“Mollie’s Pack survived the hunt,” said Wyoming Untrapped founder Lisa Robertson, who traveled to Evanston for the commission meeting. “For more than three decades, they have taught us about resilience, family, adaptation, and the enduring nature of the wild.”
Empty horse trailers and camps were found in Sunlight Basin on the opening day of Wyoming’s 2026 wolf hunting season. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
Yellowstone officials declined an interview Monday, saying the wolf hunt is a state issue. Packs crossing park boundaries, mostly into Montana, have altered the park population at times. Wolves that spend most of their time in Yellowstone are poorly suited to survive hunting because they generally lack a fear of humans, and sometimes even badly habituate to crowds.
Where wolves are managed as trophy game, Wyoming’s hunt is already tightly managed relative to Idaho and Montana. This year hunting opportunities were reduced as a result of a distemper outbreak that has dropped the population to its lowest level in two decades. The state OK’d hunting regulations that allow the killing of up to 22 wolves — half of 2025’s limit — during a season that runs through the end of December. 
Game and Fish set a quota of four animals that could be killed in hunt areas one and two. Hunters reached that limit over the weekend, Smith said. 

Dan Smith, interim deputy director of internal affairs, during a Sept. 21, 2026, Wyoming Game and Fish Commission meeting in Evanston. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

Statewide, 10 of 22 wolves that can be killed in Wyoming’s wolf trophy game area have been dispatched by hunters during the first week of the season, according to the state’s mortality database. No other hunt areas have reached their mortality limit. 
Wolf hunting is a notoriously difficult pursuit. Wyoming’s hunters devote about 500 days of effort per animal they kill. Especially early in the fall, the pups of the year are the most vulnerable. 
Wyoming’s trophy game area covers just 15% of the state. Across the rest of Wyoming, wolf hunting regulations are scant and wolves are managed as predators. No licenses are required in the remaining 85% of the state, and killing takes place without limit and few restrictions on method year-round.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa harvest behind schedule due to ‘extremely soggy’ conditions
description: Iowa corn and soybean crops are slightly behind typical harvest and maturity schedules as farmers had less than two days suitable for field work due to rainy conditions over the past week. The latest crop progress and condition report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture shows Iowa farmers had harvested 4% of corn acres and […]
text:
A flooded corn field near Alleman on Aug. 7, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa corn and soybean crops are slightly behind typical harvest and maturity schedules as farmers had less than two days suitable for field work due to rainy conditions over the past week.
The latest crop progress and condition report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture shows Iowa farmers had harvested 4% of corn acres and 2% of soybean acres as of the Sept. 14-20 reporting period. Both of those figures are behind the 2025 harvest pace and the five-year average. 
State Climatologist Justin Glisan said the preliminary statewide weekly precipitation average for week was “higher than the 30-year climatological normal for all of September.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The statewide average rainfall was 3.57 inches for the week, with many stations logging totals in excess of 4 inches. Ainsworth had the highest recorded precipitation for the week, according to Glisan’s report, with 10.63 inches. 
Glisan said rainfall was reported in the state every day of the reporting period, but the biggest precipitation events occurred at the beginning and end of the reporting periods. 
The heaviest rainfalls hit east central and eastern Iowa, where Glisan said flash flood warnings were issued in multiple counties and “major flooding” was reported in Muscatine County along the Turkey River. 
Prior to the heavy precipitation week, Glisan said the state had already experienced “anomalous wetness” for the month. The most recent precipitation totals meant farmers had just 1.7 days suitablel on average, for field work according to USDA.
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig called the conditions “extremely soggy” and said the heavy rainfall led to flooding in several areas. 
“We’re hopeful for a few dry days ahead, but more rain is in the forecast. Conditions are good for flying on cover crops, and the moisture can help get them germinated and growing,” Naig said in a news release, referring to aerial seeding of cover crops. “When fields finally firm up, Iowa farmers will get combines rolling and harvest will be fully underway.”
Corn maturity reached 56% during the reporting period, putting it behind last year’s crop which had 63% maturity by the reporting period. Corn maturity was only 2 percentage points behind the five-year average for the period. Nearly all, 95%, of corn acres have dented, which is one percentage point ahead of the 2025 crop and the five-year average. 
The share of soybean acres dropping leaves, according to the report, was also behind previous years at 46% while last year’s report showed 58% dropping leaves by Sept. 20 and the five-year average has 53% dropping leaves by the reporting period. 
Iowa’s dominant crops continue to rate well, with soybeans rated 75% good to excellent and corn rated 76% good to excellent. 
Farm safety 
In accordance with National Farm Safety and Health Week, Naig urged all Iowans, farmers or not, to “keep safety top of mind” as harvest ramps up.
“Farmers should take the time to work safely, get enough rest and look out for one another,” Naig said in a news release Monday. “Drivers can do their part by slowing down, putting away distractions and being patient when they encounter farm equipment on the road.”


Mental health hotlines:
Iowa Concern: 
1-800-447-1985 (call or text) 
FarmAid: 
1-800-FARM-AID


The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship said farmers should stay alert, avoid shortcuts and remember to follow safety protocols. Naig said in addition to physical safety, farmers and farm communities should be cognizant of the stress and mental health challenges that can arise during harvest season. 
IDALS encouraged farmers to make time for stress-relieving activities throughout harvest, to get adequate rest and to talk about their stress with family, friends or mental health professionals if needed. 
“The stress and economic pressures facing agriculture can also take a toll, so I encourage farmers and ag workers to check in on family, friends and neighbors and reach out when help is needed,” Naig said. “A safe and successful harvest means everyone makes it home at the end of the day.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Gov. Cox signs executive order aligning Utah with Trump’s addiction recovery initiative
description: Shoulder to shoulder with leaders in the Trump administration, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox on Monday made Utah the first state to officially take action to join the White House’s national effort meant to reduce addiction, homelessness and serious mental illness.  Kathryn Burgum, White House senior adviser for addiction and recovery who is married to Interior […]
text:
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, joined by White House Senior Adviser for Addiction Recovery Kathryn Burgum, signs an executive order establishing the Recovery Utah Initiative during a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 21, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)Shoulder to shoulder with leaders in the Trump administration, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox on Monday made Utah the first state to officially take action to join the White House’s national effort meant to reduce addiction, homelessness and serious mental illness. 
Kathryn Burgum, White House senior adviser for addiction and recovery who is married to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, sat next to Cox as he signed an executive order creating the Recovery Utah Initiative. 
Trump admin aims to shift homelessness grants toward addiction treatment, enforcement

The order directs state agencies, local governments, healthcare, faith-based organizations and private businesses to better coordinate with each other to improve homelessness and addiction services on multiple fronts. 
Cox’s state executive order aligns Utah with President Donald Trump’s Great American Recovery Initiative, which the president created through a national executive order in January to “prioritize addiction treatment and recovery” across the nation. 
Addiction, Trump’s order says, “contributes to declining workforce participation, increased healthcare costs, homelessness, family instability, and lost productivity that together cost the United States hundreds of billions of dollars each year.”
Cox’s executive order creates the Recovery Utah Initiative Council — including State Homeless Coordinator Tyler Clancy and two people who have experienced addiction that will serve as vice chairs — to steer the effort. 
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox announces an executive order establishing the Recovery Utah Initiative during a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 21, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
It also incorporates Cox’s “three pillars” that have been driving his administration’s strategy to improve the state’s homeless system over the past year. Those pillars include accountability for “high utilizers” in the criminal justice system, emergency shelter and affordable housing, and mental and behavioral health infrastructure.
Earlier this year, the Utah Legislature approved about $45 million (including ongoing and one-time money) to carry out Cox’s three-pillar strategy, which state officials developed while in talks with the Trump administration. 
Utah homeless board proposes ‘initial framework’ to respond to Trump’s executive order

The governor’s executive order comes as the Trump administration has proposed funneling more money to localities that prioritize “treatment-first” policies like sober living, more cooperation with law enforcement and more temporary and transitional housing. It’s a reversal from a decade-long federal approach known as Housing First that houses people experiencing homelessness without requiring sobriety or participation in treatment programs as a condition to keep their housing. 
National housing advocates have railed against the move away from Housing First, arguing it’s a proven strategy that can reduce taxpayer spending on emergency services and the criminal legal system. 
Leaders of Republican-controlled Utah, including Cox, have criticized Housing First as lacking “accountability” measures, though the state once led out on the strategy, while calling for more emphasis on addiction and behavioral health treatment before or alongside housing services. 
Kathryn Burgum, White House senior addiction recovery adviser for the Trump administration, speaks alongside Utah Gov. Spencer Cox during a news conference announcing the Recovery Utah Initiative at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 21, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
Cox said he views the Recovery Utah Initiative as an extension of the Trump administration’s moves away from Housing First and toward a more holistic strategy that places more focus on “recovery.”
But when asked if the Utah initiative will shift any resources away from homelessness and toward addiction recovery, Cox told reporters, “I don’t know if it shifts any directly, but they’re part and parcel. They’ll be working closely together.” 
Utah sees slight decline in homelessness — a first in years

“Look, housing is important. We want people to have shelter, but that can’t be the first and only goal,” Cox said. “It hasn’t proven effective in alleviating the suffering that we’re talking about today. Recovery has to be a part of that, and making sure that we have the resources in place to hold people accountable absolutely matters. … We think we’re being compassionate by just giving people whatever they want whenever they want it. And there’s nothing compassionate about it.” 
That prompted applause from the audience in the Gold Room of the Utah Capitol where the governor signed the executive order. The room was filled with state officials, along with about a dozen people who have experienced homelessness, addiction or other life challenges. 
Many of them have participated in The Other Side Academy, a Utah-based training program that state leaders in recent years have applauded as an accountability and recovery-focused provider. In recent news coverage, some past participants have criticized the program’s aggressive approach to treatment.
Joseph Grenny, co-founder of The Other Side Academy, chats with Randy Shumway, chair of the Utah Homeless Services Board, before a news conference announcing the Recovery Utah Initiative at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 21, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
“When you talk to people who have actually been there and made it out the other side, every single one of them will tell you that they needed accountability,” Cox said. “It doesn’t mean we abandon them when they fall. It means we’re there to pick them up again, and that recovery often takes many, many attempts at sobriety.” 
In an interview after Monday’s news conference, Clancy told reporters “Housing First means a lot of different things to a lot of different people,” but he doesn’t expect Utah programs that use Housing First strategies to take a negative hit. Instead, he said Cox’s administration is working on “expanding our toolkit.”
“Utah’s approach has always been very straightforward, which is whatever your needs are, we want to serve those needs,” Clancy said. “I think Housing First on a federal level lost its way when it became housing only, when it prohibited people from doing treatment, when it prohibited programs that did have success. So for us, we don’t take a one-size-fits-all approach. So some programs that do a Housing First model, that’s fantastic, we want to continue that work. But we’re expanding our toolkit, rather than limiting it.” 
Kathryn Burgum, White House senior addiction recovery adviser for the Trump administration, listens during a news conference announcing the Recovery Utah Initiative at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 21, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
Burgum, the former first lady of North Dakota, has been open about her own challenges with addiction. During her husband’s time as governor, she was the face of North Dakota’s Office of Recovery Reinvented, focused on ending the stigma around the disease of addiction. Earlier this year, she was appointed as a White House adviser to co-chair the Great American Recovery Initiative. 
“My connection to this work is personal,” she said. “I took my first drink in high school, and spent the next 20 years living in blackouts, shame, and repeated attempts to stop.” 
Sharing addiction story ‘so worth it,’ Kathryn Burgum says

Burgum said she thought she was “broken, and after years of relapsing, I was hopeless and suicidal.” One day, she said aloud to herself “‘I need help,’ and I have been sober since I said those words.” 
Burgum said addiction needs to be treated as the chronic disease that it is, and that means “building a genuine continuum of care” and “changing how we define and pay for success.” 
“The sooner we build the system, the sooner those benefits can compound across generations,” Burgum said.
She said Trump’s executive order set the “federal framework for this work,” while Cox’s order translates that “into state action.” 
“The federal government cannot accomplish this transformation by itself,” she said. “State cannot accomplish it alone. And healthcare systems cannot accomplish that alone. We need recovery organizations working with healthcare systems and everyone working together to accomplish this.” 
Asked if the partnership with the White House means more federal funding will be heading Utah’s way, Burgum told reporters, “We’ll be looking at how states can use funding.”
From left, Josh Romney, chair of Shelter the Homeless Board; Laurie Hopkins, director of Shelter the Homeless, and Steve Waldrip, senior housing adviser for Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, listen during a news conference announcing the Recovery Utah Initiative at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 21, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
“A lot of that funding is already set up in a lot of different departments, but that’s something that would be in the works,” she said. 
Cox said in his administration’s conversations with U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy about homelessness, “they’re very excited about what they’re seeing here in Utah, and as those resources become available, we know we’ll be applying for those.” 
It’s also possible that governor will ask for more funding from the Utah Legislature in the upcoming general session that starts in January, Cox said, “but we want to make sure that we’re using the resources we’ve been given in the appropriate way, that it’s getting where it needs to go and providing the most help before we come and ask for anything more.” 
Monty Burks, executive director of the Great American Recovery Initiative who also serves as director of the Center for Faith in the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, also spoke during Monday’s news conference. 
Monty Burks, executive director of the Trump administration’s Great American Recovery Initiative, speaks during a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 21, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
He said Trump and Cox’s executive orders create a “visibility campaign” with “leadership in executive-level government that advocates for people that are in long-term recovery.” 
“This empowers people with lived experience who’ve lived in shame and guilt to share the true story of how broken people that have had opportunity to heal can help other people find the tools to heal themselves,” Burk said. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Destiny Garcia, director of Clean Slate Utah, which helps people clear their criminal records to access jobs, told reporters she was happy to see that people who have experienced addiction will serve on the Recovery Utah Initiative Council. Garcia has also been outspoken about her own experience with addiction to heroin. After she was arrested on the streets of Salt Lake City in 2017, she said her life changed for the better. 
“We know that people that were closest to the problem are also very close to the solution,” she said. “Centering people with lived experience at the table is what is needed in order to solve a problem like this.” 
Will it work? Garcia said “even if it doesn’t work, at least we’re trying another avenue. I think trying and failing is better than not trying at all.” 
People who have experienced homelessness stand to be acknowledged during a news conference announcing the Recovery Utah Initiative at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 21, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana’s affordable housing dollars redirected to storm-proof roofs
description: Louisiana has found more money to allow homeowners to upgrade their roofs to withstand hurricanes, but it will come at the cost of affordable housing.
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry spoke at a press conference announcing $20 million federal dollars earmarked for affordable housing will be redirected to a fortified roof program. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana has found more money to allow homeowners to upgrade their roofs to withstand hurricanes, but it will come at the cost of affordable housing.
Gov. Jeff Landry confirmed Monday that $20 million in federal funds earmarked for affordable housing across the state will instead go toward fortified roof improvements. Insurance Commissioner and state Sen. Kirk Talbot, R-River Ridge, who chairs the Senate Insurance Committee, joined the governor Monday for the announcement at the insurance department.
The money comes from the Piggyback Resilience Initiative Mixed-Income (PRIME) program, administered by the Louisiana Housing Corp., the state agency that handles federal and state housing assistance. PRIME funding has previously been used to help build more than 4,100 apartments in the state.
When asked why the affordable housing money is being redirected, the governor said reducing insurance costs with fortified roofs was a top priority. 
“There are many other programs under which we can get affordable apartments,” said Landry. “When we start employing that money in a fortified roof program, we start to reduce the overall premiums in that area.”
So far this year, the state has committed $100 million toward subsidizing roof improvements. The Louisiana Legislature appropriated $30 million this spring, and the insurance department added $50 million from a Louisiana Citizens Property Insurance surplus. 
The insurance department’s Fortify Homes provides homeowners with grants of up to $10,000 each to build or replace their roofs to a higher standard, though the awards typically don’t cover the entire cost. The program’s intent is to lower the home’s risk of storm damage and, in turn, the owner’s insurance premiums.
While the insurance department will continue administer grants for the $80 million previously allocated, the $20 million announced Monday will be doled out through the state Office of Community Development, which is in charge of dispensing the federal money in question from the Federal Housing Finance Agency. Landry said these grants will cover the entire cost of new roofs.
The new program is known as the Restore Resilient Opportunities for Overhead Fortification program, or Restore ROOF. The only strings attached to its grants is that the money must go to homes impacted by major hurricanes from 2020-21 — Laura and Delta. 
One of the state’s leading housing advocates disagrees with the governor’s assessment that there are enough resources to address the need for affordable residences in the state, saying the need is immense. 
“A lot of them have huge waiting lists. By no measure is any program that is creating affordable rentals meeting the need,” Andreanecia Morris, executive director for HousingNOLA, a coalition of affordable housing developers and advocates, said in an interview Monday.
The Restore ROOF program will start immediately, Landry said, with more information on how to apply available soon through the Office of Community Development. 
The insurance department’s Fortify Homes program is expected to reach 13,000 roof upgrades once the $80 million allocated this year is awarded, Temple said earlier this year.  
A Legislative Auditor’s report last year calculated homeowners receiving a Fortify Homes grant averaged more than $6,200 in out-of-pocket costs to pay for their roofing improvements. Recipients also reported a median 22% reduction in their homeowner’s insurance premiums.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Judge orders release of 24 unlawfully detained individuals
description: A federal judge ordered immigration officials to release 24 individuals being unlawfully held in Cascade County, some for more than six weeks, Upper Seven Law announced in a news release. Upper Seven Litigation Director Molly Danahy said in a statement those people will be allowed to return to their families. “In Montana, we know how […]
text:
(Photo illustration by Getty Images.)A federal judge ordered immigration officials to release 24 individuals being unlawfully held in Cascade County, some for more than six weeks, Upper Seven Law announced in a news release.
Upper Seven Litigation Director Molly Danahy said in a statement those people will be allowed to return to their families.
“In Montana, we know how important the rule of law is,” Danahy said. “And we will not stop holding federal officials to the basic rules set out in our constitution that keep us free.”
The release order from U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris came Friday.
It said proper arrests require a warrant or a belief a noncitizen is in the country in violation of the law and presents a risk of escape, but no evidence indicates either condition existed.
“This practice of after-the-fact arrest warrants can be called many things — illegal, improper, and unconstitutional, among them,” the order said, citing a similar case. “But whatever label one wishes to apply, the practice is fundamentally at odds with and offensive to lawful, constitutional behavior in this country.”
The case is part of a class-action lawsuit.
The court order said the judge agreed the federal government’s warrantless arrests were illegal, but the government “declined to abide by the court’s” judgment.
Instead, the government “continued to hold wrongfully detained class members” anyway, so the court ordered the class members to file individual petitions for release.
Monday, Upper Seven senior legal counsel Andres Haladay said the firm has filed 37 petitions for release of individuals held after warrantless arrests by immigration officers since the order.
The case started with the unlawful arrest in late July near Lewistown of Jesus Verde Hernandez by U.S. Customs and Border Patrol.
The judge ordered his release and also the release of a father and child arrested under similar circumstances — without a warrant, and also without suspicion they’re breaking the law and likely to escape before a warrant can be issued.
The government has said it issued warrants after the arrests, and it disagrees with the court’s determination.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office could not be reached for comment in time for this story.
Haladay said the list of class members changes as people’s specific circumstances come to light. He said the government agreed 24 of the 37 people who petitioned for release had situations similar to the father and minor whose requests the court granted.
But 13 people are still detained and in limbo pending additional arguments from the federal government to the court about their respective situations, Haladay said. He said Upper Seven will continue to file petitions for remaining class members.
In an order, the court has said it will consider them on a rolling basis to give the government time to respond.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Haley Stevens urges Democrats to hold steady on Israel
description: For U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), support for Israel was never just a campaign slogan. As she stares down her final months in Congress, she’s doubling down on her support for the nation, its people and Jewish Americans across the nation as antisemitism and the war in Gaza continues to loom large in politics, especially […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), a former Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate, speaks during a candidate meet and greet with the Lansing Regional Chamber in downtown Lansing, Mich. July 29, 2026 | Photo By Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceFor U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), support for Israel was never just a campaign slogan. As she stares down her final months in Congress, she’s doubling down on her support for the nation, its people and Jewish Americans across the nation as antisemitism and the war in Gaza continues to loom large in politics, especially within the Democratic Party.
The soon-to-be retired Michigan representative lost the U.S. Senate primary race for the U.S. Senate to nominee Abdul El-Sayed, and the contrast between them on the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, increasingly labeled a genocide by many Democrats, was one of the major flashpoints in the campaign.
Stevens was heavily backed by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, and which became a hurdle for her campaign as support in the United States for Israel wanes. 
El-Sayed, in turn, focused on AIPAC’s influence in the race, and the turning tide of public opinion on the plight of the Palestinian people. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
El-Sayed is one of several emerging Democratic Party candidates who have called for ending military aid to Israel, or at least conditioning it so it does not help perpetuate Israel’s fight against Hamas, the terrorist organization that has governed Gaza for nearly two decades and started the war with the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks that killed about 1,200 Israelis, mostly civilians. The ensuing war has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and displaced some 2.1 million according to the United Nations.
Although El-Sayed faces new challenges with Jewish voters, some of whom have vowed to support his opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, Stevens has been targeted by activists over her support for Israel even as she exits public life.
Following a trip to Israel after her campaign for the U.S. Senate, Stevens reiterated her support for the nation in a U.S. House floor speech. Last week,  she was harassed by an activist from Code Pink and another individual who did not identify themselves, Stevens’ office told Michigan Advance.
Video from one of the confrontations showed a person aggressively accusing Stevens of supporting the bombing of Palestinian children in the midst of a supposed cease fire between Israel and Hamas. The encounter shows Stevens pushing back. 
Stevens said in the video clip that she still supports a two-state solution. When the person claimed Stevens supported a genocide, Stevens responded by saying that there was no genocide ocurring in Gaza.

Reporter: You support genocide.
Haley Stevens: There’s no genocide.
Reporter: You don’t care about the ethnic cleansing.
Haley Stevens: There is no genocide going on, sir.
Reporter: You don’t care about women being raped, men being raped.
Haley Stevens: There’s no genocide… pic.twitter.com/FIe9CaZksU
— Ounka (@OunkaOnX) September 17, 2026

The social media influencer called Stevens “disgusting,” but Stevens responded that anti-Zionism is a hate movement. The influencer responded by saying, “We will see you at the gallows.”
El-Sayed, on Sept. 19, released a statement condemning the incidents.
“Congresswoman Stevens and I might disagree on some important things — but we agree on so much more,” El-Sayed said. “If we believe in a more peaceful and just world, we have to express our disagreements without harassment or aggression. Harassment like the kind she’s experienced is unkind and unproductive, and it puts her personal safety at risk. This behavior is not representative of our movement and should cease immediately.”
When a vacation teaches lessons on humanity
In an interview with the Advance, Stevens said that she visited Israel soon after her campaign for the U.S. Senate ended. She made the journey almost on a whim, as she was traveling in Italy with her mother and her new fiancé, who is Jewish and has close familial ties to Israel. 
Stevens has been on the Congress hostage task force since 2022. Her role on the committee broadened to Israel after the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on the Nova Music Festival, when Hamas massacred nearly 400 concertgoers and took hostages at an electronic music event near Kibbutz Re’im in the southern portion of Israel.
Her position with the Congressional task force allowed her to coordinate with Israel Seminars, which sometimes helps plan trips for members of Congress and other dignitaries. 
She met with people who were held hostage by Hamas, including a 24-year-old woman who was captive for 728 days. She met with Israeli military leaders and was shown border crossings where food assistance travels into the nation and into Gaza.
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), left, speaks to Routhie Rousso, with World Central Kitchen, right, during a trip to the nation in late August 2026. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens)
The trip further bolstered Stevens’ Israeli support but also illustrated the hardships of the war for people on both sides.
“People have a lot of criticisms,” Stevens told the Advance. “I certainly and rightfully do, and the people who live there do, too. Hamas, who started the war, still hasn’t put down their weapons … and you don’t have peace yet.”
Seeing t innocent people still being harmed on both sides affected her deeply, Stevens said. She also visited Gaza, but was limited in what she was able to see.
“People don’t really get in there,” Stevens said. “It’s not a state government. You’re on the Egypt-Israel-Gaza border. You can see them all and it’s very interesting. … I looked out in Gaza and toured around with a 22-year-old gal who wants nothing more than peace.”
From there, she visited Hadassah Medical Center, the main medical organization with hospital campuses in Israel. She was surprised at how many people from Michigan were involved in the operation, and by how the hospital included both Israeli and Palestinian doctors working side by side to heal the sick and wounded.
“Here’s the humanity,” Stevens told the Advance. “The humanity of people outside of governments, or whatever we call Hamas, this rogue non-state group, with a purpose.”
Stevens told the Advance that those glimpses helped her further understand the plight of oppressed people in Palestine, but also the fact that many Israelis do not want continued war with its neighbors.
“They all deserve and want peace,” Stevens said. “I have always taken very seriously what it means to be a federal representative, someone who holds that voting card, who carries the weight, the hopes and dreams and the aspirations of a state, a congressional district, of a country, to do the best I can.”
A not-so-warm welcome at home
When she returned back to the United States Sept. 2, she gave a floor speech in the U.S. House of Representatives, calling on her fellow lawmakers — and specifically Democrats — to continue supporting Israel.
“We do not have to choose whose humanity matters,” Stevens said “I stood at the Nova Festival site where young people went to dance and 364 never came home. I walked through Kibbutz Kfar Aza and saw the remains of bloodshed and attacks on peaceful people, and I sat across from people who survived captivity and somehow found the courage to tell us what it means to come home. Their humanity matters. I also met World Central Kitchen workers feeding Palestinian families in Gaza, and at Karem Shalom, I saw the urgent work of getting food and medicine to innocent people trapped in a war they did not choose. Their humanity matters too.”
“We can mourn the victims of Oct.  7 and demand dignity for innocent Palestinians,” Stevens added. “We can demand security for Israelis and humanitarian relief for Gaza. And when the world asks us to choose whose humanity matters. America should have the answer: Everyone’s.”
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), center right, pictured with survivors of the Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attacks in Israel. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens)
Weeks later, on Sept. 15, Stevens was leaving her post on the House Science Committee following a hearing. She was approached by an activist from Code Pink and also a social media influencer, who Stevens called “rogue, paid actors” attempting to intimidate her.
On social media, Stevens reiterated that she would not be backing down in the face of harassment.
“Let me be clear: I have always wanted the wars in the Middle East to end. I believe in a two-state solution that gives Israelis and Palestinians peace, security, dignity and a home. People are free to disagree with me, challenge me, and protest my positions. That is democracy,” Stevens wrote. “But disagreement is not license for intimidation or harassment. I’m not on the ballot anymore. So, what exactly are we accomplishing by continuing to tear each other apart?”
Stevens added that “there is too much at stake to spend our energy villainizing people on our own side or like me who are not coming back to Congress.
“We should be putting our energy into protecting Social Security, defending voting rights, lowering costs, standing up for science, and defending the people who sent us here,” Stevens wrote. “Disagreement is democracy. Intimidation isn’t. Let’s get back to work.”
Despite some Democrats choosing to step away from Israel, Stevens said she still believes that Israel is an ally of the United States — even as she maintains Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “has some real problems and hasn’t done a great job, and has failed in terms of the goal of long-term peace.”
Michigan Democrats continue to grapple with Israel and Palestine
Speaking to the Advance, Stevens said she will continue to stand steadfast with Israel with what little time left she has in office.
“Why would we choose and accept it as normal to just hate one country, one tiny country that is the size of New Jersey? It is not responsible for all of Michigan or America’s problems,” Stevens said. “And in fact, the way that aid packages have always worked is that it is not blank checks. It is not even a direct check. It is money invested into our small businesses from materials, tools, equipment, information technology that then gets sent over to a chosen ally.”



Quotation







They really need to win the next election, and it’s a high risk to go all in and expect those people, who say they’re going to show up, who are advocating for this different policy stance, to show up. They’re trying to do enough to satisfy a broad spectrum of voters and do enough to satisfy young people.


– Nura Sediqe, an assistant professor for Michigan State University’s political science department with a focus on Muslim studies.


It’s a question that the Michigan Democratic Party, and Democrats nationally, are still grappling with as the 2026 general election looms on the horizon. Democrats are making a push to try and take back the majority in both chambers of Congress, and the issue of Israel and Palestine continues to be a flashpoint in some of those campaigns — namely, the U.S. Senate race in Michigan.
Nura Sediqe, an assistant professor for Michigan State University’s political science department with a focus on Muslim studies, said that the Democratic Party has an ingrained “big tent” mentality that aims to draw in as many diverse voters as possible.
That has some caveats, as there are generational divides between younger and older Democratic voters on their policy preferences and values.
“The interests of southeast Michigan and their voter preferences, as we found at least with polling data, look a lot different than what you can find in Northern Michigan,” Sediqe said. “So in a lot of ways, especially in states like Michgian, it’s almost a case study of what’s happening or playing out in the country.”
Sediqe said Michigan Democrats have relied on their older constituent spaces for votes, but there are now much younger and much more vocal elements of the party speaking out and turning out in ways the party hasn’t traditionally seen.
The Israel-Gaza divide was a palpable example of that new push and pull, and Sediqe said some of the double talk from Democrats — supporting Israel but also calling for awareness of the plight in Palestine — was just an example of Democrats being cautious.
“They really need to win the next election, and it’s a high risk to go all in and expect those people, who say they’re going to show up, who are advocating for this different policy stance, to show up,” Sediqe told the Advance. “They’re trying to do enough to satisfy a broad spectrum of voters and do enough to satisfy young people.”
If they do too much, Sediqe said, then the older generations of Democrats who are more in line with Stevens foreign policy stance may not show up to vote on Nov. 3, either.
“They are hedging their bets and I think they are nervous,” she added. “Chuck Schumer is very invested. Everyone’s met with Abdul, and I think they’re invested in the race. If it didn’t hinge so much on Michigan in this way, I think there’d be less pressure.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Videotaped assault of teen at youth jail spurs NJ mom’s demand for justice
description: A teen was injured at a state-run youth jail Saturday in an assault that was video-recorded and posted online. His mom wants justice.
text:
The New Jersey Training School in Monroe Township, one of two youth jails for boys, is slated for closure. Pictured is a housing unit. (Photo courtesy of N.J. Office of the Attorney General)A Burlington County mother is demanding accountability from state youth justice officials after her teenage son was seriously injured during an assault Saturday at the New Jersey Training School in Middlesex County and video of the incident appeared on social media.
Zion Green, 18, of Willingboro, suffered a concussion and was coughing up blood after about six inmates ambushed him outside the showers at the juvenile jail, his mother, Gabrielle Covington-Green, told the New Jersey Monitor. He spent two days recovering in the hospital, she said.
The family learned of the assault by coincidence, when her older son spotted the video Saturday while scrolling Instagram, Covington-Green said. She alleges prison officials did not contact her to let her know her son had been assaulted, injured, and hospitalized. She couldn’t reach anyone at the jail until Sunday to learn what had happened.
“My son was being beat. I wanted to die, I just was so upset and frantic,” she said. “These young men, they commit these crimes but they’re still young men with families. Like my son is not what you would call an adult male, so for you not to contact his mother after he’s had a concussion and was throwing up blood?”
Officials wouldn’t allow the family to do a video visit but permitted a phone call Sunday afternoon, when Green — who sounded “very lethargic and out of it” — told his mother he fell unconscious during a beating he estimated lasted about 10 minutes.
“I said, ‘Where were the guards?’ So at this point, I’m yelling, I’m frantic, and he’s like, ‘There was a guard standing right there,’” Covington-Green said. “He said he watched the whole thing. He said at some point, he told them, ‘Y’all, just chill! Just chill!’”
A lieutenant told her Sunday that the officer guarding the area had been redirected elsewhere to check something, leaving the shower area where Green was assaulted briefly unsupervised, Covington-Green said. The lieutenant blamed a staffing shortage, she said.
He also told her six young men were charged in the incident, she added.
The use of phones and social media is prohibited in prisons, so it’s unclear how someone recorded and posted video of the incident. Covington-Green shared a 42-second clip of the incident with the New Jersey Monitor that her older son was able to screen-record from an Instagram story. In the chaotic, soundless clip, multiple young men appear to hit and wrestle a teen Covington-Green identified as her son, with several participants briefly posing and smiling for the camera.
Tara Oliver is a spokeswoman for the Youth Justice Commission, which oversees the state’s juvenile lockups. She said Monday the incident remains under investigation but declined to comment further.
“The safety and security of YJC residents and staff are priorities,” Oliver said.
William Sullivan, who heads the union that represents correctional officers, confirmed an assault occurred outside a dorm’s downstairs shower area that should have been supervised, but he was still awaiting details on the incident, staffing, and the prison’s response.
He agreed understaffing at the state’s youth jails is “a huge problem,” and that the lockup — known as Jamesburg — has struggled to stop youth there from getting contraband cellphones that outsiders have hurled over the fence along the prison’s wooded perimeter.
“I think the executive staff is kind of turning a blind eye. I really don’t think they know what they’re doing over there because we keep bringing up problems, and they don’t really fix them,” Sullivan said.
About 430 youth now are under state supervision between the state’s three youth jails and probation and parole, according to September data. Jamesburg, which can house about 200 boys, is the state’s largest juvenile lockup.
The prison, which opened in 1867, has long been slated for closure and has a history of abuse.
Green has been there for 13 months on a two-and-a-half-year sentence, Green-Covington said.
She decided to share her concerns publicly because she wants her son’s attackers and prison staff held accountable — and doesn’t trust the system to do so.
“I just want my son to not have to do his time in fear. That’s it,” she said. “I wanted to get the word out, because I know how sometimes they cover up. I wanted to get the word out before there was a cover-up.”
