name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: 2 years into K-12 voucher program, SC leaders don’t know how students are performing
description: Just one in 10 of the students initially enrolled in the program's first year submitted viable testing results, an oversight agency found.
text:
Rep. Neal Collins, R-Easley, pictured the House floor, Wednesday, May 6, 2026, said legislators need better data to decide whether to fund school vouchers in coming years. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — As the third year of a program that gives state money to K-12 students for educational needs, including private school tuition, begins, state leaders don’t know how those students are doing academically.
Under state law, students receiving the roughly $7,500 scholarships to spend on private school tuition, tutoring and other educational needs must take an end-of-year test. Legislators added that requirement to the program, known as the Education Scholarship Trust Fund, to track student performance and make sure the money helped students improve, they said during legislative debates.
But only about one in 10 of the 2,880 students who received funds during the program’s inaugural year reported usable test results, according to a report the Education Oversight Committee heard Monday.
That number wasn’t enough for the agency to present data or draw meaningful conclusions about student performance, executive director Dana Yow told a subcommittee of legislators, educators and business leaders Monday.
SC senators request investigation into use of K-12 vouchers for homeschooling

The lack of testing data means any conclusions likely wouldn’t represent the student population as a whole, Yow said.
On top of the lack of test results, the agency couldn’t measure how scores changed, since the Department of Education didn’t give any data on how students performed the year before. Nor did the department provide demographic information, which the agency uses to account for other factors in a student’s life, or graduation data, which is required by law.
“Before the program’s effect on student learning can be appropriately reported, the data describing that learning must be more complete, more accurate and more transparent,” the report reads.
The Department of Education attributed the gaps in data to growing pains.
In 2024, after the school year started, the state Supreme Court struck down a portion of the program that allowed the money to go toward private school tuition as unconstitutional. That hobbled a program just trying to find its legs, said Meka Childs, director of education choice for the Department of Education.
Legislators reinstated that portion of the program last year, routing the money instead through a trustee tasked with distributing the funds.
As the agency began collecting testing data, officials ran into technical snafus, including rounding up test results directly from parents, who often handwrote their responses, she said.
Those sorts of issues are expected during the first year of a program, said Rep. Shannon Erickson, who leads the House education committee.
“I kind of would like us to think of this first year that we are discussing right now as building a ship in the ocean while it’s floating and a hurricane hits,” the Beaufort Republican said. “That’s really what happened.”
The oversight agency received testing data for the 2025-2026 school year Sept. 12. Agency leaders plan to present that data and what they can use of the 2024-2025 test results during the committee’s December meeting, Yow said.
By the numbers
Nearly 800 students receiving state funds submitted test scores to the state agency.
That’s out of roughly 1,440 students who finished the 2024-2025 school year in the program, which at the time offered $6,000 for up to 5,000 students.
That school year started with around 2,880 students, but roughly half withdrew before the end of the year. Some left after the state Supreme Court’s decision ended the use of funds for private school tuition, though private donors stepped in to fund tuition for most of those students, allowing them to use the money for other purposes. Around 1,000 students were removed from the program for failing to switch schools as the law required.
Up to 1,000 ineligible SC students booted from voucher program, report finds

Other students and parents left because they decided the program wasn’t for them, Childs said. She didn’t give numbers for how many students fell in each category.
Out of the nearly 800 test results the oversight agency received, most were unusable for data analysis, according to the report.
Students in kindergarten through second grade submitted about a fifth of the tests, which the oversight agency didn’t use because students in those grades are exempt from the testing requirement.
The agency chalked about 50 of the tests up to errors, since they were dated outside of the 2024-2025 school year.
About a third of the tests, 273 of the total, fell outside the agency’s parameters for various reasons. State law requires tests to have approval from the department, fall in line with state standards and include research showing how they compare to other tests.
In some cases, students took a test designed for a grade level other than the one they were in, which would violate the requirements of state standards. Others took tests the department didn’t approve. Some took tests that had department approval but didn’t align with South Carolina’s standards.
The oversight agency doesn’t report data that applies to fewer than 20 students because smaller sample sizes could make it possible to track down specific students, causing the numbers to dwindle further.
After tossing most of the data, the agency decided the results left created “a sample too limited and too unlikely to represent all participants to serve as a reliable basis for conclusions about student outcomes,” the report reads.
The oversight agency didn’t receive test results for nearly 630 students.
Most weren’t required to submit a test. Of those, 446 were in kindergarten through second grade, and six had a documented disability, another exemption from the testing rule. Those students are required to submit separate coursework to prove they’re taking classes.
The agency removed 42 children from the program for the next year because they didn’t submit testing data. Another 102 were seniors in high school, meaning they were supposed to submit test results but had no consequences if they didn’t, since they aged out of the program the next year anyway, according to the oversight committee.
The department is working with 19 families who submitted testing data but had some sort of technical issue, according to the report.
‘A failure’
Inaccurate test results can hurt students, said Melissa Pender, a member of the committee and executive director of schools for Beaufort County School District.
If a child who took an unapproved test dropped out of the program and went back to public school, teachers can use their previous test results to gauge how well that student is performing in a certain subject, she said.
“Having a state-aligned assessment that a school can use when they come back in is very valuable for a school,” Pender said.
SC Senate spending plan would disallow K-12 vouchers for homeschoolers

Testing requirements go beyond the test itself, Pender said. Research also suggests ideal timelines for children to take assessments, when they are at the peak retention for information they learned.
Testing too early or too late in the year could skew results. Although the Department of Education encourages schools to give tests within the same window as public school districts, the law has no requirement about when they have to take them.
Without test results, legislators have no way to make sure the program is working, said Rep. Neal Collins, a member of the oversight committee and a frequent critic of the voucher program.
The vouchers were initially pitched as a way of helping low-income students stuck in failing schools get access to resources their parents couldn’t otherwise afford.
This year, the money can go to students whose parents make up to 500% of the federal poverty level, or $165,000 for a family of four.
Legislators have spent more than $170 million on the program. They have to know that money is going toward actually improving outcomes for students, Collins said.
When a student fails to comply with the program’s rules, including failing to submit test results, removing them from the program isn’t enough, Collins said. Since test results typically come at the end of the year, parents have already spent thousands of taxpayer dollars the state can’t get back, he said.
“We need proof up front,” the Easley Republican said. “Show us that your voucher works. Then we’ll fund you. Don’t fund and then all bets are off.”
With the entire first year of testing data unusable, legislators essentially spent that money without any idea whether it actually helped students improve, he said.
“I think it’s a failure,” Collins said.
What comes next
Legislators need to know exactly how students performed, and they need to know as quickly as possible, Collins said.
State agencies start submitting their requests for state funding in September, and legislators begin to assemble their annual budget in January. That includes any spots in the program the Department of Education wants legislators to fund beyond the floor of 15,000 students.
“I need the data, I need the accountability, to see if it’s worth investing in,” Collins said.
He asked for the education department to give results as soon as the school year ends and for the Education Oversight Committee to analyze the data right away.
The data is difficult to analyze and understand, Yow said. In 2024-2025, students submitted results from 23 different tests, and agency staff have to go through and figure out how they compare.
When legislators revived the law last year to reinstate the private school tuition portion, they also expanded the testing options families can use, Yow said.
SC students booted from K-12 voucher program spent $64K. The problem didn’t repeat, report says

“That’s too much, when we’re talking about a very small subset of students,” Yow said. “We can’t get our arms around that.”
The Department of Education also needs longer to collect the data than it does with traditional public schools because the results are coming from public schools, private schools and, in some cases, parents, Childs said.
“While I understand the desire to have everything immediately, the reality is, it does take time to pull the data in,” Childs said.
The oversight committee recommended the Department of Education start delivering test results on a regular schedule, similar to when the department releases public school testing data.
The oversight agency also asked that the department digitize all of its results, avoiding the difficulty of analyzing handwritten submissions, and that it collect all the required data, including graduation data and students’ testing data for the prior year.
The education department is in the process of making some of those changes, including standardizing systems and setting deadlines for the data, Childs said.
“We do have to bear in mind that this is a new program and we are building out those systems and we are much better than we were and will continue to strengthen,” she said.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Departing congressman says voter choices and Trump’s ‘lost focus’ contribute to DC’s troubles
description: SIOUX FALLS — Partisan squabbles are keeping Congress from effecting change, and President Donald Trump has made it worse when he has “lost focus,” said South Dakota Republican U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, who added that he finds many of Trump’s personal characteristics “lacking.” Johnson, who will leave office in January, aired his frustrations about national [[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, speaks to members of the Downtown Sioux Falls Rotary Club on Sept. 21, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS — Partisan squabbles are keeping Congress from effecting change, and President Donald Trump has made it worse when he has “lost focus,” said South Dakota Republican U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, who added that he finds many of Trump’s personal characteristics “lacking.”
Johnson, who will leave office in January, aired his frustrations about national politics and celebrated his staff and some colleagues at a Sioux Falls Downtown Rotary Club meeting Monday. During a question-and-answer session, he reflected on his eight years in Congress.
“I won’t miss the circus, but I’ll miss the clowns,” Johnson said.
Q&A: Dusty Johnson analyzes his defeat and future, saying ‘I want to lead a life of consequence’

Afterward, Johnson told reporters he believes the Republican Party is “well positioned” on national policy and is “going to get some much needed wins” by January, before a new Congress convenes. Beyond that, it’s more complicated.
The central problem, Johnson said, is voters choosing to vote for “somebody they think is fighting rather than for somebody who is getting things done.”
“If the voters don’t start voting for thoughtful problem solvers a little more often, then I think we’re going to continue to find it hard to get things done quite as often as we should in D.C.,” Johnson said.
He said the anger and frustration in politics at all levels will eventually shift and the “fever will break,” but that’s “clearly not where we’re at today.”
Johnson chose not to run for reelection to the U.S. House and lost his bid for South Dakota governor in the June Republican primary. He previously served as a member of the state Public Utilities Commission and as chief of staff for former Gov. Dennis Daugaard.
Johnson did not share specific plans Monday about his future.
“I want my next 20 years to be as impactful as my last 20 years,” he said.
The following Q&A is excerpted from the Rotary meeting and has been edited for length and clarity. Questions came from a Rotary moderator and a Rotary member.
Q: You’re heading into the final months of your eighth year as South Dakota’s lone representative. What was it like coming into the office as a freshman representative and what did you learn in those first few years?
A: I think I was a little surprised. I had run in no small part because I just thought there were too many jerks in politics, and, of course, there are, although the ratio is a lot lower than I expected. In the end, I sort of felt naive. I had done what most people do, which is assume that the 10 or 15 members of the United States House that you can name — your Marjorie Taylor Greenes or your Alexandria Ocasio-Cortezes — are representative of the whole. And they’re really not. 
So the big surprise for me was how many decent human beings, really successful inventors or nonprofit executives or four-star generals, successful educators, nurses, just really great human beings are there. 
I’m not going to try to convince you that we do a good job, for reasons I still don’t entirely comprehend. The whole is less than the sum of our parts, but the inputs, the human beings, I was surprised by how decent most of them are. 
Q: How have things evolved or how has your approach to tackling issues evolved?
A: I try to be an optimist, but I don’t want to just whisper sweet nothings in your ear. I think things are markedly worse in D.C. than when I arrived eight years ago. I don’t blame me, but I do think the tribalism is much higher. I think the populist rage and angst is much higher. 
All of the incentives in the system reward bad behavior and so most members, of course, they’re good people, so they do want to serve, they want to make the right decisions. They also want to survive. But I think they understand that, walking through the field of public policy, there are almost an inexplicably large number of landmines that can just end a career on any given day because you say this about data centers, or you say that about January 6th, or you say this about vaccines or that about Lake Ontario. I think it creates that survival versus serve dichotomy. 
I think that there’s more tension there than there would have been five years ago and 10 years ago. I think it is a very, very difficult time to serve. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
More of my colleagues in the House have lost their primaries for Senate, for governor — not to pick any scabs — or their own House race than at any point that I can recollect. Two dozen of them, which is really unusual. 
Normally if you’re running for the U.S. House, for your own job or higher office, you’re very well positioned. People generally know you, you generally have a campaign team, you know how to raise money, you’ve got some accomplishments to run on. Now, service of that kind is a pretty substantial albatross around someone’s neck. 
Fewer and fewer of my colleagues are excited about running, and I think fewer and fewer really decent people are running for the first time. Now, the problem for all of this is that we’re getting a barely functional government with great inputs. If we get only mediocre inputs, I’m concerned that we will not even meet the functional standards. 
Q: What’s the Dusty spin on that?
A: I still think there’s tremendous optimism in the American private sector. We’re going to cure cancer and we’re going to cure Type 1 diabetes and we are figuring out how to do a better job of housing people in an increasingly inflationary environment. Outside of D.C., there’s a lot of reason for optimism.
I think city governments in this state are generally run pretty well. Most local governments in this state choose progress over drama, and I think that’s true for our state government as well. Always be hesitant when someone wants to centralize more power in Washington, as, unfortunately, more and more in my party seem to want to do. We’re the party of federalism and yet we sometimes like big government conservatism. Be wary about centralizing more power into the less functional level of government.
Q: You’ve experienced three different administrations while you’ve been in Congress. What was different between the three?
A: I would focus on the commonalities between those three, and that is when the administration was focused it was pretty effective and it got good things done — regardless of whether you’re talking about Trump 1.0, Biden or Trump 2.0.
I think we do get into trouble when there’s a lack of focus, and I try to tell the president and his team that, “If we’re talking about the border, middle class tax cuts, a return to common sense and some of the social issues where most Americans believe the pendulum has swung too far, that’s where we’re going to be able to build. If we are fighting about the reflecting pool and renaming Lake Ontario, we’ve lost focus. I think that can make it more difficult for your party to do well in November, sir.”
Any of those three administrations, when they lost focus and discipline, our country was poorly served.
Q: You’ve been a close adviser to Speaker Mike Johnson over the past several years. Tell us about how you were tapped for that role and what it’s been like to help lead him as he became a new speaker.
A: It really started with Speaker Kevin McCarthy. I went to D.C. and I thought that the lane I was going to carve out was being the dorky little policy guy, which of course I am, but I really was going to be a committee leader not in title but that people knew that if they wanted to understand Title I programs and how they interact with crop insurance or county averages they’d say, “Go to Dusty. He understands the issue.”
I was lucky enough to be in the right time and the right place to give the right people counsel. McCarthy said, “Hey, I’ve got to have you in some of these rooms. We’re negotiating the Fiscal Responsibility Act with a Democratic Senate and a Democratic president. We don’t want to default on debt, we do need to spend less money, we do need to reform welfare. I need you in the room as part of the negotiating team behind the scenes.”


Let us know what you think...


 

That was like being a backup quarterback. You never know when you’re going to get the call, but you go out and understand the playbook and assignments, and you make sure you hit people, run the routes, then you’re going to get an opportunity to help the team again.
When McCarthy was thrown out of office, the natural inclination for Mike Johnson is to get rid of the old team because they’ve just been fired. Mike and I had a pre-existing personal relationship and I was held over in Mike’s cabinet. I’m sure everybody here has very legitimate criticisms of Mike Johnson, but I have to tell you it would not be easy to govern in an incredibly dysfunctional time with an incredibly dysfunctional U.S. House. The fact that we haven’t defaulted on the debts that we have, I would say the U.S. House has been somewhat more functional than people had any right to expect, and I think Mike Johnson is a huge part of that.
Q: How do you assess the personal character of President Trump?
A: I find many of his personal characteristics lacking. Particularly, as I talked about, the lack of focus can be problematic for our country. That being said, I do think that we’re so tribal in this nation anymore. While some are too ready to celebrate his every act, some are too willing to denigrate his every act. I think securing the southern border — that kind of clarity of conviction and willingness to get it done, I think, is the kind of bold leadership that caused his supporters to continue to view him favorably.
Clearly, he is too quick to criticize others, particularly with personal insults. I think he doesn’t value our allies and friendships abroad as much as I do, and I don’t think he values some of these institutional norms, which I think are part of the American success story.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Residential property insurance projected to jump in North Dakota, analysis shows
description: Residential property insurance rates are projected to increase 26% from 2025 to 2028 in North Dakota, according to American Property Casualty Insurance Association figures presented Monday in Bismarck. Insurance Commissioner Jon Godfread said the projected jump follows an average increase of about 14% that North Dakota property owners saw between 2024 and 20[...]
text:
North Dakota Insurance Commissioner Jon Godfread speaks to members of a Residential Resiliency Roundtable, hosted by the American Property Casualty Insurance Association, at the Bismarck Event Center on Sept. 21, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Residential property insurance rates are projected to increase 26% from 2025 to 2028 in North Dakota, according to American Property Casualty Insurance Association figures presented Monday in Bismarck.
Insurance Commissioner Jon Godfread said the projected jump follows an average increase of about 14% that North Dakota property owners saw between 2024 and 2025.
“It doesn’t mean that every North Dakotan is going to face a 26% increase; this was commercial, residential and multi-family businesses,” Godfread said during a North Dakota Residential Resiliency Roundtable. “But it’s absolutely a signal that’s worth taking seriously.”
Godfread said insurance premiums are increasing in part because the costs of labor and materials are going up. 
“Labor costs more, materials cost more, if homes cost more, then the same storm produces more expensive damage that eventually does show up in your premiums,” Godfread said.
The state has done a good job in mitigating potential flooding, Godfread said, with projects in Grand Forks, Fargo, Minot and the Garrison Dam.
“We’ve taken that very seriously to address the flood mitigation problems, and we need to put that same kind of energy and effort into community resiliency,” he said.
Godfread said North Dakota has a statewide building code but no dedicated enforcement division to conduct inspections. He added that lack of enforcement can give insurers pause when determining insurance rates.
“It’s generally left to the local communities to enforce that code, and that means inspections, and that means going out and making sure that these buildings are built to appropriate standards,” Godfread said. “And I question how much we are doing that.”
He said fire inspections are conducted through the State Fire Marshal’s Office and local fire departments, but they are only looking at fire concerns, not the types of materials being used during construction and whether the structures are up to code.
The construction contractors are typically responsible for ensuring new buildings adhere to building codes, Godfread said. The only time his office or the insurance industry discovers a problem with a structure is after a catastrophic loss or collapse, he added.
“I think we need to start having some serious conversations on doing what the rest of the country does and start investing in some of those inspections,” Godfread said. “Every citizen in North Dakota deserves safe buildings to go into.”
Godfread said he was not accusing the construction industry of not following the state’s building code, but the insurance industry won’t know if building codes are being followed unless inspections take place.
Jill Beck, CEO of the North Dakota Association of Realtors, said she worries homebuyers are not pricing in the increasing insurance rates when they are shopping for a home.
Older roofs are also a concern, Beck said, as more buyers are not able to acquire insurance or mortgages for some homes with dated roofs.
“We need to do education with homesellers about the age of their roof, and they might not be able to get a typical mortgage buyer because of the age of the roof,” she said.
Brad Nold, chief claims officer for the North Dakota Farmers Union, said cheaper insurance plans may not cover everything that farmers need to be fully insured. He said he recommends farmers sit with a licensed insurance agent, shop around to compare insurance plans and understand everything that is in their policy before making a commitment.
“The No. 1 thing is education,” Nold said. “Too many people go out and buy an insurance policy based strictly on price.”
Farmers may need to make decisions on whether to insure older outbuildings as a way to keep costs down, Nold said. 
“If you have two old buildings that are about to fall down anyway, why would you want to pay a premium to insure that?” Nold said. 
Godfread said North Dakota is still a “good risk” state for insurance providers to conduct business due to predictable weather patterns and fewer potential losses, which can drive down insurance costs.
“The challenge that we have is that we’re 800,000 people and the economies of scale get a little bit tough,” he said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan House committee probes canvassing process amid dispute over citizen-only voting signatures
description: Frustrations from proponents of a failed ballot initiative that would have required Michigan residents to verify their citizenship in order to cast their vote had led members of a state House panel to examine how state officials determine which questions should make the ballot. That work started last week with the House Select Committee on […]
text:
Flags atop the Michigan State Capitol dome. April 30, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Frustrations from proponents of a failed ballot initiative that would have required Michigan residents to verify their citizenship in order to cast their vote had led members of a state House panel to examine how state officials determine which questions should make the ballot.
That work started last week with the House Select Committee on the Rules and Procedures of the State Board of Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections, as the joint committee held an introductory meeting.
Work from the committee continued on Monday, with House lawmakers hearing from Paul Jacob, the chair of Americans for Citizen Voting-Michigan. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The citizen-only voting effort died on Aug. 24, when canvassers failed to certify petitions for the initiative as the bipartisan board split along party lines, with the two Democrats on the panel voting against certification. 
Prior to the meeting, Bureau of Elections staff advised against certifying the ballot measure, after a random sample of signatures gathered by the ballot committee failed to meet the threshold of valid signatures to receive approval.
After the Michigan Supreme Court and the United States Supreme Court declined to hear Americans for Citizen Voting-Michigan’s bid to overturn the Board of State Canvassers decision, the group is looking towards another attempt in the 2028 election cycle.
Jacob voiced frustrations with several steps in the canvassing process, from the amount of time it took members of the Board of State Canvassers to consider the ballot proposal, to the board’s decisions on whether certain signatures should be considered valid.
Jacob contended that the group submitted more than enough valid signatures when they dropped off their petitions with the Board of State Canvassers in March, and that they had worked to verify the names and addresses of those who signed their petitions — crossing off duplicate signatures and making other checks to their petition sheets.
He raised concerns with the bureau’s timeline in reviewing the effort’s  signatures, telling committee members that when the Bureau of Elections released its Aug.17 report, which found that their signatures had fallen short of the threshold needed for certification, the group had but days to respond.
Paul Jacob, the chair of Americans for Citizen Voting-Michigan, testified before members of the House Select Committee on the Rules and Procedures of the State Board of Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections on Monday Sept. 21, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
In its report, the Bureau of Elections reviewed a random sample of 1,000 signatures, determining 308 of the signatures in that sample were invalid. 
Ninety-two of those signatures were invalid, meaning an entry either lacked a signature, or the signature included did not match that person’s signature in the Qualified Voter File. 
“Neither we nor our attorney were allowed to review those voter signatures, the evidence used against us, serious denial of due process,” Jacob said. “Nothing is more un-American than not being able to see the evidence used against you.”
Ahead of the Board of State Canvassers meeting, Jacob said they set out to find as many of those individuals as possible, ultimately filing 23 sworn affidavits from individuals attesting that their signature was on the petition.
Of the 23 affidavits submitted, 14 were accepted by the bureau and agreed upon by the Board of State Canvassers, though Americans for Citizen Voting-Michigan ultimately came up three signatures short of the 629 valid signatures it needed within the sample.
In reviewing their petitions, Jacob said the Bureau of Elections had adopted a “when in doubt, throw it out” mentality.
“The behavior of the Bureau of Elections toward this petition and the partisan deadlock that is the nature of the Board of Canvassers denied Michigan voters their rights and squelched this citizen participation,” Jacob said. “The citizen-only voting petition met the legal requirement to be on the ballot and is not on the ballot. This is what voter suppression looks like.”
After the hearing, Jacob said the bureau’s rules should be placed into state law.
Jacob told Michigan Advance that “laws are all about clarity and fairness, and if they’re not fair, you can take them to court. Rules can be slippery.”
He also criticized the bipartisan makeup of the Board of State Canvassers, noting that while its design is intended to prevent partisanship, the two-Republican, two-Democrat makeup means the board is designed to deadlock.
Jacob also argued that the Bureau of Elections should adopt a first-in, first-out approach to processing petitions.
However, Mark Brewer, a longtime election attorney and former Michigan Democratic Party chair who represented Promote the Vote Action in opposing the citizen-only voting effort, said the bureau has other jobs to do and deadlines to meet.
During the Board of State Canvassers’ March meeting, Michigan Director of Elections Jonathan Brater said that there are three petition timelines that run in tight windows. 
The petitions are processed in the order of those deadlines, Brater said, noting that if the bureau has a window, they will process efforts that come in ahead of the deadline as quickly as they can.
The bureau would not have been able to finish canvassing the citizen-only voting initiative before it needed to shift to processing candidate nominating petitions, Brater added.
If Americans for Citizen Voting-Michigan wanted to address their timeline concerns, they should have filed their signatures earlier, as the group was cleared to begin gathering signatures in July 2025, Brewer said.
“These are like two- and four-year projects, right?” Brewer said. “You got to plan it all out, and again, you can control much of this if you think ahead. Because none of this is secret. All this is laid out in the statute, in the procedures of the board.”
While Jacob argued that the bureau shouldn’t be invalidating signatures that the proponents of petitions don’t get to see, Brewer said allowing outside parties to see the signatures housed in the qualified voter file could open voters up to identity theft and forgery.
In addition to comparing the information on the petitions with address and voter registration information in the Qualified Voter File, committees can  also validate their signatures by reviewing past petitions and requesting absentee ballot applications or envelopes through the Freedom of Information Act, Angela Benander, the chief communications officer for Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, said in an email.
“Their goal was simply volume,” Brewer said of the citizen-only voting effort. “They thought if we just collect enough signatures, we’re going to be okay, and that was their fatal mistake.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: New lawsuit alleges unfair secrecy around Effingham data center
description: A group of plaintiffs is asking a judge to declare that the Effingham County Industrial Development Authority unfairly did public business in private and to throw out the agency’s deals with OpenAI affiliate Octans Georgia for a data center near Rincon. Five county residents plus the nonprofit environmental group One Hundred Miles allege that the […]
text:
A pine forest covers the future site of the OpenAI data center at the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub in Effingham County on July 27, 2026. The $20 billion project was announced last week, surprising many local residents. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for AmericaA group of plaintiffs is asking a judge to declare that the Effingham County Industrial Development Authority unfairly did public business in private and to throw out the agency’s deals with OpenAI affiliate Octans Georgia for a data center near Rincon.
Five county residents plus the nonprofit environmental group One Hundred Miles allege that the county development authority didn’t provide proper notice or a meaningful agenda for the key July board vote that bound the community’s land to the maker of ChatGPT software and granted the company a 50% property tax break.
The plaintiffs, represented by counsel from the nonprofit Southern Environmental Law Center, also claim that the authority has failed to publicly discuss the sale of land to Octans or to hand over information about the transaction.
“Georgia’s public process rules exist because communities should not learn about major decisions only after deals have been negotiated behind closed doors,” said SELC attorney Zachary Henneesee, in a press release announcing the lawsuit filed in Effingham County Superior Court. “The Effingham County Industrial Development Authority must follow the law and give the public a real opportunity to be heard.”
The development authority “respects the legal process and will carefully review the allegations once it receives formal notice,” an authority spokesperson said via email Monday afternoon. “It would be inappropriate to comment on the claims before the ECIDA and its legal counsel have had an opportunity to review the filing.”
The lawsuit comes as the county commission has given itself more time to review Octans’ plan for the roughly 1,440-acre site. A vote was originally set for the commission’s regularly scheduled meeting on Sept. 15, the same day the conservative AI Data Center Revolt bus rolled into town and speakers protested the secrecy around the deal. Democratic U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock made the same charges about secrecy last month, when he visited Effingham County and called for a data center moratorium in the state.
The county development authority has spent tens of thousands of dollars on countering public anger about the data center, which will use as much electricity as about 2 million houses, generated at thirsty and polluting power plants.
A separate lawsuit alleges that the county itself skipped a required public review of the zoning rules that have paved the way for Octans to plan a data center.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Trump ‘can make his own decisions,’ governor says after witnessing president’s rant about journalism
description: After pledging to protect press freedoms throughout his nearly two years in office, Republican South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden found himself standing in front of reporters Friday with President Donald Trump as the president defended a decision to ban three news organizations from the White House. Rhoden was in the Oval Office for an unrelated […]
text:
President Donald Trump is joined, from left, by South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden, Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Dr. Mehmet Oz, U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves as Trump speaks to reporters about healthcare in the Oval Office at the White House on Sept. 18, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)After pledging to protect press freedoms throughout his nearly two years in office, Republican South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden found himself standing in front of reporters Friday with President Donald Trump as the president defended a decision to ban three news organizations from the White House.
Rhoden was in the Oval Office for an unrelated reason: to talk about Trump administration efforts to save money on prescription drugs in the federal-state Medicaid health insurance program for people with low incomes.
Earlier that day, Trump announced on social media that he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House. Reporters asked Trump about that decision when Trump, Rhoden and several other officials — who were standing behind Trump as he sat at his desk — finished speaking about the prescription drug program.
CNN, MS Now, Politico sue Trump over White House ban

Trump responded by alleging that the news organizations report “fake news,” and he expanded at length on those allegations. The three news organizations have since sued to regain their access.
South Dakota Searchlight asked Rhoden’s office Monday for the governor’s reaction to Trump’s actions and comments. Rhoden’s office sent a written statement that said “the president can make his own decisions.”
“I’ve built a strong relationship with all of you by being open and responsive, and you’ve lived up to my trust,” Rhoden said in the statement, referencing journalists in South Dakota. “You’ve shown me a tremendous deal of respect, and I am grateful for the role you play in helping us serve the people of South Dakota.”
Searchlight then asked if Rhoden was implying his office would not be open and responsive to journalists who haven’t “lived up” to the governor’s trust.
Rhoden’s spokesperson, Josie Harms, responded.
“That implication is inaccurate,” Harms wrote. “Openness and responsiveness will continue to remain pillars of the Rhoden administration — the governor is simply acknowledging his respect and gratefulness for your reciprocation of that commitment.”
The governor’s initial statement also said it was “ironic” that the president “was being criticized for being against free speech while Trump was actively taking questions from dozens of media.”
Searchlight asked if the governor recognized that three news organizations were losing their access to ask questions of Trump. Harms replied, “As the governor said, ‘The president can make his own decisions.’”
Rhoden’s past comments on open government
Since becoming governor in January 2025, Rhoden has repeatedly emphasized government transparency and has made improving relations with the press one of his stated goals.
In a 2025 column he sent to media outlets titled “Protecting Our Free Press,” Rhoden wrote that “tough, investigative reporting can lead to much-needed policy reforms.”
“I’m committed to making my administration the most transparent in our state’s history,” he wrote.
During the annual NewsMedia Day at the state Capitol earlier this year, Rhoden responded to questions from reporters about open government.
“We’ll always do our best to respond to your questions, and you might not always like the answers you get, but you’ll always get a response of some kind,” Rhoden said.
Rhoden’s opponent in the Nov. 3 election is Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, a former legislator from Dell Rapids. Ahlers said Trump’s strategy since becoming president the first time has been to criticize and belittle reporters when he doesn’t like their reporting.
“I don’t hold a grudge against the press,” Ahlers said. “I don’t not communicate with the press when something doesn’t go my way.”
Trump suggests his face on Rushmore amid healthcare talk
Rhoden’s Friday appearance at the White House was for Trump’s announcement that all 50 states will join a program providing “Most Favored Nation” pricing to some drugs in Medicaid, with a goal of bringing the price of selected drugs down to prices paid in some other countries.
Rhoden’s office issued a press release Friday saying South Dakota has so far identified three drugs that would benefit from the program, saving the state approximately $750,000 a year. This year’s budget for Medicaid in South Dakota is about $2 billion, and the state’s share is about $715 million.
After Rhoden’s comments on the prescription drug program during the Oval Office event, Trump turned to him and made a comment about Mount Rushmore National Memorial that sparked laughter in the room.
“I’m being very nice to him,” Trump said of Rhoden, “because maybe he’ll get my face on that beautiful wall.”
Rhoden jokingly replied, “You want it on Crazy Horse?” He was referencing the other massive mountain carving in South Dakota’s Black Hills. The Crazy Horse Memorial, which has been in progress for decades, honors a late Lakota war leader.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. sheds 7,100 jobs in August as losses mount
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: The total number of job losses in the last two months –  about 11,100 – almost matches the jobs gained since September.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS LOST 7,100 JOBS in August, bringing the total number of job losses in the last two months to about 11,100 – almost matching the jobs gained since September, according to preliminary data the Executive Office of Labor and Workforce Development released on Friday.
The labor office also revised its July estimate to a loss of 4,000 jobs, from an initially reported loss of 4,600 jobs. Labor officials say the state has netted 11,300 new jobs since September 2025. State data shows Massachusetts added 8,300 jobs from August 2025 to August 2026. October 2025 data are missing due to a federal government shutdown.
According to the labor office’s data, sectors seeing job losses in August were professional and business services (down 6,400); trade, transportation and utilities (down 1,400); construction (down 1,400); private education and health (down 700); and other services (down 300). Sectors with job growth were manufacturing (up 1,400); information (up 800); leisure and hospitality (up 400); financial activities (up 300); and government (up 200).
The Massachusetts unemployment rate dropped to 4.3 percent, down from July’s 4.4 percent, according to labor officials. That marks the state’s lowest unemployment rate since March 2025, according to Mark Rembert, chief economist at the Department of Economic Research. The U.S. jobless rate was 4.1 percent in August.
“While retirements among older workers continue to limit labor force growth, Massachusetts is experiencing relatively low unemployment among workers aged 25 to 54,” Rembert said. “Over the past twelve months, the unemployment rate among workers aged 25-54 in Massachusetts was lower than peer states like Texas, New Jersey, New York, and California.”
The state’s labor force participation rate was 65.3 percent in August, compared with the nation’s 61.6 percent, according to labor officials. Last month, the labor force rose by 900, with 3,100 more people employed and 2,200 fewer unemployed residents. Labor officials say those figures include residents who have retired or left the workforce as well as self-employed workers and entrepreneurs.
The latest jobs figures come about six weeks out from the November 3 general election. Republicans, including gubernatorial nominee Mike Minogue, are seeking to gain traction by criticizing the state’s scarce job growth under Democrats’ leadership and the Bay State’s low economic growth metrics compared to other states. Meanwhile, Democrats like Gov. Maura Healey have highlighted business expansions and additions as well as state investments aimed at creating jobs and bolstering the workforce development pipeline.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Journalist, attorney honored with Freedom of Information awards
description: The Montana Freedom of Information Coalition honored two Montanans at a ceremony last Thursday for work done to increase the public’s right to know about state government.  Missoula broadcast journalist Anna Rau and Bozeman attorney Kyle Nelson were awarded the organization’s John Kuglin FOI Champion Award, according to a press release.  “We usually give one[...]
text:
Kyle Nelson and Anna Rau are honored for their work by the Montana Freedom of Information Coalition. (Courtesy photo)The Montana Freedom of Information Coalition honored two Montanans at a ceremony last Thursday for work done to increase the public’s right to know about state government. 
Missoula broadcast journalist Anna Rau and Bozeman attorney Kyle Nelson were awarded the organization’s John Kuglin FOI Champion Award, according to a press release. 
“We usually give one annual FOI Champion award, but Anna and Kyle each made such vital contributions to advancing the public’s right to know in Montana this past year, that we decided to honor them both,” said Mike Dennison, president of the coalition.
Rau, a journalist with Montana PBS, produced a half-hour show this spring revealing that Gov. Greg Gianforte’s administration had suppressed a report showing dangerous levels of chemical contaminations in fish found in Montana waterways. 
The state released the report in April, one day before Rau’s investigative piece aired on Montana PBS’ “Impact” news series. 
Nelson was involved in two major freedom of information court victories for Montana media this year, including unsealing charging documents in a 2025 homicide case in Anaconda and maintaining public access to legislative bill drafting information. 
Jim Strauss, an FOI Coalition board member, said that Nelson’s work not only was critical in those cases, but also provided at an affordable rate – at a time when media resources for legal battles are stretched thin.
The Daily Montanan was part of a media coalition that sued for access to the charging documents and Nelson argued in a court appeal that the district judge in the case had failed to consult the media, which is part of state law. 
The Montana Supreme Court unanimously ruled in favor of the press.
“The win preserves transparency in a high-profile homicide case and it also prevents a dangerous precedent that would have allowed public officials to keep documents secret,” Montana FOI Coalition board member Keila Szpaller said Thursday in her nomination speech for Nelson.
Nelson also won a victory in state district court in 2025 that said materials used to draft legislation must remain open and available to the public. That case is currently pending before the Montana Supreme Court. The Daily Montanan was also involved in this lawsuit as part of a media coalition. 
Rau’s award-winning story found state scientists prepared a 2024 report warning anglers not to eat many types of fish found in Montana waterways due to elevated chemical levels above acceptable safety standards. Rau found records that showed Gianforte’s office had blocked the release in February 2025, and ultimately did not release it for more than a year, just before Rau’s report aired. 
Rau said she often relied on help from the Montana Freedom of Information Coalition when preparing information requests for her reporting. 
The coalition’s John Kuglin FOI Champion Award is named after the late former Associated Press Montana bureau chief, who was instrumental in establishing the coalition 38 years ago.
The Montana Freedom of Information Coalition, formerly the Montana FOI Hotline, has helped provide free open records and open meeting legal advice to members of the public since 1988. 
The coalition is supported by the Associated Press, the Montana Newspaper Association, the Montana Broadcasters Association, the University of Montana School of Journalism and the Montana Transparency Project as well as individual newsrooms, including the Daily Montanan. 
Editor’s Note: Daily Montanan deputy editor Keila Szpaller is a board member with the coalition. Szpaller was not involved in the editorial process of this story.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Election Commission violated open meetings law, ACLU alleges
description: The SC chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union is suing the state Election Commission, accusing its members of illegally conducting public business behind closed doors.
text:
State Election Commission Chairman Dennis Shedd, along with commissioners Scott Moseley, Clifford Edler and JoAnne Day, meet on Wednesday, Oct. 15, at the elections office in Columbia, S.C. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A civil liberties watchdog is alleging the South Carolina elections office violated public meetings law when it fired its previous director.
The state chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union is suing the state Election Commission in a Richland County court, accusing its members of illegally conducting public business behind closed doors.
In court filings, the organization accused the former chairman of the five-member board, appointed by the governor, of calling other members to lobby for the removal of former state elections chief Howard Knapp. The group also alleges the board polled its members on Knapp’s removal in a closed-door meeting before taking the official vote in public.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State Election Commission spokeswoman Sydni Bain said the agency is aware of the complaint, but as a matter of policy, it does not comment on ongoing litigation.
“Last year, the State Election Commission removed South Carolina’s top election official after a secret trial, secret deliberations and a secret vote. We’re going to court because the Freedom of Information Act guarantees more transparency than that,” the ACLU’s legal director Allen Chaney said in a statement.
State public records law states “no chance meeting, social meeting or electronic communication” may be used to circumvent a public meeting. And “a public body may not commit the public body to a course of action by a polling of members in executive session.”
The State Election Commission fired Knapp on Sept. 17 in a 3-2 vote. At the time, former Chairman Dennis Shedd said in a statement the commission fired Knapp out of a desire for new leadership.
Chairman of SC Election Commission resigns, saying recent chaos is over

Shedd also said the decision was “unrelated to the conduct of any election in South Carolina.”
“The Commission’s leadership and staff remain dedicated to ensuring South Carolina’s elections are accurate, secure, and accessible,” Shedd said.
The commission declined to make any further comment.
Knapp’s firing came amid a lawsuit trying to stop the Election Commission from providing the information of about 3.3 million registered voters to the U.S. Department of Justice over privacy concerns.
Earlier that month, the state Supreme Court overruled a circuit court’s pause on providing that information, clearing the way for the commission to begin handing over names, birthdays, addresses, driver’s license numbers and final digits of Social Security numbers.
Knapp resisted the federal government’s demands for access to South Carolina voter data, the ACLU wrote in court documents.
“That resistance provoked the ire of President Trump’s allies in South Carolina, including the Governor and some members of the SEC,” the organization’s lawyers wrote.
Judge refuses to block voter data transfer, noting election agency’s promise to sign agreement first

In phone discussions with other board members, Shedd accused Knapp of colluding with opposing lawyers in the lawsuit seeking to block the information’s release, the ACLU said.
In its court filing, the ACLU did not state how it came to learn about these phone discussions. Nor did its lawyers say how they learned of the poll taken behind closed doors.
The organization did not respond to the SC Daily Gazette’s questions about the phone discussions or poll.
The organization’s court filings alleged Shedd also had used similar methods to try to oust Knapp in early 2024. In March of that year, the SC State Law Enforcement Division, at the request of the state attorney general’s office, had launched an investigation into Knapp over unspecified allegations of misconduct.
About a month after Knapp’s firing, police arrested him on embezzlement and misconduct-in-office charges related to his use of state-provided vehicles over eight months starting in 2023.
He faces 11 charges total, brought by the Attorney General’s office. They include eight counts of using his official position or office for financial gain — one for each month he’s accused of using state vehicles for personal travel and a public credit card to fuel up. He’s also charged with embezzlement of public funds valued at less than $10,000 (for the fuel), misconduct in office and accessory to a felony after the fact, according to Richland County court records.
Fired SC elections chief charged with embezzlement, misconduct

That case is ongoing.
Knapp’s lawyer, Joe McCulloch, did not immediately respond to a message from the SC Daily Gazette.
At Knapp’s bond hearing last October, McCulloch told reporters: “This is all about politics. We look forward to a very public trial.”
In a third allegation of open meetings law violation, the ACLU argued the Election Commission denied Knapp his right to a public hearing and barred him from the closed-door session in which his employment was discussed.
Public records law says a state employee “has the right to demand that the hearing be conducted publicly” instead of in an executive session.
If asked, Knapp would have demanded a public hearing, the ACLU’s lawyers claimed. The court filing did not state how the group knew Knapp would have made this request.

name: VTDigger
title: Federal grants invigorate efforts to address veteran homelessness in Vermont
description:
The Department of Veterans Affairs awarded over $18 million to Vermont and New Hampshire community organizations.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Federal grants invigorate efforts to address veteran homelessness in Vermont.
text:
The Veterans’ Place in Northfield. Photo by Elizabeth Hewitt/VTDigger

The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs recently awarded more than $18 million to community organizations across Vermont and New Hampshire, helping those organizations to continue to house and support veterans without homes. 
“Having the funding solidified again and the grants to these organizations really helps ensure veterans are being seen and heard, and getting the opportunities to get their feet back underneath them,” said Katherine Tang, public affairs officer for the White River Junction VA Medical Center.
Veterans made up 3% of Vermont’s unhoused population in 2025 — 111 total individuals according to the 2025 State of Homelessness in Vermont report. That was a 3% increase from the 2024 count of 107 veterans experiencing homelessness statewide.
The $18 million is part of $1.17 billion awarded to 680 organizations nationwide, according to a press release from the White River Junction VA Medical Center. The funding follows a nationwide push in 2025 to house veterans, when 51,936 veterans found homes — the highest number in seven years. The White River Junction VA Medical Center helped find homes for 107 local veterans in 2025, according to Vermont Business Magazine.
According to the press release, the Supportive Services for Veteran Families program and the Veterans Affairs Grant and Per Diem program will distribute the grant funds, which total $18,499,223.
The Supportive Services program will allocate funds to three different efforts: securing housing for veterans who are facing imminent homelessness, finding more appropriate housing for veterans and their families, and quickly finding housing for veterans and families experiencing homelessness, the press release said.
Funds distributed through the Grant Per Diem program will go to two transitional housing programs located in Northfield and Bradford, according to Brooke Whalen, the Grant Per Diem liaison at the White River Junction VA Medical Center. The programs, called Veterans’ Place and Veterans Inc., offer both housing and care to veterans with the goal of securing permanent housing within a year.
“The GPD programs provide a sense of community and also assist Veterans with connecting to their new communities and assist them with applying for employment, and exploring ways to increase their income including becoming service connected,” Whalen wrote.
“Veterans’ Place provides a home to help people get back on their feet, rather than simply being a place to lay your head for a few days,” offering resources including clothing, food and counselling, according to Raylene Meunier, managing director of the center.
The journey home from war can be a painful one, according to Tang, the spokesperson at the White River VA hospital. Many veterans struggle with the loss of the found family they built with their fellow servicemembers and the emotional effects of war, she said.
“You struggle with the depression that comes after that, the feeling of loneliness, and then isolation happens,” Tang said, “and that can lead to just not getting your feet underneath you, which is why veterans do experience homelessness, specifically after the transition period.”
Readjusting to civilian life is difficult for practical reasons as well, Whalen wrote in an email. For veterans who joined the military at 18, it can be especially challenging.
“Many entered the military at the age of 18 and had a limited idea of how to live independently,” Whalen wrote. “When they re-enter civilian life they are sometimes doing things for the first time, such as applying for jobs, completing housing applications, enrolling in healthcare.”
Tang emphasized the power of community members in helping veterans readjust to civilian life. She encouraged landlords and housing providers to offer rental opportunities to veterans in homelessness programs. 
For veterans who may be struggling with housing, Tang urged them to reach out to the National Call Center for Homeless Veterans.
“No veteran should be homeless in the country they fought to defend,” Tang said, “and so that is why we have a group of highly trained professionals to go out into the community and try to make that connection with veterans that are at risk of homelessness or are currently experiencing homelessness.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Native American tribes wanted to join the Chesapeake Bay partnership. Not anymore.
description: Seven federally recognized Native American tribes are ending their bid to formally join the Chesapeake Bay cleanup, saying they have been disappointed by the response from Bay Program leaders.
text:
Virginia Indigenous tribe chiefs observe the Dec. 2, 2025, meeting of the Chesapeake Executive Council, where the Chesapeake Bay partnership agreed to study how to formally include the tribes in bay cleanup planning. It was supposed to issue recommendations by July, but tribal leaders say they have been stonewalled. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Seven federally recognized Native American tribes are ending their bid to formally join the Chesapeake Bay cleanup, saying they have been disappointed by the response from Bay Program leaders.
The Virginia-based tribes began their quest last January, hoping to be added as a single signatory — the status awarded to each of the state governments surrounding the bay — when elected officials in the Chesapeake Bay region approved a new agreement for restoring the bay in December.
Their effort fell short, but the state governors in the bay region commissioned a Chesapeake Bay Program committee to study the idea, approving a document that called Indigenous knowledge “vital to the health of the Chesapeake Bay.” Several chiefs were in the front row of the crowd as the governors approved the directive during a December convening at the National Aquarium in Baltimore.
But discussions reached an impasse earlier this month, according to a statement shared on Monday by the Indigenous Conservation Council of the Chesapeake Bay, a consortium of all seven tribes, at a Bay Program committee meeting.
Tribal leaders say the bay partnership proved unwilling to offer signatory status, a failure to recognize tribal sovereignty, said Melissa Ann Ehrenreich, executive director of the council.
Board members of the Indigenous Conservation Council gather for a meeting in 2024. (Photo courtesy of Pam D’Angelo)
“If people are not willing to create a seat at the table, why should you sit under the table?” Ehrenreich asked in an interview. “That was what they were suggesting: For tribes to sit under the table and catch crumbs.”
In its statement, the council said that it voted “to withdraw from all discussions and formal engagement with the Chesapeake Bay Program,” until tribal sovereignty is respected.
The Chesapeake Bay Program said in a statement Monday that it “remains committed to working with Tribes, to the extent that they would want to engage.”
“While the partnership did not extend an option for adding signatories, we remain committed to working together on the foundational elements of advancing and respecting Indigenous guardianship and Indigenous knowledge within watershed restoration planning and implementation,” read the statement.
Chief Anne Richardson of the Rappahannock Tribe said she walked out of a September meeting with Bay Program officials before its conclusion because of her frustrations.
That meeting was convened to prepare a formal resolution that the Bay Program could approve in December. Richardson said she and other tribal leaders believed the resolution would set the tribes on a path to signatory status.
But more than an hour into the meeting at the Upper Mattaponi Tribal Center in Virginia, Bay Program officials broke the bad news, Richardson said. To her, it felt like tribal leaders had been “led down a primrose path,” only for the door to be slammed in their faces more than a year later.
“It was insulting, and I thought it was very disrespectful to the tribal leaders,” Richardson said.
But the tribes got support Monday from organizations including the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, among the largest bay-focused nonprofit groups, along with the Choose Clean Water Coalition and the Nature Conservancy.
“It’s unacceptable that the Chesapeake Bay Partnership is not following through on promises to engage in good faith and meaningfully include tribes in the partnership,” Chesapeake Bay Foundation senior policy director Keisha Sedlacek said in a statement. “Enough delays. We urge decision-makers to make things right.”



Quotation







If people are not willing to create a seat at the table, why should you sit under the table? That was what they were suggesting: For tribes to sit under the table and catch crumbs.


– Melissa Ann Ehrenreich, executive director of the Indigenous Conservation Council


During the Bay Program meeting Monday, the tribes also received support from Bill Dennison, provost and vice president for academic affairs at the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science. Dennison, a longtime bay scientist, is an executive board member on the Chesapeake Bay Program’s Scientific and Technical Advisory Committee.
“To move forward, we’ve got to engage with all knowledge that we can integrate to restore this magnificent bay and watershed,” Dennison said during the public meeting.
In its statement, the Indigenous council wrote that tribal leaders were “stonewalled” when they tried to discern why the other states had decided not to allow the council to become a signatory, on a level playing field with the governors of Maryland, Delaware, Pennsylvania, New York, Virginia and West Virginia, and the mayor of Washington, D.C.
As a signatory, the council would be able to cast a vote in decisions about the bay clean-up effort. In addition to each of the states and Washington, D.C., the federal government and the Chesapeake Bay Commission —which represents legislators in the region — are also signatories with voting power.
The seven tribes, which all earned recognition from the federal government between 2015 and 2018, formed the Indigenous Conservation Council of the Chesapeake Bay in 2022. The council includes the Upper Mattaponi Indian Tribe, Rappahannock Tribe, Pamunkey Indian Tribe, Nansemond Indian Nation, Monacan Indian Nation, Chickahominy Indian Tribe and the Chickahominy Indian Tribe – Eastern Division.
Maryland officials grapple with ‘bizarre’ Trump executive order on Chesapeake Bay

The Chesapeake Bay Program decision is particularly “ironic,” Ehrenreich said, given that President Donald Trump (R) last week signed an executive order signaling a possible retreat from federal agencies involved in the bay cleanup, and railing against “rain taxes” collected by some bay jurisdictions in order to fund stormwater management programs.
“These are tough times for the Bay Program when it needs leadership,” Ehrenreich said. “And tribes are willing and ready to step up, when their tribal sovereignty is acknowledged and respected.”
If it changed course, the Chesapeake Bay partnership would not be the first clean water partnership to add Indigenous leadership. The Puget Sound Partnership, for example, includes several tribal representatives on its leadership board.
“When the Chesapeake Executive Council decides it is ready to uphold tribal sovereignty and provide space at the leadership table for us, then we will be happy to renew our conversations,” read Monday’s statement from the council.
But in the meantime, the tribes plan to continue their environmental projects in their homelands, Richardson said, including efforts to rebuild oyster and herring populations and restore shorelines and wetlands — projects that employ indigenous knowledge and focus on adding to, rather than extracting from, the land.
“Western science didn’t need what we had,” Richardson said. “And so we’ll just keep doing what we’re doing.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico State Ethics Commission asks judge to toss much of former WNMU president’s lawsuit
description: Attorneys for the New Mexico State Ethics Commission last week asked a federal judge to toss much of a new lawsuit from former Western New Mexico University President Joseph Shepard. In a new lawsuit, Shepard accused the State Ethics Commission and Executive Director Jeremy Farris of violating his civil rights in a 2025 court case.
text:
The New Mexico State Ethics Commission on Sept. 14, 2026, asked a federal judge to toss much of a lawsuit brought by Western New Mexico University’s former president. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Attorneys for the New Mexico State Ethics Commission last week asked a federal judge to toss much of a new lawsuit from former Western New Mexico University President Joseph Shepard.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
News reports in late 2023 detailed how Shepard and his wife, former CIA agent and congressional candidate Valerie Plame, used taxpayer money on international travel, five-star resort stays and exotic home furnishings. State Auditor Joseph Maestas in 2024 issued a report detailing nearly $364,000 in “wasteful” spending, including a trip to a Ritz-Carlton resort in California. And the State Ethics Commission in 2025 filed a lawsuit against Shepard, alleging that he used American with Disabilities Act money intended for campus projects to instead build a patio where he hosted events for his daughter’s wedding.
Shepard left his post as president in early 2025, and the New Mexico Department of Justice subsequently filed a lawsuit seeking to recoup his “golden parachute” severance payment. That case is scheduled to go to trial next year.
In August, Shepard filed a suit of his own against the State Ethics Commission and Executive Director Jeremy Farris in U.S. District Court, accusing them of violating his civil rights with the 2025 lawsuit.
The lawsuit repeats many of the claims he made in a late 2025 lawsuit against WNMU and several current and former state lawmakers. In both suits, Shepard alleges that in 2023 he sought to blow the whistle on state lawmakers who appropriated taxpayer money to improperly benefit their families, and they subsequently orchestrated a “smear campaign” against him.
The commission’s attorneys wrote that Shepard’s legal team has created “a conspiracy theory uniting” the various lawsuits he is facing.
Court sets trial in NM State Ethics Commission suit against former WNMU president

In the latest lawsuit, Shepard said that the State Ethics Commission sought to “harass and extort him.” The commission has sought to claw back the roughly $177,000 of ADA money it accused him of spending on the patio near his on-campus home. That case is also scheduled to go to trial next year.
A. Blair Dunn, the attorney representing Shepard, told Source NM Monday that the 2025 State Ethics Commission lawsuit was secretly targeting the $1.9 million severance payment Shepard received when he left his job as university president.
“He lied in why he brought that lawsuit, which is unconstitutional to do to a citizen,” Dunn said. “It’s a vindictive prosecution made up for an improper purpose. The real point of that lawsuit is to try to extort that money from the severance.”
Attorneys for the State Ethics Commission in filings of their own counter that Shepard’s federal lawsuit is “a belated reaction to the lawsuit the commission” filed against him over the patio allegations in 2025, and that Farris has immunity from litigation as he was acting on behalf of a state agency.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘The family is an entire town’ in Hinesburg
description:
Event celebrates Hinesburg winning Vermont Tree Farmer of the Year
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘The family is an entire town’ in Hinesburg.
text:
Stevie Spencer, member of the Town Forest Committee, kneels down to search for salamanders. Photo by Kylie DelMaestro/Community News Service

Kylie DelMaestro and Maddy Upston are reporters with the Community News Service, part of the University of Vermont’s Reporting & Documentary Storytelling program.HINESBURG – Hinesburg Town Forest was an unusual pick by the Vermont Woodlands Association for Tree Farmer of the Year.
Winners are usually families, said Kathy Beland, program administrator for Vermont Tree Farm.
“In this case, the family is an entire town,” Beland said. 
Earlier this month, more than 60 members of that family came together to celebrate that award through a variety of experiences in the town forest. 
Beland said forest supporters “have gone the extra mile” through the opening of the land for education, their serious conservation efforts and thoughtful management.
She said the award recognizes the town’s shared commitment to preserving the forest while cultivating the space for education and recreation.
Hinesburg Town Forest started in 1936 with a donation of 100 acres and has expanded over time to its current 1,125 acres. It’s now one of the state’s largest town forests, according to the Vermont Land Trust.
A variety of entities partner to support Hinesburg Town Forest. It is owned by the town of Hinesburg and managed by the nine-person Hinesburg Town Forest Committee, which advises the selectboard.
In 2022, the town partnered with Vermont Land Trust and the Hinesburg Land Trust to expand and conserve the forest, according to the Vermont Land Trust.
The nonprofit group Fellowship of the Wheel stewards the 18-mile trail system. Fellowship of the Wheel helps build and maintain local trails, principally for mountain biking.
In addition to mountain biking, the trails are popular for hiking, snowshoeing and observing wildlife.
The celebration Saturday began at Town Hall. Attendees could choose one of four different walks and experiences: one centered on forestry and birding, another outlining the history of the land, a mountain bike tour, and a family-friendly reptile and amphibian expedition.
Before each group dispersed for their preferred forest experience, all attendees gathered for a photo. A voice emerged from the crowd: “Say trees!” 
The reptile and amphibian walk was led by herpetologist Kate Kelly, chair of the Hinesburg Conservation Commission. She said she focused on frogs and salamanders for practical reasons.
“Reptiles and amphibians are very hands-on,” Kelly said. “You can’t grab a black bear!”
Kelly engaged a group of children during the walk, encouraging them to get their hands dirty and celebrating all the reptiles and amphibians they managed to find. The group found an Eastern newt, two Eastern redbacked salamanders, a pickerel frog, and many Northern two-lined salamanders. 
Throughout the event, the children were invested in the activity, running around the forest, laughing, turning over rocks and admiring each and every creature.
Breeding a love of reptiles and amphibians in the next generation is good for more than just getting them off their phones.
From an environmentalist standpoint, reptiles and amphibians represent the importance of preserving the intersections between different types of habitats, as opposed to preserving just one type of habitat or another, she said.
“Because reptiles and amphibians live in between different types of habitats, it is easy to understand the kind of conservation we are interested in through them,” Kelly said.
