name: Florida Phoenix
title: Uthmeier embraces DOJ opinion finding federal handgun sales ban unconstitutional
description: The campaign to lower the legal age for Floridians to purchase long guns got a boost after the Trump’s administration’s Department of Justice issued an opinion declaring that the federal ban on handgun sales to 18-to-20-year-olds violates the Second Amendment. On Friday, the Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel released a 49-page document arguing[...]
text:
The Trump administration may have added fuel to the debate over Florida's ban on long gun sales to people under 21 years of age. (Photo by George Frey/Getty Images)The campaign to lower the legal age for Floridians to purchase long guns got a boost after the Trump’s administration’s Department of Justice issued an opinion declaring that the federal ban on handgun sales to 18-to-20-year-olds violates the Second Amendment.
On Friday, the Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel released a 49-page document arguing that two federal statutes that ban federally licensed dealers from selling handguns or handgun ammunition to individuals under 21 is inconsistent with the Second Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.
“Eighteen-year-olds may vote, serve on juries, be drafted, and face adult criminal penalties, including capital punishment,” said Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser for the Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel in a written statement.
“The Constitution protects the people’s right to keep and bear arms. The Department of Justice may not constitutionally seek to impose criminal penalties on dealers who sell handguns to law-abiding adults who, in nearly every other relevant respect, are members of the political community.”
That news cheered Floridians opposed to the state’s ban on individuals under 21 from buying a shotgun or rifle. That provision was part of the 2018 gun-safety law passed by the Legislature and signed by Gov. Rick Scott in the immediate aftermath of the mass shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas Public High School in Parkland.
Critics of the law include Gov. Ron DeSantis and GOP gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds, who has previously stated that he will work to overturn the age limitation if elected in November.
Another Florida Republican celebrating the opinion was Attorney General James Uthmeier.
“Glad DOJ has followed suit in the fight for Second Amendment rights of Americans who are old enough to sign up to defend our nation!” Uthmeier wrote Friday on X. “We took this position at the Supreme Court a year ago and look forward to working with the Florida Legislature to right this wrong!”
Just a few months after DeSantis appointed him last year, Uthmeier declared that in his opinion the Florida law was unconstitutional, and that he was directing his office not to defend it in a court challenge.  The National Rifle Association had filed that lawsuit in 2018 after the Parkland law was implemented, but the high court denied its petition to hear the case on June 30.
Florida Republicans in the House of Representatives have approved legislation during the past four legislative sessions to repeal the restrictions, but the bill has never become law because of opposition in the Florida Senate. The Phoenix reached out to incoming Senate President Jim Boyd last month to inquire about his stance on the law, but he did not respond.
Donalds told the Phoenix last month, “We’re going to remove that provision,” adding, “It’s gotta go.”
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly has said the law “should stay in place.”
Florida Second Amendment advocates say the DOJ’s opinion should pave the way for the Legislature to finally repeal the provision in the 2027 session.
No excuse
“If the federal government is declaring that an under-21 purchase ban is unconstitutional, then Florida’s under-21 purchase law is unconstitutional!” declared Luis Valdes, Florida state director for Gun Owners of America. “Tallahassee no longer has any excuse to delay repealing it!”
The Florida law only pertains to long guns, which include rifles, carbines, shotguns, and submachine guns. It never included handguns, since it has been illegal on the federal level for licensed dealers to sell handguns to young adults under 21 since 1968.
Gun-safety groups denounced the DOJ’s legal opinion.
“The math here is simple: 18-to-20-year-olds commit gun homicides at triple the rate of people 21 and older, which is why more than 80% of Americans want 21 to be the minimum age to buy a gun,” said John Feinblatt, president of Everytown for Gun Safety.
“Trump’s MAGA DOJ is handing the gun industry something it could never win in Congress or at the ballot box, and America will pay for it in lives lost and shattered communities.”
The Florida Department of Law Enforcement’s Supplementary Homicide Report from 2020 identified 18-to-20-year-olds as perpetrators in fatal shootings at “three times the rate of 16-year-olds” and about “three times the rate of a person in their 30s.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: South Korean defense contractor will build $2.2 billion factory at Pine Bluff Arsenal
description: WHITE HALL — A South Korean company announced Monday it will build its first United States facility that produces artillery ammunition at Arkansas’ Pine Bluff Arsenal, creating about 400 jobs with an average wage of $50 per hour over seven years. Hanwha Defense USA’s $2.2 billion factory “is the kind of transformational investment Jefferson County […]
text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Westerman chats with Col. Matthew Mason, commander of the Pine Bluff Arsenal, before a news conference at the U.S. Army facility on Sept. 21, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)WHITE HALL — A South Korean company announced Monday it will build its first United States facility that produces artillery ammunition at Arkansas’ Pine Bluff Arsenal, creating about 400 jobs with an average wage of $50 per hour over seven years.
Hanwha Defense USA’s $2.2 billion factory “is the kind of transformational investment Jefferson County and the Delta need,” Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders said at Monday’s news conference and ribbon-cutting ceremony that celebrated the opening of new administration headquarters. 
The Army awarded the company a lease solicitation for a munitions campus at the Pine Bluff Arsenal in January, and the new office is the first step in that project, according to a Hanwha news release.
The factory will build propellant charges and base bleed units for 155-millimeter ammunition, according to the release. CEO Michael Coulter said the company’s output “will enhance the speed and range” of the U.S. Army’s weaponry at a time when the federal government aims to bolster its military industrial base.
The Pentagon has been pushing the defense industry to replenish military stockpiles depleted by the war in Iran.
“Our goal is to maximize automation to ensure safe manufacturing and enhanced quality,” Coulter said. “The idea is to transform Pine Bluff Arsenal into a modern asset that advances both national defense priorities and U.S. Army priorities, including readiness that protects America’s warfighter.”

Jordan Gillis, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment, speaks at a news conference announcing South Korea munitions company Hanwha Defense USA’s planned $2.2 billion factory at the Pine Bluff Arsenal on Sept. 21, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

Hanwha’s choice of Pine Bluff for the factory “represents what can happen when Army and industry and our local communities come together around a shared objective,” said Jordan Gillis, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment.
The Hanwha factory is one of four capital investment projects, totaling $6 billion, planned for Jefferson County over the next three to five years, Arkansas Commerce Secretary Hugh McDonald said.
The state’s business discussions with Hanwha began in March 2024 with help from U.S. Rep. Bruce Westerman and U.S. Sens. Tom Cotton and John Boozman, all Republicans.
Those discussions continued in May 2025 when Westerman, Cotton and Boozman traveled to Japan, Taiwan and South Korea with the goal of “convincing people that this is the arsenal of the future,” said Westerman, whose district includes Jefferson County.

Army program to support $1 billion investment in Pine Bluff Arsenal

 

Sanders said Monday that she met with Hanwha leaders in July at the Farnborough International Airshow in England, part of a three-country overseas trade mission.
The Pine Bluff Arsenal was built in 1941, the same year the United States entered World War II. The facility “remains a key national security asset that is ripe for greater defense investment,” Cotton said in Hanwha’s news release.
South Arkansas is a hub of defense contracting. The 2,000-acre L3Harris arms manufacturing campus in East Camden produces more than 115,000 rocket motors per year. 
The region is also home to a $33 million missile plant, a joint venture that Raytheon Technologies and Israel-based Rafael Advanced Defense Systems announced in October 2023.
In February, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth praised Arkansas’ munitions industry at the L3Harris plant as part of a national speaking tour.

name: VTDigger
title: Drug injection sites are a good thing for Vermont
description:
Fear, not evidence, is driving opposition to overdose prevention centers — Denmark's results show why Vermont shouldn't back down.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Drug injection sites are a good thing for Vermont.
text:
Dear Editor,
As a person who has seen people slowly die from dirty needles, I’m confused by the slow reaction from society. Drug addiction and overdoses cost millions of dollars. Lifesaving surgeries don’t always work out. “Philly dope” infections turn people black from the inside out, leading to amputations that our taxpayers fund. 
The Danes have already proven the success of injection site systems. Vermont’s program is funded by opioid settlement money — Vermont’s share of lawsuits against drug manufacturers — and doesn’t cost taxpayers a dime. If you’re a fiscal conservative and want to save money over the long haul in healthcare, this is a good place to start.
The establishment of “fix rooms” in Denmark in 2012 led critics to fear a decline in public safety. Many worried the plan would increase drug use, attract crime and make neighborhoods worse. Sound familiar? We hear it all the time from certain politicians in Vermont who understand that creating fear wins elections. 
However, the data and research provided a different result. The European Union Drugs Agency reported that Denmark saw recordable improvements. One benefit was the decrease in needles collected from streets and school grounds. Reports showed that instead of picking up thousands of needles a week, just one year after opening the rooms, the number had dropped by 80%. The program also removed the normalization of drug use in public. A highly visible open drug scene moved entirely behind closed doors. You can’t change the culture of drug use unless you remove the visibility of it. European studies confirmed that safe injection sites actually lowered crime rates. They acted as a bridge to healthcare because addiction is a healthcare issue. 
The fearmongering has to stop for the sake of humanity. Stop using people as a political tool to turn society against each other for votes. It’s sickening. If you’re a Vermonter, you probably know someone who has lost the battle of addiction. Let’s stop judging each other’s mistakes and create cherished moments that lead people out of the gates of hell back into the community so we can grow and live. 
We need leaders to stand up and say, “enough is enough.” Are we Vermont Strong? Or are we a state of fear and hate? 
Jeremy Ayotte, 
Fletcher, Vt.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Election officials played key role in Supreme Court mail ballot decision
description: This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access. Election officials exhaled when the Supreme Court recently ended months of uncertainty by blocking the Trump administration from restricting mail ballots this November. The Supreme Court decision clears the way for millio[...]
text:
Absentee ballots are prepared to be mailed at the Wake County Board of Elections on September 17, 2024 in Raleigh, North Carolina. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images)This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access.
Election officials exhaled when the Supreme Court recently ended months of uncertainty by blocking the Trump administration from restricting mail ballots this November.
The Supreme Court decision clears the way for millions of Americans to vote by mail, just as they have in previous elections, though availability ranges widely from state to state.
“It’s a relief and it’s palpable,” said Marybeth Kuznik, the elections director for Pennsylvania’s Fayette County. “I honestly don’t know how we could have complied with (the Postal Service’s restrictions) at this point in the election cycle.”
But the administration’s efforts to tighten access and the chaotic legal battle that ensued left voters worrying that voting by mail could be disrupted or unreliable.
Now election officials are working to reassure them.
For months, people across the political spectrum voiced concerns about the new proposed U.S. Postal Service rules pushed by President Donald Trump. Election officials from both major political parties played a central role in the Supreme Court debate. More than 80 of them, including Kuznik, signed onto a brief warning that they wouldn’t have time to meet the new requirements before the November election. Several Republican secretaries of state, including officials from Kentucky, Georgia, and Kansas, urged the court to freeze the plans because of the chaos they would create for an election now less than 50 days away.
Those pleas appear to have been decisive for at least one justice, Brett Kavanaugh, who wrote a concurring opinion saying he thought there was a fair chance the rules would hold up to legal scrutiny, but applying them in the 2026 elections would be “arbitrary and capricious” because “state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule.”
Now, election officials who have been for months raising concerns about an entirely new vote by mail system have to communicate to voters that the old one is safe to use, even as Trump continues to denounce it. Despite voting by mail himself last month in Florida, Trump attacked the process on social media as a “disaster” and “Nation Destroying SCAM” that made America the “laughing stock all over the World.”
Some election officials and experts said they are seeing fewer absentee ballot requests than expected.
“It has already caused all sorts of voter confusion, and even though the rule is not in place for this election, that’s not to say that there won’t be some voters that think that it is,” said Tammy Patrick, the chief program officer at the Election Center, a national nonprofit association for election administrators. “So it’s going to be incumbent on all of us to make sure that we just keep up the mantra that nothing has changed as a result of the rule.”
Patrick, who filed an expert declaration in the court cases challenging the Postal Service rules, said the best thing voters can do is get their ballots in as early as possible.
Dana Lewis, the recorder who oversees elections in Arizona’s Pinal County, joked that she wears six-inch heels so she can pivot on a dime, something that gave her the dexterity to keep up with this topsy-turvy election season.
Lewis, a Republican, has invested heavily in her county’s drop box system, which includes 24/7 video monitoring and GPS-locked ballot boxes for tighter security, something she believes should give voters confidence that their ballots will be kept safe. Roughly three-quarters of Arizona’s voters cast mail ballots in 2024, federal data show.
“Trust the system,” Lewis said.
But not everyone does. The court ruling came in parallel with a new poll showing a precipitous decline in public confidence in the nation’s electoral system. The University of California, San Diego survey found that just 55% of respondents trust that the vote would be counted fairly, compared to 71% in 2024.
The poll also found just 49% of Americans expect the upcoming election to be free and fair.
That’s in line with other polling, including a recent Pew Research Center survey in which 55% of respondents said they thought the upcoming election would be free and fair, an historic low for the question they have asked over the past six years.
Dion Nissenbaum is Votebeat’s senior national reporter and is based in Houston. Contact Dion at dnissenbaum@votebeat.org.

name: Maryland Matters
title: DOJ presses case against in-state tuition for undocumented Maryland students
description: The Justice Department is asking a federal judge in Maryland for summary judgment in its lawsuit challenging a 2011 state law that provides in-state tuition and other education-related assistance to undocumented immigrants living in the state.
text:
Students walk across a college campus on a sunny day. The Justice Department is challenging laws in 21 states, including Maryland, that grant in-state tuition at state campuses to undocumented immigrants who live in the state. (Photo by Klaus Vedfelt/Getty Stock Images)The Department of Justice is asking a federal judge in Maryland for summary judgment in its lawsuit challenging a 2011 state law that provides in-state tuition and other education-related assistance to undocumented immigrants living in the state.
Maryland is one of 21 states where federal attorneys have filed similar lawsuits. Last month, the Maryland Office of the Attorney General asked that the federal government’s case be dismissed, a motion the Justice Department pushed back on.
“Maryland does not challenge the sufficiency of the factual allegations in the complaint, but rather challenges the legal bases for the claims,” federal attorneys said in a brief filed last week. “The United States now opposes that motion and cross-moves for summary judgment on all claims.”
The Justice Department originally filed suit in July seeking to block a 2011 state law known as the DREAM Act. The law — which went into effect following a referendum challenge — grants in-state tuition rates to some undocumented immigrants.
To be eligible, the law requires students to have attended a public or private high school in the state and received a diploma or its equivalent in Maryland; to register for college within six years of receiving that diploma; and to prove that the student or a parent or guardian paid taxes in the state for the two years prior to enrolling in college.
Immigrant rights, advocacy groups sue Trump administration for ‘warrantless arrest’

If successful, the DOJ lawsuit could also end other education-related programs such as legislative scholarships and in-state community college tuition rates that incorporated the DREAM Act eligibility standards.
The Justice lawsuit claims the state act is superseded by federal law.
The department is also seeking a permanent injunction barring the state from providing any financial aid or scholarship programs that might benefit undocumented immigrants who are residents of the state.
Two weeks ago, Attorney General Anthony Brown’s office filed a motion to have the case dismissed, citing the Justice Department’s “failure to state a claim upon which relief may be granted.”
“Indeed, courts throughout the country have already rejected the federal government’s express-preemption challenges to state laws similar to Maryland’s that do not condition eligibility on residency, but rather on residence-neutral factors such as high school attendance and graduation,” lawyers for the state wrote in their motion.
Maryland is one of 21 states with laws providing in-state tuition to undocumented immigrants that have been challenged by the federal government. Those include four new lawsuits filed last week in Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon and Washington.
Federal attorneys won court orders in five states — Illinois, Kentucky, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Texas. In Florida, the state Board of Education voted to bar people who do not legally reside in the United States from attending a state college or university.
“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division said in a statement issued by the Department last week. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Why Nebraska Republicans say they want to reelect Sen. Pete Ricketts
description: Some of the people who showed up for Pete Ricketts' annual steak fry said they’ll vote for him because he shares their conservative values.
text:
Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts speaks at his annual steak fry in Weeping Water on Sept. 20, 2026. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)Editor’s note: The Examiner talked to Dan Osborn supporters at a July rally.
WEEPING WATER. — Some of the roughly 1,000 people who showed up for Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ annual steak fry said they’ll vote for him this November because he shares their conservative values.
Ricketts and Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy — along with other elected Nebraska Republican officials – sought Sunday to energize Republican voters to turn out this November, pointing to the tax cuts in President Donald Trump’s tax and spending bill, Republicans’ efforts to secure the southern border and Ricketts’ record as governor.
The former Nebraska governor is seeking his first full six-year term in the Senate after winning in 2024 to serve out the term of former U.S. Sen. Ben Sasse, R-Neb., who resigned to lead the University of Florida. Ricketts is in a heated race with nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn, which has drawn national attention for its nontraditional political dynamics. 
Ricketts supporters who spoke to the Examiner said they want to send him back to Washington, D.C., because he has responded to their needs and his opponent is “ultra-liberal.” 
Erich Tiemann, chairperson of the Gage County Board of Supervisors, said Ricketts continues to be as responsive as a U.S. senator as he was as governor. Tiemann said Ricketts always checks in and stays engaged, asking what needs to be done for the state. 

“It’s unbelievable,” Tiemann, 48, said. “Here’s somebody that doesn’t need a job by any means, and he cares about us in so many different ways and works for us.” 
Ricketts served two terms as governor from 2015 to 2023. During his tenure, he reshaped the Legislature and state law. He pressed for passage of tax and spending cuts, managed the COVID-19 pandemic and focused on improving the efficiency of state agencies, efforts he has since tried bringing to Washington, D.C., and the federal government.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bob Rose, a 74-year-old Scottsbluff resident, said he doesn’t agree with Ricketts on everything, but he thinks the former governor has worked diligently for Nebraska. 
“(Ricketts) has conservative values that I greatly value,” Rose said. “I’m terrified of the craziness that the far left is trying to bring across the country, and so when I have an opportunity to vote for a conservative over an ultra-liberal, I’m going to do it.” 
When asked for some things he disagrees with Ricketts on, Ross didn’t provide specifics but said it was “very few things.” He also said he doesn’t like some of Ricketts’ “tactics” every once in a while. 
Ricketts is a force in state politics; his endorsements and opposition carry weight, having helped elect a governor and flip legislative seats. He has Nebraska’s dominant political operation behind him, known for its no-holds-barred approach to campaigning.
Skip McPheron, a 70-year-old Wymore resident, said Ricketts may come from a wealthy family, but he is approachable.

“He’s just like the carpenter that lives next door to you,” McPheron said. 
He added that Ricketts is effective and gets things done. Nina Head, a 71-year-old Elkhorn resident, said she is supporting Ricketts because he has done so much for the state and the nation, pointing to his time as governor and adding that she loves Ricketts dearly. 
Head called Ricketts’ opponent a “wacko.” 
Ricketts and National Republicans have been relentless in painting Osborn as a “secret ” Democrat. Osborn has been dealing with leaked audio of comments he has made throughout the campaign. 
The audio leaks have included Osborn saying he would be “f—ed” as a candidate if he said that he wanted to “abolish ICE” or that President Donald Trump’s border wall is “a symbol of racism” that “does nothing.”
The most recent leak has him talking about why he thinks some Nebraskans voted for Trump. Osborn later apologized to anyone offended by those comments. 
The former labor leader said some of the other leaks are taken out of context. Ricketts and other speakers Sunday pointed to those audio leaks as examples of Osborn being dishonest to voters. 
“[Osborn] is not the moderate independent that he claims to be … this guy is a fake,” Ricketts told the crowd. “Those liberal donors want a senator from California or New York. … Folks, I will always be a senator for Nebraska.” 
Nebraska was Kennedy’s last stop on a campaign blitz to red states with “close” races. He also went to Iowa and Kansas. He told D.C. reporters he believes that the GOP will win those races, but they “oughta be fat-guy layups for us.” 
The Osborn campaign released a statement about the steak fry, saying that national Republicans are “panicking” and “their only solution is to pour over $10 million to run attack ads because they have nothing nice to say about Pete. The billionaire Epstein Class are terrified of losing one of their own.” 
“Dan looks forward to working with Sen. John Kennedy come January,” the end of the  statement reads. 
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Kosta Diamantis is a fugitive who hasn’t quite disappeared
description: Kosta Diamantis has conducted many interviews with CT media since he failed to appear at his sentencing last week. His goal: a pardon.
text:
If there is such a thing as a typical international fugitive, it clearly is not Konstantinos “Kosta” Diamantis.
He’s done at least three print interviews since fleeing the U.S. rather than face a prison sentence Thursday. He was live on WTIC-1080 talk radio Monday afternoon, and a television interview conducted via Facetime on Sunday was to air Monday night on WTNH, News 8.
In addition to the TV and radio interviews, Diamantis has spoken to reporters from Hearst Connecticut, the CT Examiner and the Connecticut Mirror. His intended audience is not known to be a consumer of news from any of those five sources.
Diamantis, who has a pardon application pending at the White House, acknowledges he is trying to make sufficient noise in the hope President Donald Trump will make his troubles disappear with a stroke of his black Sharpie.
“And if the president hears that message, which I hope he does in a pardon, then I would be eternally grateful,” Diamantis said in an interview with Connecticut Mirror on Monday.
He’s made a public a 10-page email broadly outlining his claim he is the victim of a “weaponized” Department of Justice and a conspiracy implicating the governor, three former U.S. attorneys and others. 
At the heart of the email is a claim he is facing retribution for his opposition to a no-bid contract for COVID-19 testing to a company with ties to Lamont’s wife, Annie Lamont. The administration gave contracts to all four companies that responded to a request for a testing in the early days of the pandemic.
He said juicier stuff includes allegations and evidence in his pardon application.
“They’re in my pardon, and my pardon is not public,” Diamantis said.
The governor’s press office said the media should turn down the volume of the Diamantis show.
“It’s obvious that Diamantis is putting on this dog and pony show to try to win a Presidential pardon,” said Cathryn Vaulman, Gov. Ned Lamont’s spokesperson. “If the media is going to give him the attention he craves, he needs to be held to some standard of proof.”
His claims of being a victim are consistent with complaints raised the night he was fired from a political appointment as the deputy secretary of policy and management and pushed towards retirement from his second classified job overseeing school construction grants. 
“I put information in my pardon. That is is not a public document, and to then open up those things in in public defeats the purpose of it being something that they are investigating,” he said. “And everybody has to wait, I guess, including the public and you.”
Diamantis said he is opting for flight, a pardon application and media-tour-in-absentia due to lack of confidence in the federal courts. He said he is bitter that no mistrial was ordered after evidence that one or two jurors had read media accounts while sequestered.
He said the government’s claim he extorted bribes from contractors in return for help getting contracts was a public humiliation, albeit one attested in sworn testimony by three witnesses the government considered both victims and co-conspirators. The jury believed them — not Diamantis, who had testified in his own behalf.
“The thought process was I just felt that I had been humiliated to the point where I needed to redeem myself and I needed a voice. I needed to be able to have a voice without fear of of retribution or reprisal,” he said. “And it was a knee-jerk reaction to do so, I suppose, but I needed to let the public know.”
How knee-jerk was it?
Diamantis declined to discuss when he decided to depart for Greece, the nation where he says he currently is residing — and where was conceived. His mother was three-months pregnant when she and his father emigrated to the U.S.
He speaking out is evidence of of a man trying to clear himself, he said.
“If I was a guilty person,” he said, “I would have come to Greece and never told anybody.”

name: WyoFile
title: Lead contractor pulls out of Gates’ Natrium nuclear power plant project in Wyoming
description:
TerraPower says construction will continue as planned as it seeks a new contractor, with its in-service date of 2031 intact.
The post Lead contractor pulls out of Gates’ Natrium nuclear power plant project in Wyoming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Construction will continue as planned at TerraPower’s Natrium “advanced” nuclear reactor power plant near Kemmerer, the company says, even though its lead engineering and construction contractor announced it will exit the project.
Bechtel, a global engineering giant, first mentioned the split in a Worker Adjustment and Retaining Notification letter sent to Virginia officials earlier this month indicating it will terminate its involvement with the project and that the split would result in eliminating 200 positions at its nuclear engineering headquarters in Reston, Virginia, beginning sometime in November.

TerraPower’s proposed Natrium nuclear power plant will be located outside Kemmerer. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)

“TerraPower and Bechtel were unable to reach an agreement on the next phase of the project and have decided to move forward separately,” Bechtel stated in the Sept. 15 letter. The letter did not offer additional details about the cause of the split.
Bechtel will complete work on a “sodium test-and-fill facility,” and bidding is underway to find a replacement firm, TerraPower told WyoFile in a statement Monday.
“Construction in Kemmerer will maintain its current schedule with the exemplary subcontractor teams and [engineering, procurement and construction] support services from commercial-grade firms that have been working on site. TerraPower is managing this transition to protect the overall construction schedule for [Kemmerer Unit 1] and will rebid the EPC contract.”
TerraPower, backed by Microsoft billionaire Bill Gates, selected Kemmerer in 2021 for its pilot Natrium nuclear power plant, a liquid-sodium cooled “advanced” nuclear reactor. The term advanced, these days, is typically applied to nuclear reactor designs that are smaller than nuclear plants built decades ago, and that do not rely on water for cooling. Gates has billed the project as critical for meeting the global challenges of climate change and growing demand for electricity.
Bill Gates addresses a crowd of local leaders May 5, 2023, in Kemmerer. He is joined by Chris Levesque, Tara Neider and Mark Werner of TerraPower. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Bechtel was tapped in 2020 to lead design and construction for the bulk of the nuclear energy campus, which includes nonnuclear portions — a workforce training center and liquid-sodium testing facility — and the “nuclear island” that includes the actual nuclear power plant and ancillary components that fall under the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s authorities. Bechtel was expected to maintain its lead role through completion of the power plant, expected to commence operations by 2031, according to TerraPower statements that still appeared on its website Monday. 
Bechtel, however, wasn’t expressly under contract to continue to the next “nuclear island” phases of the project, according to Lincoln County Board of Commissioners Chairman Kent Connelly, who said TerraPower has kept commissioners apprised of progress and changes.
TerraPower has been “very open about it,” Connelly told WyoFile. “There’ll be a new contractor coming in. So this is not about somebody being pulled off the site. They’re just changing contractors.”
The WARN notice that was sent to Virginia officials was a “legal requirement,” Bechtel told WyoFile in a statement. “Our people will move to other nuclear projects underway across the company, where demand for these skills continues to grow.”
In addition to the nonnuclear facilities at the site, Bechtel was instrumental in “major procurements” for materials, it said, as well as “beginning foundational work for Kemmerer Unit 1.”
“This work was performed under an earlier phase of the contract, prior to full [engineering, procurement and construction] scope,” Bechtel added. “As we considered the next phase of the project, Bechtel and TerraPower decided to move forward separately.”
First-of-its-kind nuclear plant
The Natrium plant at Kemmerer is designed to generate 345 megawatts of electricity with an energy storage component to ramp up to 500 megawatts to meet demand peaks, according to the Bellevue, Washington-based company. One megawatt is enough electricity to power about 750 homes. 
The $4 billion project is backed by $2 billion from the Department of Energy — a commitment made under the first Trump administration.
TerraPower Director of Construction Andy Chrusciel shows renderings of the completed project during a press event Wednesday, April 22, 2026, at the site of TerraPower’s Natrium nuclear power plant near Kemmerer. (Ryan Dorgan/WyoFile)
Construction on nonnuclear portions of the project began in 2024 and 2025. The NRC issued a construction permit for the nuclear portions of the campus in March, making it the first commercial reactor approved in nearly a decade in the U.S. 
The next major permitting milestone will be an operating license from the NRC, which TerraPower says it hopes to secure in 2028. The plant is expected to be fully operational by 2031, according to the company. 
TerraPower has indicated that it plans on building similar Natrium-design nuclear power plants throughout the U.S. and in other countries.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Turek says he’s ‘happy’ Iowa Republicans joined his push for diesel export pause
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek said Monday he was happy to see Iowa Republicans, including his opponent, Republican Ashley Hinson, join his call to take steps to lower diesel costs. Fuel costs have gone up nationwide because of the U.S. war with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major trade […]
text:
Erich Bockman, co-owner of Fontenelle Supply Co., gave Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, who is running for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat in 2026, a tour of the  store in Des Moines' East Village Sep. 21, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek said Monday he was happy to see Iowa Republicans, including his opponent, Republican Ashley Hinson, join his call to take steps to lower diesel costs.
Fuel costs have gone up nationwide because of the U.S. war with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major trade route for petroleum. In Iowa, diesel costs are at a record high, sitting at $6.31 per gallon, according to AAA-Iowa, and regular gas prices are up to $4.36 per gallon compared to $2.95 last year.
Turek, a state representative from Council Bluffs, released a plan Sept. 16 calling for the U.S. to pause diesel exports, temporarily suspend the federal gas tax and open the strategic oil reserves to lower fuel costs. On Monday, he told reporters he believed these steps were needed to “some temporary relief” on fuel costs — an especially important topic in Iowa, Turek said, because Iowa farmers are preparing for harvest season.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“With those proposals alone, at least on gas, we’re looking at a reduction of you know maybe 75 cents per gallon, and I think you can see a real reduction in diesel,” he said. “Because everywhere I’m going — particularly in rural communities as we’re in harvest season — they’re talking about … it’s just an all-time bad moment for them. High interest rates, commodity prices being low, diesel prices being at all-time high. I think the tariffs and the war have hurt Iowans and Iowa rural communities and farmers more than any other state.”
Turek said “even Senator Grassley agreed with me” on calling for the U.S. to stop exporting domestically produced diesel, a stance Grassley posted about on social media Saturday, when he wrote “why doesn’t Pres Trump put an embargo on diesel exports like presidents in the 70s put embargoes on ag products bc food prices were inflated.”
Diesel prices shoot upward as Sen. Chuck Grassley begs Trump for export embargo

On Monday, Hinson released her proposal to lower fuel costs in a social media post. Hinson wrote that she would support suspending the federal gas tax and pause diesel exports, in addition to reinstating the $1 per gallon biodiesel tax credit, creating a diesel relief program for farmers and truckers, and “unleashing E-15 everywhere we can” to address high costs.
“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson, a U.S. representative from Iowa’s 2nd District, wrote. “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.”
When asked about Hinson’s proposal, Turek said, “I’m happy that she saw my proposal and decided that it was a good idea.”
“I’m strongly in favor of E15, year-round E15 — would love to be able to to fight for that in the U.S. Senate,” Turek said. “I mean, look — diesel’s at an all-time high, and especially as we’re going … into harvest season, farmers are hurting, and they’re hurting uniquely. Everywhere I’m going, I’m hearing farmers saying, ‘this is just one gut punch after another. I’m looking at what my input prices are going to be, this isn’t going to work.’ I mean, I’m hearing that from century farmers saying, ‘I’m really, really concerned I’m going to go into foreclosure.’ And so, whatever we can do to provide relief to individuals, I think we need to do it.”
Turek also criticized Hinson for voting against a war powers resolution to curb President Donald Trump’s military powers in Iran. Two Iowa Republicans, U.S. Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, voted in favor of the measure last week, though Iowa Democrats have criticized the federal delegation for opposing previous measures to require congressional approval for Trump to continue war in Iran.
In a social media post responding to Hinson, Turek said, “it’s easy to send a tweet but when you had the chance to vote to end this war, you chose not to.”
“You voted seven times to continue it, including just last week,” he wrote. “It’s time to actually end the forever wars and put Iowa and Iowans first.”
Turek made a campaign stop at Fontenelle Supply Co. in Des Moines Monday, where he discussed the impacts of inflation, tariffs and high fuel costs with store co-owner Erich Bockman. Bockman said his business was working to avoid offloading higher costs onto consumers “as much as possible.”
“But it is a very delicate sort of dance,” Bockman said. “And then, the rising cost of everything else — I don’t know what our winter shipments are going to look like with the gas crisis going on — like, diesel trucks carry our stuff across the country too. So it’s all kind of we just play by ear for the most part.”

title: Administrative judge sides with teacher punished for Charlie Kirk Facebook post
description: The state should drop charges, including an allegation of gross immorality, against a Duval County teacher who posted about Charlie Kirk after he was killed, an administrative law judge has recommended.  The decision came last week, addressing charges against Hope McMath, who was an advanced placement art history teacher at Douglas Anderson School of the […]
text:
People visit a memorial set up in honor of Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University in Orem on Tuesday, Sept. 16, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The state should drop charges, including an allegation of gross immorality, against a Duval County teacher who posted about Charlie Kirk after he was killed, an administrative law judge has recommended. 
The decision came last week, addressing charges against Hope McMath, who was an advanced placement art history teacher at Douglas Anderson School of the Arts, a magnet high school in Jacksonville, when Kirk was killed in Utah in September 2025. 
Her Facebook post positioned the shooting as “Karma,” referring to Kirk’s comment, “I think it’s worth to have a cost of, unfortunately, some gun deaths every single year so that we can have the Second Amendment to protect our other God-given rights. That is a prudent deal. It is rational. Nobody talks like this. They live in a complete alternate universe.”
Additionally, according to the state, she “posted or reposted an artist’s rendition of an individual holding the screaming severed head of what clearly is intended to represent the President of the United States, Donald Trump.”
Even so, Administrative Law Judge Garnett Chisenhall wrote that the state provided “no competent, substantial evidence that the social media postings at issue impaired Ms. McMath’s service in the community.”
“The social media postings did not reflect any use, attempted use, or threatened use of violence by Ms. McMath,” the judge wrote, adding that the state “has not argued that Ms. McMath’s post was a legitimate threat to sever President Trump’s head.”
Chisenhall recommended the Education Practices Commission dismiss the charges against McMath, which include gross immorality, personal conduct that seriously reduces effectiveness of an employee, violating the principles of professional conduct required by the Florida Board of Education, reasonably protecting students from conditions harmful to learning, and taking responsible precautions to distinguish between personal views and those of the institution.
Also in September 2025, the school board adopted a policy establishing that an employee’s “inappropriate or unbecoming Material on publicly accessible websites” “has the potential to disrupt the educational process, damage the reputations of the District, it’s [sic] teachers and staff, damages the District’s reputation and stature, and subject the District, its teachers and employees to ridicule.”
McMath’s post did none of that, Chisenhall concluded.
“In short, there is no evidence indicating that anyone could reasonably conclude that Ms. McMath’s sentiments were shared by her employers,” he wrote.
‘I was not celebrating’
The district issued McMath “a verbal warning” with “coaching/counseling,” and “a temporary reassignment to the School District’s Art Resource Center with no teaching duties.”
“I was not celebrating, and the language in that post and the intention behind that post was not celebratory,” McMath said during the proceedings, per the court record. She didn’t post the comments while on the clock at school.
A district investigation did not determine McMath had disrupted district operations. Furthermore, the evidence shows no teacher, administrator, or student complained, and no student viewed the social media posts.
According to the principal at the school, “The content of the posts never came up at the school. Students weren’t talking about it. Teachers weren’t talking about it. Parents weren’t talking about it. They were aware because it was in the news, but nobody ever brought it up as far as a concern of her being in front of their children.”
Shortly after Kirk’s killing, then-Education Commissioner Anastasios Kamoutsas wrote a letter to school superintendents statewide, reminding them that he has the power to discipline educators and sanction their certificates for probable cause, including “personal conduct that seriously reduces that person’s effectiveness as an employee of the district school board.”
McMath, according to the court record, has not been in the classroom since the incident.
“Content that trivializes a homicide and that generally depicts the decapitation of a national figure is a condition harmful to learning and to the mental health of the adolescent students who encounter it,” the state argued.
Chisenhall said he has seen no “persuasive explanation for why” McMath was reassigned away from students.
Federal lawsuit
McMath is plaintiff in a federal lawsuit against the Duval County school district, Florida Department of Education, and Moms for Liberty and its Duval chapter. “While not state entities, they are in some way managed, run or have significant influence on the individual Defendants herein,” that complaint says of the organization.
In that suit, she alleges retaliation, content and viewpoint discrimination, malicious prosecution, defamation, and tortious interference.
In May, the state settled with a state-employed biologist fired after posting about Charlie Kirk after his killing. The state owes half-a-million dollars to the now-former state employee.

name: VTDigger
title: Fund recovery, not active addiction
description:
Building a system with treatment on demand, not a safe injection site, is the real path to compassion.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Fund recovery, not active addiction.
text:
Dear Editor,
As a former three-term progressive Burlington city councilor who spent the last 12 years of my career working in the recovery field — as the executive director of both the Turning Point Center and Recovery Partners of Vermont — I feel compelled to write about the state of our city. 
I’m opposed to opening a safe injection site in Burlington. Our city is in trouble, and our viability as a destination for vacations and regional leisure activities like dining and shopping is in jeopardy. 
Instead of investing millions of dollars in supporting active addiction, I suggest we invest that money in building a treatment and recovery system that provides treatment on demand. If someone is ready to go to a treatment program, that request should be met with an open door for treatment at the point of request. Today, people must wait up to two weeks before a treatment bed is available. That is a huge barrier for someone who is ready to go and a delay that could — and has — cost many people their lives. 
We lost a 41-bed treatment program, Maple Leaf, about 10 years ago. The state has never made up that loss. It was not only a loss to the state but a huge Chittenden County resource lost. 
I drive by City Hall Park every day on my way to the YMCA. It is absolutely shameful that we have let things get this bad. The park that was redesigned for families is frightening and out of control. When I recently ran a booth as part of celebrating the nation’s 250th birthday, I was presented with a woman who pulled her pants down and urinated right in front of me on the grass. 

READ MORE

Battery Park is going in the same direction. Recently, I was giving a Burlington history tour, and we were confronted with a mob on the walkway at the front of the park. There was fighting, drinking and loud music. I could not get close enough to show my customers a special view of the beautiful lake and mountains. I was embarrassed. We stopped and turned away.
Adding a safe injection site where people can continue their active addiction will only bring us further down in a spiral that breaks my heart. Some say that if we have any compassion, we will open this injection center. I say building a more comprehensive treatment and recovery system is our way of showing compassion and putting the emphasis on recovery, not active addiction. 
People in recovery will tell you that they want to be held accountable for their actions. For some reason here in Burlington, we have decided accountability is not all that important. It seems to me it’s the bedrock of a civil society. We do no favor to people by bending and breaking the law. I hope that, as the guardians of this city, Burlington City Council will steer us to a better future. I’m certainly available for any discussions on this matter.
Gary De Carolis,Burlington, Vt.

title: Diesel prices shoot upward as top farm-state GOP senator begs Trump for export embargo
text: WASHINGTON — Diesel prices hit a record average of $6.51 a gallon Monday, and some in President Donald Trump’s own party are breaking their support for the ongoing war in Iran that has driven fuel prices to staggering levels in the United States and across the globe.Already House Republicans locked in tight races as the November midterms approach have distanced themselves from the president’s conflict and his administration’s stagnant negotiations with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital passage for global petroleum products. Another major vote on Iran support is expected later this week in the U.S. Senate.The cost of diesel, which fuels the movement of goods through the United States, is up nearly $1 since last month, and up from just over $3.69 a year ago, according to AAA. The national average cost for a gallon of gasoline landed at just over $4.47 Monday, up more than a dollar from last year’s average at $3.18, according to the motor club’s daily monitor.Trump has an opportunity this week to potentially meet with Iranian officials, as leaders head to the United Nations General Assembly in New York City. Trump told Fox News on Sunday he is “open” to meeting with Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian.Trump said he is in “deciding mode” about next steps in Iran, and that “big things” will happen in the “not so distant future,” he told the network’s Trey Yingst. Grassley wants diesel embargoLongtime Iowa Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley urged Trump throughout the weekend to embargo diesel fuel exports as costs impact farmers in his largely agricultural state. “W(ith) diesel $6.57 in Iowa why doesn’t Pres Trump put an embargo on diesel exports like presidents in the 70s put embargoes on (agricultural) products bc food prices were inflated. High diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME,” Grassley wrote Saturday on X, followed by two more posts on Sunday urging the president to put “AMERICA FIRST.”The administration does not have plans at this time to ban or restrict diesel exports, according to a White House official Monday. Seven House Republicans broke ranks last week and voted in support of stopping Trump’s war with Iran unless Congress approved further action. The Republicans included two vulnerable Iowa representatives, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, who are facing tough reelection bids in the fast-approaching midterm elections.Democratic senators are expected to move on a War Powers Resolution vote this week. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Wednesday he will force the vote to continue applying pressure on Trump to stop the military campaign that has not been authorized by Congress.“We’re gonna force a vote to end this illegal war every week until we succeed,” Kaine said in a video posted to X. Two Republicans who will not serve in Congress next year, largely due to Trump’s public opposition to them, have also spoken out against the Pentagon leadership.House Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who has consistently supported War Powers Resolutions on Iran, unexpectedly introduced articles of impeachment last week against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, citing his leadership during the Iran conflict. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina told reporters on Capitol Hill Thursday that Hegseth “needs to go.” Tillis has voted no on multiple War Powers Resolutions aimed at ending hostilities in Iran.Energy commodities up 16.3%Inflation continued a steady march upwards in August, with fuel leading the way, according to the government’s latest consumer price index. The cost of all types of gasoline and fuel oil rose 3.9% from July to August. All energy commodities and services, like electricity, shot up 16.3% over the past 12 months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.Trump and his administration officials have downplayed the squeeze on Americans at the pump, and Trump has promised fuel prices will drop “quickly” once the conflict ends.On Monday he shifted the blame for skyrocketing diesel prices on to Russia’s war in Ukraine.“Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine. A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission. This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended,” he wrote on his platform Truth Social.Vice President JD Vance told reporters Monday that the administration “is doing everything we can” to reduce energy prices, and suggested that states should suspend gas taxes.“We're very cognizant of the fact that because the Iranians are terrorizing international shipping, energy prices are elevated,” he said.Meanwhile the conflict has expanded in the Middle East as Iran -backed Houthi rebels in Yemen fight for control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key route for Saudi Arabian oil exports. The State Department issued a safety alert Saturday to U.S. citizens in the Middle East, warning “the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation.”“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” according to the warning, which instructs American travelers to make sure cell phones are charged at all times and to “keep a low profile.”

text:
Emily Donovan, Clean Cape FearOne of the most important and worrisome threats to our natural environment and human health to emerge in recent decades is a group of chemicals commonly referred to as PFAS. Also known as “forever chemicals,” PFAS are especially pernicious because they’re toxic, cause all kinds of health problems, and don’t break down in the environment. For the last several decades, corporate polluters spewed vast quantities of PFAS into the air and water in southeastern North Carolina, thus contaminating public water systems and thousands of private wells.
Thankfully, one especially important and effective group that’s emerged in response to this problem is the nonprofit Clean Cape Fear, and recently Newsline caught up with the group’s co-founder Emily Donovan as she returned from testifying before the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva, Switzerland.
Click here to listen to the full interview with Clean Cape Fear co-founder Emily Donovan.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico general election 2026: Public Education Commission
description: Two races are on the ballot come November for seats on New Mexico's commission that oversees and approves charter schools. The District 2 race sees the incumbent Democrat face a Forward Party candidate and a Democrat and Republican face off for an open seat in District 7.
text:
Two seats on the New Mexico Public Education Commission, which oversees charter schools, have contested races in the Nov. 3 general election. (Photo by kali9/Getty Images)The New Mexico Public Education Commission approves public charter schools applications, and reviews and supports the over 100 charter schools currently in the state. The commission is administratively attached to the New Mexico Public Education Department, which supplies the commission with staff. Ten partisan commissioners serve four-year terms with no term limits representing 10 districts across the state.
Charter schools are public schools that are governed by an independent governing board instead of being administered by a school district like traditional public schools. 
In the Nov. 3 general election, the Democratic incumbent faces a challenge from a Forward Party challenger to represent the Albuquerque-area district.
Two candidates, a Republican and a Democrat will vie for the open seat in southern New Mexico’s District 7, and hope to replace Patricia Gipson, who did not run for re-election.
Source NM posed several questions to the candidates about their races. Their answers have been edited for clarity and concision.
District 3
District 3 covers western parts of Albuquerque in Bernalillo County. There are currently 14 public charter schools in the district, according to the PEC.
Dennis Dinge
Dennis Dinge, Forward Party candidate for the Public Education Commission. (Courtesy of Dennis Dinge)
Forward Party candidate Dennis Dinge is a physicist, researcher and educator who previously worked at Sandia National Laboratories and is state treasurer of the Forward Party, which was certified in May as a minor party in New Mexico. He previously ran for New Mexico’s first congressional district in the 2018 Democratic primary, but dropped out of the crowded race in 2017.
Why do you want to serve on the PEC and what makes you the best choice?
The PEC felt like a natural fit for my background in research and makes me a better candidate. I worked at the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, which was the largest database in the world that mapped galaxies. I want to bring that same data-centered approach to New Mexico’s public charter system.
What is the biggest challenge charter schools face in New Mexico?
Barriers like lack of charter school options and transportation. Public charter schools need to be available to all students in the state. There are rural areas of the state that could use them, and parents may lack the transportation to get their kids there. 
What role do charter schools play in the larger educational landscape in New Mexico?
Public charter schools provide educational experiences that usually may not be offered in the state, such as ones that focus on trades or art. They have some wiggle room to experiment with different teaching methods, and if those methods are successful, lawmakers can consider adopting on a statewide level.
Do you think the Trump administration’s massive investment in charter schools while also cutting federal funds meant for public schools is a step in the right direction for national education policy? 
To cut funding for public schools is never a step in the right direction. Federal funding should not prioritize one type of public school over a different one — money is best spent helping all schools. It’ll be rare to find me in agreement with the Trump administration.
As the Yazzie/Martinez education equity case continues, how will you hold charter schools accountable for enrolling and serving the student populations affected in the case and satisfying the court’s order?
Prospective charter schools have to include how they will help affected Yazzie-Martinez students in their initial application. If they don’t, then an objection will be raised. The same goes for renewal applications, though it will be easier since the commission can look at the track record to see if the school has been successful in satisfying the court’s order.
What type of charter-school legislation would you back/hope to see in the coming session?
I would like to see the Legislature promote charter schools in rural parts of the state and ensure that underserved populations are cared for. Virtual charter schools may be a way to address that. I want to also make sure that charter schools are not allowed to discourage unions in any way.
Jacob Trujillo
Public Education Commission District 3 incumbent Jacob Trujillo. (Courtesy of Jacob Trujillo)
Jacob Trujillo is the Democratic incumbent of District 3, appointed by Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on June 17 after former commissioner Alan Brauer resigned due to moving from the state.
Trujillo cites his status as a charter school graduate — he attended  Albuquerque Institute for Mathematics and Science — as a point of pride. He has served as the chair of the Democratic Party of Bernalillo County since 2025 and as a field representative for U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.). 
Trujillo was appointed to the position by Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on June 17 after previous commissioner Alan Brauer resigned.
Why do you want to serve on the PEC and what makes you the best choice?
I feel a need to fill a gap of representation because the PEC consists of people who never went through the educational system they govern.
What is the biggest challenge charter schools face in New Mexico?
We need to better educate the public that public charter schools are not private schools. The charter schools under PEC are also public schools and do not hand-pick like private schools do.
What role do charter schools play in the larger educational landscape in New Mexico?
Charter schools allow us to test out different education styles to see what is working and then implement at other schools. This improves the public education system as a whole.
Do you think the Trump administration’s massive investment in charter schools while also cutting federal funds meant for public schools is a step in the right direction for national education policy? 
I do not think that is a good direction. Republicans want to privatize education, and the way they start getting there is by promoting charters while cutting public schools. That is why charter schools need to be very well regulated.
As the Yazzie/Martinez education equity case continues, how will you hold charter schools accountable for enrolling and serving the student populations affected in the case and satisfying the court’s order? 
One of the things I took my oath on was a copy of the Yazzie/Martinez case. If applicant schools are not supporting the Yazzi-Martinez student population, I will vote against their application. They have no reason to be a school in New Mexico.
What type of charter-school legislation would you back/hope to see in the coming session?
Funding in order to hire and pay staff for the PEC. Currently, the PEC doesn’t have its own staff. A dedicated staff would make the PEC have better technical assistance for schools, families and students.
District 7
District 7 primarily covers Doña Ana County and a portion of Otero County in southern New Mexico, including Las Cruces. There are eight charter schools in the district, per the commission. The current District 7 commissioner is Patricia Gipson, a Democrat, who also serves as chair, but is not running for reelection.
John Foreman
Republican PEC District 7 candidate John Foreman. (Courtesy of John Foreman)
Republican candidate John Foreman is a lifelong educator who taught high school history, social studies and economics in New Mexico public and private schools. He previously ran as a Republican for New Mexico House District 52 in 2022 and lost to state Rep. Doreen Gallegos (D-Las Cruces).
Why do you want to serve on the PEC and what makes you the best choice?
I have always been a fan of school choice and charter schools are the only version of that for parents in New Mexico. My background in the education system is extensive — teacher, coach, administrator — which makes me qualified to sit on the commission.
What is the biggest challenge charter schools face in New Mexico?
The challenge going forward is to keep charter schools autonomous so they can do their mission and not feel pressure from teachers unions or funding mechanisms.
What role do charter schools play in the larger educational landscape in New Mexico?
They give parents a choice and fill a role that maybe wasn’t there before. Students interested in a specific trade or career can have the opportunity to learn the skills required through charter schools which can keep them engaged in order to graduate.
Do you think the Trump administration’s massive investment in charter schools while also cutting federal funds meant for public schools is a step in the right direction for national education policy? 
Some of the federal moves were in the spirit of competition and competition is good. We need to look on a case-by-case basis, regardless if a school is charter and public, and see who is succeeding and progressing and shift funds accordingly.
As the Yazzie/Martinez education equity case continues, how will you hold charter schools accountable for enrolling and serving the student populations affected in the case and satisfying the court’s order? 
I previously was a principal in the Navajo Reservation and I know that students in the Yazzie/Martinez population can accomplish great things with the right classroom leadership that starts with the teacher. 
What type of charter-school legislation would you back/hope to see in the coming session?
I support legislation that supports the autonomy of charter schools and that promotes increased vocational training.
Fred Parker
Democratic PEC District 7 candidate Fred Parker. (Courtesy of Fred Parker)
Democratic candidate Fred Parker spent close to 30 years as a New Mexico public educator  prior to retiring. He started his career cleaning computers for an elementary school before becoming a teacher and later an administrator. This is his first time running for an elected position.
Why do you want to serve on the PEC and what makes you the best choice?
As a prior district level leader that oversaw a local charter school, I understand the intricacies and knowledge needed for the position. 
What is the biggest challenge charter schools face in New Mexico?
Declining enrollment rates, which we see across the country. We need to reengage families and students in a way that is responsive to their needs and get enrollment back on track.
What role do charter schools play in the larger educational landscape in New Mexico?
Since charter schools are smaller, they are more agile to respond to student needs and pivot if needed. They hit the niche needs for families that want something different. 
Do you think the Trump administration’s massive investment in charter schools while also cutting federal funds meant for public schools is a step in the right direction for national education policy? 
Federal funds being allocated for charter schools is, in some cases, a good thing since they do not have access to certain types of funding that our traditional public districts have. 
As the Yazzie/Martinez education equity case continues, how will you hold charter schools accountable for enrolling and serving the student populations affected in the case and satisfying the court’s order? 
Equity has to show up in actual opportunities and outcomes than just what comes from written plans in applications. The commission needs to track the outcomes during each charter school review on how well they’re serving Yazzie/Martinez student populations.
What type of charter-school legislation would you back/hope to see in the coming session?
I’d like to see some funding increases to support charter schools for lease reimbursement that is matched to inflation and a clearer mechanism for charter schools to acquire and build facilities.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Federal appeals court rules Lafayette County permit policy violates First Amendment
description: Lafayette County Courthouse in Oxford as seen from the west side of the square.
text:
A federal appeals court panel last week ruled that Lafayette County’s policy prohibiting an Oxford filmmaker and professor from using the exterior of its picturesque county courthouse at night was unconstitutional. 
The opinion, written by Judge Andrew Oldham and joined by Judges Jaques Wiener and Kurt Engelhardt, said the county’s stated reason of protecting public safety was not enough to justify instituting a blanket nighttime curfew and violates the First Amendment.  
“The County has not shown the curfew provision is narrowly tailored,” Oldham wrote. “Even though trial evidence showed that nighttime activity on the town square varies, the nighttime ban applies from sundown to sunup.” 
The litigation began in 2020 when John Rash, a University of Mississippi film professor, applied for a permit to project art onto the exterior of the county’s courthouse. The county denied the application because it had a nighttime curfew and only allowed access during the day. 
John Rash
U.S. District Judge Debra Brown ruled in Rash’s favor and prevented the county from enforcing the curfew. But she said Rash did not have legal standing to challenge the other portions of the county’s permit policy.
Both Rash and the county appealed to the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals, which ultimately sided with the plaintiff in the ruling released Thursday. The three-judge appellate panel went further and ruled that Rash did have standing to challenge all portions of the permit policy and sent it back to the district court for further proceedings. 
The American Civil Liberties Union of Mississippi and private law firm Simpson Thacher represented Rash in the litigation. 
Joshua Tom, the ACLU of Mississippi’s legal director, said in a statement that Americans have the right to assemble, protest and debate the issues of the day in a public forum like that county courthouse. 
“Lafayette County tried to stifle that right,” Tom said. “With this ruling, the Fifth Circuit has reaffirmed it.” 
Attorneys for the defendants did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The county could ask the full slate of judges on the 5th Circuit to reconsider the case. It’s unknown when the trial court will schedule future legal proceedings.
Correction 9/21/26: The federal appeals panel ruling in this case was Sept. 17. An earlier version of this article had the incorrect day of the ruling.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Gulfport program helps nursing home residents stay connected
authors: Michelle Pinto, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center, Justin Glowacki, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center and McKenna Klamm, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center
description: Vanessa Welch uses larger equipment to make video calls because some patients have vision, hearing or accessibility impairments. Welch also uses large equipment to show more than one resident at a time how to operate phones.
text:
GULFPORT — Juanita Wallace has lived at Gulfport Care Center for six years. With several family members out of state, her phone helps her stay connected — but using it has not always been easy. 
“I really appreciate (Gulf Coast Connection Services) because I really needed (help), because I sure did not know how to operate my phone,” Wallace said. 
Wallace is one of the residents receiving help from Gulf Coast Connection Services. Founder Vanessa Welch helps residents make video calls, adjust accessibility settings and troubleshoot phones, tablets and computers. 
Her company aims to help nursing home and assisted living residents overcome technology barriers that can leave devices unused and make it harder to communicate with relatives who cannot regularly visit. 
Mississippi’s Digital Skills and Accessibility Plan identifies people 60 and older as one of several populations facing barriers to digital access. Among the challenges for older Mississippians, the plan identifies limited digital skills and cybersecurity knowledge and calls for expanded digital literacy training and technical support.
One-on-one assistance 
Vanessa Welch, founder of Gulf Coast Connection Services, goes to Gulfport Care Center twice a week to teach residents how to use technology or assist with technology questions. Credit: Michelle Pinto/RHCJC
Welch meets with residents at Gulfport Care Center on Tuesdays and Fridays, working with groups and going room to room to reach those who cannot leave their beds. 
Lisa Perdue, the center’s activity director, said the program provides one-on-one technology assistance that staff may not have time to offer. 
“One-on-one, for that amount of time, it is pretty impossible for a CNA to take two hours, an hour with a resident to help them with things like that,” Perdue said. “That’s where Vanessa comes in.” 
Welch developed the idea after volunteering at another local nursing home, where she saw residents struggling with isolation from their families. 
She started Gulf Coast Connection Services in June and began reaching out to assisted living facilities. Gulfport Care Center joined the pilot in July. 
Perdue, who has worked in nursing home activities for 26 years, said her experience during COVID-19 visitor restrictions drew her to Welch’s plan. 
“We gave iPads any way we could during COVID, to keep them connected with their families,” Perdue said. “That’s why I was so on board with (Welch), because I saw what the video calls did during COVID, what they did for families.” 
A 2023 systematic review published in JMIR Aging found video calls and other communication technologies were used in long-term care facilities during the pandemic to help residents maintain social connections and address isolation and loneliness. 
Although pandemic-era visitor restrictions have ended, Perdue said residents with limited mobility can still experience isolation. 
“Imagine that you cannot move. You can’t do anything for yourself,” Perdue said. “The only touch you get that day is from a CNA who is positioning you in a different way. You know, no hugs, no physical interaction with anyone besides care.” 
Staying in communication 
Welch arranges video calls through Google Meet. When a resident requests a call, she contacts the family member, explains the service and schedules a time. 
She also helps residents enlarge text, turn on closed captions and access games, digital books and audiobooks. She creates reference sheets for residents to use after lessons and teaches them to identify possible scams.
Linda LaHood, who lives at the center with her husband, Gerald, said she had learned previous phones on her own but struggled with her newest one. 
“She’s helped us learn this phone like we had never been able to learn before,” LaHood said. “It’s complicated for older people because we don’t know how it all works.” 
Welch said closed captions transformed one resident’s video calls with his sister. Because he has hearing loss, his sister normally used a whiteboard during FaceTime calls. 
“I was able to turn on the closed captioning so he could read it as she was saying it, and they were able to just have a conversation,” Welch said. 
For Lashona Lewis, the calls help close the distance between Texas and Gulfport, where her mother lives at the center. 
“You get a free visit. You didn’t have to travel to do it. You don’t have to take off from work,” Lewis said. “It’s not to replace your in-person connection, but in the event that the person has a family dynamic where there’s not a lot of in-person visitors, this video visit is really important.” 
Beyond the pilot 
Gulfport Care Center is part of the Gulf Coast Connection Services pilot program. The care center connected with Welch’s Gulf Coast Connection Services after Welch sent surveys to multiple nursing homes on the Gulf Coast.  Credit: Michelle Pinto/RHCJC
Welch volunteers her time, and the facility, residents and families do not pay for the service. Donations help provide chargers, phone cases and educational materials. 
Outside of her work at Gulfport Care Center, Gulf Coast Connection Services offers paid assistance to people living at home or in privately-owned assisted living facilities. 
Welch initially planned to serve several nursing homes for two hours at a time. But her experience at Gulfport Care Center showed her that there was not enough time to answer questions and provide individual assistance. 
For now, she is focusing on Gulfport Care Center while determining how to make the program sustainable. She hopes to expand to other nursing homes along the Mississippi Gulf Coast and eventually make the service her full-time work. 
For Wallace, learning to use her phone is about maintaining relationships with people who cannot always be in the same room. 
“Communication is the most important thing with family,” Wallace said.
