name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Republican House candidate under fire for comments about Black women, Muslims
description: Republican candidate Chris Clagett, who is running in Berkeley County for a seat in the West Virginia House of Delegates, posted several racist posts on social media that targeted Black women and Muslims.
text:
Chris Clagett is the Republican candidate for House of Delegates District 91, which represents southern Berkeley County. (Photo courtesy of Chris Clagett’s campaign website)Republican candidate Chris Clagett, who is running in Berkeley County for a seat in the West Virginia House of Delegates, posted several racist posts on social media that targeted Black women and Muslims. 
Clagett is on the ballot in the 91st District in the upcoming November election. The district has seen a string of controversies involving its Republican House candidates, including a candidate arrested after making terrorist threats against sitting lawmakers. 
A lengthy list of Clagett’s social media activity is now under scrutiny. 
A screenshot of Chris Clagett’s social media post.
In January, Clagett posted on X, “Maybe because black women are the most ill-mannered, ill-behaved, loud-mouthed demographics on the face of the Earth. Does that clarify it for you … ?”  He responded to a post that said, “They always think saying I’m not doing anything means they’re not resisting arrest.”
That same month, Clagett posted on X “their children are roaming the streets,” in response to someone saying, “No black woman would willinging bring their babies to an active arrest situation.”
In an X post on Jan. 6, 2026, Clagett responded to a photo of the Confederate flag and called it “a beautiful flag compared to so many drab three horizontal or vertical bar flags.”
West Virginia Watch reached out to Clagett on Monday by phone, email and social media. He answered the phone asking for an interview later in the day, but didn’t return the second phone call.
Clagett fielded questions last week from radio hosts with Eastern Panhandle station WRNR about the social media posts. During that interview, Clagett confirmed that he posted it. 
Clagett told the radio hosts, “context is everything.” He later said the post he responded to with the words “ill-mannered” included Black women “behaving in exactly the manner I described.”
“It does represent me poorly … if I had been more accurate, I should have put liberal Black women and I should have described it that way,” Clagett said. “I was also guilty of not being even handed because the truth is the awful, white female liberals are just as bad. We’re talking about a world view and the behaviors that go with it.”
Clagett added that, “There are many Black women I admire greatly.”
There are other posts made by Clagett that were not discussed in that radio interview.
In a Facebook post in 2023, Clagett said, “I want to announce that I now identify as Trans … racial that is. As a penance for my heretofore underserved status as a privileged white male, I now identify as a Black man. May the police hunt me down.” 
West Virginia Republican Party Chair Josh Holstein declined to comment on Clagett’s comments at this time. 
West Virginia Democratic Party Chair Mike Pushkin. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Mike Pushkin, chair of the state Democratic Party, said Clagett’s social media posts include repeated references to African Americans as “savages,” and to Black women as “sheboons.”
“These statements are abhorrent and should receive universal condemnation,” Pushkin told West Virginia Watch. Pushkin also serves in the House of Delegates.
“That’s why I am calling on House Speaker Roger Hanshaw and West Virginia Republican Party Chairman Josh Holstein to state clearly whether they condemn this language,” Pushkin said. “West Virginians deserve to know where their political leaders stand when hate-filled statements like these are made by someone seeking public office. Silence on matters this serious implies consent, which is why a clear public response is warranted.”
House of Delegates Minority Leader Sean Hornbuckle, D-Cabell. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Ann Ali, communications director for the House, said she hadn’t yet been able to speak with Hanshaw on Monday about the situation. 
“I am unfamiliar with this candidate’s language, and while context is always important, Speaker Hanshaw has never condoned hate speech,” Ali said. 
House Minority Leader Sean Hornbuckle, D-Cabell, condemned Clagett’s comments on his own social media page. Hornbuckle is the first Black man elected to the Minority leader position in West Virginia.
“Personally, I could care less about how many members I have in my Caucus, party or any of that because I’m never going to sit back in silence on disgusting behavior. The seat, the control, all the things that come with just don’t mean that much to me that I’m willing to allow people to be dehumanized,” Hornbuckle wrote Monday on Facebook.
“To my elected peers of all walks of life, this is beyond ‘politics.’ This spits in the face of West Virginia … the state was created by literally separating slavery and the worst behavior we’ve seen in our country,” he continued. “Don’t wait ‘til Nov. 4 to act like you care because you were power hungry and acting selfishly when these things could happen.”
Clagett also made comments online about the country’s Muslim population, responding on an X post with a photo that said, “MAGA care more about their dogs than Muslim immigrants, is that right?” In response, Clagett said, “Depends on your definition of ‘care.’ If ‘care’ means ‘to have affection for,’ then yes, we care more about our dogs.”
Clagett clarified on the Eastern Panhandle radio show that the post “was intended as an insult to conservatives. “I reposted it because I said, yes, this is accurate,” Clagett said.
“They’re not here to assimilate to enjoy the American dream,” he said.
In a separate social media post on Jan. 27, Clagett said he supported banning all Muslims from entering the West.
Clagett’s campaign website describes him as an experienced Navy leader who served as a member of the U.S. Navy Medical Corps. He retired in 2019 after 34 years of service, according to his website. Clagett’s biography says he earned a medical degree.
His political platform focuses on medical freedom from vaccinations, immigration enforcement and curriculum reform in public school.
Clagett ran unopposed in the May primary election, winning 796 votes. David Michaels, the
Democratic challenge in the race, won 435 votes.
(Photo courtesy of David Michaels)
Michaels said he was appalled by Clagett’s comments.
“I’m surprised that you know the West Virginia GOP hasn’t stepped in and said, ‘Hey, this is enough.’ We need better candidates,” Michaels said in a phone interview.
“I feel bad for the minorities that have to hear that sort of language, and it saddens me that it’s still thick. It’s still in the United States, and it’s still in West Virginia,” he said.
Berkeley County district’s controversial candidates
Del. Ian Masters, R-Berkeley, currently holds the House seat for the district. He is not seeking reelection.
Last summer, Masters denied allegations that he was responsible for an antisemitic comment made by a private Instagram account that used his name and is linked to an organization he recently led.
House Majority Leader Pat McGeehan, R-Hancock, supported Masters in the ordeal, saying there was proof that Masters did not post it. McGeehan later said that Masters gave his old phone to a person who was “basically homeless,” living with substance use disorder and very ill and that individual had posted the antisemitic comment.
Gov. Patrick Morrisey had appointed Masters to the House seat after Republican delegate-elect Joseph DeSoto, who won the November 2024 election, was arrested and accused of threatening to harm and kill lawmakers ahead of the 2025 Legislative Session.
There were also concerns about whether de Soto was truthful about his military career or if he was actually a physician.
Joseph de Soto (West Virginia Division of Corrections and Rehabilitation)
House Republicans in January voted to vacate the seat instead of expelling de Soto, saying it was the correct way to deal with the seat since de Soto was on house arrest and never sworn in.
DeSoto had won the 2025 general election as a Republican but he further complicated the arrest fallout since he switched his party affiliation to Democratic shortly before being arrested.
The vacate move prompted a legal challenge from the state Democratic Party, who argued that the seat should have gone to Democrats due to de Soto’s party switch.
The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals dismissed a challenge from the Democrats in one of their challenges over the seat. The party’s other appeal is still ongoing and will be heard by the Supreme Court this week.
Michaels had been on the Democratic list to replace de Soto before the seat was secured by the Republican Party.
He said the de Soto ordeal had inspired him to run since he thought the area, which he has called home for more than 40 years, deserved better candidates. Berkeley County is growing quickly, Michaels said, and he’s running on a platform of improving roads and instituting locality pay to keep teachers in the county.
The southern part of Berkeley County is very Republican, he noted.
“(It) looks like there’s very little vetting that’s done on the Republican side and their choice of candidates,” Michaels said. “Unfortunately, we have yet another candidate that is being lifted up by the GOP that says, ‘Hey, this is your choice,’ and that just really saddens me.”

title: Two Michigan residents charged with making terrorist threats against state officials
description: Attorney General Dana Nessel on Monday announced charges against two Michigan residents accused of making terrorist threats against public officials in unrelated incidents, including the mayor of Dearborn, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and members of the Michigan Supreme Court. Alicia Choucair, 33, of Roseville, Michigan, and Antho[...]
text:
The office of Attorney General Dana Nessel in the G. Mennen Williams Building in Lansing, Mich., on May 15, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Attorney General Dana Nessel on Monday announced charges against two Michigan residents accused of making terrorist threats against public officials in unrelated incidents, including the mayor of Dearborn, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and members of the Michigan Supreme Court.
Alicia Choucair, 33, of Roseville, Michigan, and Anthony Dekinderen, 61, of Lake Orion, Michigan, were arraigned late last week, Nessel’s office said in a news release.
Choucair is alleged to have called a local police dispatch threatening violence against a mosque and Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud. She was charged with two counts of making a false report and a threat of terrorism, and one count of committing a hate crime. Choucair allegedly threatened the mosque and Hammoud by saying the threat would occur if “your people” weren’t kept out of town, a reference to Arabs and Muslims in the predominantly Arab and Muslim city. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Choucair was arraigned Sept. 17 before a Wayne County 19th District Court judge. She was given a $20,000 cash or surety bond and is scheduled to next appear for a probable cause hearing on Sept. 30. She remained in custody as of Monday afternoon. If convicted, she faces up to 20 years in prison for each count of a false report and threat of terrorism and a two-year sentence for committing a hate crime. 
Dekinderen is alleged to have sent two threatening emails to Michigan Advance, part of the States Newsroom network. The emails allegedly contained threats to kill members of the Michigan Supreme Court, Whitmer and Benson, Nessel’s office said.
Dekinderen was charged with nine counts of sending a false report or a threat of terrorism, the attorney general’s office said, each carrying a 20-year prison sentence. He was arraigned before an Oakland County 52-3 District Court judge in Rochester Hills on Sept. 19 and was granted a $5 million bond with a requirement to wear a GPS tether. 
Oakland County jail records indicate that Dekinderen was still incarcerated as of Monday afternoon. He is scheduled to next appear in court on Sept. 28.
“Thousands of Michigan residents answer the call to serve through elected office, be it as the local mayor or in statewide office. Unfortunately, hate crimes and threats of terrorism against officials at all levels of government are becoming increasingly common,” Nessel said in a statement. “Let these charges serve as a warning that Michigan takes threats of violence very seriously and will prosecute these cases to the fullest extent of the law.”
Denkinderen sent two emails to the Advance on Sept. 14, containing slurs and threats to a reporter and threats to the officials.
A message seeking comment from Dekinderen’s attorney was not returned at the time of publication. This story will be updated once a response is received.
“We take threats of violence seriously,” said Jon King, Michigan Advance editor-in-chief. “The emails our journalist received were alarming, so we turned them over to the Michigan Department of Attorney General’s office immediately. The safety and security of our staff and the public officials named is our top priority.”

name: VTDigger
title: UVM and USDA researchers hope to improve local agriculture
description:
The Food Systems Research Station is a long-term collaboration between the University of Vermont and the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Agricultural Research Service.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM and USDA researchers hope to improve local agriculture.
text:
The research warehouse at the Food Systems Research Station in Charlotte, Sept. 17, 2026. Photo by Tierney Flavin/VTDigger.
Matthew McIntosh’s family says he came out of the womb loving cows. 
Now, McIntosh, who works for the Agricultural Research Service in the U.S. Department of Agriculture, is trying to help Vermont farmers improve the quality and quantity of their cows through the University of Vermont’s new Food Systems Research Station.
At the station, researchers are seeking to innovate solutions to agricultural problems, sharing  what they learn with the rest of New England, Kirk Dombrowski, UVM vice president for research and economic development, said in an interview. 
“It’s one of those new collaborative spaces where we can get students with their hands literally in the dirt,” he said.
UVM opened the research station to a crowd of researchers, staff and stakeholders Thursday. Located on an approximately 400-acre former dairy farm in Charlotte, the research station is housed in an 18,000-square foot warehouse where researchers have begun studying crop behavior, livestock and food system challenges. The station is the first of its kind in New England, according to Food Systems Research Institute Director Polly Ericksen.
Ericksen, who coordinates research opportunities and collaborates with the USDA, said in an interview that the center’s researchers are able to alleviate some of local farmers’ burdens.
This includes dairy farm consolidation, which McIntosh is working to address with his upcoming research studying dairy and beef cow crossbreeding, as well as various other impacts on cow behavior and production performance. 
Limited research started at the station in May, including a study of cow grazing preference inspired by discussions with other scientists, USDA Agricultural Research Service research leader Chris Peters said in an interview.
The research station is the newest step in the collaboration between UVM’s Food Systems Research Institute and the USDA’s Agricultural Research Service. The partnership began in 2019 through a $3 million congressional appropriation.
In 2024, UVM signed a 30-year lease on Nordic Farm to establish the research station.
In the two years since the signing, UVM and USDA teams have been working to prepare the land, determine equipment needs, establish preliminary research needs and begin building a research barn and acquiring livestock, Ericksen said during Thursday’s opening remarks.
She said that she envisions more “field days” like Thursday’s, where community members, researchers and stakeholders can see what work is being done.
Food systems research adds to a long-standing practice of trying to understand how agriculture works from all angles, Peters said, adding that researchers can’t keep their “blinders on.”
“The work that we do is not just studying farm products but whole systems, multiple products at one time,” he said, “kind of getting to the whole picture writ large.”
The hope for McIntosh and other researchers is to help local farmers produce healthy food that can stay in the Northeast.  
“We could have a huge impact on keeping it local,” McIntosh said. “I’m just so delighted to be here.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM and USDA researchers hope to improve local agriculture.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Democrat Don Coover objects to U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt’s approach to unreleased Epstein files
description: TOPEKA — Kansas congressional candidate Don Coover expressed frustration with U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt’s refusal to help trigger a House vote on a bill pressuring the administration of President Donald Trump to release more documents in the Jeffrey Epstein case. Coover, a Democrat seeking to oust Schmidt in the 2nd District of eastern Kansas, urged […]
text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt, seen March 12, 2026, at the Kansas Secretary of State's Office in Topeka, refused to sign onto a procedural move to bypass House leadership and force a vote on legislation to bring transparency to the Epstein files. Democrat Don Coover, who is running against Schmidt, criticized Schmidt's decision. (Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas congressional candidate Don Coover expressed frustration with U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt’s refusal to help trigger a House vote on a bill pressuring the administration of President Donald Trump to release more documents in the Jeffrey Epstein case.
Coover, a Democrat seeking to oust Schmidt in the 2nd District of eastern Kansas, urged the Republican congressman to join more than 200 Democrats and a handful of Republicans working on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II. The bill was a response to the U.S. Department of Justice’s failure to fully comply with a 2025 law mandating disclosure of Epstein documents. Critics also accused the DOJ of heavily redacting documents to hide names of alleged Epstein associates.
Schmidt, a former Kansas attorney general, told constituents during a recent town hall that he wouldn’t sign the bipartisan “discharge petition” directing GOP House leadership to bypass normal committee procedure and bring the new Epstein bill to a vote of the House.
“Once again, Derek Schmidt decided to stand behind D.C. insiders covering up the Epstein files instead of standing with survivors of sexual abuse,” said Coover campaign spokesperson Lily Johnson. “Like many Kansans, Don Coover is disgusted with what is happening in Washington. He will be a strong voice for Epstein survivors.”
 Epstein was awaiting trial on federal charges of sex trafficking of minors when he died in his jail cell in 2019. During the 2024 presidential election, Trump vowed to voluntarily comply with public demand for release of government documents linked to the case. Trump later broke his campaign promise to make Epstein files public, calling the inquiry a hoax perpetrated by Democrats.
U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kansas, signed the 2025 discharge petition related to the initial Epstein transparency bill. No Republican member of the state’s congressional delegation joined her. Under political pressure, Trump reversed course to endorse that bill. In the House, the measure passed 427-1. It received unanimous backing from the Senate. Trump signed the legislation in November 2025.
The New York Times reported the president’s name appeared in the government’s Epstein files at least 38,000 times.
On Thursday, House sponsors of a discharge petition attached to the second piece of Epstein disclosure legislation said they secured the minimum 218 signatures to bring about a vote. The follow-up Epstein legislation likely wouldn’t reach the House floor until after the Nov. 3 election.
Schmidt’s congressional office didn’t respond to telephone and email requests for comment about the Epstein files, but he said during the town hall that he objected to the petition process because it was often driven by lawmakers intent on making Congress appear dysfunctional.
“I have not yet signed a discharge petition on any subject since I’ve been in Congress,” said Schmidt, who was elected in 2024. “I prefer to work with the leadership to get items scheduled on the floor. This has the potential to sound glib and I don’t mean it to, but there’s a lot of politics around this place.”
“On lots of issues,” he added, “what happens is folks join up and try to run over the leadership. Not only because they care about an issue, but because they want to render the place nonfunctional. They want to basically hijack the ability of the (House) speaker and the leadership to control the floor schedule and to do that, usually, for political reasons.”
Schmidt committed to voting on merits of legislation regardless of how it got to the House floor.
In terms of the latest Epstein disclosure bill, Schmidt said during the town hall that “I’d probably vote for it.”
Schmidt said his preference would be for the Justice Department and Attorney General Todd Blanche to meet obligations under the 2025 Epstein law. So far, the DOJ says about half of 6 million pages of documents have been released.
Blanche has been accused by Epstein victims of undermining DOJ transparency. U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan threatened Blanche with civil contempt if DOJ failed to meet court deadlines. While Blanche defended the DOJ, the state of New Mexico sued after the agency refused to release information relevant to a probe of alleged sex crimes at Epstein’s ranch.
“I’m not sure we have to have another law,” Schmidt said. “What we have to have is DOJ follow the one we’ve got. Don’t make us pass another law. Just release what you’ve got. I think it would be potentially quicker and maybe fruitful. I’m happy to be part of those efforts.”

text:
Photo of a grizzly bear (Photo by Gregory Smith | Wikimedia Commons | CC-BY-SA 2.0)A grizzly bear was killed last week by wildlife management officials near Augusta, following several cases of livestock depredation and an attack on an archery hunter.
It is not known if the bear was the same one involved in the human attack, but a Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks press release stated that the bear was feeding on a cow carcass just three miles from the attack last Monday.
The attack was determined to be a surprise defensive encounter, and the hunter sustained significant, but not life-threatening injuries.
The grizzly was an adult female without cubs, and was determined to have killed three cattle in the area.
Montana FWP, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and U.S. Department of Agriculture Wildlife Services made the joint decision to kill the bear.

name: Delaware
title: Eight proposed changes to Delaware Constitution await new General Assembly
description: Four amendments involve voting rules, while others address marriage, the death penalty and vacancies in the lieutenant governor’s office DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s next General Assembly will inherit eight proposed amendments to the state Constitution, including four that could change voting rights and election procedures. Vil Ramunno, a public policy researche[...]
text:
Four amendments involve voting rules, while others address marriage, the death penalty and vacancies in the lieutenant governor’s office
DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s next General Assembly will inherit eight proposed amendments to the state Constitution, including four that could change voting rights and election procedures.
Vil Ramunno, a public policy researcher and Delaware LIVE contributing journalist, outlined the proposals during an appearance on “A Better Discussion,” hosted by former Delaware Attorney General Jane Brady for A Better Delaware.
The amendments already received the required approval from two-thirds of the members elected to each chamber of the 153rd General Assembly. However, none is part of the Constitution yet.
Under Delaware’s amendment process, the same proposed changes must receive two-thirds support in the House and Senate again after a general election. Unlike most states, Delaware does not routinely place individual constitutional amendments before voters for ratification. The governor also has no power to sign or veto them.
That means the lawmakers elected in November will decide whether the eight proposals become part of Delaware’s foundational legal document.
Four voting amendments
Ramunno said four of the pending amendments involve elections or voting rights:

Senate Substitute 1 for Senate Bill 2 would authorize 10 days of early, in-person voting before general, primary and certain special elections.
Senate Substitute 1 for Senate Bill 3 would create a constitutional right to vote by absentee ballot without providing an excuse. Voters generally would still have to request a ballot for each election cycle unless they qualify for permanent absentee status.
House Bill 180 would generally restore voting rights to people convicted of felonies after they are released from incarceration. It would prohibit making restoration contingent upon restitution or another monetary payment and remove obsolete residency and literacy provisions.
House Bill 430 would specify that only natural persons may vote in Delaware elections, preventing corporations and other artificial entities from being granted voting rights.

Ramunno said she did not immediately see significant negative consequences in the four voting measures, but emphasized that was her personal assessment.
Brady disagreed, raising concerns about the details lawmakers could later establish through statute. She particularly questioned the no-excuse absentee proposal and argued that voting rights should not be restored before restitution to crime victims has been addressed.
Their exchange demonstrated why the second round of legislative consideration could produce significant debate, even though each proposal secured the supermajority needed to clear its first constitutional hurdle.
Marriage, death penalty and state offices
The four remaining amendments would address other parts of the Constitution:

Senate Substitute 2 for Senate Bill 100 would establish marriage as a fundamental right that cannot be denied based on gender or another characteristic protected by the Constitution. It also contains language protecting religious freedom.
House Substitute 1 for House Bill 35 would constitutionally prohibit the death penalty. Delaware currently has no enforceable death penalty statute, but the amendment would prevent a future General Assembly from restoring capital punishment without another constitutional change.
Senate Bill 264 would establish a special-election process for filling most vacancies in the lieutenant governor’s office.
House Substitute 1 for House Bill 320 would make a series of technical corrections to the Constitution, including removing duplicated words, correcting punctuation and clarifying several provisions.

Brady cautioned against treating the Constitution like ordinary legislation, saying it should remain a foundational document that is changed carefully and infrequently.
Making legislation easier to follow: CivicDelaware.com
Ramunno’s analysis is informed by nearly a decade in public policy. She previously served as a senior editor at the Caesar Rodney Institute, where she worked to make policy reports accurate, readable and understandable in plain English.
She now covers government and politics for Delaware LIVE and conducts public policy research.
Ramunno also created Civic Delaware, a legislative information platform designed to help residents follow bills moving through Legislative Hall. Its primary tool, Dover Dash, tracks legislation from introduction through committee hearings, floor consideration and final action.
She said she developed the platform after watching complex bills move from introduction to passage in a matter of days during the final weeks of a legislative session.
Dover Dash uses automated updates from the General Assembly’s website and organizes bills according to the people most likely to be affected. Users can select profiles such as homeowner, parent, young professional, retiree, senior or veteran.
Instead of displaying only bill numbers, the platform gives proposals descriptive names, plain-language summaries, their official legislative synopses and current status. Users can also browse bills by subjects such as taxes, energy, alcohol and cannabis, and the state Constitution.
“You want to only know the ones that affect you, and it helps you to be more engaged,” Ramunno said. “And it makes it a little personal, too.”
She said Civic Delaware will archive legislation from the outgoing General Assembly when the new session begins. The eight proposed constitutional amendments will remain active because they must be considered again by the incoming lawmakers.
Ramunno said the goal is to help residents learn about proposals before they become law, ask informed questions and engage directly with their elected representatives.
“You can actually go on this web app yourself and look up what bills passed, what bills got introduced or what bill is in committee that is affecting you,” she said. “The purpose in this is so everyone would be more engaged.”





TO GO: Track legislation with Civic Delaware

What: Civic Delaware’s Dover Dash helps residents follow bills moving through the Delaware General Assembly.
How it works: Select a profile — such as homeowner, parent, young professional, retiree, senior or veteran — to find legislation that may affect you. Users can also browse bills by subject.
What you’ll find: Plain-language summaries, official bill synopses, legislative status updates and information about where each proposal stands in the lawmaking process.
Visit: CivicDelaware.com
Why it matters: Bills can move quickly through Legislative Hall. Civic Delaware allows residents to identify important proposals, follow their progress and ask lawmakers informed questions before final votes are taken.

description: Glacier National Park officials announced last week a beaver discovered on the east side had tested positive for a rare but serious bacterial disease. text:
North American beaver, Castor canadensis. (Courtesy Glacier National Park)Glacier National Park officials announced last week a beaver discovered on the east side had tested positive for a rare but serious bacterial disease.
Tularemia occurs naturally and can affect both wildlife, pets and humans, according to a press release from the park. The beaver was discovered between Upper and Lower St. Mary Lakes.
The disease is most commonly transmitted through bites from infected ticks or flies, and can cause wildlife illness and death, especially in voles, rabbits, beavers and other small rodents.
Humans and pets can contract tularemia through contact with infected animals, contaminated food or water, inhalation, or tick bites. Person-to-person transmission is rare, but exposure can cause serious health risks.
Park officials said visitors can reduce reduce the risk of tularemia infection, by following these precautions:

Apply insect repellent regularly.
Wash hands thoroughly and often.
Keep a safe distance from wildlife.
Drink only water that has been treated or boiled.

In humans, tularemia can cause a wide range of symptoms, including fever and chills, joint pain, muscle aches, headaches, dry cough, chest pain, skin ulcers or sores at the site of a tick bite, and swollen lymph nodes. Anyone who develops these symptoms within two weeks of visiting an affected area should seek medical attention and tell their healthcare provider about possible exposure to tularemia. The disease is treatable with antibiotics when diagnosed early.
For additional information on Tularemia visit Tularemia (U.S. National Park Service).

name: Delaware
title: Delaware Art Museum exhibit reveals Howard Pyle’s British influences
description: New research connects two of the Wilmington museum’s most important collections and offers fresh insight into the development of American illustration WILMINGTON — A new Delaware Art Museum exhibition is challenging the long-held view that two of the institution’s most important collections tell separate stories. “Pyle and the Pre-Raphaelites,” which opened[...]
text:
Photo: “Pyle and the Pre-Raphaelites,” which opened Sept. 5, brings together works by Wilmington illustrator Howard Pyle and British Pre-Raphaelite artists whose detailed, romantic style helped influence his approach to visual storytelling.
New research connects two of the Wilmington museum’s most important collections and offers fresh insight into the development of American illustration
WILMINGTON — A new Delaware Art Museum exhibition is challenging the long-held view that two of the institution’s most important collections tell separate stories.
“Pyle and the Pre-Raphaelites,” which opened Sept. 5, brings together works by Wilmington illustrator Howard Pyle and British Pre-Raphaelite artists whose detailed, romantic style helped influence his approach to visual storytelling.
The exhibition’s larger significance lies in new research showing that Pyle and Wilmington textile manufacturer and art collector Samuel Bancroft were more closely connected than historians previously understood.
Bancroft assembled what became one of the museum’s signature collections of British Pre-Raphaelite art. Pyle’s work formed the foundation of another.
Although the two men were related by marriage, questions remained about whether Pyle influenced Bancroft’s collecting, whether Bancroft introduced Pyle to the British artists or whether their interests developed independently.
The museum’s research indicates that Pyle was already studying and drawing inspiration from the Pre-Raphaelites before Bancroft began acquiring their work in 1890.
Two collections become one story
The Pre-Raphaelite movement began in England during the 19th century. Its artists rejected some conventional academic approaches to painting in favor of vivid colors, close attention to detail, symbolism and stories drawn from literature, medieval history and Arthurian legend.
Those qualities are also visible in many of Pyle’s best-known illustrations.
The exhibition places Pyle’s medieval and Early Renaissance scenes beside works by Pre-Raphaelite artists and their followers, including Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Edward Burne-Jones and William Morris.
Among the works displayed are Pyle’s illustrations for stories about the Knights of the Round Table and Rossetti’s “Water Willow,” Burne-Jones’ “Cupid’s Hunting Fields” and a Rossetti study depicting Lancelot and the Lady of Shalott.
The side-by-side presentation allows visitors to compare the artists’ compositions, subjects and storytelling techniques instead of simply being told that a connection existed.
A Delaware link to American illustration
The exhibit matters locally because Howard Pyle’s legacy is closely tied to Wilmington and the Brandywine Valley. His illustrations appeared in prominent books and magazines, and his teaching influenced a generation of artists who helped establish American illustration as a distinct art form.
The Delaware Art Museum itself traces its origins to the Wilmington Society of the Fine Arts, founded in 1912 to preserve Pyle’s work following his death.
By demonstrating that Pyle encountered Pre-Raphaelite ideas early in his career, the exhibition adds a new chapter to the story of how American illustration developed. It suggests that the dramatic, story-driven images associated with Pyle and his students had meaningful roots in an earlier British art movement.
The result is more than a comparison of artistic styles. It is an examination of how artistic ideas crossed the Atlantic, took hold in Wilmington and helped shape images seen by American readers across the country.
The exhibition also gives the museum an opportunity to connect two collections central to its identity: its founding collection of Pyle’s work and the Samuel and Mary R. Bancroft collection of British Pre-Raphaelite art.
“Pyle and the Pre-Raphaelites” was curated by Katherine Feldkamp, the museum’s curatorial associate. It will remain on view in Galleries 11 and 12 through Jan. 24, 2027.
Feldkamp will lead a gallery talk from noon to 1 p.m. Friday, Sept. 25, examining how Pyle incorporated Pre-Raphaelite art into his teaching and how his students also found inspiration in the movement. The program is free for museum members and included with general admission for other visitors.
To Go Box

What: “Pyle and the Pre-Raphaelites”
Where: Delaware Art Museum, Galleries 11 and 12, 2301 Kentmere Parkway, Wilmington
When: On view through Jan. 24, 2027
Hours: 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday. The museum remains open until 8 p.m. Thursdays from April through December.
Admission: $18 for adults, $16 for seniors, $7 for students with identification and $6 for youth ages 7 to 18. Admission is free for members and children 6 and younger. General admission is free from 4 to 8 p.m. Thursdays through December.
Special program: Curator Katherine Feldkamp will lead a gallery talk from noon to 1 p.m. Friday, Sept. 25.
Parking: Free on-site parking is available behind the museum.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Rep. John Larson won’t seek third-party run after primary defeat
description: Larson lost the four-way primary to Luke Bronin in August. Larson's term ends in early January, marking the end of his 28-year tenure.
text:
U.S. Rep. John Larson, D-1st District, won’t seek a third-party run in the November general election after his loss in the Democratic primary, formally marking the end of his 28-year congressional tenure that winds down early next year.
Larson conceded his loss to former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin in the August four-way primary a couple of hours after the polls closed. He wouldn’t give a firm answer that night about whether he was calling it a career.
But Larson’s spokesperson Charles Perosino confirmed Monday that he won’t pursue another path to get on the Nov. 3 ballot. The deadline for minor parties in Connecticut to select their candidates and submit for certification to get on the general election ballot was Sept. 2.
In a statement provided to the Connecticut Mirror, Larson said the party must unify to take on President Donald Trump. 
“As the president prosecutes an illegal war in Iran and costs continue to rise for working families, now is the time for Democrats to come together to hold Donald Trump accountable and deliver for the American people,” Larson said in a statement.
Larson had offered a similar characterization of his time left in Congress to the dozens of supporters who attended his election night party in the summer. On the night of the August primary, he indicated in his speech that he’s focusing the remaining months of his term on battling the president.
“The people of this district have spoken, and it’s time for us to come together and make sure that we all join forces,” Larson said that night. “Because the issue here, as I said throughout this campaign, is Donald Trump and what he’s doing to this country.”
“There’s still a lot of fight left and a lot to be done,” Larson added. “And I intend to fulfill my responsibility until the last day.”
When asked by reporters at the time whether he would seek the Working Families Party line or mount an independent bid in the fall, he quickly brushed aside those questions by saying, “take the night off, relax, take a deep breath.”
Larson’s decision not to run was first reported by CT Insider.
Larson was seeking a 15th term in the Hartford-based seat in an election cycle that’s been dominated by calls for generational change within the Democratic Party and some backlash to incumbency and the political establishment.
He faced Bronin, state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest and Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune in the Aug. 11 primary. It was the first primary Larson as a sitting member of Congress faced since he was first elected in 1998.
Bronin was able to break out of the crowded field of candidates because of his name recognition and his ability to raise money. Bronin and Larson frequently tangled over the sources of their fundraising, which played out on the campaign trail and in advertisements.
Following the primary and the month-long August recess, Larson returned to Washington, D.C., for a couple of weeks before Congress was to leave again for the election.
But the U.S. House wrapped up its work much earlier than expected and left town in the middle of last week. Lawmakers will have seven weeks back in their home districts, primarily meant for campaigning ahead of a pivotal election that will determine control of Congress.
Larson and the rest of the lawmakers now won’t return to D.C. until after the election. They’ll have several more weeks in the lame-duck session to finish up any remaining work before the holidays. Members try to pass last-minute priorities, but the final weeks of session are typically dominated by government funding bills and an annual defense policy bill that is crucial for Connecticut’s defense industry.
Larson’s signature issue of Social Security was a centerpiece of his reelection campaign. He had said he could be chairman of the House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security if Democrats regain the House majority. The issue recently gained some steamed in Congress as a reports estimate the trust fund for retirees could dry up by the early 2030s. Larson recently applauded the attention to the issue by others in Congress and continued to push for passage of his own bill to strengthen Social Security, even as he gets ready to depart.
Larson’s 14th term will finish up early next year. The new session of Congress will begin Jan. 3, 2027, when new members are sworn in.
Bronin will square off against Republican nominee Amy Chai on Nov. 3.
Bronin served as the mayor of Hartford for two terms, leaving office in 2024. He joined a crowded field in the summer of 2025 to take on Larson in the primary. He led the pack in fundraising and had also clinched the party’s endorsement in an upset at the nominating convention this spring.
“This is a political earthquake in Connecticut,” Bronin said following his primary victory in August, while also thanking Larson for a “lifetime of service.” “The goal is to shake things up in Washington D.C., and we’re just getting started.”
Chai has sought elected office before, running as an independent against U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-3rd District, in 2022. She was previously an independent but “realized she couldn’t win” unless she was affiliated with a major party.
“My motto is listen more, hate less,” Chai said as she stood at the polls on the August primary day. If elected, Chai, who’s a doctor, wants to focus on the prevention of mental illness and addiction. She believes politics is making mental health disorders worse.
But Bronin is considered the heavy favorite in the general election. Of the five U.S. House seats in Connecticut, the 1st Congressional District is the bluest.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa State University leads efforts to prevent contaminant exposure for firefighters
description: Iowa State University researchers and partners are working to learn about how modern fires impact firefighters’ health due to toxic contaminants on their gear and to find practical solutions to keep them safe. Guowen Song, an ISU professor of apparel, events and hospitality and director of the NextGen Personal Protective Technology Program, and his research[...]
text:
Iowa State University professor Guowen Song shows the system for burning contaminants and studying the smoke. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa State University researchers and partners are working to learn about how modern fires impact firefighters’ health due to toxic contaminants on their gear and to find practical solutions to keep them safe.
Guowen Song, an ISU professor of apparel, events and hospitality and director of the NextGen Personal Protective Technology Program, and his research team are burning materials to generate the invisible residue the fire and smoke leave on firefighters’ gear in order to study how it hangs on after the fire is put out.
They’ve already grasped the fundamental science behind carcinogens sticking on personal protective equipment, even after washing, Song said, and are trying to create a platform where their basis of knowledge can be shared and solutions for safer gear and new methods of cleaning can be disseminated.
“The current technology we call decontamination, regular washing things, does not work,” Song said. “The reason is that thing is not designed for this nature of emission, pollution, contamination, right, so there is no foundation (for) fully understanding the nature of this kind of contamination.”

The team also launched the Iowa Firefighter Cancer Prevention and Exposure Reduction Program in July, with partners in the University of Iowa Holden Comprehensive Cancer Center, Iowa Cancer Consortium, Iowa State Fire Marshal Division, Iowa Fire Service Training Bureau and Iowa fire departments.
Together, they’re more deeply examining this topic and how firefighters are being impacted by the contaminants on their gear, and working on solutions to develop modernized equipment and decontamination methods.
Kent Brix, past president of the Iowa Firefighters Association, said this kind of research is “vital” for Iowa’s career and volunteer firefighters. The hazardous conditions firefighters face in the line of duty can act as a “multiplier” for their risk of cancer, he said, and it’s important that Iowa’s institutions are trying to help.
“Anything to make our firefighters safer,” Brix said.
According to the Iowa Firefighters Association, in September 2024, Iowa housed around 850 fire departments, 92% of which were volunteer departments. This is more than 20 percentage points higher than the national average, and it means that most of Iowa’s firefighters may be bringing their carcinogen-laced gear into their personal vehicles and back home after the fire is put out.
Firefighters in big cities across the U.S. are also at a greater risk but for a different reason — their structure fires can be much more complex in terms of the involved materials, leading emergency responders to become exposed to more dangerous contaminants through their clothes.
Iowa State University is working with statewide partners to find solutions for firefighters carrying contaminants on their gear. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The Federal Emergency Management Agency, or FEMA, has funded Song’s work for six years, he said, because this is such a large issue. Song also leads ISU’s NextGen Personal Protective Technology program.
In that time, he and his team have developed chambers for burning materials like batteries, plastics and other synthetic materials and tested them with different parts of firefighting gear to understand how contaminants like polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) stick to clothing and the effectiveness of normal cleaning measures on removing them.
PFAS, or per- and polyfluoralkyl substances, can also be a problem, researchers said, as some pieces of personal protective equipment contain PFAS-based materials due to their resistance to heat and moisture and smoke from fires can also hold the substances.
With the fundamental science of their research established, Song said the cancer prevention program partners are working to create a wearable exposure monitoring system to track exposure to contaminants at the scene of a fire, in transit, in the fire station and other areas.
“Eventually, we hope these findings from fundamental practice (help) develop a national monitoring system so we know what the true exposure could be,” Song said.
Along with greater monitoring, Song said he hopes that the work he and other partners are doing will lead to better equipment, cleaning and storage systems to keep firefighters healthy. Rui Li, co-principal investigator and a research assistant professor of apparel, events and hospitality, said their work could even lead to helping firefighters deal with insurance and other areas related to their health by tracking their personal exposure.
“We try to prevent the happening of this cancer, not like we’re developing some cure for cancer, right,” Li said. “Prevention in the first place (is) much more effective if we have enhanced understanding about how these small particles interact with the PPE system, so we can develop new material, or we can do some treatment to the PPE material to just make some improvements about the protection (to) help them with their safety and health.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: RI judicial selection panel to weigh campaign contribution disclosures to applicants
description: The panel tasked with selecting Rhode Island’s judges on Tuesday will consider whether its members must disclose campaign contributions to judicial applicants and recuse themselves from considering those candidates. That question before the Judicial Nominating Commission comes from a petition filed Aug. 21 by H. Philip West Jr., the former executive director[...]
text:
Zachary Mandell, chairman of the Rhode Island Judicial Nominating Commission, prepares to begin the  panel's meeting on Tuesday, July 28, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)The panel tasked with selecting Rhode Island’s judges on Tuesday will consider whether its members must disclose campaign contributions to judicial applicants and recuse themselves from considering those candidates.
That question before the Judicial Nominating Commission comes from a petition filed Aug. 21 by H. Philip West Jr., the former executive director of Common Cause Rhode Island, after revelations that four commissioners had donated to former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi’s campaign account months before he applied for a seat on the state Supreme Court.
“Any contributions at all, I think should be disclosed,” West said in an interview Monday. “You’re talking about a judgeship —  a life tenure without review at a very high salary.”


What: Judicial Nominating Commission meeting
When: Tuesday, Sept. 21, at 4 p.m.
Where: Department of Administration Executive Director’s Conference Room, Fourth Floor
Good to know: Members of the public may attend, but there is not a public comment period.


West’s proposal would require commissioners to disclose campaign contributions, expenditures or other covered transfers made to support or oppose a judicial applicant during the previous 10 years. Commissioners who had made any contributions would then have to recuse themselves from discussing, voting on or otherwise considering the applicant.
Commissioners are scheduled to discuss and vote on West’s petition after announcing which candidates they intend to interview for the vacant chief judge position at Rhode Island District Court, a seat left open by Judge Jeanne LaFazia’s retirement in June.
Zachary Mandell, chairperson of the Judicial Nominating Commission, did not immediately respond to request for comment. 
The state’s Code of Ethics does not consider campaign contributions when determining whether a conflict of interest exists. West said that makes it “hard to press” an ethics complaint based on donations alone, which is why he wants a clearer standard for the all-volunteer commission tasked with recommending who gets to fill a judicial vacancy.
John Marion, Common Cause Rhode Island’s current executive director, called West’s proposal a straightforward way to address concerns from good government advocates and some lawmakers about former General Assembly members seeking judicial appointments.
Marion said Shekarchi’s application brought the issue into sharper focus because he was still serving in the General Assembly and still has an active campaign account with over $4.7 million in the bank.
After seven commissioners voted to advance Shekarchi’s application along with four others, GoLocalProv reported that four of the seven commissioners who voted to advance his application, including the panel’s chairman, had collectively contributed more than $30,000 to Shekarchi’s campaign account since he first ran for office in 2012.
“People who’ve been out of the legislature for a while were somewhat removed from politics, but in some instances still had campaign accounts,” Marion said. “It’s been a problem, a growing problem, but then Shekarchi really put the spotlight on it because of his position.”
Ultimately, Gov. Dan McKee selected Superior Court Judge Luis Matos to fill the vacancy on Rhode Island’s highest court. 
“The system worked, but it was close,” West said. 
Shekarchi’s challenge to the appointment process is still pending before the Rhode Island Supreme Court following a legal dispute between the former House speaker and the state’s Ethics Commission over whether his judicial application violated the state’s “revolving door” provision.
Marion commended West for pushing the issue and said the proposal could be a first step toward broader changes to the  judicial appointment process, some of which may require action by the General Assembly.
Lawmakers this year considered legislation that would have required the Judicial Nominating Commission to conduct a “blind review” of applications before interviews or public hearings. But the bills stalled at the committee level, which did not surprise advocates like West.
“When there’s an attempt at reform, there’s a pushback,” he said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: Congress winds down ahead of November elections
description: WSHU's Ebong Udoma and CT Mirror's Lisa Hagen discussed the end of the U.S. Congressional session ahead of the midterm election.
text:
The U.S. House of Representatives is out until after the November elections, and the Senate isn’t far behind them.
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Lisa Hagen to discuss the end of the Congressional session as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read Lisa’s coverage here.
WSHU: Hello, Lisa. When lawmakers returned to Washington last week, the House was expected to be in for a week, and the Senate for three weeks. But after a couple of days, the House was shuttered by Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA). Why?
LH: Actually, the House was going to be in even longer. They were supposed to be in for kind of the same amount of time as the Senate, and so they had already once cut it short, and so that’s when it kind of came down to that week, and then they cut it down to, you know, basically three days last week. So it was even shorter than expected. It’s an election season, so lawmakers and leaders always have it on their mind that they want to get their members back in the districts as soon as possible, and they don’t want to put them essentially in the line of fire if they have to vote on controversial legislation. And so, one of the bills that had come up was from a Republican, Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky; he was trying to force a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and so that had been on the docket. And then they basically punted on that, and then they sent members home.
So, you know, various different reasons why that was the case, but they always keep it in mind. They don’t want anything controversial, and they want to get their members home for campaign season.
WSHU: So, what actions did they take? And I know they acted on a bill because the Connecticut House delegation sent press releases saying they didn’t vote for it, and it was sponsored by fellow Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) as part of the Russia sanctions bill. Could you tell us a little bit about that and why the entire state delegation in the House voted against it?
LH: Yeah, it was a really interesting dynamic because Connecticut’s congressional delegation – you know, the five members in the House and the two senators – they’re all Democrats. They usually vote pretty much in uniform a lot of the time. Obviously, sometimes some take different votes, and so there was the Russia sanctions bill that got fully through Congress last week, and so that was something where Congress was able to see some legislative action ahead of the election. And as you said, Senator Richard Blumenthal from Connecticut, a major champion behind this bill, worked on it for years with the now-late Senator Lindsey Graham, and so the Senate got it through. And then one of the final actions of the House last week was voting on that Russia sanctions bill. Ultimately, it got through the House; they sent it to President Trump’s desk. But interestingly enough, the five-member delegation in the House from Connecticut all voted against the bill, and so they, you know, put out a pretty lengthy statement. They had thanked Senator Blumenthal for the work. They had reiterated their support for Ukraine, wanting more military aid for them, but they had basically boiled it down to, which was a point of contention for a lot of Democrats, that they didn’t want to give President Trump more tariff authority and give him more leeway to be able to make that decision on whether to implement various tariffs on those countries that import a lot of oil and gas from Russia. So that is essentially where that came down to. But a very interesting split in a delegation that doesn’t typically split very often.
WSHU: Yeah, and also Connecticut’s other U.S. Senator Chris Murphy proposed legislation on ICE. What exactly is he proposing? And it seems as if a lot of what happened in Danbury in the past month with the ICE raids helped propel him to introduce this legislation.
LH: Yeah, it definitely seemed like it was in direct response to what had happened in Danbury. It was a trio of bills, pretty simple, all one-pagers, and they all essentially said the same thing: that it would bar immigration enforcement operations at playgrounds, childcare facilities, and school bus stops, and so he introduced all that. There are similar pieces of legislation that Democrats have introduced, kind of barring similar operations at what we call sensitive locations, and so a lot of the time that’s at churches, at hospitals, what have you. The ones that he proposed are definitely places that are frequented by kids and by families, and definitely in more school settings and daycare as well. And so, it’s reflective of work that Senator Murphy has already tried to pursue a lot of. He and other Democrats, especially over the past year, were trying to push for various different immigration reforms- sorry, ICE reforms- and so those have all largely been stalled. They were kind of at play when Congress was negotiating government funding. That all got tied up in a bow earlier this year. Republicans were able to act on it alone, and because of that, and because they have a majority, those reforms fell by the wayside, and so Senator Murphy is proposing new reforms or putting this in new legislation. But again, you know, the Senate is about to recess at the end of the month. We have an election, and then they have only several weeks afterward, and it’s very difficult for Congress to get big legislation passed after an election and before their work wraps up before the holidays.
WSHU: Okay, so basically, no more action for Congress. We, voters, cannot expect any particular action from Congress on legislation before the election.
LH: The Senate will do a few things. They’re trying to put a bow on fully passing, on the Senate side, this college sports bill that I also wrote about that both Senator Murphy and Senator Blumenthal are opposed to. But even if it gets past the Senate, it still has to go through the House, and the House is off through the election. So they’re basically in a holding pattern, and so the Senate, the best-case scenario for the Senate is that they can pass nominations, or at least for Senate Republicans, they can pass some of President Trump’s nominees because you don’t need the House to act on that. Otherwise, again, they’re kind of in limbo until after the election.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: New poll shows NC voters across party lines see childcare as workforce, affordability issue
description: North Carolina’s midterm elections are on Nov. 3, and some voters in both parties are thinking about childcare before they hit the polling place. A share of the state’s voters say finding and affording childcare is an issue, with many also saying the cost of care is affecting their finances and availability to work. The […]
text:
Child care workers press NC legislators in 2024 to fund their industry as federal stabilization grants ended. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)North Carolina’s midterm elections are on Nov. 3, and some voters in both parties are thinking about childcare before they hit the polling place.
A share of the state’s voters say finding and affording childcare is an issue, with many also saying the cost of care is affecting their finances and availability to work.
The statewide poll from the WNC Early Childhood Coalition and First Five Years Fund — a childcare advocacy organization based in D.C. — found that 78% of North Carolina voters say the ability to find and afford childcare is a crisis or major problem.
The concern crosses party lines, with 62% of Republicans, 78% of independents and 90% of Democrats in agreement among those surveyed.
Child care advocates rallied in Raleigh over the summer to support daycare centers. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
Joseph O’Hern, director of coalition and campaigns for First Five Years Fund, said the organization conducted the poll in August and spoke with 820 voters, many of them from Western North Carolina.
“Affordability is top of mind for voters, and childcare costs are a huge part of that affordability crisis voters are facing,” he said.
Among North Carolina parents who pay for childcare, half said the cost is preventing them from saving or making financial gains. Another 34% said they’re cutting back on other essentials to pay for care.
The costs are also affecting families’ plans for the future. About one in four voters said they’re putting off starting a family because of childcare costs.
Voters also saw childcare as an important part of the state’s economy. About 77% of them agreed that increasing access to care would strengthen North Carolina’s workforce and economy. That percentage increased to 83% among voters polled in the western part of the state.
Greg Borum, director of the WNC Childcare Coalition, said he isn’t surprised to see Western North Carolina voters poll at higher percentages regarding childcare.
NC announces $20 million to expand childcare in storm recovery areas

“Our coalition had been charting childcare as an urgent and crisis issue in western counties before the pandemic came along,” he said. “But this crescendo of build-up and awareness that has been growing since that time is really reflected in this poll.”
 As childcare centers struggle, voters want more state support 
North Carolina voters also support state efforts to keep childcare centers open and help families afford care, according to the poll.
About 72% support the state subsidizing childcare for low-income families, while another 62% say the state should pay providers enough to cover the actual costs associated with childcare rather than at current funding levels.
The findings come as families continue to grapple with childcare shortages and higher costs.
During and after the pandemic, many providers were able to keep their doors open because of stabilization funds from the federal government. But that funding dried up with the expiration of federal American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) dollars, forcing some to close.
However, earlier this year, in the state budget,  lawmakers increased the amount of federal funds going to childcare providers that serve children through the state’s subsidy program. The program helps low-income families afford childcare.
The budget also created a new floor rate that will help stabilize funding for childcare centers across the state. Providers will now receive funding based on the state’s average rate for subsidized care.
But although childcare advocates celebrated the success, many say more work needs to be done to help providers.
Leanna Martin, director of early childhood education policy and research at NC Child, said many centers are also struggling with hiring and retaining staff because state and federal funding doesn’t adequately cover competitive pay for childcare workers.
“This is a critical first step, but we also know that our goal and our hope is that those reimbursement rates will eventually mirror the true cost of providing that care for children,” she said.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘We have more deer than our forests can support’: Norwich walk highlights browse damage
description:
Saplings with torn leaves and chewed stems are telltale signs of deer browse.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘We have more deer than our forests can support’: Norwich walk highlights browse damage.
text:
Dan Healey, center, a Vermont county forester based in the White River Junction office, at an event organized by the Upper Valley Land Trust at Brookmead Conservation Area in Norwich, Vt., on Monday, Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

This story by Alex Driehaus was first published in the Valley News on Sept. 14, 2026. 
NORWICH — About 30 people walked through the woods at Brookmead Conservation Area recently clad in hiking gear and armed with printouts of a deer browse assessment index. Attendees scanned the forest understory looking for saplings with torn leaves and chewed stems and other telltale signs of deer browse.
The Aug. 31 event, organized by the Upper Valley Land Trust, brought together foresters and deer biologists from both sides of the Connecticut River to teach members of the public about the impact that overabundant deer can have on forest ecosystems.
Brookmead is a good example of that impact because “it has been hit extremely hard by deer,” said Holly Henderson, naturalist and outdoor programs leader with the Upper Valley Land Trust. 
Deer eat a variety of food sources, from herbaceous plants and fresh leaves on saplings to beech nuts and acorns. They eat around 7 to 10 pounds of food per day, about what would fit in a 5-gallon bucket, according to Vermont wildlife biologist and deer project leader Nick Fortin. When deer density gets too high, heavy browsing can limit forest regeneration and allow for the proliferation of invasive species.
Warmer winters and increased suburbanization have contributed to an increase in the deer population over the past several decades, according to New Hampshire Fish and Game Department deer project leader Becky Fuda. 
“We have more deer than our forests can support,” Fortin said.
New regulations in Vermont — like allowing hunters to fill antlerless tags with rifles during the regular season in November — will help address the problem, Fortin said, but won’t be enough to fix it. While regulation changes can make it easier for hunters to harvest deer, managing deer density would require more landowners to allow hunting on their properties.
“What we’re seeing today is an artifact,” Fortin said. “It took decades to get to this point.” 
During the event, foresters discussed other management strategies to help promote forest regeneration. Attendees visited a sample deer exclosure, which helps support the growth of saplings and other native plants by protecting them from deer. Dan Healey, a Vermont county forester based in the White River Junction office, talked about the benefits of creating large clearings with no canopy, which allows saplings to grow because deer are less comfortable in areas with no cover.
Henderson said she hopes that attendees left with a better understanding of the impact of deer browse and the many approaches that can be implemented to support the northern hardwood forests around the Upper Valley.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Pearson put Tennessee front and center at forum during Congressional Black Caucus week
description: WASHINGTON, D.C. — Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson told some of the nation’s best-known Black journalists and media leaders Wednesday that national Democrats should not write off Black candidates running in the South, pointing to a recent poll showing him 4 percentage points behind in a congressional district Republicans redrew this year to favor their [[...]
text:
Rep. Justin J. Pearson, second from right, talked about the importance of Black and independent media in a forum held during Congressional Black Caucus Week 2026. Pearson is running for Tennessee's 5th Congressional District. Also pictured from left is Lauren Williams, founder of Capital B news, journalist Joy-Ann Reid, Errin Haines, president of the National Association of Black Journalists and Alexis McGill Johnson, CEO of Planned Parenthood. (Photo: Angela Dennis for Tennessee Lookout) WASHINGTON, D.C. — Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson told some of the nation’s best-known Black journalists and media leaders Wednesday that national Democrats should not write off Black candidates running in the South, pointing to a recent poll showing him 4 percentage points behind in a congressional district Republicans redrew this year to favor their party.
Veteran journalist Joy-Ann Reid, who joined Pearson on the panel as part of Congressional Black Caucus week, said assumptions about whether Democrats can compete in places like Tennessee can influence media coverage and where national political organizations invest.
“The media covers the South as someplace only Republicans can win,” Reid said. “Anybody can win if enough people vote for them.”
“When this young man decided he was going to run for Congress, the immediate thought inside of Democratic officialdom was, ‘Well, he can’t win. That’s Tennessee, and so the spending won’t go there,’” Reid said.
Tennessee US House District 9: Republican Taylor and Democrat Pearson set for general election

A Hart Research poll conducted in September found Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor leading Pearson 48% to 44% among 400 likely voters in Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District. The survey, the only publicly available poll of the race, was conducted for Tennessee Rise PAC, a Democratic-aligned group supporting Pearson.
Republican lawmakers redrew Tennessee’s congressional map during a May special session, eliminating the state’s only majority-Black congressional district and splitting Memphis and Shelby County among three districts. An analysis by Inside Elections found the newly configured 9th District would have supported President Donald Trump by 21 percentage points in the 2024 election.
Pearson faces Taylor in the Nov. 3 general election. Independents Dennis Clark and Michelle Davis Head are also on the ballot.
 Independent and Black media critical for midterms

Pearson and Reid spoke during “Reclaiming Our Narrative,” a panel hosted by URL Media, the National Community Reinvestment Coalition and the Washington Association of Black Journalists during the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation’s Annual Legislative Conference. 
The discussion examined the role of independent and Black media in covering the 2026 midterms. URL Media President Sara Lomax moderated the panel, which also included Don Lemon, Errin Haines, Lauren Williams and Alexis McGill Johnson.
Washington Association of Black Journalists President Phillip Lewis pointed to Tennessee’s 2023 legislative expulsions as an example of how independent and Black media can bring national attention to local political developments.
Lomax asked Pearson about differences between mainstream and Black media coverage after Republicans expelled him and Rep. Justin Jones, a Nashville Democrat, from the Tennessee House in 2023 following a gun-control protest.
Pearson said Black media placed the expulsions within a longer history of Black political representation, including the Georgia House’s refusal to seat civil rights activist Julian Bond in 1966.
“I think the lens by which a lot of Black media started to pay attention to what was going on in Tennessee was yes, this is an affront on democracy in the now, but it is also a part of a deep-seated history in our country,” Pearson said. “These moments are connected to a long lineage and the way that we articulate that and speak about that can help us find our way out of it. That’s the perspective that Black media was able to provide that no one else could.”
‘What do we have in common’: Traveling the 250 miles through Tennessee’s House District 9

 ‘Memphis no longer has a congressional district’

Pearson turned to the congressional map that transformed the district where he is running.
“Memphis no longer has a congressional district; it’s stretched across 200 miles,” Pearson said. “I’m still running in that district for District Nine now. 191 miles, 15 counties, majority rural, 32% Black, 43% people of color.”
Pearson told the group his campaign is focusing on economic concerns shared by voters across the district.
“The message that we are sharing is really simple, we have to build an economy that works for everybody, not just the billionaires,” he said. “If you’re in rural Giles County or you’re in the center of Memphis, Tennessee, you are struggling. Gas is high, groceries are high, wages are low.”
 Reid discusses national investment in Tennessee, the South

Reid said Pearson’s campaign illustrates how perceptions of Southern states can affect political investment.
“Does the Democratic Party want the seats? Yes,” Reid said. “Do they want Black Power? Because that’s a different question.”
Pearson pointed to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s Red to Blue program, which provides campaign support to selected Democratic candidates.
“There are no Black candidates from the South on the DCCC Red to Blue list,” Pearson said. “We are building something pretty extraordinary, and we are fighting with all we’ve got to be on that list.”
The DCCC expanded the program to 40 candidates on Sept. 15. Pearson is not currently among them.

title: Medical groups, patients sue Trump administration over Medicaid work requirements
description: Medicaid enrollees from five states and leading medical organizations filed a lawsuit Friday challenging new Medicaid work requirements. The broad tax and spending law that President Donald Trump signed last summer, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, established work, school or community service requirements for low-income adults who receive Medicaid u[...]
text:
Medicaid enrollees from five states and leading medical organizations filed a lawsuit Friday challenging new Medicaid work requirements. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Medicaid enrollees from five states and leading medical organizations filed a lawsuit Friday challenging new Medicaid work requirements.
The broad tax and spending law that President Donald Trump signed last summer, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, established work, school or community service requirements for low-income adults who receive Medicaid under expansion provisions and waiver programs across 44 states. The law exempts people who are medically frail from work requirements, but the lawsuit argues a new administration rule severely restricts who qualifies.
Plaintiffs in the lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland include Medicaid enrollees from five states — Kentucky, Illinois, Indiana, Missouri and North Carolina. 
They also include the American College of Physicians, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine, Doctors for America, the New Hampshire Medical Society, the New Hampshire Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics and the city of Columbus. The National Health Law Program and the Democracy Forward Foundation are representing the plaintiffs.
“Creating barriers to healthcare coverage for the most vulnerable needlessly puts people’s lives at risk and inevitably drives up the cost of care for everyone,” Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein said in a news release. “These are folks who should be focused on getting the help and care they desperately need, not overcoming even more obstacles.”
The federal government in June issued a rule that specifies “medical frailty” exemptions from the work requirements. Those include people who are blind or disabled, or have any physical or developmental disability that interferes with daily living; people with substance use disorders or disabling mental disorders; or those with “serious or complex” medical conditions. People who fall in these categories still must prove that their conditions hinder their ability to work or participate in community engagement.
Judge rejects states’ bid to block Medicaid work rules

Republicans argue that work requirements would push people into the workforce and allow them to come off government aid. Research shows the majority of Medicaid recipients already work or are in school.
The plaintiffs argue that the new designations are narrow and that work or exemption verification processes will create red tape that threatens Medicaid coverage for people with serious or chronic health conditions. Those who could be harmed under the new rule include people with cancer, diabetes, HIV, substance use disorders and other behavioral health conditions, the lawsuit argues. 
Individuals represented in the lawsuit have health conditions ranging from autism spectrum disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, bipolar disorder, severe vision impairments, HIV and narcolepsy.
Work requirements will be costly for cities and localities that provide public health and emergency care services, the plaintiffs argue, as many people may lose coverage.
“When they (cities and localities) provide services for residents who lose their Medicaid coverage, they do so without compensation,” the lawsuit reads.
Medical groups are concerned the reporting burdens will cause interruptions in care and coverage for low-income, vulnerable adults.
“We should not and must not be implementing policies that place this already vulnerable population at increased risk of interrupted treatment, disrupted coverage, or losing healthcare access altogether,” said Dr. Jan K. Carney, president of the American College of Physicians.
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.
