name: WyoFile
title: University of Wyoming optimistic on academic freedom despite censorship lawsuit naming new president
description:
Faculty leadership largely back Shane Reeves in wake of litigation stemming from his time at West Point. 
The post University of Wyoming optimistic on academic freedom despite censorship lawsuit naming new president appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
On the cusp of his first academic year as president of the University of Wyoming, retired Army Brig. Gen. Shane Reeves made national headlines in late August, though not for his new post leading the state’s sole four-year public university.
Instead, as The New York Times first reported, Reeves was named in a federal lawsuit against the U.S. Military Academy, filed by a civilian climate scientist who alleges he was fired after 17 years at West Point “because he taught that humans influenced climate change,” the complaint states. 
Prior to taking the helm at UW, Reeves served as West Point’s dean of the academic board. The lawsuit accuses him and two other academy leaders of violating Dr. Adam Kalkstein’s First Amendment right to freedom of speech. The complaint also points to the Trump administration’s “hostility to the accepted scientific notion that human activity was a major cause of present-day climate change.” 
The defendants, including Reeves, have not yet filed a legal response to Kalkstein. Reeves declined WyoFile’s request for an interview for this story. 
West Point, like the University of Wyoming and other institutions of higher education across the country, is not new to questions over the rights of instructors, researchers or students to teach, investigate or discuss ideas without undue interference from the government, donors, university boards or administrators. 
In Laramie, that tension has grown more acute in recent years as the Wyoming Freedom Caucus gained power in the Legislature and sought to restrict the university’s autonomy through legislation and the power of the purse. A 2024 budget footnote, for example, forbade UW from using any state money for diversity, equity and inclusion programming and curricula. The school closed its DEI office as a result. Earlier this year, the Freedom Caucus, citing specific concerns with environmental courses, tried but ultimately failed to reduce UW’s block grant by about 11%. But the group’s message was made clear by its members.

Rep. Ken Pendergraft, R-Sheridan, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheynne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

“We’re going to pull this money back,” Rep. Ken Pendergraft, R-Sheridan, said on the House floor in February. “And we want you to focus on ag, we want you to focus on engineering, we want you to focus on education, these other things that benefit Wyoming specifically, rather than training people in majors, minors, ideas and concepts where they’re not going to be, frankly, at home in Wyoming.”  
Before voters ousted most Freedom Caucus incumbents in the primary election last month, the group had already taken aim at Reeves, accusing him of “bringing woke academics to West Point.” 
However, Reeves’ arrival to Laramie has been marked largely by optimism. Much of that is thanks to the first impression the Rock Springs native has made on campus, including via a charming social media presence. The new president’s bullish outlook for the university’s future, despite challenges like declining enrollment and a $15 million budget shortfall, has also contributed to his early popularity. 
“I think it’s on the ascent,” Reeves told WyoFile in August during a wide-ranging interview. “I absolutely think it has a lot of momentum behind it, and accelerating what already exists is going to be part of my job. And I’m really honored to have the opportunity to do it.” 
President Shane Reeves (University of Wyoming)
News of the federal lawsuit began to circulate on campus earlier this month, including via the faculty email listserv, according to The Laramie Reporter. But it hasn’t necessarily soured the mood on campus, according to Faculty President Rob Godby. 
“I think the majority opinion on faculty is that they’re willing to give President Reeves the benefit of the doubt, and you know, are positive and hopeful that he’s as successful as he can be” Godby told WyoFile this week. 
Godby, an associate professor of economics, also said faculty are eager to move forward after a tumultuous period with university leadership. In 2025, the faculty senate voted to adopt a no-confidence resolution against former UW President Ed Seidel amid the controversial ouster of a popular dean. 
“It’s no secret there were some potential leadership challenges based on decisions that the previous president made,” Godby said. “And a lot of faculty just want to move forward and are glad to have those behind them” 
Earlier this year, Godby served on the presidential search committee, and said Reeves stood out from the other candidates for a reason. 
“One of things that impressed us the most about President Reeves was he was among the candidates who gave the strongest explanation and description of academic freedom and the importance and its value on a campus,” he said. 
“And I’ll be honest with you,” Godby said, “not all of our candidates actually did a very good job on that question.” 
In August, Reeves told WyoFile that “intellectual discourse is a very traditional Wyoming value, right?” 
“We can talk about anything, and we can disagree and at the end of the day, we’re still neighbors,” he said. “As a son of the state of Wyoming, I was brought up with a healthy level of cynicism from being told what to think or what to believe. I think that this effort to have real discussion, real discourse, to have students engaged in ideas is a real commitment to the free marketplace of ideas that is the very purpose of an institution of higher education.” 
Cautious optimism
Recently retired professor of philosophy and creative writing Jeff Lockwood is among those in UW’s community who are taking a wait-and-see approach. 
“We’re in the honeymoon, right?” Lockwood told WyoFile. 
“Actions speak louder than words. You know that’s kind of trite, but also, we’ve got some very nice words from the president,” Lockwood said. “He’s a wonderfully engaging, warm person. I mean, his interpersonal skills are on another planet compared to what we’ve had, without being too blunt about that. So we got that right.”
However, Lockwood said, “when resources get allocated and priorities get made via action and budget, that’s when we exchange words for actions, and we find out what’s really going to be going on.”  
A sculpture on campus drew the ire of state lawmakers and the energy industry during Lockwood’s time on campus in 2011. Using charred logs arranged in a 36-foot-wide pinwheel design in the lawn south of Old Main, artist Chris Drury’s “Carbon Sink” sought to draw a visual connection between climate change driven by fossil fuel emissions and the region’s pine beetle epidemic. 
Many considered the removal of Carbon Sink, an art installation seen here, from the University of Wyoming campus, as an example of institutional censorship and the threat to academic independence in action. (Chris Drury)
After lawmakers and energy industry leaders objected to the sculpture, it was removed from campus earlier than planned. University officials denied bowing to political pressure, though documents obtained by Wyoming Public Media in the aftermath indicated otherwise. 
In the years afterwards, Lockwood wrote a book about the controversy and the larger theme of censorship imposed by corporate wealth and power. In 2017, he told Wyoming PBS he was inspired to write the book after “people started coming to me with stories, stories that they couldn’t tell because they were at much more risk than I am as a tenured professor.” 
Lockwood told WyoFile this week that UW faculty are not naïve to Wyoming politics or the institution’s financial reliance on the Legislature. They’re also keenly aware, he said, that “there have been consequences for speaking or writing or teaching freely on subjects that might be uncomfortable to the political environment.”
“When resources get allocated and priorities get made via action and budget, that’s when we exchange words for actions, and we find out what’s really going to be going on.”Jeff Lockwood, retired professor
The hard question becomes, Lockwood said, “how much will we, as an institution, or we as a faculty, or we as a bunch of administrators, compromise on principles in order to, if you will, protect the funding of the institution?” 
There’s a certain point, he said, “at which the constraint on academic freedom is so egregious that it no longer functions as what it was supposed to be, or what the people want it to be.” 
While Lockwood said he expects the university’s relationship with lawmakers to change in the wake of  the Freedom Caucus’ defeat at the polls last month, the greater dynamic will persist. 
“The conflict between the perceived interests of our industries and the perceived interests of our legislature and the principles of academic freedom on the campus, that’s not going to go away,” he said.
Seidel’s initiative
In 2022, Seidel, who Reeves replaced in July, launched a free-speech initiative. 
He tasked a working group of faculty, staff, administrators, students and a trustee with defining the university’s “core principles in the areas of freedom of expression, intellectual freedom, academic freedom, and constructive dialogue.”
In 2023, the working group’s recommendations were officially adopted by the university. 
“A fundamental principle is that the university plays a unique role by providing a neutral forum for the deliberation and debate of public issues,” Seidel said at the time. “Providing such a forum does not mean the university either endorses or condemns the different perspectives expressed. What it does mean is that, as our free expression group states, UW’s adherence to impartiality reaffirms the intellectual freedom of all at UW to seek and receive information without restriction and enjoy unfettered access to all expression of ideas through which any side of a question, cause or movement may be explored.” 
The group was co-chaired by Martha McCaughey, who was then appointed in 2025 to lead the initiative fulltime. In an emailed statement to WyoFile, McCaughey said she had “no information” on the West Point lawsuit and pointed to the university’s statement of principles, which includes a section on academic freedom. 
“UW is an R1 institution with strong academic standards where people examine evidence, discover new knowledge, and put knowledge to practical use,” McCaughey wrote. 
Matt Burgess, an associate economics professor, has also been involved with UW’s free speech initiative. Burgess told WyoFile he’s confident in Reeves and the direction the university is taking. 
“Everything I’ve seen from him publicly and everything I’ve heard about what he’s been doing behind the scenes suggests very strong, very unequivocal support for free expression, free academic freedom, for the initiative,” Burgess said. “And as somebody who studies climate change, I have no concerns at all about any kind of censorship or pressure coming from Old Main about that.” 
Like Lockwood, Burgess said public pressures are certain to exist, but it’s not the sole responsibility of the university’s president to ensure academic freedom.
“We decide whether we censor ourselves,” Burgess said. “And I think that we academics would do ourselves and our professions a service by doing that less.” 
WyoFile reporter Dustin Bleizeffer contributed reporting.
The post University of Wyoming optimistic on academic freedom despite censorship lawsuit naming new president appeared first on WyoFile .

name: WyoFile
title: How Election Day looks from the inside
description:
Guest columnist Paul Hansen, a first-time election judge, reflects on his experience and looks ahead to November’s general election.
The post How Election Day looks from the inside appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
During the Aug. 18 primary election, I was a Teton County election judge. It was a wonderful experience. 

Opinion

Our county clerk, Maureen Murphy, assigned me to the Old Wilson Schoolhouse. The team included two Teton County Clerk’s Office employees, an information technology expert from the Teton County Sheriff’s Office and eight volunteers.
It was a long day — 14 hours — during which we recorded 674 votes. We never left the building. 
It was a very rigorous process. Unlocking the ballot counting machine involved multiple numbered tags, several seals and signatures from three judges who witnessed each step of the process. Individual ballots — there are 42 varieties depending on where you live — were carefully sorted and counted at the beginning of the day.
 At the end of the day, we counted the unused ballots and the spoiled ballots, i.e., ballots where people made a mistake and wanted a redo. Spoiled ballots were carefully marked so they would not be processed, and then put in a secure file. All of this was reconciled with the number of ballots cast.
I spent most of the day on a computer, checking people in. The computer program was pretty simple. In most cases, it took about 30 seconds. If someone had an address change or had not voted recently, then we needed to update their information or reregister them. Any mistake on the form and it would not print. The voter then reviewed and signed the printed form, which I also signed, dated and immediately filed in a secure location.
We even kept all the trash in a secure location. (Let the record show that Hansen ate two meat sticks.)
I have a few takeaways from the experience. There was a great vibe in the room all day. People were unfailingly polite and friendly. 
This was my first election judge rodeo, so a few times I took longer than I should have. Everyone was pleasant about it. A few voters grumbled about now having to show identification, but it was basically a nonissue. The clerk has records on everyone. There have been only four cases of voter fraud in Wyoming in the last 25 years, and none since 2014, according to the Heritage Foundation.
However, people really did not like being told they had to choose by May 13 whether to vote in the Republican or Democratic primary. This is more than three months prior to the primary election and before we know who is running for office. 
I probably checked in close to 200 voters. I sent about 10 home without voting since they were registered as “unaffiliated” and could not change their party status and vote. For decades, Wyoming voters could show up at the primary and choose whether to vote as a Democrat or Republican. The so-called Freedom Caucus and Secretary of State Chuck Gray took that right from us. 
Ironically, if you had never voted, you were allowed to register on the spot and choose the party ballot you desired. Even crazier, if you did not vote in the previous election and were purged, you could show up, reregister, and choose your ballot. So, only regular voters get punished by the early declaration date.
At our primary election on Aug. 18, it was overwhelmingly clear that voters — Republicans and Democrats — cherished the voting process. Given what I saw that day as an election judge, if Trump tries to interfere in the Nov.3 general election, it will not go well for him and his sycophants.

title: Ahead of 2026 midterm elections, Idaho officials begin mailing ballots to overseas, absentee voters
description: With less than two months before the 2026 midterm elections, election officials across Idaho mailed the first round of mail-in ballots to voters who are overseas or who requested absentee ballots locally. The finalization of ballots in Idaho follows after a weekslong crunch to change contested language for an abortion legalization ballot initiative and attem[...]
text:
Absentee ballots are prepared to be mailed at the Wake County Board of Elections on September 17, 2024 in Raleigh, North Carolina. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images)With less than two months before the 2026 midterm elections, election officials across Idaho mailed the first round of mail-in ballots to voters who are overseas or who requested absentee ballots locally.
The finalization of ballots in Idaho follows after a weekslong crunch to change contested language for an abortion legalization ballot initiative and attempts by the Trump administration to implement a federal rule that could’ve made last-minute changes to ballots. 
Idaho election officials worry about mail-in ballot changes proposed by Trump administration

“Everything is on track,” said Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, the state’s top election official who’s running for re-election as a Republican.
More than a month before the Nov. 3 general election, local election officials are expected to finalize ballots. That’s because federal law requires the first slate of mail-in ballots be shipped 45 days before federal elections to voters who are overseas, such as members of the military or missionaries. In Ada County, Idaho’s largest, election officials were expecting to mail out more than 24,000 ballots on Friday, Trent Tripple, the Republican county clerk, told the Idaho Capital Sun. That includes overseas and military voters, along with everyone who had already requested an absentee ballot, he said. 
Voters still have more than a month to request absentee ballots or register to vote before Election Day. Oct. 23 is the deadline to request absentee ballots or pre-register to vote, according to an election calendar on VoteIdaho.gov, a website run by the Secretary of State’s Office. 
This year, all statewide constitutional offices — such as governor, lieutenant governor, and attorney general — are up for election as well as all 105 seats in the Idaho Legislature. Three of Idaho’s four congressional seats will also be on the ballot.

 The crunch to finalize ballots in Idaho

Election officials in Ada County — which is home to Boise — had told the state they were working on a Sept. 9 deadline to finalize the design of ballots ahead of shipping the first round of absentee ballots out. 
Idaho Secretary of State candidate Phil McGrane talks with a supporter during the Idaho Republican Party primary celebration on May 17, 2022. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
One legal dispute came close to that deadline. 
With just four days left to go until Ada County’s deadline, the Idaho Supreme Court quickly finished its work resolving a lawsuit by the organizers of the abortion ballot initiative. On the Friday before Labor Day weekend, the state’s high court required state officials, including McGrane, to rewrite statements about what votes on the initiative would do. Before the work week started, the court had approved redrafted language.
“It could’ve gotten a lot closer to the wire,” McGrane said in an interview. “It is impressive that the Idaho Supreme Court was issuing decisions on Sunday during Labor Day weekend in an effort to meet the deadline.”
Making changes to ballot design close to the deadline is more than changing a single ballot, election officials say. That’s because there’s many variations of ballots that can change based on which taxing, legislative and congressional districts that voters live within.

In Ada County, Tripple said there’s 202 different ballots — and that election officials are juggling state regulations that require ballots to randomly rotate candidate names.
“It’s not a one ballot for everybody. It depends on where you live,” he said, adding that “making sure all of those various requirements flow nicely within a document is a real hurdle.”
Ada County also ran into one more hitch preparing for the elections, which wasn’t related to laying out ballots. 
This year, the Legislature passed a law to make elections for the Ada County Highway District partisan and districtwide, with the expectation that those changes wouldn’t take effect until the next election cycle in 2028, the Idaho Press reported. But Tripple said the county has interpreted the districtwide requirement to already be in effect for this election cycle.
Not all ballots are printed in Ada County. For others, the county prints ballots on demand as voters come in, Tripple said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Democrats face uphill battle in winning any Tennessee U.S. House race
description: Tennessee Democrats seem unlikely to be part of any national congressional blue wave during the midterm elections, election experts say.  During the 2018 midterm election, during President Donald Trump’s first term, his low approval rating led to a nationwide backlash that elected 41 new Democrats to the U.S. House. In that blue-wave election eight years […]
text:
State Rep. Justin J. Pearson, a Memphis Democrat, is running in Tennessee's 9th U.S. Congressional District in 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee Democrats seem unlikely to be part of any national congressional blue wave during the midterm elections, election experts say. 
During the 2018 midterm election, during President Donald Trump’s first term, his low approval rating led to a nationwide backlash that elected 41 new Democrats to the U.S. House.
In that blue-wave election eight years ago, the Democratic Party’s best flip was a seat Trump won in upstate New York by around 15.5 percentage points in the previous election. But this year in Tennessee, Trump would have won in all nine of the state’s newly drawn U.S. House districts by at least 20 percentage points if they had been reshaped two years ago, according to Dave’s Redistricting, an online tool allowing users to create and adjust election district boundaries.
At Trump’s urging, Tennessee lawmakers redrew all nine of the state’s U.S. House seats in May after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that states no longer have to draw districts that favor minority voters, as had long been required under the Voting Rights Act. 
Tennessee Republicans pass US House map carving up Memphis days after SCOTUS guts Voting Rights Act

“It’s a really effective gerrymander,” said Erin Covey, the head of the Cook Political Report’s U.S. House ratings. Cook is a nonpartisan election-rating organization that analyzes federal and gubernatorial races, classifying them by partisan leaning and likelihood of being competitive. 
The 2026 midcycle redistricting allowed Tennessee Republicans to crack a Democratic-held seat in Memphis by splitting the predominantly Black city among three congressional districts. The drawing pattern was similar to what Republicans did to Nashville during the 2022 redistricting cycle. 
As a result, Republicans are now heavily favored to win every congressional race in Tennessee, and even in a “great year for Democrats,” the map might be “tough to overcome,” Covey said.
In Tennessee, the six U.S. House districts stretching from Middle to West Tennessee are all rated in the same cluster of “Solid” Republican seats, with a Cook rating of a Republican advantage of  9 to 11 percentage points. The other three congressional seats in East Tennessee have an even stronger Republican rating. 
Covey said the Democratic Party’s best shot is in Tennessee’s new 9th District, followed by the 5th. 
“Those two races follow the same pattern,” Covey said. “Democrats are running serious campaigns that have raised a lot of money and have enthusiasm.” 


Dynamics in the 9th and 5th
U.S. Rep. Steve Cohen, a Memphis Democrat, held the 9th District seat for nearly two decades but decided not to run after the redistricting. 
State Sen. Brent Taylor, a Memphis Republican, faces state Rep. Justin J. Pearson, a Memphis Democrat, in the 9th District race. Pearson’s campaign released an internal poll in September showing him trailing Taylor 48% to 44% in a head-to-head matchup.
Pearson entered the race in 2025 and raised a large amount of his nearly $2.3 million for a primary challenge to Cohen that never happened. Pearson had $845,000 in the bank, and Taylor $420,000 as of July 17, according to Federal Election Commission, FEC, filings. Taylor entered the fray after state lawmakers redrew the maps.
U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles, a Columbia Republican, has represented the 5th District since 2023. But Ogles lost the Republican primary this year to former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher. 
Ogles’ primary defeat hurts the Democratic Party’s chances of winning the seat, since the two-term congressman raised little money and faced several ethics investigations over allegedly fabricated campaign finance reports. 
Hatcher faces Chaz Molder, Columbia’s Democratic mayor, in the general election. When Molder entered the race more than a year ago, the 5th District looked markedly different. The previous version was centered in West Nashville and Molder’s hometown of Columbia.
The new 5th includes only a sliver of Columbia, covers the northwest rural part of Tennessee, and runs down the state’s border with Missouri and Arkansas to incorporate a third of Memphis. 
Hatcher had $105,000 and Molder $1.5 million in the bank as of July 17, FEC filings show.
Molder also released an internal poll showing he trailed Hatcher 48% to 40%.
Both Pearson’s and Molder’s campaigns are betting on boosted Democratic turnout in Memphis triggered by a backlash to the gerrymandering and the Trump-created Memphis Safe Task Force as a path to overcoming the partisan leaning of the districts. 
The Memphis Safe Task Force has been trumpeted by Republicans, but criticized locally for its heavy-handed, outdated and harrassing approach to law enforcement. 
Memphis typically has low voter turnout but also hasn’t had a competitive U.S. House midterm election since Cohen’s first run in 2006.
“It’s going to be very difficult to pull off,” Covey said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Republicans fear GOP apathy could give Democrats boost
description: Several Alabama Republican Party candidates have expressed worries about signs of flagging GOP enthusiasm in the fall campaign and fear it could give Democrats a boost in November. While turnout for the May primary elections was 23% statewide, the number of people taking Democratic ballots jumped from four years before, while turnout in Republican areas […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile (third from left, in Blue shirt) addresses a crowd attending the All Roads Lead to the South rally in Montgomery, Alabama on May 16, 2026. The Republican-controlled Legislature redrew Figures' seat to favor Republicans, but several GOP officials have voiced concerns that low Republican turnout could give Democrats a boost.  (Andi Rice for Alabama Reflector) Key Points




Several Republican candidates expressed concerns that continued lower voter turnout could have a negative impact on their chances for getting elected to office.
Turnout among Republicans has been relatively stable compared to the previous midterm elections, but Democratic turnout surged in the May primary.
Political analysts said that Republicans still have the advantage in the state and that many should survive the challenge.
However, turnout could affect some races, such as the race between U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, and Republican Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, in Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District.




Several Alabama Republican Party candidates have expressed worries about signs of flagging GOP enthusiasm in the fall campaign and fear it could give Democrats a boost in November.
While turnout for the May primary elections was 23% statewide, the number of people taking Democratic ballots jumped from four years before, while turnout in Republican areas was flat. In the August 13 special congressional primaries in four districts, most of which featured Republican races, turnout was just 5%.
“Republicans control the state. Most of the people in this state are Republican, they vote Republican reliably,” said State Auditor Andrew Sorrell, a Republican seeking re-election, in an interview Thursday. “If we ever perform poorly in an election, it is not because people woke up and decided they were Democrats today. Anytime we lose, it is when our people stay home and don’t go vote.”
Multiple messages were sent to Scott Stadthagen, chair of the Alabama Republican Party, seeking comment.
Democratic voting turnout surges, Republican turnout falls during May 19 primary

Alabama state government has been fully controlled by Republicans since 2012. Democrats have been a superminority in the Alabama Legislature since 2010 and have not won a governor’s race since 1998.
But Republicans are facing significant headwinds entering the midterm election cycle, due to concerns over inflation and President Donald Trump’s unpopularity. GOP legislators earlier this year redrew the 2nd Congressional District, currently represented by U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, to favor a Republican.
But Sabato’s Crystal Ball, which analyzes races, recently shifted the contest from “Likely Republican” to “Leans Republican,” due in part to expectations of strong turnout by Black voters, who tend to vote Democratic. Black turnout is expected to climb across the South after Republican efforts this spring to draw Figures and other Black members of Congress out of their seats.
“Maybe if it is higher Black enthusiasm, maybe if turnout is lower in, let’s say, the Wiregrass part of the state, you could see Rep. Figures getting a large turnout in Montgomery, whereas keeping the rural areas a little closer because they might have lower turnout, him holding his seat in that way,” said J. Miles Coleman, associate editor at The Center for Politics.
Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, the Republican nominee for the 2nd Congressional District, has been vocal about expressing his concerns about the low voter turnout during the primary election. During a campaign event, he said that “voting is going to matter, not only for this state but for the direction of our country.”
Tabitha Isner, former vice chair of the Alabama Democratic Party, said she was encouraged by the vote totals during the primary election season earlier this year.
“Big picture, I think we are seeing higher than normal levels of Democratic engagement and we are seeing lower than normal levels of Republican engagement,” she said in an interview Monday.
Others said that voter turnout matters regardless of party.
“There is not an elected official or candidate in the United States of America who is not concerned about voter turnout,” Rep. Chris Pringle, R-Mobile, said in an interview on Tuesday. “We are candidates, we need people to come out and vote.”
Midterm lag
Midterm turnout tends to lag presidential turnout. In 2024, voter turnout in Alabama was almost 59%, which was a 30-year low in the state. In the midterms in 2022, it was only about 38%, according to the Election Lab at the University of Florida that tracks voter turnout numbers.
However, the particulars of the political environment for the current cycle add to the Republican Party’s problems.
“With the emergence of Trump, Trump was able to win the popular vote in 2024, and he was able to do that because he realigned the Republican Party, bringing in these voters who had never participated before, bringing in a lot of rural Americans, a lot of, what we could call in political science, ‘low propensity voters,” said Spencer Goidel, assistant professor of political science at Auburn University.
Trump, who can rally his voters to the polls, is not on the ballot, and that could be problematic for Republican candidates. Trump implored supporters to vote in the coming election at a recent midterm convention in Texas.
“You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell,” he said at the convention. “Go out and vote, go out and vote!”
Other Republicans expressed alarm over possible Republican apathy as Democrats appear engaged.
“The Democratic base is excited,” said John Wahl, former chair of the Alabama Republican Party and the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor. “They are not happy with what is going on in Washington. They don’t like Donald Trump, and they are engaged in this election process, they are going to turn out to vote. And I think Republicans have to give our base that same excitement in order to get out and vote.”
Alabama 2nd Congressional District race could have national implications

In the May primary, the percentage of Democratic primary ballots chosen reached 43%, up from 22% four years ago. Democrats also saw significant jumps in primary votes cast in Madison, Mobile and Tuscaloosa counties, all critical for the party’s success.
“If the same thing happens in the general election where Democrats are seeing the same level of increase, we ought to be winning some statewide seats,” Isner said. “I think that is making a lot of Democrats feel really excited and hopeful and making a lot of Republicans very nervous.”
According to data on the Alabama Secretary of State’s website, almost 170,000 people voted to nominate the party’s nominee for Governor in 2022. Earlier this year, that same contest garnered more than 365,000 votes, an increase of about 117%.
“I think Democrats are really motivated by what we have seen in terms of attacks on the Voting Rights Act, attacks on basic liberties, the way in which standards and norms for governance have been broken,” Isner said. “The people feel disrespected by those things.”
Will it matter?
A line of voters runs out the door and outside the building at Woodland Methodist Church in Pike Road, Alabama on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. Alabama is one of a handful of states where all in-person voting takes place on Election Day. (Jemma Stephenson/Alabama Reflector)
It is not clear whether voter turnout for the coming general election contest will remain as low as it was for the primaries. And even if it does, it is unclear how much that will benefit Democratic congressional candidates. Alabama Republicans have benefitted from straight ticket voting in the state: in 2024, about two-thirds of all ballots cast were straight-ticket, and of those, about two-thirds were cast for the Republican Party.
“It feels like a real long shot to me,” said Mitchell Brown, a professor of political science at Auburn University. “If you look at the margins in the last midterm, they were pretty big. The closest race was 67% Republican and 29% Democrat. I would be really surprised if, all of a sudden, the Democratic turnout was so high and Republican turnout was so low that a Democrat could ever overcome these margins.”
She also said that the margin for the governor’s race favors Republicans.
“It will matter in some places, local level races, or where the numbers are really small because that is where funny things happen,” Brown said.
Brown said low voter turnout will matter in places where the electorate features a mix of registered voters between Republican and Democrats, and the size of the eligible voting population is less.
Democrats are pushing in Madison County, where demographics have shifted in their favor in the last several years, though Republicans continue to dominate elected offices.
“There are swing legislative districts in Madison County, for instance, that I think could be in trouble,” Sorrell said. “I also have some opinions on a couple of statewide races that look like they will be closer than they should be, but I don’t want to give you names there.”
Wahl said the 2nd Congressional District would probably be “the biggest battleground in the state of Alabama.”
“This is a must-win district for the Republican Party,” he said.
Sorrell said Republicans have got to keep our voters enthusiastic whether Trump is on the ballot or not.”
“That is on us as candidates,” he said. “If voter turnout is poor, that is on the candidates. It is nobody’s job but the candidates to motivate people to go vote.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Data Centers: The Weekly Download
description: In a letter to Ypsilanti Township and University of Michigan Leadership, U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) expressed opposition to a proposed computing center under development as a partnership between U-M and Los Alamos National Laboratory. In a separate letter, Dingell requested the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Michigan Department of E[...]
text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration Updates

In a letter to Ypsilanti Township and University of Michigan Leadership, U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) expressed opposition to a proposed computing center under development as a partnership between U-M and Los Alamos National Laboratory. In a separate letter, Dingell requested the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy conduct an environmental review of the proposed project site, arguing that the development “should not move forward without a clear understanding of the site’s environmental history, remaining contamination, applicable restrictions, and the protections necessary to safeguard public health and the surrounding community.”
After the dust settled at Mason’s data center town hall discussion, Lansing State Journal’s Ken Palmer writes that city officials and data center opponents both saw some good from the event, though their reasons were vastly different. While Mayor Russell Whipple said it was a success in the sense that it allowed city officials to answer questions and exchange differences, Paula Caltrider, who founded No Data Centers in Mason, said the town hall highlighted the disconnect between city council and the city manager.
During the same event, Whipple shared that he is a member of a group looking to rewrite the city’s zoning ordinances to include stricter guidelines on data centers than what was contained in a now-repealed zoning change, WKAR’s Andrew Roth reports.

Legislative Action

After the Michigan Economic Development Corporation declined to identify the companies seeking tax breaks under a 2024 law exempting data center equipment and construction from the state’s sales and use tax, more than 30 environmental groups called on state leaders to ensure data center developers cannot receive these incentives without the public knowing who is benefitting, and how much they are receiving. While the MEDC argued state law bars them from revealing the information, environmental groups sent a letter to Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) and Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) asking them change the law and ensure transparency for Michigan residents.

News of Note

MLive’s Danielle James looks into a set of ads from Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and a political action committee backing U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) as the two candidates for governor continue to contend with concerns around data center development.
William Lawrence, a political organizer seeking to unseat U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, released a multi-step plan aimed at regulating data center development and artificial intelligence.

title: North Dakota livestock relief program funds 470 projects as most of state remains in drought
description: The Drought Disaster Livestock Relief program has exhausted its $4.1 million in funding roughly a month after it was activated by an executive order from North Dakota’s governor.  Reice Haase, director of the Department of Water Resources, told lawmakers on the Water Topics Overview Committee last week that the program has helped fund 470 projects […]
text:
A little water remains in a stock pond near Marion, North Dakota, on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Torie Piehl/LaMoure County Extension)The Drought Disaster Livestock Relief program has exhausted its $4.1 million in funding roughly a month after it was activated by an executive order from North Dakota’s governor. 
Reice Haase, director of the Department of Water Resources, told lawmakers on the Water Topics Overview Committee last week that the program has helped fund 470 projects proposed by 369 ranchers across the state. 
“What our drought disaster livestock program is intended to do is to provide relief and cost share for individual ranchers across the state to fund water projects for long-term drought resilience,” Haase said. 
North Dakota governor declares drought emergency, activates livestock water assistance program

The bulk of the approved projects are located west of the Missouri River and south of Lake Sakakawea, according to a map in Haase’s presentation. Ranchers could apply for up to $10,000 in cost share assistance per project to help fund items like new water wells, pipeline extensions, pasture taps and rural water connections. 
Gov. Kelly Armstrong activated the program via executive order on Aug. 18 and expanded it a week later. Haase said his staff spent late nights, weekends and “a significant amount of overtime” in order to review more than 500 applications during the subsequent two weeks. 
“At this point we have exhausted all funding available that the water commission had approved for this,” Haase said. 
Haase said the projects funded by the assistance would provide permanent relief and help during future droughts as well. 
Nearly 92% of North Dakota is affected by drought or abnormally dry conditions, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor’s Sept. 17 update. Around 31% of the state is in severe drought. Almost 14%, primarily in the southeast and southwest regions of North Dakota, is rated as extreme drought. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: If a diabetes screening is free, get it. An upcoming event in Southwest Idaho can help.
description: Here’s something that you should not pass up. The Kuna Lions (my club) is sponsoring health screening for vision, hearing and diabetes from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Oct. 10 at Kuna’s community center. The vision and hearing screening will be conducted by Envision, and Terry Reilly Health Services will be doing the diabetes testing. […]
text:
The Kuna Lions Club is sponsoring health screening for vision, hearing and diabetes from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Oct. 10 at Kuna’s community center. (Photo by Getty Images)Here’s something that you should not pass up.
The Kuna Lions (my club) is sponsoring health screening for vision, hearing and diabetes from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Oct. 10 at Kuna’s community center. The vision and hearing screening will be conducted by Envision, and Terry Reilly Health Services will be doing the diabetes testing. People living in surrounding communities are cordially invited.
If there were a poster boy for diabetes screening, it would be me. This has been a summer of amputations – one toe on my right foot and two partial toe amputations on my left foot. I have not been able to do summer activities that I enjoy, such as daily walks around the neighborhood and golf.
Yes, these amputations were the result of diabetes. On the bright side, losing a couple of toes is a lot better than losing a foot or a leg.
But there’s more to my diabetes story. Twenty-two years ago, I had a five-way heart bypass surgery – which has given me more than two decades of quality living. But veins from that surgery don’t last forever, and some of mine have shown signs of wear.
In football terms, I may be getting close to the two minute warning. But as fans know so well, a lot can happen in those last two minutes. I have a great life, and it isn’t done yet.
I might have been spared from some of these health challenges if I had diabetes screening 30 years ago. Instead, I ignored some of the obvious symptoms.
Recently, I had a chat with Dr. Stuart Black with Terry Reilly Health Services, and he knows all about the importance of the screening.
“Some studies show that 10 percent of the population, and as high as 13 percent have diabetes and maybe a fourth of the people with diabetes don’t know about it,” he said. “If screening shows an indication of prediabetes, people can get the care they need and prevent the complications that come with the disease, such as heart disease and kidney problems. Diabetes also is one of the leading causes for blindness.”
Dr. Black says that random glucose readings at a screening event may not paint the true picture. For instance, numbers may be on the high side for those who had something to eat before the screening. But high numbers are worth watching.
“The more information that a person has, the better,” he says. “I think there are people who are afraid to find out they have diabetes, because they think it’s a death sentence. But that’s not the case. There are great options to help control blood sugars if you have diabetes or prediabetes.”
Terry Reilly’s service doesn’t stop with the screening. It’s also a resource, and a relatively affordable one, for those who show signs of prediabetes or diabetes.
Terry Reilly Health Services, based in Nampa, has other area clinics – including one in Melba.
“We have physicians and clinical pharmacists who are well versed in dealing with diabetes,” Dr. Black said. “Our doors are open to help anyone who is diagnosed, or at risk, for diabetes or prediabetes.”
Of course, he says, there are steps people can take without a doctor’s help.
“Getting 150 minutes of exercise in a week; eating a healthy diet that focuses more on fruits, vegetables and less on fast foods or processed foods; getting enough sleep; decreasing stress in your life,” he said. “All those things are basic lifestyle choices that people can take, with or without diabetes.”
I wish I had followed that advice 30 years ago.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas health department schedules free flu clinics statewide
description: The Arkansas Department of Health will host free community flu vaccine clinics across the state beginning Monday.  No appointment is needed and vaccines will be provided at no charge, according to a press release from the department. Arkansans should bring their insurance cards to the clinic. If you don’t have insurance or your policy does […]
text:
(Photo by Parker Michels-Boyce for the Virginia Mercury)The Arkansas Department of Health will host free community flu vaccine clinics across the state beginning Monday. 
No appointment is needed and vaccines will be provided at no charge, according to a press release from the department. Arkansans should bring their insurance cards to the clinic. If you don’t have insurance or your policy does not cover flu shots, the vaccine will still be available at no charge.
The flu vaccine cannot give you the flu, according to the health department. If you get the flu after being vaccinated, the vaccine can help reduce how sick you get. There were 91 flu-related deaths reported during the 2025-2026 influenza season. 
“Getting your flu vaccine is a simple step you can take to protect yourself and the people around you,” said Dr. Sarah Labuda, ADH Medical Director for Immunizations. “By offering vaccines at community clinics across the state, we try to make it as easy as possible for Arkansans to get vaccinated and stay healthy this flu season.”
The flu is caused by a virus that spreads easily when a sick person coughs, sneezes or talks, according to the health department. Most people start feeling sick about two days after being exposed to the virus. Symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, muscle or body aches, tiredness and headaches.
Everyone 6 months and older is encouraged to receive an annual flu vaccine, according to the health department. Vaccination is particularly important for high-risk groups, including pregnant women, adults age 65 and older, younger children and people with long-term health conditions or weakened immune systems.  
A schedule for flu clinics in all 75 counties is available on the health department’s website.

text:
A wind turbine is pictured east of Wilton in central North Dakota. (Photo by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)The public will have a chance to comment on a planned wind farm in northwest North Dakota. 
The state Public Service Commission has set a hearing for 9:30 a.m. Sept. 29, at the Grand Williston Hotel and Conference Center for the Homestead Wind Project in northwestern Williams County.
The project proposes 67 wind turbine generators across 25,000 acres. It would be capable of producing about 256 megawatts of electricity. The estimated cost of the project is $750 million. 
Homestead Wind is part of Apex Clean Energy Holdings, which also has been involved in wind development in McLean and Bowman counties. 
Public comments must be made in person at the hearing to be part of the official PSC record. 
Commission hearings are livestreamed at psc.nd.gov. The commission has siting authority over energy projects such as wind farms and solar farms.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Tontitown traffic stops led to ICE detentions months before 287(g) agreement
description: At least 20 people were detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after routine traffic stops by Tontitown police before the department formally joined the federal 287(g) immigration enforcement program. What began as traffic stops for minor violations resulted with several passengers being taken into federal custody despite facing no state or lo[...]
text:
Screenshot from video of an Oct. 10, 2025 traffic stop in Tontitown, Arkansas. (Photo courtesy of Arkansas GRITA)At least 20 people were detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after routine traffic stops by Tontitown police before the department formally joined the federal 287(g) immigration enforcement program.
What began as traffic stops for minor violations resulted with several passengers being taken into federal custody despite facing no state or local charges.
The findings predate Tontitown Police Departments’s June 12, 2026, signing of a 287(g) Task Force Model agreement with ICE, which authorizes local police officers to perform some federal immigration enforcement functions that would otherwise be handled by federal agents.
Read more about 287(g) in Arkansas
Arkansas GRITA compared Tontitown traffic warnings and citations with available federal ICE detention records in Washington County to identify traffic stops that resulted in immigration detentions before the city signed its 287(g) agreement. Federal intake records became publicly available on the Washington County Detainee Intake Roster in mid-September 2025, establishing the earliest point for comparison.
The 13 traffic stops identified resulted in the federal detention of 20 people, including several passengers. Ten of the stops ended with warnings and three resulted in citations. Several of the passengers were detained despite not being accused of any traffic offenses. The majority of the vehicles involved in the identified traffic stops were work vans or trucks.
 An October traffic stop

On the morning of Oct. 10, 2025, Tontitown police pulled over a work van. Although no one was arrested on state or local charges related to the traffic stop, Tontitown police officers called ICE to the scene.
Five of the van’s six occupants were detained by ICE and booked into Washington County Detention Center before being transferred to federal custody. Among them was 18-year-old Vicky Ramirez, a Guatemalan woman whose mugshot went locally viral.
In bodycam footage obtained by Arkansas GRITA through a Freedom of Information Act request (FOIA), Officer Darrin Bentley, who initiated the stop, can be heard saying “we’re going to ID everybody” before exiting his police cruiser.
Within 30 seconds of approaching the work van Bentley opened the van’s sliding door, making multiple passengers visible in the back. Within 90 seconds, the officer asked for the identification of all the passengers of the van.
After going back to his cruiser, Bentley told a second responding officer that he can “make the phone call,” apparently to ICE. In a phone conversation with a third officer, he said, “I’ve got a truck full.”
After issuing a traffic warning to the driver for speeding one to 15 miles per hour over the speed limit and driving continuously in the left lane, the van’s occupants were fingerprinted, then detained roadside for approximately one hour in total until ICE officers arrived. ICE then detained five of the van’s six occupants.
Irvin Camacho, an organizer with the Alliance for Immigrant Respect and Education (AIRE), told GRITA that Ramirez was sent to a detention facility in Louisiana and ultimately deported to Guatemala.
Tontitown police chief Corey Jenison declined to respond to a detailed list of questions about the traffic stop. The questions, and Jenison’s response, are reproduced below this story.
Excerpts from the bodycam footage are embedded below. This is a compilation of bodycam footage from three officers on scene, shortened for time. GRITA has redacted parts of the footage to protect the privacy of the people detained.



 Attorney raises constitutional concern

Connor Thompson, an attorney with the Arkansas chapter of the National Lawyers Guild, said the body camera footage raises several potential constitutional concerns.
“Here, we have a traffic stop seizure that ends up ranging over an hour in length and appears to include waiting for an ICE officer to show up, patting down the occupants of the van, and fingerprinting them,” Thompson wrote in an email to Arkansas GRITA.
Thompson also questioned officers opening the van’s sliding door without reasonable suspicion and fingerprinting passengers who had not been arrested, calling both potential constitutional violations.
“Generally, police lack the authority to force the subject of a traffic stop (short of an arrest) [to] provide biometric data like fingerprints. To collect fingerprints outside of a custodial arrest, officers would need probable cause that a crime has been committed, a warrant, or valid consent,” Thompson wrote. “Based on the videos alone I’m not satisfied that any of these criteria were met before fingerprinting took place here.”
He also said officers generally lack the authority to open a vehicle door without reasonable suspicion that the occupants are armed and dangerous, if contraband is in plain view or if exigent circumstances exist.
“In my eyes, none of those criteria were met here, nor did the officer have consent from the van’s occupants to open the sliding door,” he wrote.
An Arkansas community founded by Italian immigrants becomes a flashpoint over ICE

Tontitown chief Jenison declined to respond to detailed questions about officers’ actions and potential constitutional violations during the stop.
 Police denied plans to join 287(g)

On Dec. 23, 2025, local immigrant advocates with AIRE had a meeting with Tontitown Police Department officials. Jenison was one official from the department in attendance.
The meeting was requested after AIRE received numerous reports from community members about immigration-related incidents in Tontitown. Audio from the meeting was later shared with Arkansas GRITA. (The recording is audio-only, and individual speakers are not easily identifiable beyond their roles as community advocates or Tontitown Police Department officials.)
During the meeting, one Tontitown police official said the department did not intend to join the 287(g) program.
“We don’t have an agreement with ICE. We haven’t signed any of that. We don’t have intentions to sign,” the official said. “That is their task and their purpose. Ours is not that.”
“Getting deputized and [becoming] part of a task force to go out and do [immigration enforcement] is not benefiting Tontitown, in our opinion,” the same official said later in the recording.
Jenison told GRITA via email that the intent behind the department signing a 287(g) agreement “is not to make local officers responsible for broad immigration enforcement or to target members of our community. Rather, the agreement is intended to enhance public safety by allowing law enforcement to more effectively identify and coordinate with federal authorities when they encounter individuals who are wanted for serious crimes in other countries or who present a legitimate public safety concern. The goal is to help ensure that dangerous criminals do not evade justice simply because of international jurisdictional boundaries.”
Jenison previously told the Arkansas Advocate that federal funding promised to departments who join 287(g) programs was a benefit to the department, which is planning to build a new police station.
During the December meeting, police officials also said officers may call ICE after a traffic stop if they cannot identify a person. They did not say how often officers contacted ICE and said the decision was left to individual officers. Officials also said it would not be typical for officers to delay a traffic stop while waiting for ICE to arrive.
Thompson, the NLG attorney, told Arkansas GRITA that stalling a traffic stop for ICE to arrive could violate the Supreme Court’s decision in Rodriguez v. United States, which held that “a police stop exceeding the time needed to handle the matter for which the stop was made violates the Constitution’s shield against unreasonable seizures.”

GRITA-questions-for-Tontitown-1- 
After the meeting, Camacho, who attended the December meeting, said immigration-related encounters involving Tontitown police appeared to decline temporarily.
“We heard less arrests [were] happening in Tontitown – less photos, less videos, less people reaching out to us,” he said. “We thought that they had actually made a good difference with their policy.”
Camacho said that changed when the news broke that Tontitown Police Department signed the 287(g) agreement in June.
“You signing an agreement as a police department, you’re going the extra step, you’re purposefully being harmful to immigrant communities – and that’s the part that makes me sick,” Camacho said.
Cities are not required to sign 287(g) agreements under the legislation Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders signed into law last year. However, including Tontitown, 66 municipalities across the state currently have such agreements with ICE, almost all of them under the Task Force Model.
As Arkansas GRITA previously reported, DHS announced last year that it would reimburse police departments who signed onto 287(g) under the Task Force Model for trained officers’ salaries, benefits, and overtime.
Tontitown’s 287(g) memorandum allows trained local law enforcement officers to carry out immigration enforcement during routine policing activities, such as traffic stops or patrols. The Task Force Model of the 287(g) partnership, which was discontinued under former President Barack Obama and reinstated by the Trump administration in 2025, has been criticized for civil rights abuses and racial profiling.
This story was originally produced by Arkansas GRITA, and was republished with their permission. Email staff@arkansasgrita.com if you’re interesting in republishing this article.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota Supreme Court races are nonpartisan, but Republicans play a big role
description: North Dakota voters have a rare contest for a state Supreme Court seat this fall, one that raises questions about Republican politics in the nonpartisan race.  Judicial races are nonpartisan by state law. Justice Jerod Tufte is seeking a second 10-year term, challenged by Watford City attorney Ariston Johnson. Each says his campaign is nonpartisan. […]
text:
North Dakota Supreme Court candidates Jerod Tufte, left, and Ariston Johnson. (Photos courtesy of the campaigns)North Dakota voters have a rare contest for a state Supreme Court seat this fall, one that raises questions about Republican politics in the nonpartisan race. 
Judicial races are nonpartisan by state law. Justice Jerod Tufte is seeking a second 10-year term, challenged by Watford City attorney Ariston Johnson. Each says his campaign is nonpartisan. They have attended or appeared at events put on by Republicans, including a fundraiser held by prominent party members for Tufte. Various Republicans also have endorsed a candidate in the race.
Tufte said his campaign committee has handled fundraising and endorsements because he cannot. Johnson said part of his campaign platform is that he is “genuinely nonpartisan,” and he is uncomfortable accepting politicians’ endorsements and asking for support. 
North Dakota Supreme Court upholds ban on transgender healthcare for minors

Longtime attorneys affiliated with the Republican Party said they would avoid partisan mingling because the judiciary’s integrity is crucial to uphold.
Bob Wefald, a former state district judge and long-ago attorney general, said he “avoided any kind of political contact whatsoever” as a judicial candidate and a judge — even removing his name from GOP programs alongside his wife Susan’s when she was a Republican member of the Public Service Commission.
“A lot of people felt we were divorced because everybody else would have their spouse listed, and Susan would be all by herself,” Wefald said. “I just avoided it. I think it’s the proper thing to avoid it.” 
Rules
North Dakota has a sprawling judicial code of conduct that includes rules for campaign activities. Those rules begin with: “A judge or candidate for judicial office shall not engage in political or campaign activity that is inconsistent with the independence, integrity or impartiality of the judiciary.” 
Judicial candidates cannot directly or personally seek campaign contributions, or know the names of donors, but they can ask groups of 25 people or more for donations.
They are barred from participating in a variety of political activities, such as accepting political groups’ endorsements and attending political organizations’ events. But judicial candidates may speak on behalf of their candidacy “through any medium,” whether or not they are at a gathering sponsored by a political organization, according to the rules.
North Dakota Supreme Court Justice Jerod Tufte asks a question during oral arguments on Dec. 18, 2023. (Photo by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)
Judges or judicial candidates appearing at political events or with partisan officeholders gives an impression “you are going to be favorable toward people in that political party,” said Richard Painter, who was chief ethics lawyer to President George W. Bush, White House employees and other officials. 
“Impartiality is a critically important factor in the effectiveness of the courts, the fairness of the courts and public confidence in the courts,” said Painter, who is now a professor of corporate law at the University of Minnesota Law School. 
Judicial candidates shouldn’t attend partisan political events because courts handle state, federal and presidential election disputes, he said.
“When they do things like show up at a partisan fundraiser or political events, they give ammunition to the extremists of the far left and the far right who say that judging is nothing more than an exercise in partisan politics,” Painter said.
Fundraisers
Last month, Sandi and Brent Sanford — a former NDGOP chair and former lieutenant governor, respectively — hosted a fundraiser for Tufte at their Bismarck home. Other hosts included U.S. Sens. Kevin Cramer and John Hoeven and U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak — all Republicans. 
Tufte’s campaign wanted “some elected officers with stature” to be a part of the fundraiser, and the federal officeholders are less likely to appear before the state Supreme Court, campaign co-chair Shane Goettle said. 
“There just aren’t any Democratic officeholders here to turn to and ask them to be part of it,” said Goettle, who ran for NDGOP chair last year.
The invitation included a disclaimer that Tufte cannot know who does and does not give to his campaign, and people shouldn’t hand him contributions or say they have given. 
“This rule protects the very thing he’s asking your help to preserve: a court where everyone stands equal, contributor or not,” the message said. 
The invitation also listed a suggested individual donation of $200, which Goettle said was not required of attendees.
The fundraiser had a sign at the entry explaining the rules about judicial campaign donations, Tufte said. He also said he sought advice from the Judicial Ethics Advisory Committee, “and I was advised that I was going above and beyond in what I had to do to make sure that we were taking reasonable efforts to shield me from donations, specific knowledge of donations.”
Wefald said he would not have attended the fundraiser, as Tufte did. 
“I myself would want to avoid that appearance. I think we need to keep partisan politics out of judicial races, and that’s all I’ll say about that,” Wefald said. 
North Dakota Supreme Court candidate Ariston Johnson poses next to the entrance of the Ralph J. Erickstad Courtroom at the Capitol on Sept. 18, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Johnson said his campaign has held a few meet-the-candidate and fundraising events conducted “within the judicial code of conduct.” 
“I speak. If it’s a large enough group, I uncomfortably, because of my nature, ask for support. If it’s a smaller group, I am very cautious to not ask for financial or other material support,” Johnson said. 
Endorsements
Tufte’s campaign website touts endorsements of prominent Republicans including Cramer, former governors Jack Dalrymple and Ed Schafer and state Sen. Janne Myrdal. 
Endorsements come from people his campaign committee has sought out from those who “would have a perspective and that the public would be interested in their views on this judicial race,” Tufte said. 
“It’s basically unavoidable that some of the public officials are going to be partisan people who have opinions on these races,” he said. 
Republican endorsement of Tufte “goes down that path of creating a partisan theme to the judiciary when historically that has been not commonplace,” said attorney Bob Harms, a former NDGOP chair. But he said he isn’t sure it should factor into voters’ decisions.
Johnson said he would be uncomfortable accepting a politician’s endorsement in the nonpartisan race. The less there’s an appearance of impropriety for a judge, the better, he said. 
Sen. Dale Patten, R-Watford City, recently offered his endorsement at a Johnson meet-and-greet. He said he’s known Johnson since he was born, respects his broad background and agriculture and energy expertise, and wanted to offer his endorsement as “the local guy.” Johnson did not know he would endorse him, Patten said. 
Judicial candidates cannot seek, accept or use endorsements or letters of support from political organizations. 
Events
Both Johnson and Tufte attended a North Dakota Federation of Republican Women event and separate Fedorchak events earlier this year.
Tufte appeared in social media photos with multiple Republican statewide officeholders running for office this year.
Johnson said he was “a guest of a guest” at the Republican Women and Fedorchak events, and did not seek or receive support at those gatherings.
Tufte said the code of judicial conduct “expressly permits candidates for judicial office to speak on their own behalf at events like that,” including those that are party-sponsored, private or run by organizations.  
“I think those rules recognize that judicial candidates need to have opportunities to make their case for why they are a good candidate,” he said. 
North Dakota abortion ban deemed constitutional in split opinion from state Supreme Court

Tufte noted he went to state and district conventions of both parties during his first campaign in 2016, which he said the rules allow. He said he did not do the same this year because he had no opponent until the last day for candidates to file, at which point the convention season was over. 
Tufte said he has good relationships with Republicans and Democrats in the Legislature and state government, and has spoken at events of both parties in the past. 
“I go where I’m invited to speak to any group that’s interested in hearing about my campaign,” he said. 
Johnson said he has not appeared at any party conventions. Before he considered running, he did appear by request as a parliamentarian at a district GOP meeting in Watford City, he added.
Patten said it’s almost impossible to run a race in North Dakota and do meet-and-greets without doing it at a Republican event or events with a significant Republican showing. 
How should voters decide? 
Johnson and Tufte say their individual records and experiences are key for voters.
Tufte’s campaign is somewhat educational as he reintroduces himself to voters after 10 years. He cites more than 400 opinions he has written that voters can read. “They don’t have to guess at what kind of a judge I’ll be because I have that record that they can trust,” he said.
He said his varied background gives him a unique perspective on the separation of powers and roles of the three branches of government. Tufte has been a state district judge, general counsel to the governor, a judge advocate in the North Dakota Army National Guard, a prosecutor and a solo civil attorney. He also cites his computer engineer background as crucial to understanding a changing technology landscape for courts and lawyers.
Johnson said his perspective as an attorney representing clients in mineral rights and civil rights cases is missing from the court. He’s spent two decades seeing how the law affects people in their lives and businesses. 
He cites his experience and relationships from having appeared in cases in every one of the state’s eight judicial districts. He also points to his technology background, having a computer science degree and working on the user end of court technology. 
In the last year, the Supreme Court has handled such high-profile decisions as the constitutionality of North Dakota’s abortion ban and transgender care for minors and a ballot measure from the Legislature to change term limits. 
No sitting justice has lost an election since 1992.
Justice Douglas Bahr, appointed in 2023 by then-Gov. Doug Burgum, is running unopposed for an eight-year term. He is not campaigning.

The full-service grocery in North Omaha  — to be run as a social […]
text:
A ceremonial groundbreaking was held over the weekend for a nonprofit grocery store supported partly by a state grant. The enterprise, to be operated by Heart Ministry Center, will rise on a few acres shown here near 25th and Lake Streets. Among those who scooped dirt to mark the occasion were Omaha Mayor John Ewing Jr., Heart Ministry Center's Damany Rahn and Omaha City Council member LaVonya Goodwin. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — A jingle created and sung by Omaha Mayor John Ewing Jr. especially for the occasion kicked off a groundbreaking Saturday for a grocery store described as key to restoring dignity and economic vitality to one of Nebraska’s most distressed areas.
The full-service grocery in North Omaha  — to be run as a social enterprise by nonprofit Heart Ministry Center — is to span 25,000 square feet, about half the size of an American football field.
It is funded partially by a state grant program intended to boost revival of impoverished areas most hurt by the pandemic. An official previously estimated the price tag at about $7 million. The state awarded $1.5 million.
Yet to be named, the market will rise on a few vacant acres southwest of 25th and Lake streets and offer fresh, affordable food while creating jobs for community members and graduates of Heart Ministry’s Fresh Start job training program. That program serves as a hands-on workforce pipeline for people overcoming crises and on the path to self-sufficiency.
Ewing commended supporters for promoting job creation and economic growth.
Planned grocery store aims to not just feed but uplift historical heart of Omaha’s Black community

“A grocery store may seem like one building, but what we’re really celebrating today is access, dignity, opportunity and investment in the future of North Omaha,” Ewing said.
He said that something “as basic as fresh food” should not depend on one’s zip code.
Omaha City Council member LaVonya Goodwin, whose district includes the project site in the heart of North Omaha, said it has been 58 years since the neighborhood had a full-service grocery store. 
She used words like “monumental” and said the effort represented a commitment to “holistically restoring a people and a community.”
Reflecting on how a grocery store might help rebuild a neighborhood, Goodwin recounted strategic discussions she’s had with economic development experts. There’s a burning question: “What comes first? The housing, the infrastructure, the safety, the security — or the services and amenities?”
She said programs and infrastructure can be built. “But what’s really going to holistically support the community? Does anybody deliberately move back to a community where there is not a grocery store,” or perhaps a dry cleaner, shoe repair, dentist or doctor’s office?
Goodwin and others said they view the grocery project as another catalyst that can improve “livability” in its North Omaha area and snowball into broader economic development.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Also at the event, which drew about 150 people, were Chris Rodgers of the Douglas County Board, Heart Ministry board members and a representative of the Nebraska Department of Economic Development.
The DED-administered North and South Omaha Recovery Grant program, which awarded about $235 million to multiple projects and organizations in the target areas, directed $1.5 million of public funds toward the effort. 
Damany “Dom” Rahn, Heart Ministry’s chief executive, said previously that key philanthropic donors asked for anonymity. 
But zoning and other agreements identify RH Land Management Co. as owner of the land and the corporation proposing to build the project and make site improvements. RH Land Management is affiliated with Susie Buffett’s nonprofit Sherwood Foundation. The Heart Ministry continues to raise funds for the effort.
The planned market, an interior view from the floral department looking north toward the check-out area. (Courtesy of Alley Poyner Macchietto Architecture)
Rahn, also speaking at the project site, said the center is seeking community input on what to name the grocery store he describes as more of an investment in the area’s health and stability. It’ll be a disrupter to a food desert and operate as a nonprofit, with a mission to provide affordable food.
Ewing, who grew up in North Omaha, called Saturday a milestone. The Democrat who unseated three-term Republican Jean Stothert in 2025 said he was encouraged to write a tune for the occasion, and kiddingly said he took a “huge risk” at sharing it on stage. 
“I cannot sing,” the mayor told those gathered, including his wife, Viv. But he said that one of his goals when he retired from the Omaha Police Department was to have more fun than anyone else. He first sang alone, then asked the audience to join in. 
“Here we go: 
“Down the road there’s a grocery store. Thank you, Heart Ministry Center. Dignity for all. That’s our battle cry.”

text:
Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti is asking a Hamilton County Chancery Court to dismiss Chattanooga’s lawsuit to reverse an airport board takeover. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The state of Tennessee is asking a Hamilton County Chancery Court to dismiss Chattanooga’s lawsuit to reverse an airport board takeover.
Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti filed the request, saying in part that Chattanooga doesn’t have standing to sue the state, nor has it shown any injury from a new state law giving the governor and Senate and House speakers the majority of appointments to boards that oversee airports in Nashville, Memphis, Chattanooga, Knoxville and Tri-Cities. The legislation came after courts ruled a previous state effort to take over appointments to the Nashville airport authority was unconstitutional.
The filing is made on behalf of Gov. Bill Lee, House Speaker Cameron Sexton and Senate Speaker Randy McNally.
The city of Chattanooga and the previous locally appointed Chattanooga airport board sued the state earlier this year to prevent the state-appointed board from taking over airport operations. The new board subsequently voted to withdraw from the lawsuit.
The situation in Chattanooga is similar to the case in Nashville where Metro Nashville and the former airport board sued the state, arguing a federal law prevents the Federal Aviation Administration from recognizing the new board until the legal dispute over changing the entity that operates the airport is resolved.
Skrmetti’s new filing says federal law does not require the FAA to take action, only that the agency’s administrator has the legal authority to approve a change “in the event there is disputed change in sponsorship.”
