name: Alabama Reflector
title: The grocery tax must go. But Alabama’s tax system needs a complete overhaul.
description: There’s a political ad I’d like to see. I know it’s just a dream. But let’s break out the Alabama Campaign Spot Construction Set anyway. Get my candidate in a field with 64 spotlights on him. Put him in a $90,000 pickup truck. Play that 2003 bar band guitar riff. Burmp ba-da-da-da burp-bum bop. “My […]
text:
General Manager Brian Horak walks down an aisle at Post 60 Market in Emerson, Nebraska in 2024. A growing number of Alabama politicians are calling for the abolition of Alabama's grocery tax, which has been in place since 1939. (Kevin Hardy/Stateline)There’s a political ad I’d like to see. I know it’s just a dream.
But let’s break out the Alabama Campaign Spot Construction Set anyway. Get my candidate in a field with 64 spotlights on him. Put him in a $90,000 pickup truck. Play that 2003 bar band guitar riff.
Burmp ba-da-da-da burp-bum bop.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“My name is Bill Fratbrother. And I work for hard-working Alabamians. That’s why I’m going to shift taxes to people who can pay them.”
Cut to my man in a polo shirt next to a barn. For political authenticity.
“When I’m in Montgomery, I’m going to make sure rich Alabamians start shouldering the burden they’ve pushed on us.”
Shred that guitar like you’re being paid in beer. Burmp ba-da-da-da burp-bum bop.
“No grocery tax. No breaks for timber barons. And no welfare for wealthy families paying federal taxes. Because this is our government, not theirs.”
Cut. Upload. Play a bazillion times on Saturday afternoons through November.
This was inspired in part by the growing consensus that it’s time to bounce Alabama’s grocery tax. And I’m all for grabbing it by the shirt collar and throwing it out the door. State officials with hair-trigger tempers over the slightest federal regulation have intruded on this essential household expenditure for decades, with zero sense of irony.
The fate of the grocery tax will depend on next year’s budget and whether state officials can swallow losing $230 million in a year where everyone expects money to be short.  
I’d cut it regardless. Find another solution. Don’t tax hunger.
But this push to dump the food levy stands out for another reason. We’re talking about cutting a tax that hurts Alabamians outside of the country clubs.
You could believe from our state’s political culture that Alabama soaks people like a Scandinavian country, where personal tax rates approach 60%. If that were the case, you’d have a lot fewer worries about paying for childcare, higher education and medical emergencies. In fact, Alabama consistently appears on lists of states with the lowest tax burdens.
But this is a bit misleading. We’re not Sweden, but most people in Alabama don’t really experience low taxes. That state sales tax is insidious. Worse, it’s applied in a ham-fisted manner, with a raft of business exemptions that tell you who counts in our state. We have taxed human food since 1939. We don’t tax chicken feed.
Compare that to New York, which I am informed is a Stalinesque hellscape. They don’t tax groceries. Nor do they tax clothing purchases under $110.
That’s a helpful exemption for families with children.
But not the kind Alabama ever thinks about extending. For all the pickup truck preening and agricultural playacting, our state government generally believes that taxes should be borne by those least able to pay.
So if you own a forest, send your children to private school or (shudder) find yourself in the highest federal income tax bracket, Alabama lawmakers will trample the masses to help you.
If you rent your house, send your kids to public school or drive to work each day? Sorry. Hope you find your way into a higher caste.
And those tax breaks for some raise the cost of living for the rest of us. Many local government services get funded through vehicle registration taxes — excuse me, “fees.” Fees that are often raised in local bills that slide frictionlessly through a Legislature allegedly filled with low-tax advocates.
The reason for that dependency? Our property tax caps.
Do Alabama homeowners pay less tax than those in other states? Yes. Do families experience a lot more anxiety about the quality of education in a resource-strapped public school? Particularly in rural areas forbidden from properly taxing property owned by a handful of timber barons? You bet.
So you may feel compelled to pay thousands or tens of thousands of dollars a year to put your kids in private academies, even though modest property tax hikes would almost certainly be cheaper, give your local school adequate resources and maybe raise your home value.
But we can’t do that. Racist white planters who hated public education put those caps in the state constitution at the end of Reconstruction. Groups built to protect big landholders, like the Alabama Farmers Federation, laser-eye anyone who dares to address them.
Nor can we do much with the state income tax, with rates and income thresholds frozen in a 1933 constitutional amendment.  Tinkering with exemptions eased some of the regressivity. But it can’t be called a fair tax system by any stretch of the imagination.
So don’t tell me Alabama’s taxes should be cut. I want Bill Fratbrother and every other aspiring official to make taxes fair.
Tell me how you’re going to shift the burden to the Big Mules. Show me that you have the fortitude to tell the exalted Alabamians that they have to give back to a state where they’ve prospered.
Because that’s the actual problem with Alabama taxes: some people are too important to pay. Which means the rest of us have to make up the difference.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia should end tax breaks for unpopular data centers
description: Public opposition to data centers is real and growing across the political spectrum.
text:
A server room in a data center. (Photo by Getty Images)Public opposition to data centers is real and growing across the political spectrum. 
Residents largely see data centers as bad neighbors — emitting air and noise pollution, gobbling up huge tracts of land and water and raising utility costs, all while creating few if any permanent jobs for locals. The artificial intelligence they power is then used to raise the prices on goods we buy, surveil us, deny medical procedures, and — as industry insiders are warning — could even end humanity. Despite that, data center developers are set to receive massive tax breaks and special carveouts that will equal lost revenue for local schools and public services, which cannot be ignored in the public debate around data centers’ costs and benefits.
 While state officials tout billions of dollars in proposed data center development as a benefit to West Virginia, in reality those figures represent corporate investment for private profit. These dollars are not going to public budgets or even to West Virginians, but to private companies for out-of-state profits. The way our communities would benefit from data center development is via the tax revenue they generate, but in West Virginia, we provide stacking tax breaks, allowing multi-billion-dollar companies to dramatically reduce or even zero out their tax liability. They are exempt from paying sales tax on the expensive equipment that fills their data centers including computers, servers, software and other purchases; pay a heavily discounted rate on their property taxes; and can dramatically lower their income tax liability if they create just 10 jobs.
An analysis from the West Virginia Center on Budget and Policy found that the sales tax exemption alone could exceed $1 billion for every $20 billion in data center buildout. Gov. Patrick Morrisey has announced $96 billion in possible investment, and while all of that is unlikely to come to fruition given our history of economic development promises that later fizzle out or underwhelm, this demonstrates the potential billions of dollars in tax revenue our state could be leaving on the table. 
While any merits of data centers are dubious, if they are going to exist in West Virginia, they should have buy-in from the communities in which they locate and pay their fair share in taxes just like any other business or household. As we look around the state, there is no shortage of needs that are currently on hold due to a lack of public funding: building out flood-resilient infrastructure, roads and bridges; ensuring the southern coalfields have broadband internet and clean drinking water; fixing the public school funding formula to better accommodate rural communities and students with disabilities; investing in job training and higher education; and addressing the state’s worst-in-the-nation child welfare crisis. 
At the very least, we shouldn’t be begging data centers to locate in West Virginia with a race-to-the-bottom strategy to have the least regulation and lowest taxes in the nation. Take it from data center corporations in their own words — they need us. Nscale officials say they chose West Virginia for our energy. TransGas, developers of the Adams Fork Energy site in Mingo County, say they chose West Virginia for a “proprietary fresh-water reserve” and the site’s location near “low-cost natural gas reserves.”
Notably, none cite our state’s tax breaks. Rather, they make clear they are here for our abundant but finite natural resources. When understood that way, one might recognize parallels with our state’s experience of timber, coal, and natural gas extraction. If we do not ensure our people are prioritized rather than sacrificed amid potential data center developments, we will be stuck with a similar result where our resource wealth is extracted and shipped out of West Virginia, making out-of-state corporations even wealthier while leaving our local communities no better off in the long-term. 
The debate over data centers should continue in the public arena, with our people having the final say over whether they want them in their communities. But policymakers should not wait to take action. They should eliminate all tax breaks for data centers to ensure West Virginians see a real and lasting benefit from the data centers that may locate here, restore local community control by repealing HB 2014, and codify requirements that data centers report on their environmental impact, local hiring, and water and electricity use.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Dems think ‘affordability’ gives them a shot in 6th District, but GOP touts historical patterns
description: PAINT LICK — Kevin Brown, an attorney whose family has owned a subsistence farm in Garrard County for several generations, says cost of living is a big issue in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District race.  Brown’s farm was the site of a meet-and-greet for the Democratic candidate, Zach Dembo, in the election in mid-September. A few dozen […]
text:
Republican Ralph Alvarado, left, and Democrat Zach Dembo, right, are running in Kentucky's 6th Congressional District. (Photos provided by campaigns)PAINT LICK — Kevin Brown, an attorney whose family has owned a subsistence farm in Garrard County for several generations, says cost of living is a big issue in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District race. 
Brown’s farm was the site of a meet-and-greet for the Democratic candidate, Zach Dembo, in the election in mid-September. A few dozen people showed up in what Brown said is “definitely a red county.” 
“If you go talk to the neighbor next door here, who’s a Republican, we’re going to probably agree on 90% of things about cost of living, about different things,” Brown said. “And Zach is, I think, the type of person that can bring people together like that.” 
Zach Dembo speaks to constituents at a campaign fundraiser on Sept. 11, 2026, in Paint Lick, Kentucky. Photo by Arden Barnes for KY Lantern
The November election between Dembo, 40, a former federal prosecutor and veteran, and Ralph Alvarado, 56, a doctor and former state senator, is about 40 days away. Both candidates launched their first general election ads the week after Labor Day, and PACs are funding ads — one aligned with Gov. Andy Beshear and one aligned with President Donald Trump. 
Democrats in the 6th District say the race is shaping up around affordability issues among Kentuckians, but Republicans say Democrats don’t have the best track record with the central region of the state. The current seat holder, Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Barr, is running for Senate. Barr first won the House seat in 2012. 
Still, Dembo, in Garrard County, told the Kentucky Lantern that people in the district “are ready for a change.” 
“The race is not about Democrat versus Republican,” Dembo added, sounding a bit like Beshear, whom he worked for during the governor’s first term. “It’s about people being fed up with both parties and the system.” 
Dembo said voters in the central Kentucky district “are seeing “very tangible impacts of the cost of corruption in D.C” through the effects of the war in Iran and high gas and grocery prices. Dembo said Congress should “do its damn job.” 
Zach Dembo speaks to constituents at a campaign fundraiser on Sept. 11, 2026, in Paint Lick, Kentucky. Photo by Arden Barnes for KY Lantern
“They have the power to stop it, and they just aren’t,” he said. “So it’s the perfect parable for self-serving politicians serving themselves and getting rich instead of working for us.”
In another part of the district, Kate Bixler, the chair of the Madison County Democrats, said she is hearing not just from members of her party, but also independent and Republican voters that the election is “coming down to the back-breaking costs and corruption versus affordability, and people wanting to see some accountability.” As of August, about 12.5% of registered voters in the 6th District are independent or third-party voters. 
Nevertheless, in the largest county in the district, Fayette County, local Republican Party Chairman Fran Anderson said Democrats as a whole are not offering something voters want and he sees enthusiasm for Alvarado. He said the party has become “so socialist and communist that people are starting really to turn against them.” Other Kentucky Republicans on the ballot this year, including Barr and U.S. Rep. James Comer, have also framed the November elections as GOP values versus “socialism.” 
Republican candidate for Congress, Ralph Alvarado, at the podium, accepts an endorsement from the Kentucky Fraternal Order of Police. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
“We can talk about affordability and all that stuff, but this is what I’m hearing,” Anderson said. 
Alvarado defended Republicans’ policies to address the cost of living during a press conference at the end of August, pointing to the Working Families Tax Credits passed during Trump’s second term. 
The road to Election Day
Alvarado also said during that press conference, where he received an endorsement from the Kentucky Fraternal Order of Police, that he believed there are still a lot of undecided voters in the race between him and Dembo. 
“It’s a matter of understanding what Kentuckians need and want, and earning the trust of Kentuckians every day,” he said. “As having been a doctor here who’s advanced the policies that matter to people in Kentucky, I think I’ve done a good job for that, and I’m going to continue to tell my story. The things that we’ve done, the things that we plan to do, and having proper vision.”
Though anchored by Lexington, a college town that is the second largest city in the state, the 6th District is surrounded by red, rural counties. During the last presidential election in 2024, Trump carried the district by 15 points. Barr was also on the ballot that year and won reelection by 27 points. 
However, Beshear, who won two terms in Kentucky, has carried the district by 19 points in the past. The governor endorsed Dembo after the primary and has been on the campaign trail with him. 
In the weeks ahead, both Dembo and Alvarado will continue to make their pitches to voters. At this point, it’s unclear if they will do that at the same time. In early September, Alvarado’s campaign said he agreed to a debate with Spectrum, while Dembo’s campaign said he will do debates with WKYT and KET. 
Ralph Alvarado is the GOP candidate for the 6th District Congressional race in Kentucky. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Chris Hughes)
A poll from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which is backing Dembo, had the race tied at 47% between Dembo and Alvarado in early August. However, race watchers like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball still have the outcome of the race favoring Republicans. 
Bixler, the Madison County Democrat, said that “no matter what happens in November, there will be progress one way or the other.”
“And I really do believe it’s only the beginning for the party reviving and redefining itself here,” she said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Before you say yes to a data center, listen to this advice from coal country
description: The mayor of Russell learned in June that a Barcelona company wanted to build a two-gigawatt data center on the old AK Steel site in his town. He learned it from a consultant’s email, and the consultant’s first concern was that the moratorium Russell had just passed might get in the way. That is how […]
text:
This map shows proposed hyperscale data centers across Kentucky. (Lantern Screenshot)The mayor of Russell learned in June that a Barcelona company wanted to build a two-gigawatt data center on the old AK Steel site in his town. He learned it from a consultant’s email, and the consultant’s first concern was that the moratorium Russell had just passed might get in the way. That is how an $8-$12 billion-dollar project that would draw more than a tenth of Kentucky’s summer electricity announced itself, as the Kentucky Lantern reported in July.
Russell is not alone. Kentucky utilities told regulators in May that as many as 30 data centers were under discussion in the state, the Lantern found. TeraWulf is building on the industrial park Greenup shares with Boyd County and at the idled aluminum smelter in Hancock County. Pikeville has signed a memorandum with a Lexington developer, WYMT reported in June. The response has been the only one the law allows a county. Bell County, Cave City and Russell passed moratoriums, a Burgin council member walked out on September 9 to deny a quorum, and the day before, the Woodford County Fiscal Court had voted unanimously to ban data centers outright, the first county in the state to do so, with no project even proposed.
The General Assembly gave the industry a sales-tax exemption and then let bills from both parties on water use, siting and ratepayer exposure die on the last day of the session. Gov. Andy Beshear filled the gap in August an executive order which requires developers to show the state they will not raise other customers’ bills. It is the strongest statement any Kentucky official has made, but it is an order rather than a statute, and it does not say what happens to a developer who ignores it.
So, the counties are largely on their own, and they should know what they are getting. A hyperscale data center consumes electricity on the scale of a power plant and, once built, needs surprisingly few people. The Russell project promises 200 permanent jobs on $12 billion dollars of investment. Pikeville’s first phase is 40. In Mason County, W.Va., the Monarch campus will employ 645 people on a $69 billion first phase, roughly one job for every hundred million dollars, according to figures from Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s office reported by the Charleston Gazette-Mail. Neighbors whose yards flooded during site grading have been selling their homes, West Virginia Public Broadcasting reported in August.
What a data center does produce is property tax. Loudoun County, Va., collected $875 million from data centers last year and runs a third of its government on them. For an Eastern Kentucky county that has watched its coal severance money vanish, that is the first serious new tax base anyone has offered in a generation. It is worth having, and worth pricing correctly. The coalfields once gave away their minerals for a dollar an acre to people who knew exactly what they were worth.
Good advice
Here is what a county or city can put on the table before it signs, my research shows.
Buy time first. A moratorium is not obstruction. It is the only tool the legislature left local governments, and it can be used to write a zoning ordinance that covers setbacks, noise, water, generators and stormwater. Wythe County, Va., learned what happens without one when its board chairman conceded in December that a data center could become anyone’s next-door neighbor without a hearing, Cardinal News reported. Nine months later the county still has no zoning and the project is proceeding.
No code names. A project that will use public water, public roads and a public tax exemption should not be negotiated under a nondisclosure agreement. The developer, not its consultant, should appear by name before the fiscal court or council votes.
Get the numbers from someone other than the developer. Hire an independent analyst and make the developer pay for it. The Kentucky Center for Economic Policy has already warned that developers may claim the manufacturing and industrial-processing tax breaks in state law, which would shrink the windfall school districts are counting on, the Lantern reported Sept. 2.
Turn promises into obligations. Pikeville’s instinct, to demand enforceable commitments on jobs and wages before signing, should be the state standard. If the jobs do not appear, the tax abatement should disappear with them. Add local hiring and an apprenticeship line at the community college, because the durable jobs are electricians, pipefitters and plant operators. And make every obligation bind whoever owns the property next. The company making promises today may sell the campus in 10 years to one that never made them.
Put the electric bill in a contract. Kentucky is not starting from zero here. On August 21 the Public Service Commission approved the contract between Big Rivers Electric and TeraWulf for the Hancock County project after finding that it made the data center bear the cost of serving its own load and protected existing customers, the Lantern reported. Every project should be subject to a commission-approved tariff or contract of that kind, and citizens should follow the PSC docket in Frankfort as closely as the courthouse agenda, because that is where the money is decided.
Water on the record. Russell’s developer says it will use 55 million gallons a year from a system that produces about 500 million, according to the company’s answers to the city. Put it in the agreement, with a cap, monitoring and priority for households in a drought.
Plan for the end at the beginning. Senate Bill 319, introduced in March and never heard in committee, would have required a decommissioning plan and a surety bond for data centers built on farmland. A county can require the same on its own, so taxpayers are not left with an empty shell and a field of dead generators if the project fails. Make the developer pay for the road damage its construction causes and for the fire equipment and training that a campus full of generators, fuel and battery storage will require. And require a short public report every year on actual jobs, taxes paid, and power and water used, so the community can see whether the bargain it was promised is the one it got.
One demand belongs in Frankfort. The coal severance tax was the mountains’ one belated victory over an extractive economy, and even then most of the money went into the state general fund, with only a share sent back to the counties that had been mined. Kentucky should do better with data centers. A per-megawatt-hour levy on their power, paid entirely to the county that hosts them, would put the machines to work paying for the roads, schools and water systems they strain. If the industry says it will go elsewhere, ask where. It is looking at Kentucky because Northern Virginia and the other older data center regions are running out of power and patience.
The data centers can be good for Kentucky if the citizens want them. But they should be negotiated, not surrendered, by communities that know what they own. The mountains have said yes the other way for 150 years, and every hollow can show you what it bought.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: A data center ban or data center regulations? Catch up on Kentucky data center news.
description: Republican Louisville Metro Council member Anthony Piagentini interrupted a committee meeting last week because he wanted someone to stop the blaring noise he heard from the gallery.  That blaring noise was the recorded sound of a data center coming from the phone from a member of the group No Data Center 502, according to group […]
text:
Mary DeLima, 65, and her dog Bo wait for the Burgin city council meeting to start on Tuesday. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)Republican Louisville Metro Council member Anthony Piagentini interrupted a committee meeting last week because he wanted someone to stop the blaring noise he heard from the gallery. 
That blaring noise was the recorded sound of a data center coming from the phone from a member of the group No Data Center 502, according to group organizer Danielle Ray. The group has confronted city leaders at public events and meetings, including Mayor Craig Greenberg, in an effort to try to stop a planned hyperscale data center in West Louisville. 
“A lot of the changes for the better and the improvements for people’s lives were achieved through direct action and protest and making officials uncomfortable,” Ray told the Kentucky Lantern in describing the group’s approach to advocacy. 
That 1.6 million-square-foot data center, being built by developers Poe Companies and PowerHouse Data Centers, received local government approval to move forward earlier this year before the city passed a moratorium, or a temporary ban, on data center construction. 
With that temporary ban in place, the council for Kentucky’s largest city is now grappling with how to craft planning and zoning regulations for data centers — particularly hyperscale data centers that can have a massive power demand to support online operations including artificial intelligence. 
It’s one of a number of Kentucky communities that are wrestling with how to regulate proposed data center projects. 
Evolving data center limits in Louisville
Louisville Public Media reported earlier this month that the city’s planning and zoning commission moved forward with stricter data center regulations, including a requirement that almost all data center proposals be rezoned and therefore have an opportunity for the public to weigh in. 
But one local group thinks the city needs a new approach, concerned that the regulations may not hold up in court. The current approach regulates data centers differently depending on their size, banning any data center larger than 500,000 square feet.
Sarah Lynn Cunningham, the executive director of the Louisville Climate Action Network, said that could be challenged in court.
“If it’s arbitrary, it can get thrown out. And it would really frustrate me if we are all working this hard and the community has invested unprecedented input into the government’s rulemaking processes, only to have it thrown out,” Cunningham said.
Instead, she is encouraging the council to rework the framework to regulate data centers based on their impact, such as having pollution limits, pointing to a template data center regulation ordinance created by an environmental legal group as a model.
Democratic Louisville Metro Council member Tammy Hawkins questioned why the city couldn’t ban data centers outright as a solution. 
Andrew Owen, the Democratic chair of the Planning and Zoning Committee, which is considering the regulations before they move to the full city council, told the Lantern he still favors regulation over prohibition. Scott Reed, the Republican co-chair of that committee, told the Lantern over the phone that he agreed. 
“My feeling is that most people that live in Jefferson County are okay with data centers with very, very thoughtful regulations in place,” Owen said in a Sept. 17 phone interview. “I think it is a very loud minority that says, ‘Don’t ever build one of these things ever.’” 
A county data center ban and a city council walkout
Woodford County just passed an outright ban on data centers. The county’s top elected official telling the Lantern a years-long desire to preserve farmland and strong data center opposition from constituents led to the strict move. 
Democratic Woodford County Judge-Executive Kay told the Lantern he wanted to avoid “divisive” debate over a potential data center proposal like what’s happening in Mercer County. 
The Lantern reported earlier this month a city council member for the small Mercer County city of Burgin walked out of a meeting to stop a vote on a proposed data center. The Mercer County Fiscal Court is holding a special meeting on Sept. 28 to discuss its own potential data center regulations, which currently wouldn’t include the city of Burgin. 
Lexington is also holding a special meeting on Oct. 6 to discuss potential data center regulations.
Legal loopholes?
Meanwhile, the GOP-controlled state legislature and Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear are also trying to tackle data center regulation, though some who watch state policymakers have pointed to potential loopholes and pitfalls. 
Beshear has stood firmly behind an executive order he issued seeking to control the impacts of large data centers, despite some questioning his ability to do so. 
A progressive think tank has also pointed to what it sees as loopholes in state law that could allow data center developers to skirt around paying local taxes, one of the key arguments data center proponents make for the projects. 
One data center developer is also using a state law meant to increase the supply of housing to try to dismiss a Simpson County lawsuit brought by a group representing concerned citizens.
In Congress on Thursday, a Democratic U.S. Senator stopped an effort to fast track the passage of a bill introduced by Republican Kentucky U.S. Rep. Brett Guthrie that would encourage state utility regulators to consider rules that would have data centers cover their electricity and infrastructure costs.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: With US House control hanging in the balance, Wittman faces Taylor in contentious VA-01 race
description: As early voting for the 2026 midterm elections ramps up in Virginia, the commonwealth’s 1st Congressional District, where Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman is battling Democratic challenger Shannon Taylor, has been thrust into the spotlight as one of the most consequential races in the country, with the potential to shift control of the federal […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, left, is running for reelection in Virginia's 1st Congressional District, as Democratic challenger Shannon Taylor aims to unseat him. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)As early voting for the 2026 midterm elections ramps up in Virginia, the commonwealth’s 1st Congressional District, where Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman is battling Democratic challenger Shannon Taylor, has been thrust into the spotlight as one of the most consequential races in the country, with the potential to shift control of the federal legislature. 
The largest portions of VA-01’s voter population are centered in Henrico, Chesterfield, Hanover, and James City counties. The district stretches from Westmoreland to Newport News and hooks around Richmond to the west.  
U.S. Census Bureau data shows the majority of residents there, nearly 72%, identify as White. About 13% are Black, 7% identify as multiracial, 6% are Asian and about 6% are Hispanic or Latino. 
Politically, the 1st District has traditionally leaned Republican, with over 615,000 registered voters living there. In 2024, President Donald Trump won the district with 51.6% and in 2021 former Gov. Glenn Youngkin won 57.8% of the vote.
That trend shifted last year, however, after Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger clinched 51% of the district’s vote, stoking her party’s hopes for a flip in the midterm races. 
National groups like the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added the district to their lists of “districts in play”. Taylor, a progressive candidate who is also Henrico County’s Commonwealth’s attorney, is aiming to force Wittman from the seat he’s held for two decades.
 Wittman, vying for reelection, defends his record on healthcare

Wittman, based in Westmoreland, has held the seat since 2007. He serves on the House Armed Services Committee and Natural Resources Committee, reflecting his past employment at the Virginia Department of Health’s Division of Shellfish Sanitation. He also served as Mayor of Montross and one term in the Virginia House of Delegates before advancing to Congress.
The seasoned lawmaker’s healthcare policy stance has drawn increased scrutiny in recent months. 
Wittman was one of just 17 Republicans to support extending Affordable Care Act credits before ultimately voting to let the credits lapse at the end of last year. He also voted 60 times to undo the ACA throughout the years.
Wittman voted 60 times to undo the Affordable Care Act, then he backed extending its subsidies

He also supported H.R. 1, the spending bill Congress passed last summer which has led 300,000 Virginians to drop their insurance, and will change how hospitals are funded in the coming years. Analysts predict it could also shut out millions from social service programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
But Wittman said in an interview with the Mercury that the impacts of H.R. 1 are being misrepresented. 
“So there hasn’t been any change in qualification. If you qualify for Medicaid, you’re going to continue to get Medicaid. If you’re able to work, we want you to go to work,” Wittman said. “But if you’re deceased, if you’re collecting in two states, that’s defrauding the government. We’re going to stop that.”
He added that lawmakers “put $50 billion in this bill for rural hospitals,” in reference to the Rural Health Transformation Fund, a shared pot of money states may dip into to shore up the cost of maintaining healthcare facilities in rural areas. 
Virginia has received $192 million in RHTF awards, but some state healthcare leaders say it doesn’t do enough to address longstanding funding gaps, characterizing the RHTF as a “$50 billion plug for a $300 billion hole.”
Looking ahead, Wittman said there is still much he wants to accomplish on Capitol Hill if he’s re-elected. Among those goals: helping veterans, lowering costs, and passing a farm bill that could ease some of the strain levied on farmers by drought conditions, high gas prices and tariffs.
When asked how he responds to increased inflation under his party’s leadership, Wittman laid blame on the previous presidential administration’s energy policies and moves by Gov. Abigail Spanberger to curb carbon emissions by rejoining the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative.
“Those additional regulatory requirements that don’t provide any value to Virginia customers are driving costs as well as the additional regulations, the additional taxes that have been put in place by the Virginia General Assembly,” Wittman said.
Congress acknowledges that prices have risen and they are doing “everything that we can,” Wittman said. “We do have a plan, these bills that we pass, we believe, will have an impact on energy production which will bring down costs.” 
On data centers, a key driver of skyrocketing energy costs, Wittman said it should be up to the localities to determine if they want them. Counties and cities that choose to allow data centers to be built should require developers to pay for the infrastructure upgrades and energy generation needed for the facility, he said.
As of July 15th, Wittman’s campaign has raised over $4 million and he has the backing of President Donald Trump headed into November.
“They’re warriors,” Trump said at a Sept. 17 telerally promoting Virginia’s Republican congressional candidates. “It’s Rob Wittman, who you know, and Jen Kiggins, who you know, and John McGuire, and we’ve had tremendous success with the great Big, Beautiful Bill and all of the things that it represents, and tremendous tax cuts.” 
 Taylor pitches fresh ideas to address inflation, energy demands

Taylor swept the district’s Democratic primary in August, beating out the crowded field of seven candidates with over 50% of the vote. 
She has spent the last 13 years as the Henrico Commonwealth’s Attorney, the first woman to hold the title and first Democrat in over 40 years to do the job. Taylor also ran for Attorney General in 2025 but lost in the primary to Jay Jones.
Taylor aims to rein in private equity in healthcare, restore Medicaid funding and ACA subsidies

In staunch contrast to her opponent, Taylor is focused on undoing the impacts of H.R. 1. 
If she’s elected, one of Taylor’s key priorities will be restoring funding for Medicaid and the ACA subsidies that were cut in the bill. She added that the $50 billion that Wittman highlighted for rural hospitals is still only a fraction of what H.R. 1 cut in total.
“It’s not true that it hasn’t changed anything because why do we have people who are already losing healthcare? Why do we have clinics that are closing? Why do we have hospitals (closing) or (that) are cutting back on services? So he is not being honest about that,” Taylor said.
Concerning data centers and rising energy costs, Taylor said she firmly believes the data center industry should pay for the infrastructure upgrades that are needed only because of the rapid expansion of the digital warehouses. 
“We must start from the premise that Virginians should not be paying one dime more for energy or for water for what these data centers are operating on,” Taylor said. 
She said data center siting should ultimately remain a local decision, but “the citizens have every right to speak up, and if they don’t want them, they should not be…having them in their areas.” 
Taylor said spiking inflation is due to politicians of both parties “who take advantage of a corrupt D.C. that allows them to work, focus on their self-enrichment, and not focus on supporting policies and laws that are beneficial to their constituents.”
She said if Democrats are able to take control of the House, the legislature could block tariffs, reinstate Medicaid funding, and find a way to extricate America from the war in Iran, a conflict launched without congressional approval and which most Republicans, including Wittman, support and have voted to fund.
“The American people here in Virginia, here in my district, no one really believes that we had an idea of why we’re getting in (the war) and we now have no way out,” Taylor said.
Taylor’s campaign has raised over $2 million, about half of Wittman’s total.
Early voting is underway and Election Day is Nov. 3. Read The Mercury’s voter guide to learn more about the congressional candidates and stakes of the races.

title: Virginia Beach schools, Civil Rights Office reach agreement over sexual misconduct investigations
description: The U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights has reached an agreement with Virginia Beach City Public Schools, after finding the division violated federal laws involving inadequate investigations and record-keeping of sexual misconduct reports.. Results of the investigation come after the Office for Civil Rights launched a national K-12 initiat[...]
text:
The Lyndon Baines Johnson Department of Education Building pictured on Nov. 25, 2024. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)The U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights has reached an agreement with Virginia Beach City Public Schools, after finding the division violated federal laws involving inadequate investigations and record-keeping of sexual misconduct reports..
Results of the investigation come after the Office for Civil Rights launched a national K-12 initiative in July to enforce Title IX, a statute barring sex-based discrimination at federally-funded schools, and to protect students from sexual misconduct while providing every child with a safe learning environment.
The initiative started with 20 directed investigations that appeared to “inadequately” address staff-on-student sexual misconduct. It’s unclear if Virginia Beach was one of those initial probes.
The agency reported last week that Virginia Beach schools recorded roughly 117 incidents of sexual harassment between 2017 and 2020 and produced 12 investigation reports for the Office for Civil Rights to review. 
As part of the agreement, the district must now strengthen policies, training, reporting and investigations to ensure students are protected from sexual misconduct by teachers and school officials. 
“We are encouraged by the district’s willingness to work with OCR to remedy its Title IX violations and take the necessary steps to comply with federal law,” Kimberly Richey, assistant secretary for the Office of Civil Rights, said in a statement. 
In a statement late Friday, the school division said OCR’s compliance review covered the 2017–2020 school years, before the division adopted its current Title IX procedures.Since then, the division has hired a Title IX coordinator and provided training for staff.“Nothing matters more to us than the safety of the children in our care,” Virginia Beach Schools Superintendent Donald Robertson Jr. said in a statement. “We take this seriously, and we welcome the opportunity to work alongside the Office for Civil Rights. This agreement gives us a shared roadmap to make sure every student, parent, and employee knows how to report a concern, knows that concern will be heard, and knows it will be addressed fairly and completely.”
 Investigation background

Between 2017 and 2020, Virginia Beach schools failed to implement proper procedures, leaving alleged victims of sexual misconduct without the necessary support to have their allegations properly addressed, according to the agency’s findings.
The investigation also found that the school division handled reports of sexual misconduct only as disciplinary issues at the school level, without a grievance process, support for the accused, or notification of outcomes to both sides, according to the agency. 
If teachers or other employees accused of sexual misconduct resigned, the Virginia Beach school district stopped investigating sexual harassment complaints against those individuals altogether, the agency said. 
The findings determined the school division violated Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex in education programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance. 
The law also requires schools with knowledge of sexual harassment or sexual assault to respond promptly and in a manner that is not deliberately indifferent. 
As part of the agreement, OCR requires Virginia Beach schools to take several actions, including updating its Title IX policies to ensure there are fair grievance procedures for both student-on-student and staff-on-student allegations of sexual misconduct or assault.
All division employees must be trained on the school system’s Title IX policies and procedures, as approved by OCR, including how to identify sexual harassment, and employees’ legal obligations to report sexual harassment, whether by students or employees.
Virginia Beach must also notify students, parents and employees that the district has a Title IX coordinator who will properly implement investigation and grievance procedures. 
The district must also communicate how it defines sexual harassment, available resources for students actions students can take if they are victims, and the Title IX Coordinator’s responsibilities. 
The school division must ensure it responds to all reports or complaints of alleged sexual harassment, including staff-on-student harassment, in a manner consistent with Title IX, even if the accused employee resigns.
School officials must create a record-keeping system that preserves all records as required by Title IX, including interview notes and witness statements, support measures, and notice of outcomes to both parties.
Virginia Beach schools will also distribute, pending OCR approval, an updated nondiscrimination statement online and in student and employee handbooks.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: The battle over data centers isn’t just about data centers, but they’re the battleground we have.
description: Virginians’ attitudes towards data centers have shifted rapidly in just a few years. Once seen as a relatively benign form of development that contributed to local coffers without harming the broader community, today data centers face united opposition.  Polling this spring showed just 35% of Virginia voters would be comfortable with construction of a new […[...]
text:
Marvell data center in Culpeper County, Virginia. Virginia has the highest concentration of data centers in the world. (Photo by Evan Visconti/Virginia Mercury)Virginians’ attitudes towards data centers have shifted rapidly in just a few years. Once seen as a relatively benign form of development that contributed to local coffers without harming the broader community, today data centers face united opposition. 
Polling this spring showed just 35% of Virginia voters would be comfortable with construction of a new data center near them, a plunge from 69% just three years ago.  
This is the rare issue that unites voters of all political stripes – mostly against their own elected leaders, since the great majority of both Republicans and Democrats continue to support the data center buildout. The about-face has clearly taken elected leaders by surprise. I wonder if they actually understand it.  
For our leaders, the unconstrained growth of data centers in Virginia is just a problem to be managed. Identify the obvious issues: energy, water, utility bills, noise. Cut some deals, pass some laws, and with a few tweaks here and there, keep the industry moving forward. 
And move forward it must, they believe, because the data center industry attracts more new investment in Virginia than all other business sectors combined (though it falls to sixth place for employment). 
No other state – heck, no other country – relies so heavily on this one industry for growth. Leaders see the dangers of having all their eggs in one basket, but a lack of options makes them keen to avoid breaking eggs.
Virginia is not alone. The U.S. economy is way more diversified than Virginia’s, but even so, data center spending is estimated to add one full percentage point to GDP growth. Nationwide, data center construction is so robust, the construction industry would be contracting without it. 
And yet, most Americans feel the way Virginians do. They don’t want policy tweaks; they want data centers to go away. 
Seen purely as a reaction to the sins of the industry, the anti-data center backlash may look overblown.
Brown water, dust and loud noises: Louisa homeowner sues Amazon over data center construction

Yes, the companies negotiate largely in secret, bring noise and pollution, and use way more than their share of energy and water. But this is how most industries operate. Paper mills, factories, developers, chemical plants – they all hide their faults, look for holes in regulations, and get away with whatever the law allows. Is this really so different? 
It is. And until leaders recognize just how different, they will continue to respond as if all we need is more careful permitting.
The data center industry stands apart because the force behind it, America’s tech industry, is comprised of the richest and most powerful corporations in the world, led by obscenely wealthy men. Their willingness to run roughshod over the communities that host their facilities is, frankly, insulting. 
Ordinary Virginia residents are having to pay more in higher electric and water bills, breathe polluted air, and see our state climate law compromised, apparently because the tech bros can’t be bothered to act responsibly. 
The conviction that the titans of tech aren’t behaving well goes beyond the data centers themselves to the major reason there are so many of them: the development, use and misuse of artificial intelligence. 
Americans are angry about what AI is doing to our children and the educational system. We are fearful of what will happen to people’s jobs. We are worried about our phones getting hacked and our identities and bank accounts stolen, and about being unable to determine truth from fiction. 
We are afraid AI developers are moving too rapidly and understand their own products too little. In a culture of “move fast and break things,” we fear we may be the things that get broken. 
Those fears were percolating before the hack of Hugging Face revealed AI agents breaking out of supposedly isolated environments and collaborating with each other to breach the defenses of an unrelated company.
The worries were brewing before a cybersecurity firm developed a “worm” that could seize the information on hundreds of millions of phones through the WeChat app, and before insiders like Bill Gates began warning that the guardrails are not in place, and that human extinction is more than a theoretical outcome of a race we never signed up for. 
Unease about AI makes the fight over how, and even whether, to site more data centers in Virginia more than just a disagreement over land use and resource allocation. Beneath the concerns that residents point out to pollsters is a growing conviction that we are fighting for our future. 
AI threats aren’t entirely within the power of a state legislature to resolve, even the state at the epicenter of the data center boom. But there is no indication the federal government will do anything, certainly not with our ever-feckless president at the helm. States have to act, because they are all that’s left.
And Virginia has to lead because we host more data centers than any other state; the others look to us for leadership.
Spanberger presents slate of data center regulation proposals, puts first directives in motion

Having long subsidized the data center industry and allowed tech companies to think that their only obligation was to secure the proper permits for construction, Virginia has an obligation to course-correct. 
Seen in this context, the governor’s just-announced “framework” doesn’t meet the moment. It proposes welcome improvements in data center regulation (though some still don’t go far enough), but they don’t get to the heart of Virginians’ fears. 
The administration and General Assembly have to pull every lever of government to hit the brakes on new development and impose stringent conditions on existing data centers until Congress puts real protections in place and the AI companies prove worthy of our trust. 
The fact that this seems too much to hope for explains why Virginians’ opposition to data centers just continues to grow.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rivals no more, can they be good sports? Gubernatorial primary battles end with different outcomes.
description: Less than 24 afters after losing a bruising primary reelection battle, Gov. Dan McKee backed his rival, Helena Buonanno Foulkes for the Nov. 3 general election. Yet endorsements have not materialized in other heated primary matchups, including the Providence Democratic mayoral race. Mayor Brett Smiley declined to endorse his progressive challenger, David Mor[...]
text:
Helena Buonanno Foulkes relishes her win over Gov. Dan McKee on primary night with supporters at Track 15 in Providence. McKee endorsed her for governor the next day. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Less than 24 afters after losing a bruising primary reelection battle, Gov. Dan McKee backed his rival, Helena Buonanno Foulkes for the Nov. 3 general election.
Yet endorsements have not materialized in other heated primary matchups, including the Providence Democratic mayoral race. Mayor Brett Smiley declined to endorse his progressive challenger, David Morales, as first reported by The Boston Globe Rhode Island.
Meanwhile, Elaine Pelino, who narrowly lost the Republican gubernatorial nomination to Aaron Guckian, appears unwilling to endorse her opponent, despite pleas for party unity by Guckian. 
But will any of it sway voters?
Not really, according to Adam Myers, an associate professor of political science at Providence College.
“These kinds of personal endorsements from former rivals can make a difference in the margins, but I don’t think there’s strong evidence they matter a lot,” Myers said. “Most voters don’t pay attention enough for it to make a difference.”
Unlike Foulkes and McKee, whose differences are more personal than ideological or generational, GOP nominee Aaron Guckian and his primary opponent, Elaine Pelino, represent vastly different brands of conservatism.
Guckian, 50, of East Greenwich, is a self-described compassionate conservative while Pelino, 72, of Smithfield is a strong MAGA supporter. Guckian cemented his place as the nominee by 259 votes on Tuesday, following a review by election administrators of the memory sticks for ballot-counting machines. 
Guckian said Friday he’s still waiting to hear from Pelino to concede the race. He has not asked Pelino for her endorsement. But that doesn’t mean he doesn’t want it.
“I would hope she would endorse me,” Guckian said in an interview. “We need to unify as a party for November.”
With just 14% of state voters registered as Republicans, the already slim path to victory for Guckian is only possible with a united base of conservative supporters, Myers said.
“Even the appearance of a divided Republican base does not look good for Guckian,” Myers said. 
Especially when matched up against former Republican-turned independent gubernatorial challenger Ken Block, 60, of Barrington, who trailed Foulkes by 20 points in August public polling. But he has nearly as much support among registered Republican voters as he does independents, according to the surveys.
Republican gubernatorial candidates Aaron Guckian, left, and Elaine Pelino, right. (Left photo by Michael Salerno; right photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)
“He could definitely peel off a lot of Republican voters,” Myers said of Block. 
Especially if he got the backing of Pelino.
Block penned a complimentary message to Pelino on Facebook Wednesday, congratulating her on an “amazing” campaign.
“Most candidates don’t get past signatures, let alone scare the other candidate,” Block said. “Well done.”
But Block insists he’s not courting Pelino — or anyone — for an endorsement.
“I don’t want to be beholden to any special interests,” Block said in an interview.
He knows, though, that he will have to chip away support on both sides of the aisle to win.
“That’s where our path to victory is,” Block said.
Pelino did not respond to multiple requests for comment. In a Facebook post on Thursday, she suggested she does not intend to make a public endorsement.
“My choices are mine and not for public discussion, as again, I am a private citizen,” she wrote. “Please respect that.”
Gov. Dan McKee, shown after voting at Bear Hill Village in Cumberland on Sept. 9, 2026, endorsed the entire Democratic ticket for state general office seats, including his primary opponent, Helena Buonanno Foulkes. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
While still very much a public figure for the remainder of his time in office, McKee’s choices for the Nov. 3 general election are also not very influential given the pending end of his political career, Myers said.
“I don’t think voters are thinking about who Dan McKee endorsed,” Myers said.
Morales might not need Smiley
Meanwhile, Smiley has avoided wading into the endorsement pool, answering questions about his general election endorsement by noting that his primary opponent did not ask for his support.
In a national headline-worthy upset, David Morales, a 28-old progressive, ousted the more moderate Smiley by 1,300 votes in a Democratic mayoral competition centered on rent control and affordability concerns. 
“I don’t plan to get involved in that race,” Smiley, 47, said in a statement Friday. “Over the next few months, my focus will be on continuing to serve my constituents as mayor and ensuring a smooth transition to the next administration.”
But Providence’s partisan bent is dominant enough that Morales doesn’t need — or maybe even want — support from more moderate Smiley voters to win the general election, where he will face Republican Dave Talan and independent Allen Waters.
“Even among people who really don’t like Morales, the sense is this November general election is a done deal,” Myers said. “To vote for anyone else would just be a protest vote.”
Morales’ campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday.
The last Republican to win the Providence mayor’s race was Buddy Cianci during his first stint as city leader from 1976 to 1984; Cianci subsequently returned to the mayor’s seat as an independent in 1990.
More than half of Providence voters are registered Democrats, while just 7% are Republicans, with the remainder unaffiliated, according to registration data with the Rhode Island Department of State.
Despite the attack-laden battle between McKee and Foulkes, there was no hesitation by the governor’s campaign team to endorse Foulkes, Sophie Mestas, a McKee campaign spokesperson, said in a text message Friday.
“The campaign is over,” McKee said in an interview with WPRI-TV after results came in on the primary night.  “We’re focused on ensuring a smooth transition.”
Also quick to bury the hatchet, Foulkes praised McKee for a “gracious” concession call in her victory speech on primary night.
“Helena is very happy to have Governor McKee’s support and will continue crisscrossing the state and meeting with Rhode Islanders to earn every vote,” Angelika Pellegrino, a campaign spokesperson, said. 
McKee has also endorsed the rest of the Democratic ticket for state general office seats: Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos, Kim Ahern for attorney general, Secretary of State Gregg Amore, and General Treasurer James Diossa. 
The Rhode Island Democratic Party has scheduled a “Unity Reception” fundraiser for Democratic nominees for federal, state and local offices on Oct. 6. The Rhode Island Republican Party has only advertised fundraising events for individual candidates.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: As they seek to flip the New Hampshire House, Democrats hold some advantages
description: There is no guarantee that New Hampshire Democrats will retake the state House of Representatives in November. But if they do, the path to victory goes through Manchester Ward 12, Goffstown, Londonderry, Sunapee, and Bedford.   An analysis of 2024 election results by the Bulletin has found that Republicans in those towns are the most vulnerable […]
text:
"To retake the 400-seat chamber, Democrats must win 23 more seats than the 178 they carried in 2024." (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)There is no guarantee that New Hampshire Democrats will retake the state House of Representatives in November. But if they do, the path to victory goes through Manchester Ward 12, Goffstown, Londonderry, Sunapee, and Bedford.  
An analysis of 2024 election results by the Bulletin has found that Republicans in those towns are the most vulnerable should a “blue wave” hit New Hampshire this fall. In each of those five voting districts, a Democrat came within 0.5% of beating a Republican in the 2024 general election. 
Two weeks after the primary, state legislative candidates have a tight six weeks until the Nov. 3 election, and recent state and national polls indicate Democrats have some advantages across the ballot. 
But whether Democrats can flip the House will come down to a couple dozen seats, each of which Republicans won by less than 2% of the vote last election.
To retake the 400-seat chamber, Democrats must win 23 more seats than the 178 they carried in 2024. That is doable if the party can outperform its 2024 results by just a few percentage points: Democrats came within 2% of Republicans in 29 seats last election, and within 3% by an additional eight seats. 
Democrats may have other numerical advantages, the Bulletin’s analysis suggests: They fielded more candidates than Republicans did across the House map this year, have nearly twice as many candidates in safe, uncontested seats than Republicans do, and saw a higher turnout in the Sept. 8 primaries. All of those conditions have not been seen in the Granite State since 2018, the last time Democrats took control of the state House, according to records by the Associated Press and Ballotpedia. 
Here’s what to know about the results of the Sept. 8 House primaries, and what the candidate map can tell us about the battle for the New Hampshire House. 
11 lawmakers ousted in primaries
The September primaries saw 11 sitting House representatives lose their seats, with 10 of them Republicans.  
But there was no clear ideological pattern to the defeats. 
One defeated Republican lawmaker, Stephen Pearson, had been an ardent opponent of his party’s “right to work” bill in 2025, joining Democrats to help defeat it, 200-180. 
Another, Brian Taylor, bucked fellow Republicans by voting against bills to prevent “sanctuary city” immigration policies, expand education freedom accounts, and establish processes for school book removals, though 74% of the time he voted with his party. 
But another defeated Republican lawmaker, Matt Sabourin dit Choinière, attracted national attention after a National Public Radio story revealed he had unsuccessfully advanced an amendment to add Holocaust skeptics to the state’s Commission on Holocaust and Genocide Studies. He also helped Holocaust deniers testify before a state committee, NPR reported. 
And the primaries claimed some longstanding Republicans, including Rep. Ralph Boehm, a 16-year state representative, and Rep. David Milz, a longstanding chairman of the House Public Works and Highways committee.
The lone Democratic incumbent defeated in the primary was Rep. John Joseph Stone, a first-term member who served on the Fish and Game and Marine Resources Committee. 
The 11 defeats of incumbents this month is less than the state’s average of 13.3 incumbent defeats from 2010 to 2024, according to Ballotpedia. And the percentage, 2.75%, is slightly below the 3.4% average of incumbents who lost primaries nationwide. 
Democrats competing for more seats this year
One metric for party enthusiasm is in the number of seats that aren’t competitive.
With 400 seats, and some areas that are traditionally staunchly Republican or Democratic, often neither party is able to recruit candidates to run in each district. But this year, for the first time since 2018, there are more Republican candidate vacancies than Democratic ones.
Democrats failed to recruit a candidate for 42 House seats this year, according to a tally of Secretary of State’s Office data.  Republicans did not field a candidate for 75 House seats. That means Republicans can count on 42 guaranteed seats and Democrats 75 — barring any successful write-in campaigns or third-party candidates. 
Meanwhile, five Republicans are facing a general election with no opponents. In contrast, 34 Democrats are competing in districts with no opponents. 
Republican candidates who have a guaranteed victory in November include Rep. Mike Ouellet, in Colebrook, Columbia, Erving’s Location, and Stewartstown; Rep. Lori Korzen, in Berlin, Carroll, Jefferson, Kilkenny and Whitefield; Rep. Sayra DeVito, in Danville; and Matthew Brooks and Kevin Major in Sandown. 
The invincible Democrats include: 

Rep. Dru Fox, an incumbent in Keene Ward 3 
Christine Parshall, a candidate in Harrisville, Marlborough, Nelson, Roxbury and Sullivan 
Rep. Jared Sullivan, an incumbent in Bethlehem and Franconia

The rest of the 42 and 75 uncontested seats are in multi-candidate districts, meaning the party gets a guaranteed seat but individual candidates must still compete. name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Some 58,000 Medicaid recipients in Louisiana might fall short of work requirements
description: As many as 58,000 Louisiana Medicaid recipients might have to take additional steps to meet the new federal work requirements for the program that go into effect in January, according to information from the state health department.
text:
Most of Louisiana's 1.3 million Medicaid recipients will be exempt from the work requirements that will be imposed on the program in 2027, according to data from the Louisiana Department of Health. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)As many as 58,000 Louisiana Medicaid recipients might have to take additional steps to meet the new federal work requirements for the program that go into effect in January, according to information from the state health department. 
A breakdown on how many of Louisiana’s 1.3 million Medicaid enrollees already fulfill the work requirements or qualify for an exemption was part of an informational packet provided to state lawmakers Thursday at a meeting of the Joint Legislative Committee on the Budget. 
The new Medicaid rules coming in 2027 will require tens of thousands of Louisiana residents between age 19 and 65 to earn at least $580 per month, or they must work or volunteer at least 80 hours a month to keep their benefits. They can also enroll in school or job training part-time to meet the requirement. 
Most Medicaid recipients will be able to opt out of the work requirements entirely. The health department’s breakdown shows the vast majority of Medicaid enrollees, 1.1 million, will be automatically granted an exemption. 

Common reasons for an exemption include being the parent or caregiver of a dependent child (50,470 people) or a person with a disability (55,268). Pregnant women (15,200) and postpartum women (11,219) can also bypass the work requirements, according to the health department. 

Approximately 80,000 people who receive Medicaid also already meet the work requirements through their current, low-paying job, according to state data. 
Around 46,000 Medicaid recipients who don’t have an existing exemption also have no income, making it more likely they would have to make adjustments to keep their benefits. Another 12,000 earn some money each month but not enough to satisfy the work requirement threshold.

Still, it’s not clear how many of those remaining 58,000 could already be in compliance with the proposed work regulations through taking part in school, job training or volunteer work. The health department has not started tracking those activities yet.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: National
title: Trump administration says developers, loggers can kill endangered species
description: The Trump administration’s top wildlife official issued a directive last week that expands a recent rollback of endangered species protections much further than the feds had told the public. Individuals and industries may kill endangered animals in the course of logging projects, developments and other activities, it said — so long as the activity’s purpose[...]
text:
Grizzly bears in the lower 48 states are federally protected as a threatened species. A new memo from U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik says that endangered animals may be killed as long as the action was not “intentionally directed at a particular animal or animals.” (Photo courtesy of Terry Tollefsbol/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)The Trump administration’s top wildlife official issued a directive last week that expands a recent rollback of endangered species protections much further than the feds had told the public.
Individuals and industries may kill endangered animals in the course of logging projects, developments and other activities, it said — so long as the activity’s purpose isn’t killing species.
The memo issued by U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik is the most drastic move yet in the Trump administration’s campaign to limit the scope of the Endangered Species Act. 
Wildlife advocates and experts said the nation’s bedrock wildlife conservation law would offer few safeguards under the new federal guidelines. 
“Unless you’re wearing a T-shirt that says, ‘I’m here to draw the blood of endangered species,’ you’re basically off the hook,” said Brett Hartl, government affairs director with the Center for Biological Diversity, a conservation nonprofit. “Wink, wink, nudge, nudge, go crazy, we’re not gonna prosecute you.”
Chris Servheen, who served as grizzly bear recovery coordinator for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for 35 years, said the agency’s current approach to the endangered species law is “ridiculously extreme.”
“It’s essentially going to be a meaningless law, and it will have no protection whatsoever for species,” he said. “It’s like taking the four wheels off your car and saying it’s still your car.”
The feds no longer protect endangered species habitat. States say they can’t pick up the slack.

Earlier this year, the Fish and Wildlife Service and other federal agencies finalized a rule excluding the destruction of habitat from the definition of “harm” covered by the law. As long as chopping trees or draining a wetland didn’t directly kill animals, the feds said, those actions were legal even if they led to a species’ demise. 
Now, Nesvik is instructing wildlife officials that even the direct killing of endangered animals does not constitute an illegal “take” as long the action was not “intentionally directed at a particular animal or animals.” Its instructions to staff on how to implement the new rule take effect immediately. 
“A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel’s course was not set against the whale,” he wrote. “Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them.”
The memo could unravel a longstanding framework in which developers and other industries undergo an environmental analysis for their projects’ impacts to endangered species, and obtain permits accounting for that harm. Wildlife advocates warned that industries using the agency’s new directive to forgo permits may still face citizen lawsuits, and a new administration could reinstate the previous interpretation of the law.
The Fish and Wildlife Service forwarded a Stateline request for comment to the Department of the Interior, which did not grant an interview request.
The memo, sent last Monday to agency staff across the country, quickly raised alarms after it was leaked to the public. 
“This is an incredibly sneaky and disingenuous way of going about things,” said Ben Levitan, senior attorney with the biodiversity defense program at Earthjustice, a legal conservation nonprofit. “They led everyone to believe they were doing one thing with the rescission of the definition of harm, and now they’ve issued a memo saying, ‘What we actually meant was this.’”
A coalition of attorneys general, tribes and environmental groups have filed lawsuits challenging the Trump administration’s rollbacks to the Endangered Species Act. Advocates said the Nesvik memo will open up a new battle ground in the ongoing legal fight, but it’s too early to say if that will come in the form of separate lawsuits. 
Jane Davenport, senior attorney at Defenders of Wildlife, a conservation nonprofit, noted that the “harm” rule and Nesvik’s memo draw heavily from the late Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia’s dissent in a landmark 1995 case. In a 6-3 decision, the Supreme Court ruled that habitat destruction constitutes harm to wildlife under the Endangered Species Act. But Scalia disagreed, saying that the “take” of wildlife describes actions “done directly and intentionally (not indirectly and by accident) to particular animals (not populations of animals).”
“(Nesvik’s) decision in every aspect of it entirely relies on Scalia’s dissent,” she said. “It’s reducing the scope of (endangered species protections) to an absurdly narrow interpretation that is inconsistent with what Congress intended.”   
While some industry groups supported the “harm” rule in public comments, few of the organizations or lawmakers who backed that change have made public statements on Nesvik’s memo about how it will be applied. But some conservatives praised the decision.
“It will shield innocent people from litigation by the country’s largest law firm, the Department of Justice,” William Perry Pendley, who served as acting director of the Bureau of Land Management during Trump’s first term, told Cowboy State Daily.
Wildlife advocates said the memo could allow developers or logging companies to knowingly chop down a forest filled with endangered owls or bats, so long as the purpose of their action was timber harvest. 
“(The memo) says you can knowingly kill an endangered species as long as you’re not killing it for the sake of killing it,” said Kate Groetzinger, communications director with the Center for Western Priorities, a conservation group. “This basically is a blank check to companies, landowners, developers, loggers — anyone operating in endangered species habitat — to both destroy that habitat and kill the animals and literally face no consequences.”   
States sue feds over endangered species rollbacks

Servheen, the former grizzly bear recovery coordinator, said the memo will allow hunters to gun down endangered species, as long as they later claim they mistook a grizzly bear for a black bear or a similar failure of species identification. 
“This tells law enforcement that they have no ability to prosecute somebody who kills a grizzly bear,” he said. “(Hunters) are basically relieved of any responsibility of what they’re shooting, you can do whatever you want and say ‘I didn’t mean to.’ It makes the outdoors a pretty dangerous place now.”
The memo could also limit environmental reviews of potentially harmful projects, some advocates warned. For instance, a new road through Florida panther territory may no longer need an environmental analysis if increased vehicle collisions with panthers are no longer considered “take” by federal wildlife officials, Davenport said. 
During the rulemaking process for the “harm” definition, federal officials argued that the change would empower states to protect wildlife under their own laws. But experts say state wildlife agencies lack the authority, resources and expertise to replace federal oversight. 
Wildlife officials in Arizona, Georgia, Louisiana, New Mexico, North Dakota, New Jersey, Vermont and Wyoming submitted public comments expressing concern with the proposal, as did the Association of Fish & Wildlife Agencies, a nonprofit that represents state wildlife managers. 
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Angus King endorses Hannah Pingree for governor
description: Independent U.S. Sen. Angus King endorsed Democratic gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree at Bowdoin College on Sunday.  Their hourlong conversation, attended by 300 people in a standing-room only auditorium, also covered the stakes of Maine’s gubernatorial election in light of the cuts to health care, food security and affordability as a result of federal p[...]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree with independent U.S. Sen Angus King. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Independent U.S. Sen. Angus King endorsed Democratic gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree at Bowdoin College on Sunday. 
Their hourlong conversation, attended by 300 people in a standing-room only auditorium, also covered the stakes of Maine’s gubernatorial election in light of the cuts to health care, food security and affordability as a result of federal policies, as well as the polarization of both parties and how the next governor needs to bridge that gap.
 “We’re going to have some challenges, and that’s one of the reasons I’m supporting you, because I think you’re the person to confront them,” King told Pingree as the crowd cheered.
Both King and Pingree represent well-known political dynasties in Maine. King is part of the state’s congressional delegation along with Pingree’s mother, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree who is seeking re-election for her 10th term this year. King’s son ran against Hannah Pingree this year in the gubernatorial primary. 
The two have known each other for years, with King remembering a note he sent the Democratic nominee more than a decade ago after she served as Speaker of the Maine House of Representatives saying she had his support if she ever ran for governor.
“I’d have to say this year she was my second favorite,” he said. 
“But I have such respect for Hannah. She has a rare combination of competence, toughness, intellect, and caring.”
King’s endorsement comes just a few days after Pingree’s campaign highlighted support for the Democratic nominee from former Republicans and independents who disagree with the current administration. While her policy positions are generally more progressive than those of Gov. Janet Mills, Pingree has emphasized her experience working with Republicans, often spotlighting her experience as Speaker of the House of Representatives from 2008 to 2010.
“I’ve had some very positive experiences in the Legislature working across the aisle to pass bipartisan bills … passing bipartisan budgets, but that work has become more challenging in this time,” she said.
“This president and this political climate has made bipartisanship much much more difficult.”
King agreed, saying “it’s certainly much harder than it once was.” Some of his Congressional colleagues he relied on for bipartisan support are no longer there, he said, and both parties are choosing candidates who are increasingly polarized. 
“You can now lose your primary, not because of your position on abortion or immigration or trade, but because you’re viewed as not sufficiently hostile to the other side,” he said. “And I have seen with my own eyes the loss of trust and willingness to just talk.”
“I think somehow we have to get back to the idea that we can have opponents who aren’t enemies,” he added.
Maine’s election laws allow unenrolled voters to choose what party’s primaries to vote in. Based on absentee voting data, unenrolled voters chose to vote in the Democratic primary roughly 3-to-1 compared with the Republican primary.
Pingree highlighted that statistic, saying “I think that level of engagement is good for our elections.”
She will face Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett in the Nov. 3 election.
